en: The Self-Establishment,
accompanied by the commentary named *Siddhāñjana*.
He whose every impurity has been destroyed by meditating upon the lotus-feet of that [Lord]—
I bow to that Yāmuna-born sage, who has attained the state of ultimate reality. // 1 //
The root [of all things]—
Prakṛti, Puruṣa, Kāla, Vyakta, and Muktas— constantly obey His will,
which is perpetually attended by many eternally perfected beings.
While the glorious one is being pleased by my own service and enjoyments, may there be an abundance of devotion in me toward the Supreme Person. // 1 //
We worship the Lord of all worlds, the Consort of Śrī, who is higher than the highest and who delights in the creation, preservation, and dissolution of the universe. (1)
I take refuge in the supreme teacher, the best of sages, the son of Yamunā, who is a treasure-trove of knowledge, dispassion, and devotion, and an ocean of compassion. // 2 //
May the noble Lord Rāmānuja, who reveals the supreme reality through his treatises such as the Śrībhāṣya, show compassion toward me. May he take refuge in me. 3.
Relying upon the essence of the compassion of the Lord of Teachers, I compose this commentary on the *Siddhitraya* in a simple manner.

Where is the collection of the noble and illustrious Yāmuna’s elegant sayings, and where is my intellect, which has such a very limited scope? Nevertheless, it is my restlessness that commits this offense.

The teachers, who are the foremost leaders in determining the doctrine of qualified non-duality (viśiṣṭādvaita) and whose very essence is compassion for those who have sought refuge, are my shelter. 6.

Having bowed to my father Kṛṣṇārya— who belongs to the Vātsya lineage, who is the venerable teacher Vādibhīkara, the ornament of the Guru-kula, rich in virtues, and the one who revealed the meaning of the Dravidian Upanishadic texts—
and also to my supreme teacher Rāmānujārya, the lamp of the lineage of the author of the Bhāṣya;
I shall expound the teachings of Yamuna, who is like a parrot of beautiful fame and an ornament to the family of the wise.
I, Aṇṇaṅgarāryadāsa, born of the noble lineage known as Śrīmannāgapura and a terror to disputants, expound the words of my Guru. (8)

Then indeed, the Blessed One Śrīmad Yāmunamuni—the grandson of the venerable Śrī Nāthamuni (who was counted as the foremost among the teachers who inaugurated the Śrī Vaiṣṇava tradition and was the author of the Yogarahasya and Nyāyatattva treatises), and the biological son of Īśvaramuni;
the preeminent leader in propagating the doctrine of Viśiṣṭādvaita; and one capable of tearing asunder the manifest arrogance of the elephants that are his opponents—[spoke].

The supreme teacher, commencing the Vedāntic treatise titled *Ātmasiddhi*, composes the verse beginning with "prakṛti" for the instruction of his disciples; this serves as both an auspicious invocation—intended to ensure the completion of the work without obstacles and its steady progress—and a statement of the subject matter (*vastunirdeśa*), taking the form of a benediction.
Here, "prakṛti" refers to *māyā*.
Its effects, which exist in both collective and individual forms, are manifest;
time is the cause of the transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti) and its evolutes (prākṛta);
and the multitude of bound souls (jīvarāśi)—all these situated within the realm of the Līlāvibhūti—are subsumed by these four terms.
"Liberated" means they have been released from the bondage of worldly existence, which is woven by the snares of karma, through the power of worshiping the Blessed One.

These [elements], beginning with *prakṛti*, always follow the will—consisting of volition—of that very Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) in their own essential nature, maintenance, and activity; the grammatical connection is that [they abide] "in that Person. And these...
Creation, protection, withdrawal, and liberation from saṃsāra—these, accomplished solely by His will, serve as the source of the Lord’s playful delight (līlā-rasa).

Thus, the connection with the manifest glory of His play (līlā-vibhūti) has been described. Now, He speaks of the connection with His eternal glory (nitya-vibhūti), beginning with the word "eternal" (nityam).
The word "eternal" (*nityam*) applies to both what precedes and what follows, according to the maxim of the central gem (*madhyamaṇinyāya*).

In the glorious Mahāvaikuṇṭha, there are infinite eternal sages (*nityasūri*), such as Ananta, Garuḍa, Viṣvaksena, and others, who— by virtue of their very nature consisting of ever-arisen freedom from sin and other attributes, and being omniscient— have attained all enjoyments solely through their constant engagement in the state of being the absolute subordinates (*śeṣavṛtti*) resulting from the love born of experiencing the Lord.

May there be an abundance of my devotion toward the Supreme Person, the Supreme Brahman, the beloved of Śrī— the most excellent among women— who eternally experiences unsurpassed bliss in the divine, imperishable abode;
for devotion to the Lord of both manifestations, the Lord of Ramā, indeed brings about all that is most auspicious.
It is most appropriate to aspire for devotion to each respective deity;
indeed, sentient beings should pray only for devotion toward the Blessed One,
for He Himself bestows the highest good.
By this it is made known that, for devotees, the prayer for one's own welfare in that regard is not at all appropriate;
for in the ultimate sense, there is only the distinction between the insentient and the sentient,
and the supreme sovereignty belongs solely to the illustrious Nārāyaṇa.

The intended meanings of this treatise, as indicated here, are as follows: that all sentient and insentient beings constitute His manifestation; that worship of Him alone—characterized by unsurpassed love—is the cause of liberation; and that service characterized by uninterrupted and full experience of the Lord is the supreme goal of human life. // 1 //
There exist many conflicting views regarding the self and the supreme self;
therefore, for the sake of purifying that [confusion], the *Ātmasiddhi* is composed.
For it is agreed upon in all systems that self-knowledge is the cause of the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*).

And it is heard in scripture: "Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct, being delighted by that [knowledge], one attains immortality"; "If one should know the Self..."; "The knower of the Self crosses over sorrow"; and "The knower of Brahman attains the Supreme. Thus, the knowledge of the reality of the higher and lower Self is the means to liberation.
While the collection of Vedānta statements is thus establishing [this],
there are various kinds of disagreements among the founders of different schools (tīrthakara) regarding this very Self and the Supreme Self.
For instance, concerning the Self first, some declare the body itself to be the Self.
Some say the sense-faculties; others, the mind; and others still, the vital breath.
Some maintain that the *ahaṅkāra* is mere consciousness (*bodhamātra*) to which the state of being a knower has been superimposed;

others hold it to be distinct from the body, senses, mind, vital breath, and consciousness, having a nature like space (*ākāśa*)—that is, non-conscious (*acid-svabhāva*)—and serving as the substrate for adventitious, specific qualities such as cognition, pleasure, and pain, which fall within the scope of the *ahaṅkāra*.
Still others, however, maintain that its very nature is solely consciousness.

They describe this [Self] as self-luminous, its nature a light that neither rises nor sets, appearing as if naturally white like a crystal gem that reflects qualities such as redness produced by a particular substrate; likewise, it appears to possess inauspicious qualities such as passion, aversion, pleasure, and pain produced by the substrate of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Others, however, maintain that its nature is knowledge and bliss (*jñānānanda-svabhāva*).

Others maintain that its intrinsic nature (*svābhāvika*) is precisely a specific state of awakening designated as bliss, happiness, and so forth, which is obtained in conformity with its basis (*āśraya*).
Likewise, it is both to be comprehended through inference and to be known solely through scripture (*āgama*).
It is cognizable through mental perception;
it is directly perceived in all cognitions of objects solely by virtue of being the subject;
and, having the nature of consciousness, it is self-luminous, its own manifestation being neither rising nor setting.

Even such a [Self] is ultimately perceived directly, exactly as it is, through the means of inference, yogic perception, and [ordinary] perception— becoming increasingly clear, clearer, and clearest by virtue of its essential nature which is distinct from everything other than itself.
Likewise, it is both supremely great and of atomic dimension.
It has the size of the body;
although it is itself devoid of size, it is delimited by the dimensions of the objects it pervades.
Furthermore, this pervasion occurs through pure consciousness alone.
"In its own nature" means:
likewise, it is momentary;
it lasts as long as the body's heat persists.
It persists until the state of primordial dissolution; it lasts until liberation; it is immutable and eternal.

Some maintain that [the self] is one in all bodies, while others hold that it is distinct in each field (kṣetra); they thus understand it in various ways. Likewise, regarding the Supreme Self (paramātman), some do not even accept the existence of a Lord (īśvara) who possesses all powers and directly perceives all things.

Even while accepting [the existence of the Lord], some describe Him as purely conceptual, consisting of a single flavor of immutable consciousness that is free from the conceptual distinctions of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), the knower (*pramātṛ*), and the object of knowledge (*prameya*), as well as the distinction between the Lord and those to be ruled; yet, due to the conceptualization of His majesty—such as His knowledge and sovereignty—which appears divided by the distinctions of space and so forth presented by beginningless ignorance (*anādyavidyā*).

Others, however, maintain that He is of the very nature already described, but through the proximity of ignorance (*avidyopadhāna*), He is manifested as the manifold variety of individual souls (*jīva*)—from Brahmā down to the stationary beings—by virtue of having the qualities [of the intellect] as His essence.

Others assert that this [Lord] is conditioned (*upahita*), having attained the perfection of omniscience and other qualities by being endowed with *māyā*, whose nature consists of various manifestations under its own control. Likewise, others honor Him as one whose sovereignty is established solely through the regulation of specific transformations of independent *pradhāna*, which is caused by the appropriation of excellent *sattva*.
Still others have maintained that He is even unconditioned (*anupahita*), yet subject to transformation.

Others favor the view that the one Consciousness alone— though itself unchanging— attains the states of Viśva, Taijasa, and Prājña by being reflected in the surface of the various internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which are portions of its own *māyā*.

Still others [favor the view of Him] who is the great ocean of the multitude of all auspicious qualities— such as innate, limitless, unsurpassed knowledge, strength, sovereignty, heroism, power, and splendor— who possesses the distinction of the nature, maintenance, and activity of the threefold conscious and unconscious entities under His own control.
They maintain that the Lord is a particular kind of person (*puruṣaviśeṣa*).

Likewise, even regarding His specific nature, they dispute whether He consists of four, three, two, or one form, by rejecting or favoring various manifestations such as Hari, Hara, Viriñca, or Bhāskara.

Furthermore, debates arise concerning these specific forms, such as whether they are eternal or non-eternal, composed of elements or not composed of elements, and whether they exist for their own sake or for the sake of others.
And [they are characterized by] their retinue, location, and so forth.
Likewise, with respect to their means of cognition: some say they are based solely on scripture (*ānuśrāvika*), while others say they are based on inference (*ānumānika*).
Others maintain that it is to be apprehended through a distinguished form of perception.

Likewise, regarding the relationship between the individual self (ātman) and the supreme self (paramātman): this relationship, consisting of the lord and the subject of his rule, has its locus in the distinction produced by the material cause of beginningless ignorance (anādyavidyopādāna).
Some hold that, in its ultimate reality, there is only one single principle (tattva).

Others maintain that even in the absence of difference, the individual soul (jīva) is distinct [from Brahman]. Still others hold that there is identity by nature, but difference due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi); thus, through the existence of a qualified nature, there is both difference and non-difference.
Only when there is multiplicity can there be non-difference, which is characterized as the relationship between part and whole;
it is inherence (samavāya), characterized by dependence,
and consisting of the nature of the subordinate and the principal.
There are various doctrinal claims, such as that the relationship is one of master and servant, characterized by the nature of a servant and a master;
likewise, even regarding liberation— characterized by the attainment of Brahman, which constitutes the supreme human goal— some claim it is characterized by the annihilation of one's own nature.
It is characterized by the subsidence of ignorance,
characterized by the total eradication of all specific qualities of the self,
and is of the nature of absolute liberation (kaivalya).
It is characterized by the conformity of being with that, characterized by the transfer of its qualities,
and characterized by the attainment of stability.

They dispute accordingly: [that liberation] is characterized by the manifestation of one’s own nature as innate bliss (*sāṃsiddhikānanda*) and so forth; or it is characterized by absolute subservience to Him, brought about by the emergence of unsurpassed happiness born from the experience of His qualities.
Also, regarding the means to attain it: it is obtainable through *karmayoga*.
It is attainable through the yoga of knowledge, attainable through either one supported by the other,
or attainable through both.
"It is attainable through the yoga of devotion, which is absolute and ultimate for one whose patience has been refined by both [means].

Thus, because of the observed disagreements among people who have not yet completed their investigation of specific distinctions, and because of the lack of certainty regarding the strength or weakness of the proofs for various respective positions, discerning individuals who remain in doubt here and there would not yet apply themselves toward the supreme human goal.

Since this individual self (*ātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) have not yet been definitively determined in terms of their essential nature (*svarūpa*), their means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), their relationship (*saṃbandha*), their attainment (*prāpti*), and the means for that attainment (*tatsādhana*), this work is commenced for the purpose of awakening them to that reality.
Although the venerable Bādarāyaṇa has already composed sūtras on these very subjects and they have been commented upon by others...
These [works] were also expanded by the author of the Dramiḍa-bhāṣya, who spoke with measured depth,
and by Śrīvatsāṅkamiśra, who spoke with the essence of profound logic.

Nevertheless, those whose intellects have been led astray by faith in the various white and black treatises composed by Ācārya Ṭaṅka, Bhartṛprapañca, Bhartṛmitra, Bhartṛhari, Brahmadatta, Śaṅkara, Śrīvatsāṅka, Bhāskara, and others,
do not understand [the truth] as it is, but rather grasp it erroneously; therefore, the commencement of this treatise is appropriate.
(Thus ends the introductory section. He states the purpose for undertaking this treatise with the words "Incompatible," etc.
For indeed, there exist various conflicting misconceptions regarding the nature of the individual self and the supreme self.
The contradiction among cognitions consists in their apprehending contradictory forms.
Since there exist disagreements among disputants and counter-disputants regarding the reality of the Self and the Supreme Self for those seeking liberation who desire to know it,

therefore, for the sake of its purification— that is, by removing the defect consisting in the cognition of the reality of the Self and the Supreme Self having as its qualifiers (prakāra) unreal and contradictory forms induced by various doctrines— [the inquiry is undertaken].
This treatise, titled *Ātmasiddhi*, is composed for the purpose of accomplishing the union with purity characterized by the penetration of the nature of things as they truly are;
its aim is the determination of the reality of the self and the non-self through valid means of knowledge and sound reasoning.
The primary subject matter is the reality of the higher and lower selves.
It has been indicated that the refutation of opposing positions is an inseparable concomitant,
while the direct purpose of this treatise is the determination of the true nature of the self (*ātmatattva*).
Furthermore, its intended goal is the attainment of supreme liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) through a successive process.
From the statement of the subject matter and the purpose, the relationship and the qualified student are understood by implication.
Thus, the fulfillment of the fourfold preliminary requirements (anubandha) has been considered.
The primary function of this treatise is the detailed exposition of the principles that lead to the ultimate liberation, which establishes the reality of the higher and lower selves.
Therefore, it should be understood that this [text] results in being useful for the contemplation of the self and the supreme self. // 2 //

Thinking that no one who acts with foresight would engage in what is essentially a useless body, he reveals his attachment to the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) as the fruit of his own work by saying "it is agreed" (*saṃmatam*).

Now, let it be granted that knowledge of the self (*ātman*) is a means to liberation; but how can this apply to the knowledge of a distinct Supreme Self (*paramātman*)? To this, he says "it is heard" (*śrūyate*).

The sense is that even though there may be disagreement among the outsiders (bāhya) regarding the self, there is no disagreement among the foremost of the Vaidikas concerning the fact that knowledge of the true nature of the Supreme Self (paramātman)—just like that of the individual self—is the means to liberation.
The Supreme Self is the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Person (puruṣottama), the illustrious Nārāyaṇa;
the lower self is the individual soul (jīvātman).
The remainder is clear.

Now, it may be objected: "The application of reasoning occurs only regarding that which is doubtful. Since the reality of the higher and lower Self has been well-ascertained by the Vedāntas themselves, how can there be any doubt regarding it?"
And how does the application of reasoning occur? It is said:

even when the meaning is understood through the Vedas (*śruti*), because doubt arises regarding the very intent of the Vedas due to hearing the various doctrines of the founders of systems (*tīrthakara*) who possess renowned intellectual power, [reasoning is applied] to the true nature of the Vedic meaning.
Even so, a doubt may arise;
keeping this very intention in mind, [the author] introduces the conflicting views that cause a mass of uncertainty regarding the reality of the Self with the words "In that regard" (*tatra*).
Here, *tīrtha* means a philosophical system (*darśana*), because it is similar to a sacred ford (*tīrtha*).
For vision (*darśana*) produces in the selves a purity consisting of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), preceded by the removal of the impurities of internal ignorance.

Those who effect this are the *tīrthakāras*—the proponents of philosophical systems (*dārśanikas*). For example, the manifoldness of their conflicting views has been stated; that is, in whatever manner [they differ].
That is to say, it is described as such. Regarding the phrase "the body alone":
this refers to the Cārvākas, who maintain that the body and so forth constitute the self.
Regarding the phrase "others say it is the mind" (*mana ityanye*):
the meaning is that some call by the name "Self" (*ātman*) something that is not commonly known as "mind.
This [word] also connects with the subsequent phrase "they call it the Self" (*ātmānamācakṣate*).
He states the doctrine of the Sugatas and the doctrine of Śaṅkara simultaneously with the word "superimposed" (*adhyasta*).
"Cognition alone" (*bodhamātra*) means pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra*).
"Free from egoity" (*anahaṅkāra*) means not being the object of the notion or the word "I."
One position is that the state of being a knower, which resides within the knot of ignorance and egoism (ahaṅkāra), is superimposed upon the Self.

Another position is that through beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā), the state of being a knower is superimposed upon cognition itself. He states the view of the Logicians (Tārkika) with the words "body and senses," etc.

"Bodha" means knowledge. The meaning is that the followers of Kaṇāda and Gautama have declared the Self (ātman) to be distinct from the body, senses, mind, vital breaths, and intellect; to be of the nature of consciousness (caitanya); to possess adventitious specific qualities such as knowledge, pleasure, and so forth; and to be the object of the notion of "I" (ahaṃbuddhi) and the word "I."
By the phrase "having the nature of non-consciousness" (acitsvabhāva), the insentience of the self's essential nature is intended, just as that of space and so forth.
"Ego" (ahaṅkāra) refers to both the cognition "I am" and the word [denoting it].
He states the Sāṅkhya view with the words "others."

It has the nature of pure awareness alone; "awareness" (bodha) means consciousness (caitanya), and that which has this as its own being (sva-bhāva) or essential nature (svarūpa) is that which is of the very nature of knowledge.
"Upadhāna" means proximity (*sannidhāna*).
"This"—that is, the self (*ātman*).

Just as a crystal or similar substance, though naturally white, appears to assume various colors such as red through the proximity of limiting conditions (*upādhi*) like the *japā* flower; so too [does the self appear].

Thus, the Self—which is eternally self-luminous and its own light—appears merely as if possessing qualities such as pleasure and pain through the proximity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which superimposes them upon it;
in reality, however, this [Self] is eternally and absolutely free from defects. This is the intended meaning.
As for the phrase "others, however": [the following applies].
These are either a certain school of Mīmāṃsakas or a certain school of Siddhāntins.
Their intention is that knowledge and bliss are the natural attributes (svābhāvikadharma) of the self. He states the view of the Siddhāntins with the words "āśraya" and so forth.
Bliss (ānanda) also is not something additional;
rather, it is simply a specific kind of knowledge characterized by the designation of bliss, happiness, and so forth, which is attained as being favorable to the self.
The intended meaning is that this alone is the true nature of the self;
its state of being subject to transmigratory existence, suffering, and so forth, is due to the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of karma.
The core idea is that the self is endowed with whatever has been described [in scripture].

Indeed, in our own established doctrine (siddhānta), it is already accepted that the self possesses as many formal aspects (ākāravattva) as are logically possible among those asserted by various disputants.

Having stated the disagreements regarding the nature of the self, [the author] now introduces those disagreements concerning the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) that apprehend it, beginning with the words: "Likewise, in inference... (tathānumāne).
This is the Sautrāntika position that [the self] is inferential.
And the inference may be formulated as follows: "I-consciousness has an object of perception because it is a consciousness, like the consciousness of blue, yellow, and so forth.
Alternatively, this might be the Naiyāyika position being cited here, namely that the self is of a different character and is the object of inference.
According to the *Agnimavivaraṇa*,
the phrase "knowable solely through scripture" (*āgamaikavedya*) represents the position of those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*).

Their intention is that the Self is knowable solely through scripture, because the notion of "I" is logically established as having the body as its objective support, and because the inference based on being a composite for the sake of another (saṅghātatva-parārthatva) is inconclusive and so forth.
The term "mental" refers to this position held by both the Naiyāyikas and the Bhāṭṭas.
"The state of being the apprehender" (grāhakatā) refers to this Prābhākara position; "by way of being the apprehender" means by way of being the knower (jñātṛtā).
Because cognition illuminates a triad, in the very perception of a jar, both that cognition and the self as the knower shine forth just like the jar itself;
thus [the author] states the view of the Sāṅkhyas and others with the words "by virtue of having the nature of cognition.
One's own being is "svabhāva," which is to say, one's own essential form (svarūpa).

Regarding the eternal self (*ātman*), because its nature is knowledge, it is self-luminous by its own nature, independent of anything else; the authors of the *Siddhānta* (the established conclusions) bring forward this intention with the words "even such as this. After the phrase "by way of being most clear," the word "grasped" (*gṛhīta*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The meaning is this: because this [Self] is self-luminous precisely by virtue of its inwardness (pratyaktva) and so forth, it is grasped with clarity through scripture in its aspects such as being distinct from the body and the like, permanence, atomicity, and knowership;
with even greater clarity through reflection (manana);

and with the greatest clarity through the perception born of yoga (yogaja-pratyakṣa). Thus, in liberation, it is experienced in its entirety by the light of one's own natural, uncontracted, and immediate knowledge.
He indicates that [the qualities] exist even in the measurement of the self with the word "likewise.
He states the Naiyāyika position with the words "supremely great," and its true nature is a magnitude that does not admit of further diminution.

[The author] states "of atomic dimension" (*aṇuparimāṇa*) to present the position of the proponents of established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), which is the counterpart to that [position] characterized by omnipresence (*vibhutva*).

He states "of the body's dimension" (*śarīraparimāṇa*) to present the view of those who argue for non-conclusiveness (*anaikāntyavādin*), who consider the atom to be of intermediate size (*mādhyama*).
He states the view of the Sāṅkhyas, who maintain that there is a single Self for all beings, with the words "from itself" (*svataḥ*).
The absence of finite dimension in the Selfs is due to their omnipresence (*vibhutva*);
for if they possessed finite dimension, the consequence would be limitation and a lack of omnipresence—this is their underlying intention.
And he states that its dimension is adventitious (aupādhika) with the words "pervading" (vyāpi).

The meaning is that in the state of bondage, this [self] possesses a dimension conditioned by the dimension of the pervasive internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa). He also states that [the self] is pervasive even in the case of consciousness (caitanya) with the words "in consciousness" (caitanye).

The position of the proponent (siddhāntin) is that pervasion occurs solely through the medium of knowledge, which constitutes its own nature (*svadharma*). This is because the proponent’s position is presented by way of analogy: just as dimension (*parimāṇa*) is dependent upon the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), so too is all-pervasiveness (*vyāpakatva*) dependent upon knowledge.
The first explanation here is "by its own nature" (*svarūpeṇa*).
The Naiyāyikas and others maintain that the self (*ātman*) is omnipresent by its very nature.
He introduces those [views] even in connection with time, saying "likewise":
momentariness is the position favored by the Buddhists (Saugatas),
while for the Cārvākas it lasts as long as the heat of the body remains.
The state of abiding beyond the ordinary pertains to Brahmā, the gods, and others;
the state of abiding until liberation pertains to the followers of Auḍulomi;
and the state of immutable eternity pertains to the Naiyāyikas and other established philosophers.
Immutability is the state of being changeless;
permanence is existence at all times.
He expresses that [permanence] even in terms of number by saying "all."
The doctrine of a single soul belongs to certain followers of the Māyāvāda;
the doctrine of a distinct self for each body belongs to the Naiyāyikas and other established schools (siddhāntins).
The word "and" (ca) serves to include other unmentioned disagreements.
"In such and such a manner" means that those disputants conceive of the self (*ātman*) in various forms contrary to their respective own preferred views.

Having stated the disagreements regarding the nature of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and so forth, he introduces those [disagreements] regarding the nature of the supreme self (*paramātman*) with the words "likewise, in the supreme... and so on.
The phrase "the various divergent views of the non-Buddhist teachers" is the ellipsis to be supplied. "Some" refers to the Cārvākas, Buddhists, Ārhats, and Karmadās.

He states that there is no consensus even among those who maintain the existence of a Lord, saying "even while accepting... Some Advaitins [hold] that the state of being a Lord is merely conceptual (kalpanika).
He states the manner of conceptualization with the words "when [all] has subsided":
"The immutable, unchanging, eternal, pure consciousness alone is reality;

wherein there is no manifoldness of distinctions such as the Lord and that which is to be ruled, nor even the distinction between the knower, the object of knowledge, and the resulting cognition delimited by them."

In such a substrate, through ignorance (*avidyā*) alone— which possesses manifold powers— there occurs the manifestation of various cognitions (*cit*) as space and so forth, like the appearance of a snake and the like upon a rope; and there also occurs the manifestation of the distinction in the majesty of knowledge, sovereignty, and so on, as delimited by the collective (*samaṣṭi*) and individual (*vyaṣṭi*) states belonging to the realm of ignorance.
Their intention is as follows: Consciousness (caitanya), appearing as possessing knowledge, sovereignty, and so forth, delimited by the totality (samaṣṭi), is the Lord (īśvara);

that same [consciousness], appearing as manifold due to possessing knowledge and so forth, delimited by individual forms such as the bodies of gods and others, is the multitude of individual souls (jīva).
In this view, it is precisely ignorance (avidyā) that serves as the limiting adjunct (upādhi) which fashions the states of being the individual soul and the Lord.

He states the view of those who maintain that the distinction [between the individual soul and the Lord] is due to the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of *māyā* and *avidyā*, beginning with the words "But others.

Pure, undivided consciousness alone, when conditioned by *avidyā*, manifests as the state of various individual souls (*jīva*), and when conditioned by *māyā*, it manifests as the state of the Lord (*īśvara*).

In this regard, because it is produced by *avidyā*, the distinction of the individual soul is characterized by the predominance of the qualities of *avidyā*—such as desire, anger, and greed—and is subject to the power of *avidyā*.

However, their intention is that Īśvara possesses the greatness of omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth, attained through the power of Māyā, which is by nature subject to various transformations under his own control.
Regarding the manner in which those established in Yoga and Tantra revere Īśvara, he says, "so others.
By the word "so" (tathā), it is intended that even in this view, the status of being Īśvara is merely adventitious (aupādhika).

The meaning is that they revere the Lord (Īśvara), whose establishment of universal sovereignty is brought about by that specific excellence of the independent transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti)— an excellence consisting in the state of being eternally augmented by *sattva*, which is caused by His having as His material cause a portion of nature predominantly composed of excellent *sattva*.
The internal organ and so forth, consisting of eternally pure *sattva*, constitute the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of the Lord.
The Lord (Īśvara) is a particular soul whose body consists solely of consciousness conditioned by that [limiting adjunct].
The sense is that His lordship is dependent entirely upon a specific limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
According to the position of Yādavaprakāśa, however, it is "even unconditioned" (*anupahitam api*).

This is the doctrine of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*), according to which Brahman becomes, like the ocean through the differentiation of foam, bubbles, and waves, the forms of the insentient, the individual soul, and the Lord.
He states the doctrine of reflection (*pratibimbavāda*) with the words "even though it is unchanging.
By the phrase "that one alone who is conscious," he means that the Lord is consciousness conditioned by *māyā*.

The individual souls (jīvas) are understood to have the nature of reflections, being the various distinct reflections of that very [consciousness] within the internal organs (antaḥkaraṇas). Alternatively, the Lord (Īśvara) is consciousness reflected in Māyā;
the meaning is that the individual souls are the various distinct reflections of that [consciousness] within the diverse internal organs which constitute the limbs of Māyā.
Viśvādi is the one who identifies with waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.
He states the view of the Siddhāntins with the words "others, however.
There are three kinds of sentient beings—those possessing the nature of knowers—who are bound, liberated, and eternal.
And there are three kinds of non-conscious entities—namely, primordial matter (*prakṛti*), time (*kāla*), and the eternal realm (*nityavibhūti*)—which are devoid of the quality of being a knower.
Although the eternal realm has the nature of knowledge, it is non-conscious because it lacks the capacity for knowing.
All of these possess the fullness of their own respective forms.

The persistence of things whose own natures are already established, consisting in their continuation through successive moments, as well as the specific activities that always depend upon Him for conformity to their respective effects— He is the Lord (Īśvara).
And He is not devoid of qualities;
rather, He is a mine of jewels consisting of an infinite multitude of auspicious qualities, beginning with His natural and most excellent sixfold attributes.
Furthermore, His state of being "without qualities" is due to the absence of even a trace of anything to be abandoned (*heya*).
And this particular Person—distinct from the three types of individual souls, the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama), the Lord of Śrī—this is their inner conviction.
Since it has been stated that "the particular Person is the Lord," in response to the inquiry as to what His name and form are, he says: "Likewise, even regarding His specific nature."
The meaning is that there is no consensus among disputants even regarding the names, forms, and other attributes of the Lord (*īśvara*).
For instance, some maintain that the one and only Lord assumes four forms according to the requirements of his tasks.
The proponents of the Trimūrti doctrine, however, discard the form of Āditya; those who maintain the identity of Hari and Hara discard even the form of Brahmā;
while the Śaivas, moreover, consider Hara alone to be the Lord (Īśvara).
The Śrīvaiṣṇavas, however, maintain that it is Hari alone;
in this same way, the respective positions of the Hairaṇyagarbhas and the Sauras regarding their singular form should also be considered.
He states the disagreements even concerning the specific attributes of the Lord’s forms with the word "mūrti."
"Possessing a purpose" means having the purpose of accomplishing one's own enjoyment. "Having another as the purpose" means having the sole purpose of favoring living beings.
"Vitarkas" refers to conflicting views.
Regarding "the retinue":
whether the retinue and so forth exist or not, and whether they are permanent or impermanent.

The distinctions between categories such as "ordinary" (*prākṛta*) and "extraordinary" (*aprākṛta*) are to be investigated in relation to their respective roles, such as those of attendants and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "also by way of measure" (*pramāṇataḥ*),
the suffix *tasil* is used here with the sense of all case endings.
The meaning is: "even regarding the object of valid cognition.
Some say that [the subject] has scripture alone as its means of valid cognition;
others say that it has both scripture and inference as its means of valid cognition.

The proponents of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) maintain, however, that [the Lord] is apprehended by the mind through hearing and reflection, as well as through inference based on what has been heard, and is grasped by a mind refined by meditation preceded by love.
Now, he points out the disagreements regarding the relationship between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para) with the words "likewise, the self" (*tathā ātmā*).
He states the position of the Advaitins with the words "beginningless" (*anādi*).

Their intention is that because the relationship of lord and subject (*īśeśitavyatva*) is based on a distinction created by ignorance (*avidyā*), it is merely empirical (*vyāvahārika*) and not ultimately real (*pāramārthika*).
With the intention of presenting the position of the reflection (*pratibimba*), he says "in distinction" (*vyatireke*).

The meaning is that even though there is no difference from the original object (*bimba*), there exists a distinction (*atireka*)—characterized by being the object of the cognition of difference and so forth—among the reflections.
He states the position of Bhāskara with the word "intrinsically" (*svataḥ*).

The intention is that there is non-difference in terms of essential nature (*svarūpataḥ*), while difference is adventitious (*aupādhika*); for it is impossible for both difference and non-difference, which are contradictory, to exist in the mere essential nature alone.
He states the position of Yādavaprakāśa with the words "nānātva" (diversity).
The phrase "characterized by the relation of part and whole" is to be connected with the word "anvaya" (conformity).
Because of this relationship of part and whole, the establishment of both difference and non-difference is possible.

The inner intention of these [authorities] is that the meaning of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is precisely identity (*tādātmya*), which is non-difference (*abheda*) coextensive with difference (*bheda*).
"Inherence" (*samavāya*) and so forth are the positions held by the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*).
In the established doctrine, because multiple relations are accepted between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), there is a mention of various relations.
The view that inherence (samavāya) is characterized by the relationship between part and whole is also possible as a tenet of our own school (siddhāntapakṣa).
The meaning is that inherence is of the nature of dependence and non-separate existence (apṛthaksiddhi), and not something distinct [from the related entities] as the Vaiśeṣikas maintain.
The distinction is as follows: *śeṣatva* (subservience) consists in having a nature and so forth established by the desire to produce an excellence in another;
*svatva* (ownership) consists in being fit for disposal according to one's will;
and *bhṛtyatva* (servitude) consists in being a conscious being who is to be impelled.
And it should be understood that the characteristic of being related as such [i.e., as a correlate] consists in being the subordinate (*śeṣitva*) and so forth.
The expression "servant-master" is a designation in which the abstract state (*bhāva*) is primary;
that is to say, it means "characterized by the state of servant and master."
Or rather, such a reading may be considered possible.
Now, he states the conflicting views regarding the nature of liberation with the words "tathā pare" (so others).

The phrase "characterized by the attainment of Brahman" is his own statement of the intended view, and it serves to indicate that the natures of liberation proposed by others cannot constitute the ultimate human goal (*puruṣārtha*).

The first position is that of the Cārvākas and the proponents of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), which maintains the annihilation of one's own nature. The second position is that of the Yogācāras or the Māyins. The third position is that of Kaṇāda and others. This is the distinction.
Thus, the Vaiśeṣika is one position;
the Sāṅkhya view is the fourth;
and for the Advaitins, it would be characterized by the similarity of being with that [Brahman].
The word "that" refers to Brahman;
liberation is the state of identity with Brahman, which constitutes the commonality [of nature].
Alternatively, it is the attainment of equality with the form of Brahman.
The three supreme states consist of the attainment of the qualities of Brahman, the attainment of the splendor of Brahman, and liberation characterized by distinction;
"inborn" (*sāṃsiddhika*) refers to the doctrine of the Mīmāṃsakas and others.
The phrase beginning with "tadguṇe" refers to the proponents of the Siddhānta.
Here, the manifestation of one's true nature (*svarūpāvirbhāva*) is also implicitly included.
"Servitude" (*kiṅkaratva*) means the performance of service.
Regarding the means to liberation as well, he says: "also by virtue of its being the means to that.
The position of the combination of action and knowledge (*karmajñānasamuccaya*) belongs to Yādavaprakāśa;
"both" refers to the position of the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*).

Only for one whose mind has been refined through the yoga of action and the yoga of knowledge does supreme devotion, known as *bhaktiyoga*, arise. This very devotion, having action and knowledge as its limbs, is the means for attaining liberation characterized by the realization of the Supreme Brahman.
Its exclusivity consists in having the Lord alone as its object.
The meaning is that "permanence" (ātyantikatva) consists in being uninterrupted,
and that this very state is the form of the fruition of both supreme knowledge and supreme devotion.
With the words "That indeed," he establishes the utility of demonstrating the conflicting views as a means for the water of inquiry.

As long as the specific quality— such as being rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and sound reasoning (*tarka*)— is not determined in any one position among the various conflicting views of investigators,
so long does doubt regarding the truth not cease. And as long as there is no determination of the aforementioned specific quality, [doubt persists].
First of all, there is no determination of strength based on the possession of the characteristics of pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) in those respective proofs.
Furthermore, it is impossible for two contradictory means of proving a thesis to possess actual pervasion and presence in the subject with respect to a single locus (*dharmin*).

Thus, when various proofs for opposing positions are perceived as being of equal strength, the determination of the probandum (*sādhya*) is difficult to achieve due to their state of counter-thesis (*satpratipakṣa*).
Liberation does not arise from doubt regarding the object alone;
thus, while various positions remain active, the occasion has arrived for an investigation into which possesses the actual reality.

Once, through such investigation, the specific nature of one particular position is determined, the counter-argument (satpratipakṣa) ceases because it is known that the proof for that position possesses superior force; thereby, the ascertainment of the true nature of the object is established.

The collective intention is as follows: it is indeed appropriate to commence this work of inquiry (*vicāra-grantha*), which aims to determine the truth regarding the reality suitable for the means of liberation and which establishes the specific distinctions—such as being rooted in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) and sound reasoning (*tarka*)—of whichever particular position pertains to the nature of the self (*ātman*) and so forth.

Now, one might object: the task should simply be to set forth the treatises of the ancient teachers (*pūrvācārya*) in order to dispel the various conflicting views (*vipratipatti*) concerning the individual self (*ātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).
Having harbored within himself the apprehension that [his work] might be considered a mere engagement in composing a new treatise, he says, "Even though...

This means precisely this: the *sūtras*—namely, the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā-sūtras*—are intended solely for the purpose of determining the reality of the self, the supreme self, their relationship, and so forth.

"The status of being a *sūtra* belongs primarily to these alone," as stated in the *Skānda*: "Therefore, the wise know that the *Brahma-sūtra* possesses the status of a *sūtra* without qualification, whereas other *sūtras* are known by the learned to be qualified. The term is used without qualification for the primary one, but with qualification for the others."
Thus have those who know the Vedas and understand the true meaning of the nature of sound declared.
Thus:
"manifested" means "limited," which is a contraction of words.
"Profundity" (gāmbhīryatvam) means the possession of an abundance of meaning.
"The author of the Draviḍa-bhāṣya" refers to the commentator on the *Chāndogya-vyākhyāna*— known as the *Vākya*— composed by Brahmanandin, also called Ṭaṅka-ācārya, who bore the name Draviḍa-ācārya.

That he has also composed a commentary (*bhāṣya*) on the *Brahmasūtras* is understood from this context of the venerable author’s own words: "And they have been expanded. These refer to the statements of the *Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya* composed by the teacher Dramiḍa.
The phrase "in the Vivaraṇa-grantha" is to be understood as the ellipsis; or it refers to those Brahma-sūtras themselves.
Indeed, sentences from the Vivaraṇa are cited in the Viṣṇucittīya, which is a commentary on the Śrī Viṣṇu-purāṇa.
"Nevertheless"—
this is the sense: although the reality of the inner self (*adhyātmatattva*) along with its adjuncts has indeed been determined in the treatises of the ancient masters, nevertheless,

because later [thinkers] have promulgated various doctrines under the guise of commentaries on the *Brahma-mīmāṃsā* and other works, there remains a lack of certainty regarding the grounds for their invalidity.

Since faith in those [non-Saiddhāntika] texts is possible just as it is in the Siddhānta treatises, and since their intellects might waver due to the abundance of contradictions therein, they would not attain the knowledge of reality directly; therefore, the commencement of this treatise—which consists of an examination of those various systems for the purpose of distinguishing between their essential and non-essential elements—is indeed necessary.
Regarding the mention of Ācārya Ṭaṅka and others, some are proponents of established doctrines (siddhāntins).

Others, however, may be followers of different schools of thought (*matāntarānuyāyin*); and in their respective treatises, the qualities of being "white" or "black"—meaning, respectively, clarity of exposition and the opposite—should be applied as appropriate.
Alternatively, the two mentioned here, Ṭaṅka and Śrīvatsāṅka, might also belong to other schools and be distinct from the author of the *Vākyavivaraṇa*.
The name Ṭaṅka as the author of the Vākya is understood from the *Vedārthasaṃgrahaṭīkā*: "And for the sake of its comprehension...
Some understand the true nature of the meaning [of the Veda] due to its lack of clarity.

Furthermore, the intention is that since some people, due to certain reasons, have faith in the treatises of other schools and— consequently having their intellects deceived— understand things otherwise, it is indeed appropriate to commence this treatise both to ensure clear understanding and to demonstrate the white and black nature of other works.

The underlying intention is that this work, such as the *Ātmasiddhi* and others, is a treatise (*prakaraṇa*) belonging to the tradition of the ancient masters (*pūrvācārya*) in the form of formal scriptures (*śāstra*). Furthermore, this treatise is a supplement to the *Śārīrakamīmāṃsā* and the *Nyāyatattva-śāstra*.

A *prakaraṇa* is that which, while being intent on explaining a portion of the meaning of a treatise (*śāstra*), is occupied with other tasks conducive to the comprehension of the treatise’s meaning, such as the refutation of opposing views. As it has been said: "That which is connected to a single part of a treatise and is engaged in another task of the treatise..."
"This is what is called the *mata-prakaraṇa*."
First, he describes the true nature of the Self (ātmatattva) with the word "therein" (tatra). Regarding the term "body" (deha):

among those things proposed for investigation, the Self—which is distinct from the body and so forth—is self-luminous, eternal, capable of pervading all due to its subtlety, different in each individual body, and of the nature of bliss.
This is the meaning:
*dhī* (intellect) is knowledge that illuminates objects, which is an attribute (*dharma*) of the self (*ātman*);
because it has that [self] as its substratum, it is distinct from it.
That whose accomplishment and manifestation are achieved by no other means than itself is "ananyasādhana.
"Eternity" (nityatva) means being devoid of origination and destruction.
By the term "all-pervading" (vyāpī), its subtlety like that of an atom is implied.

"Self-blissful" (*svataḥ sukhī*) means possessing bliss characterized by a naturally agreeable manifestation by its very own nature (*svarūpataḥ*); that is to say, its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is bliss.
Alternatively, it refers to its having bliss as its inherent quality (*svābhāvikam ānanditvam*).
The meaning is that the state of being a sufferer is merely conditional (aupādhika). // 3 //

In this regard: distinct from the body, senses, mind, vital breath, and intellect, yet not established by means other than these; eternal, all-pervading, and separate in each body, the self is inherently blissful. (3)
But surely we perceive the body itself as the self through direct perception; for the knower who manifests as "I" in the cognition "I know" is the self,
and the body is the object of the notion of "I."
Because of the perception, "I am fat" or "I am thin," for it is indeed the body that possesses such qualities as fatness;
therefore, one must necessarily admit that this ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra) has the body as its objective support, since it stands in grammatical coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇatā) with it.
Otherwise, there would be an obstruction to all the worldly and analytical conventions of experts;
nor is this a figurative convention,
because no separate basis for primary usage has been established.

Furthermore, if the manifestation of the knower had as its objective support a body composed of multiple parts, it would necessarily be accompanied by the manifestation of that body's form, parts, and so forth; since such an accompaniment is absent, the cognition "I know" would have to lead one to understand [the knower] as something distinct from the body.
For such a rule is observed only in the case of perception by the external senses.
This is because the capacity [of cognition] is restricted by the fact that it manifests only the internal substratum of qualities within the mind (*svānta*).

Furthermore, this is because the first direct perception of a triad (*tryaṇuka*)—which possesses many parts, is endowed with the quality of magnitude (*mahiman*), and whose specific constituent parts have not yet been determined—is admitted [by you].
Moreover, it is observed that air (*vāyu*) is perceived by the tactile sense-organ (*tvagindriya*) merely as the locus of touch.

Just as there is a non-apprehension of its other qualities even though the object is the self distinct from the body, so it is here as well. Just as in that case, the rule for the apprehension of number, dimension, and so forth applies only to external objects of perception,
likewise, since consciousness is not perceived in individual atoms, [it cannot belong to them].
Furthermore, if that were accepted, it would follow that there would be many thousands of conscious beings within a single body;
since a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) residing in an effect-substance cannot exist without being preceded by the qualities of its cause, consciousness is not a specific quality of the body;
and because it does not persist as long as the body exists—these and other such types of inference are unable to prevail, as their objects are sublated by perception.
Furthermore, if pleasure is denied the status of a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa), it would follow as a logical consequence that it must be admitted as a quality of the body.

Moreover, such properties as performing actions in accordance with desire, possessing sense organs, and so forth— which are observed in the body and which completely distinguish it from objects like a jar that are not admitted to possess consciousness— lead to the understanding that the body itself is conscious.

Just as redness (rāga), though not present in each individual part such as the betel nut, the leaf, or the areca nut, appears in the whole due to a specific conjunction (saṃyoga-viśeṣa), so too the manifestation of consciousness (caitanya) in the body is not untenable, arising precisely from a specific cohesion of the atoms that initiate the body.

If it is argued that the emergence of redness there occurs through the sequence of dyads (dvyaṇuka) and so forth—produced by atoms that have acquired a rosy hue through contact with fire generated by chewing, and that this follows the principle that the qualities of the cause precede those of the effect—we say: no.
Because there is a lack of valid evidence (*pramāṇa*).

Furthermore, since we clearly perceive the specific quality of variegated color (*citrarūpa*) in a cloth produced from threads—even though that variegated color does not exist in each individual white, black, or other thread—how could we determine that this quality is preceded by the qualities of its causes?
Moreover, there is no other distinct color called "variegated" existing in the whole apart from the colors of the parts.
Because it would follow that the whole (avayavin) is not visible;
for if its visibility were established solely by means of the colors of its parts, then every effect-substance (kāryadravya) would result in being colorless. This contradicts experience.
Furthermore, there would be a contradiction with all conventional usage.

Moreover, the specific quality of hardness is observed to reside in a substance that produces effects (such as a stone), yet it does not have a preceding quality as its cause; thus, your argument is inconclusive.
Nor is hardness a particular kind of conjunction; for that [conjunction] resides in two things,
whereas this [hardness] exists only in a single substance, such as a water-jar.
Furthermore, this is because those who know the nature of categories accept [the self] as being distinct from touch.
If it is asked, "How can the visible body be the seer?",
what contradiction is there?
This is precisely because it is not possible for a single entity to simultaneously possess both the status of object (*karman*) and agent (*kartṛ*) in a single action.
If this is so, then how can there be the cognition "I" (*aham*) with respect to the self (*ātman*) according to the doctrine of difference (*vyatireka-vāda*)?
If you argue that it is due to a difference in form (*rūpa-bheda*), [we reply:]...
This is the same even in the doctrine that the body is the self (*dehātmavāda*).
Furthermore, action is that which results in a fruit residing in another as its inherent substrate (*samavāyin*).
Since the body—which possesses the fruit of cognition co-inherent in itself—does not possess the status of being an object (*karman*) at all, there is no room for such an objection.
Therefore, the followers of Bṛhaspati maintain that the body alone is the self;
and thus it is said: "Earth, water, fire, and air are the principles (tattvas), and from them arises consciousness."
The aphorism states: "Like the intoxicating power [arising] from yeast and other ingredients.
First, it describes the reality of the self (ātmatattva) with the word "therein" (*tatra*). Then, it addresses the "body" (*deha*).

The meaning is as follows: among those things proposed for investigation, the self—which constitutes the core—is distinct from the body and so forth, self-luminous, eternal, capable of pervading all due to its subtlety, separate in each body, and of the nature of bliss.
"Intellect" (dhī) refers to knowledge that illumines objects, which is an attribute (dharma) of the self.
Because it is the substratum of that [consciousness], it possesses a nature distinct from it.
That whose accomplishment or manifestation is by means of nothing other than itself is "one whose accomplishment is non-other" (*ananyasādhana*).
Eternality (*nityatva*) is the state of being devoid of origination and destruction.
By the word "pervasive" (vyāpin), subtlety is implied.
"Inherently blissful" (svataḥ sukhī) means possessing bliss characterized by a naturally favorable manifestation by its very own nature;
that is to say, having bliss as its essential form (sukhasvarūpa).
Alternatively, the sense is that its state of bliss is innate, whereas its state of suffering is merely adventitious, caused by limiting adjuncts (upādhi). // 3 //
Unable to accept the reality of the Self as it has been stated, the Cārvāka, who maintains that the body is the self, objects: "But surely, it is the body alone [that is the self].
For perception is indeed the primary means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and no purpose can be accomplished by transgressing it.
The sense is that perception itself establishes the body—endowed with grossness and other qualities—as the knower, the "I-sense," and the self; thus, the body alone is the self.
He demonstrates that the body alone is the object of the notion of "I" through the two sentences beginning with "And the body... and so forth.
[He concludes with] "Therefore."
"By virtue of being in grammatical apposition with that"—meaning, by having as its object a thing non-different from the body;
the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) is used here in the sense of "being thus.
This ego-conception (*ahaṅkāra*)—the notion of "I" such as "I am fat"—is of the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*)."
"Having the body as its objective support" means having the body as its object.
The rest is clear.
He states the fault in deviating from direct perception with the words "otherwise."
For worldly transactions are observed to be rooted in perception; these are primary, as they consist of things that perform causal functions and are common to both the learned and the ignorant.
The meaning is that contradiction of that [perception] would entail the consequence of overstepping direct perception itself.
Now, one might object: "The cognition of the ignorant, 'I am fat, I know,' is indeed merely an error."
[The author] restates and refutes the objection: "But for the wise, whose own sphere of experience is swift, [the thought] 'I know' arises;

whereas the conventional usage 'I am gross' is merely figurative (lākṣaṇika) for the wise. He rejects this with the words "And this is not so. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "This conventional usage is neither [figurative] nor [merely based on characteristics]."
The word "to be stated" (*vācyam*) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. He states the reasoning for the rejection [of the opponent's view] with the words "in the primary sense" (*mukhye*).

The point is that since that which is the object of the word "I"—namely, something distinct from the body—is refuted by its non-perception, it is the body alone that possesses primacy in both the cognition of "I" and in linguistic usage.
He raises the objection— starting with "And not" (*na ca*) and so forth— that the cognition "I know" (the perception of being a knower) cannot possibly have the body as its object.

The meaning is that there is no such rule (*niyama*) that the manifestation of the parts of an object is necessarily co-extensive (*anvayin*) with the direct perception of that composite object possessing parts.
If there were such a restriction, then that which follows [from it] would be established by the word "by means of" (*ayena*);
this is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Because of the absence of its concomitance—that is, because of the absence of concomitance with the illumination of the body’s parts and so forth—and because it does not illuminate those [parts], the cognition "I know" would lead one to understand [the self] as being indeed distinct from the body.
However, the result of the rule that "the body possesses parts" is that the perception of being a knower does not have the body as its object,
because it does not have the body's parts as its objects.

Whatever has a partless entity as its object has that very entity as its domain of perception, just as a pot and so forth are perceived; this is the application of the aforementioned rule in this formal argument (*prayoga*).
He states the reason why the aforementioned rule would be impossible [if it were not accepted]:
Regarding the term "external": the cognition of a necessary rule (*niyama*) arises from the observation of concomitance (*sahacāra*).
Since concomitance is observed only through external perception, the intended meaning is that the aforementioned rule has precisely that [external object] as its domain.
Now, let it be granted that the observation of concomitance occurs only with respect to the external.
To the objection that "the restriction [of the senses] should apply to everything except direct perception because it is unrestricted," he replies with the words "of one's own mind" (*svāntasya*).
An internal quality, such as cognition or pleasure, is what is perceptible;
the mind manifests the substratum merely by being its locus.
But it does not [grasp] another property [such as shape], because the mind lacks independence regarding external objects.

Thus, since the perception of parts and spatial extension is impossible for the mind, the notion that the body is grasped merely through the mind's status as a knower cannot be maintained as a rule applicable to perception in general; this is the intended meaning.
Even though the body is external, there is the misconception that it is internal because it is colored by cognition and so forth.
Regarding the rule that "being the object of the perception of its parts" pervades "being externally perceived as a whole," he states an exception with the words "unascertained.
The point is that in the case of the visual perception of a triad (tryaṇuka), there is an exception because its part is not grasped due to being beyond the senses (atīndriya).

"Consisting of many parts" means being inherent in many parts, or being qualified by many parts through inherence in that which is inherent in itself. "Possessing the quality of magnitude" means having the dimension of largeness (*mahat-parimāṇa*).

Immediately after the perception of a *trasareṇu* (a mote of dust), its possession of parts is inferred by means of its being a visible substance (*cākṣuṣadravyatva*) and so forth; thus, the manifestation of the brought-forth (*upanīta*) dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) is possible in the perception of a triad (*tryaṇuka*) from the second moment onward. Therefore, the perception of a triad is specified as "first" (*prathama*) to avoid the fallacy of deviation (*vyabhicāra*). If it is argued that there must be a rule that the external perception of a composite whole whose parts are perceptible has as its object those very parts, [the author] states the same fault in that case as well with the words "And of the wind" (*vāyośca*).

The point is that there is an inconstancy (vyabhicāra) regarding the stated rule in the case of the tactile perception of air, because by the mere possession of touch, that perception lacks the air's constituent parts as its object.
It is held that the perception of the air's constituents occurs only when there is focused attention (*avadhāna*);
otherwise, however, there is the apprehension of the air in contact with the skin solely by virtue of its possessing touch.

Regarding the cognition "I know," since it does not have form (rūpa) and so forth as its object, he states that there is no proving power (*aprayojakatva*) in establishing that the body is not its object, with the words "distinct from the body" and so on.
This refers to the cognition of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*). Its other qualities—such as number and so forth—are those residing in the self (*ātman*).
The phrase "so it is here too" implies that [the same principle] applies immediately thereafter.
This is the intended meaning: there is a rule that a sense organ which perceives a substance also perceives its qualities when they are suitably proximate.
Thus, in the theory of a distinct self (ātman), just as in the case of number—

Because those qualities [of the self] are unmanifest (*adīna*), they are not grasped by the mind due to their unsuitability; likewise, in the doctrine of the identity of the body and the self (*dehātmavāda*), the form and other attributes of that [self] are not grasped by the mind precisely because of their unsuitability.

Nor should it be argued that the perception of color is necessarily restricted to the perception of a colored substance, for this is not invariably the case, as seen in the tactile perception of jars and the like.
"'Just as in that case' means:

just as in the doctrine of a superfluous self (atiriktātmavāda), it is restricted that external perception alone, while grasping a substance, also grasps the number and other qualities inherent in it, so too should it be restricted in the doctrine of the body as the self (dehātmavāda); such is the sense."
"The same applies here as well" is what should be further connected [to the previous argument].
Thus, by stating "I know thus," it is established that perception has the body as its object.
By this, he states that the inferences which refute the sentience of the body are themselves sublated, saying "And if this is so."
"Consciousness is not a specific quality of the body, because it is preceded by qualities of its cause,

or because it does not persist as long as the substance [endures], like conjunction"— this is the inference that serves as a sublation (*bādhaka*) against the view that consciousness belongs to the body.
In this regard, he dispels the unestablished nature (*asiddhi*) of the first reason with the words beginning "pratyekam" (each).
Now, it might be argued: "Let there be no consciousness in the atoms that constitute the body, so that the contingency of multiple conscious beings in a single body does not arise;
furthermore, color and other qualities produced by heating are observed to be preceded by qualities that are not their own causes."
To the objection that consciousness might be like that [the quality of color], he replies with the words "in the case of an effect-substance" (*kāryadravye*).
Here, the theory of *pīlupāka* (the baking of individual atoms) is intended.

Thus, there exists a pervasion (*vyāpaka*) between being a specific quality of an effect-substance and having as its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) a quality of the same kind residing in that which inheres in what inheres in itself—this being the nature of "having qualities of the cause as antecedents."
The meaning is that by the cessation of the pervader [the property of being a specific quality of a body], there follows the cessation of consciousness as a specific quality of the body.

Furthermore, in the second inference, the general negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*)—namely, "whatever is a specific quality of an effect-substance is co-existent with that substance as long as it exists"—must be stated according to the *pīlupākavāda* (the theory of baking within the atom).

By the phrase "and so forth," the following inference is to be understood: "Consciousness is not a specific quality of the body, because it differs from other specific qualities residing in that [body]."
They are not able to exert their power, nor do they dare to subvert the consciousness of the body.
Why? Because their objects are sublated by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
Due to this sublation by direct perception, those aforementioned inferences do not even arise.
The meaning is this: it is possible that these weak inferences cannot subvert perception, which is a stronger authority because it is foundational.

Furthermore, since conjunction and other qualities—which do not persist as long as the substance exists and are not preceded by the qualities of their causes—are observed to be qualities of the body, the absence of "bodily quality" in consciousness cannot be established even by the aforementioned reasons.
With the intention that this is possible, he says "in the particular" (*viśeṣe*).
Since consciousness is perceived only in the body, it is indeed a quality of that [body].
Even if its status as a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is denied by the aforementioned reasons, there is no harm.

For "specific quality-ness" (*viśeṣaguṇatva*) is a technical definition. The sense [of the objection] is this: if specific quality-ness is defined as "being a quality other than gravity, water-fluidity, and that which inheres in a property residing in what resides in air, while being distinct from those," then one might as well include the "otherness" of cognition (*jñāna*) and so forth within the "otherness" of gravity and the rest.

Intending to show that the reasons—such as "not being preceded by a quality" (*akāraṇaguṇapūrvakatva*) and so forth—are inconclusive (*aprayojaka*), and thus that there is no harm in cognition being a specific quality of the body even if it were so, he says: "Moreover, if [it is argued]...

The sense is: if it is maintained that cognition is not a specific quality of the body because it differs from other specific qualities of the body, then why is consciousness not simply accepted as belonging to the body itself, since it differs from insentient objects like jars which are commonly agreed upon? This would be simpler (*lāghava*).

In the phrase "possessing sense organs, etc.," the word "etc. (ādi) is intended to include "possessing vital breath" (prāṇavattva). The meaning is that the body's action conforms to will—that is, its activity is directly dependent on will—whereas for objects such as a jar, that conformity occurs only through the mediation of the body's own activity.

The body possesses consciousness because its activity conforms to desire, or because it possesses sense organs and so forth; for that which does not possess [consciousness] is not thus, like a jar or similar objects—this negative inference (*vyatirekānumāna*) is implied in this statement regarding the sentience of the body.

Furthermore, he states "in the case of the *kramuka*" to show that there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) in the pervasion that "being a specific quality of an effect-substance is preceded by the qualities of its cause."
The point is that there is a deviation [from the rule] in this case: when a betel leaf smeared with powder mixed with areca nut is crushed between the teeth, the prior parts are destroyed;

then, through a specific kind of conjunction (*saṃśleṣaviśeṣa*), a composite whole (*piṇḍitāvayavin*) is produced from those parts. Consequently, the red color—which did not exist in the individual parts—arises in them solely due to that specific conjunction. Thus, the rule fails in this instance.

He objects with the word "chewing" (*carvaṇa*). The objector’s point is that when the original composite substance, down to its binary compounds (*dvyaṇuka*), is destroyed by the crushing of the teeth, the atoms become independent; then, through the process of cooking (*pāka*) characterized by contact with the primary fire produced during chewing, a red color arises in the atoms.

Since the red color in the aggregated composite substance is preceded solely by the qualities of its causes (*kāraṇaguṇapūrvaka*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the rule. This is the sense of the objector.
He refutes [the objection] by stating, "It is not a case of the absence of a means of valid cognition.
One must accept that it is precisely a particular kind of conjunction (*saṃśleṣaviśeṣa*) that serves as the cause for a different color in certain cases;
for instance, in the case of turmeric powder, a red color is observed only through the conjunction of the powder with water.

The point is that here too, since such a possibility exists, there is no evidence for the hypothesis of baking (*pākakalpanā*). Even if one insists that in the case of chewing (*carvaṇa*), a change in color occurs only through baking, he points out an inconsistency in another case with the words "white and black" (*sitāsite*).
For indeed, in the case of a variegated cloth, baking is not possible in the parts (*avayava*).
Furthermore, there is no variegated color (*citra-rūpa*) in the parts;

thus, the intended meaning is that the rule—that a specific quality (*viśeṣa-guṇa*) of a whole must be preceded by a quality of its own kind in its parts—is subject to the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) in the case of variegated color.
Here, "belonging to the same kind" (*sājātya*) is intended in terms of a subordinate genus, such as "color-ness" (*rūpatva*).
For a white cloth is not produced from blue threads.
However, if one intends to assert a commonality (*sājātya*) based on the property of being color (*rūpatva*) and so forth, then that [production] would follow as a consequence.
Now, it might be argued that "variegated" (*citra*) is not accepted as a distinct type of color.
Nor should it be argued that a variegated cloth (*citrapaṭa*) produced from threads of various colors would consequently be colorless;
for it is a fixed rule that color and the like must be all-pervasive (*vyāpyavṛtti*), and thus it is impossible to admit that a single locus possesses multiple non-pervasive colors.
This is because there is no harm in the variegated cloth being colorless, since its visibility as an object of sight is established by the colors of its constituent parts alone.

If it is argued that the possession of manifested color (*udbhūtarūpa*) is accepted as the cause for the visual perception of a substance through either the relation of inherence (*samavāya*) or the relation of inhering in that which inheres (*svasamavāyisamavetatva*), then [the author] replies here with the words "all indeed.
The meaning is this: since visual perception is established by the color of the parts alone, one should not accept that every composite whole (*avayavin*) possesses color.
To the objection that this very [position] is accepted because of its parsimony (*lāghava*), he replies with the words "in experience" (*anubhava*).
The meaning is that since the perception and the conventional usage of the whole as possessing color are uncontradicted, one cannot maintain the desired position that the whole is colorless.
The point is that, because of the uncontradicted cognition and usage "the cloth is variegated," a variegated color must also be accepted [as existing in the whole].

Now, one might object: on the strength of perception, we accept that the variegated cloth possesses multiple colors that exist as non-pervasive (avyāpyavṛtti) with respect to the various colors of its parts.

And thus, there is no deviation [in the rule] in that case; to this he says: "But as for the specific quality... In the case of a hailstone (*karakā*) consisting of water, because of the particularity of the conjunction of its parts and the diversity of the auxiliary causes of its production, a hard touch is perceived even though it is devoid of fluidity; yet this is not preceded by the qualities of its cause, because a hard touch does not exist in the water-atoms (*jalaparamāṇu*).

And thus, the sense is that there would be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) from the rule that [qualities] are preceded by the qualities of their causes, in the case of the touch of a solid object (*kāraka*).

Now, one might argue: "Let hardness (*kāṭhinya*) simply be a particular kind of conjunction of parts; and in that case, where is the lack of invariable concomitance? To this, he says: "Nor in conjunction... (*na ca saṃyoge*).

If hardness were a specific kind of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) of parts, it would not reside in the whole (*avayavin*); consequently, the cognition and linguistic usage "the hailstone is hard" would be impossible.

Even if one were to somehow justify that [usage], since a conjunction residing in a visible substance is itself visible, it would follow as an unwanted consequence (*prasaṅga*) that hardness could also be perceived by the eye. This is the intended meaning. [The phrase] "as a specific kind of touch" [is used].
It is correct that hardness is merely a specific kind of tactile sensation (sparśaviśeṣa), because it is a quality (guṇa) perceivable solely by the sense of touch.
The meaning is that this has been accepted as such by the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas), who are experts in the categories of existence (padārthavid).
Having raised the objection regarding the contradiction between the status of agent and object in the doctrine that the body is the self, he refutes it with the words "of the visible," etc.
"What contradiction?"— for the question "how" arises only where there is a contradictory meaning.
The sense is: since there is no contradiction in the seer being the object of seeing, what indeed is the question of "how"?
He states the contradiction with the words "this very [person]":
it is not logical for someone to simultaneously possess both the status of agent and the status of object in relation to that same action.
