For the object (*karman*) is that which is most desired to be attained through an action (*kriyā*), and thus exists in the form of something to be accomplished (*sādhya*);
whereas the agent (*kartṛ*), who is the locus of the action, exists in an already established form (*siddha*).
Since identity between the established and the to-be-accomplished is impossible, the sense is that there is a contradiction between the states of being the agent and the object.
In order to refute the opponent's argument by means of his own logic, the proponent of the self (dehātmavādī) states a counter-argument (pratibandī), beginning with "If it is so.

The opponent states the resolution (samādhi): "Because of the difference in form" (rūpabheda). The proponent of the self provides the answer that establishes parity between the two cases: "It is the same" (samānam).

Just as in the doctrine of a superfluous self (ātmariktātmavāda), it is said that there is no contradiction because of the difference in modes— where agency (*kartṛtva*) in the act of cognition consists in being conjoined with the mind, while objecthood (*karmatva*) consists in being the "I" and so forth—
the same logic does not preclude [the application of] this reasoning to the doctrine of the body as the self (*dehātmavāda*). This is the intended meaning.
In reality, the kind of objecthood that is contradictory with agency is not the same as being the object of knowledge;
therefore, there is no fault for this reason either, as he says: "Moreover, others..."
Regarding the phrase "partaking in the fruit of the knowledge inherent in itself":

the meaning is that which possesses the objectivity (viṣayatā) as determined by a knowledge residing in itself. Since objectivity is defined by its correlate (the subject), there is a metaphorical designation of it as the "fruit of knowledge."
"The state of being an object (*karmatva*) does not exist at all"—this means that the primary state of being an object does not exist.
The intended sense is this: the primary state of being an object consists in being the locus of a result produced by an action that inheres in another [the agent].
Just as a village possesses the status of being the object of the action of going,
the status of being the object of cognition and so forth— characterized by the relationship between the object and the subject— is indeed secondary.

For it is the established doctrine of the logicians (*tārkika*) that when a verbal root has an object consisting of a thing possessing an object, the status of being an object (*karmatva*) takes the form of "objectness" (*viṣayatā*).
Since it is accepted that even the agent of cognition [is the self], there is no inconsistency in such statements as "the self does not know itself";
however, there is a contradiction only with respect to the primary [self] acting as the agent.

Nor should it be said that this [definition of] *karmatva* (objecthood) is secondary or not established by the grammatical instruction (*anuśāsana*), because the very rule "that which is most desired by the agent is the object" (*kartur īpsitatamaṃ karma*) is accepted as the authority for this case as well, through its application by way of *tantra* (simultaneous extension). Here, "agent" (*kartṛ*) means the knower (*jñātṛ*).

In this view, the literal meaning (*akṣarārtha*) should be stated as follows: by means of action—that is, by means of knowledge—the object (*karman*) is that which is most desired to be attained, being intended as something to be known.

However, regarding that which is known but undesired, it is precisely by the rule "likewise [that which is] connected [to the action] though not desired" that the undesired object of knowledge is defined as being connected with the action—that is, related to it as its objective domain through the act of knowing.
Furthermore, even though it is the object of the agent’s desire, the object [of the action] is not the primary *karman* according to the view that it is only a secondary *karman*.
Even if verbal usage (*vyavahāra*) is the fruit of cognition, the object does not possess primary *karmatva* because it lacks the status of being the locus of that [usage].

Although the self (*ātman*) is the locus of its own verbal usage, the cognition residing within itself—which has itself as its object and is the cause of that [usage]—is not inherent in another; therefore, the self is not [the primary object].

However, when there is a desire to express the fruit of knowledge characterized by conformity with worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), the status of being the object of knowledge (*jñānakarmatva*) for the subject matter, such as a jar, may indeed be primary;
we shall explain this further in the subsequent section.
He concludes the established position regarding the identity of the body and the self with the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*).

The Bārhaspatyas—namely, the Cārvākas who adhere to the Lokāyata system composed by Bṛhaspati—are well known for the tradition that the preceptor of the gods, being overwhelmed by the entreaties of the lord of the Asuras, composed a delusive treatise intended to destroy the Vedic faith and to bring about the loss of the Asuras' sovereign power and majesty.
To establish that consciousness belongs to the body alone, they cite that aphorism, beginning with "And thus... (tathā ca).

The meaning of the Sūtra is as follows: there are only four elements—earth and so forth—which are the fundamental principles (*tattva*). Consciousness, though non-existent in each of them individually, emerges when they are combined to produce the body, just as a previously non-existent intoxicating power arises in the substance *surā* produced from yeast and other ingredients.
Here is the rebuttal: The body is not the self, because that is contradicted by direct perception;
for indeed, the notions of "I" and "this" do not belong to one and the same entity. (4)
The cognition "I," which functions as inward-turned (*pratyag-vṛtti*), presents its own object as precisely extracted from the body that is the sphere of the notion "this" (*idaṃ-kāra*);
it is like [the cognition] of a jar or similar objects.

And the intellect (*śemuṣī*) which functions as outward-turned (*parāg-vṛtti*) and has the body as its object distinguishes its own object from the sphere of the "I-notion," just as in the case of "this is a jar."
Otherwise, the distinction between self and other would be untenable.
Nor does such a cognition arise from a difference in form within a single entity;
for Devadatta does not perceive himself, while holding a staff, as "this one is a staff-bearer."
Furthermore, for one whose external sensory functions are restrained and whose mind is attentive, when perceiving the self as "I," the limbs such as the hands, feet, and belly do not appear.

Moreover, if it is admitted that the gross composite whole (avayavin), the body, is the object of the cognition "I," then it must necessarily be accompanied by the appearance of its constituent parts.
For it is impossible that a gross composite whole should manifest while [its parts remain unperceived].
As for the claim that no parts whatsoever are perceived,
and the objection that there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of a triad (*tryaṇuka*); that is not so, because it is visible through an opening in a window.
There is no deviation [from the rule] because there is no reason to accept atoms apart from the *ribhāga* and *trasareṇu*,

or because there is a rule that a part capable of being perceived by the senses must appear in that manner. Nor should it be imagined that this rule applies only to a whole (*avayavin*) that is perceptible by the external sense organs.
Because there is a lack of valid means of cognition [for such a thing],
and because it is impossible for the internal organ alone to function upon a composite whole;
whereas wind, due to the absence of color and other qualities, is perceived solely as the substratum of touch.
Even in that case, there is indeed the appearance of many such parts, just as when one touches a jar or similar object; thus, there is no deviation [from the rule] by that instance.
As for the observation that the notion of "I" is seen directed toward the body—as in "I am fat" or "I am thin"—that too must be carefully examined.

Even there, the ego (ahaṅkāra) perceives some indeterminate object within the body that has the very form of "I," and not merely the physical body as the visual cognition [perceives it] in its connection with stoutness, childhood, and so forth.
For this very reason, there occurs both the appearance of difference and the linguistic usage: "This house is mine" and "This body is mine."

For it is not appropriate to resort to a metaphorical usage—such as the designation "the head of a stone statue"—for that which is being understood based on a directly perceived distinction, as in the case of "my self.
In that instance, such a resort is appropriate because the word "self" (ātman) applies to the [actual] self, resulting in identity of meaning and because there is no dispute.
But it is not so in this case.

Therefore, since the conscious self is established as distinct from the body through direct perception, the use of the word "I" with respect to the body is merely figurative (lākṣaṇika) in reference to that which is related to it.

Because the distinction [of the self] from external objects is clear through the apprehension of mutually contradictory forms, dimensions, numbers, and configurations, the delusion of the non-discrimination of the ignorant consists in the appearance of identity between the self and the body due to the non-apprehension of such other forms in the self.
Furthermore, this self has its own activity conforming to its will;
for it is by will alone that it intends, remembers, and deliberates.
Since even the body performs activities such as lying down, sitting, and rising in conformity to that will, the delusion of non-difference arises.
Just as in the case of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like,

those whose minds are concentrated indeed perceive directly— as distinct from the gross composite body that appears as a partless object shimmering as "this"— the form of the "I" which is established as the knower.
And there occurs the cognition "I know," which does not have the body as its object.
Or rather, this [cognition] has a different object as its domain;
because it manifests as having parts that are not themselves manifesting;
whatever is of such a nature is so [i.e., has a different object].
Just as this appearance [occurs],
that which has the body as its object is not so;
just as in both cases...
The body is considered to be an object of knowledge.
Likewise, the body is not the objective domain of the notion of "I," because it is apprehended as "this."
Or, [it is so] because it is perceivable by the external sense organs, like a jar and so forth.
Now follows the refutation of the doctrine that the body is the self, beginning with the words "The response here is... and so on.
In this regard— concerning the view that the body is the self—
the rebuttal is the counter-argument, which serves as a subverting proof.
Or there is sublation; the word "is proposed" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
[This refers to] "due to sublation by perception."

The meaning is that grasping [the body] as "this" (idantvena), just as one does with a hand or a house, is the very definition of perceiving a difference between the body and the self; this serves as a sublation (bādhaka) against its being the self.
He establishes this very point with the words "Certainly not" (na khalu).
"I-ness" (aham) and "this-ness" (idam)—that is, the cognitions of "I" and "this."

The meaning is that for a single person, the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya), which has itself as its object, and the notion of "this" (idaṃpratyaya), which has something other than itself as its object, cannot both pertain to one and the same thing.
He explains this with the words "I know," and so forth.
Inward-turning (pratyagvṛtti) means having the inner self as its object;
"extracted" (niṣkṛṣṭa) means distinct;
outward-turning (parāgvṛtti) means having something other than the self as its object.
"From the sphere of the ego"—that is, from one's own self which is the object of the notion of "I.
The remainder is clear. Regarding the phrase "otherwise":
Otherwise—that is, if the cognitions "I" (*aham*) and "this" (*idam*) did not have objects that are distinct in nature—the following would be the case:

the meaning of the "inner" (*pratyak*) is one's own self (*svātman*), which appears as "I" to oneself; whereas the meaning of the "outer" (*parāk*) is the "other," which appears as "this" to oneself. Indeed, the distinction between self and other is defined solely by the notions and words "I" and "this."
Since there is no difference in their objective referents (*arthavailakṣaṇya*), this [identification] would not be possible for those two;
therefore, he says "not indeed" (*na hi*) regarding the suggestion that it might be the very object of "I" (*ahamartha*) appearing under another form as "this" (*idantvena*).

The meaning is that for one's own self, which appears as "I" through its nature of inwardness (*pratyaktva*), there could only be an appearance as "this" through its being a possessor of a staff (*daṇḍitva*), such as "this person possesses a staff" (*ayaṃ daṇḍī*).
"But surely, the cognition 'I am this' and so forth does indeed occur with respect to one's own self.
True;
even there, by the word "this" (idam), there is the delineation of attributes belonging to the nature of the "other" (the external).
The manifestation of the nature of the Self is "I" (aham).

Thus, the underlying intention is that there is no inconsistency in the established distinction that the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) has an inward orientation (pratyagvṛtti), whereas the sense of "this" (idaṅkāra) has an outward orientation (parāgvṛtti).
One might object: "Could it not be that [the body] is mine, just as one says 'this is my body' or 'this is my self'? Anticipating this lack of conviction, he says, "And others.
This means that there is another reason for the body being non-self. He states that very reason with the words, "When [the self] is restricted," and so forth.
For one whose engagement of the external senses has been restrained, the mental contemplation of one's own self as "I" does not have the body as its object,
because it does not have the hands, feet, and so forth as its referent.

The sense is that when the whole (*avayavin*) is perceived as gross, the manifestation of some of its parts is unavoidable. "Of one with an attentive mind" means of one whose mind is intent on grasping the self. "Of one who discerns" means of one who knows.
*Sthavīyān* means "exceedingly gross.
What is intended is that it is inherent in parts that are perceptible by the senses.

The phrase "in the window" (*vātāyane*) excludes the possibility of an inconsistency (*anaikāntya*) in the rule that the perception of a whole depends upon its parts being within the range of perception, as this rule would otherwise fail in the case of perceiving a triad (*tryaṇuka*).

The meaning is that there is no evidence for postulating atoms as parts of the triad (tryaṇuka) beyond the triad itself, which is partless and perceivable by the rays of the sun entering through a lattice opening.

The point is that since the *trasareṇu* is partless, there is no deviation from the aforementioned rule regarding its perception. Even while accepting the postulation of atoms, he says "perceptible," etc.

The meaning is that for a whole (*avayavin*) whose parts (*avayava*) are perceptible, there is a rule that its manifestation is pervaded by the manifestation of its parts; therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of the perception of a triad (*tryaṇuka*),
because its parts are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*).
"And [the claim] that 'there is no whole'—

the assumption that the manifestation of the whole is necessarily restricted to the manifestation of its parts only in the case of perception produced by the external senses— is merely a self-contradiction.

For if one accepts that the manifestation of parts is pervaded by the perceptibility of the whole, then the observation of a subverting factor (bādhaka) serves as the proof for restricting the rule [to the effect that it applies] only to those cases where the object of that external perception is exclusively the parts."
The meaning is: "because of the absence of that.

Now, if it is argued that the restriction [that the whole is perceived by the mind alone without the parts] must be narrowed down precisely because the whole is grasped by the mind alone without the parts, he says in response: "of the internal organ" (*antaḥkaraṇasya*).

The meaning is that it is impossible for the mind, when external sense organs have not been employed as its medium, to engage in the perception of a mere specific part, or of an external object such as the body.
For logicians maintain that the internal mind lacks independence regarding external objects;
therefore, the apprehension of the body by the mind alone would not be possible.
Nor should it be imagined that because the body possesses sentience, it could be apprehended by the mind without [the mediation of] its parts.
The sense is that there is no contradiction regarding consciousness itself.
He removes the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) of the aforementioned rule with respect to the tactile perception of air by saying, "But as for air.

The meaning is that there is no fault in the rule that the perceptibility of a composite substance possessing color and other qualities consists in its having parts as its object; for even if one accepts the tactile perception of air solely on account of its possessing touch, air is devoid of color.

In fact, even tactile perception of air has as its object its constituent parts; thus he says, "In that case also. Since the contact with the constituent parts is unavoidable when there is contact with the whole, and since the manifestation of the whole is necessarily preceded by the manifestation of the constituent parts that are in contact with the senses, it follows that even though there is a rule that the direct perception of a part has as its object those very parts, this is not the case for the tactile perception of air.
There is an inconsistency (vyabhicāra),

because in that case there is also the manifestation of its constituent part, just as in the tactile perception of a jar there is the manifestation of the jar's constituent parts; such is the meaning.

Having restated the perception established by direct experience—which seeks to prove that the body is the self—with the words "But as for that... and so forth, he provides the resolution with the words "That too...
and so forth: the notion of "I" takes as its object only the inner self, characterized by "I-ness," which exists within the body and has the form of "I."
The point is this: the ego-consciousness "I am fat, I know" has as its object the inner self (antarātman) which possesses fatness, by way of the body.
In mental cognition, however, the appearance of the body occurs through the operation of mental association (upanaya).
Even in the common usage "I am fat, I know," the word "fat," though denoting the body, is used figuratively for the inner self connected with it.
In our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), however, [the term "body"] is used in its primary sense alone;
for the body is a mode (*prakāra*) that is not established separately from the conscious self,

and it is accepted that words denoting a mode that is not established separately— provided they are not abstracting terms (*niṣkarṣaka*)— function in their primary sense with respect to the substratum (*dharmin*).
Thus has been described the way in which non-erroneous cognition and linguistic usage proceed.

He states "for this very reason" to show that when the co-referential (samānādhikaraṇa) cognition has the body as its object in the sense of being the self, there is also the support of the designation of a non-co-referential (vyadhikaraṇa) cognition.
He dispels the doubt that the expression of difference, "this is my body," might be merely figurative—like the expression "the body of a stone statue"—by stating "for it is not that."
"Being extended"—that is, being stretched out or expanded;
meaning, being employed extensively by the world. The sense is that it is not a sound view to assume that the designation "extensive" is merely figurative.

However, since the expression "this is my self" must necessarily be regarded as figurative in both philosophical systems due to the lack of any other recourse, he says "therein. This is because of their identical referent— the fact that the words "I" and "self" have the same meaning—
and because of the absence of dispute— the fact that there is no disagreement regarding the identity between the referent of "I" and the self.

"And it is not thus here" means that since the identity of meaning between the body and the word "I" is unestablished, and because there is dispute regarding their identity of referent, the expression "this is my body" cannot be assumed to have a figurative sense.
Rather, the point is that it must be accepted as having a primary sense, just like the expression "this is my house."
He states that the word "I" (aham) is used figuratively with respect to the body by saying "therefore" (ataḥ).
This means that in expressions such as "I go," the word "I" is used metaphorically (lākṣaṇika) for the body which possesses the self.
However, it should be understood that for those who possess the delusion that the body is the self, such usage is rooted in a confusion regarding its primary denotation (śakti-bhrama).
Thus, by the force of reasoning, it has been established that mental perception—expressed as "I know"—has as its object a self distinct from the composite body.
Having thus established the manifestation of a self distinct from the body, [the author] asks how the delusion of non-difference from the body arises, and answers with the word "external":
"sanniveśa" means configuration, form, or the arrangement of parts.
Because of its clarity—
this implies that even when the delusion of non-difference does not arise; and "the appearance of non-difference with the body" is a *karmadhāraya* compound meaning both an appearance and a delusion.

The meaning is that the delusion of non-difference between the body and the self occurs for those who do not perceive the distinguishing features—that is, for those devoid of the perception of the distinguishing features.
This is the underlying intention: although the self has a dimension distinct from that of the body, nevertheless, that dimension is not perceptible.
Even though cognition, pleasure, and so forth are perceptible, as long as there is no apprehension of their impossibility within the body, they do not serve to differentiate [the self from the body].
Likewise, even form and other qualities do not differentiate [the self] with respect to the self, except through the apprehension of their impossibility therein.
"Number and so forth, however, are not differentiators because they are common [to both].

Having established the absence of the "grasping of the cause of difference," which would otherwise sublate [the notion of identity], he establishes the cognition of similarity as the proof for the delusion of oneness with the words "for this reason also.
The meaning is that the body's equality with the self consists in its possessing an activity that conforms to the will of the self.
Regarding the form *abhyūhati*, the *vārttika* "after a prefix, the roots *as* and *ūh* optionally take the *parasmaipada*" provides for the optional use of the active voice.
*Abhyūhana* means deliberation (*vitarkaṇa*), conjecture (*utprekṣaṇa*), or investigation.

The phrase "when it is applied" (*praṇihite*) demonstrates the cessation of the error of identity—which has arisen from the perception of common characteristics—through the perception of the specific distinguishing features.
"Attention" means focused concentration.
"Established as the knower" means manifesting solely in the form of the state of being a knower. "Partless" means devoid of constituent parts.
For the self is the object of the mind; if it possesses parts, it is perceived accordingly.
And it is not perceived in that way;
rather, it has the single form of being a knower.
Therefore, it is partless.
The apprehension of the self as having a single form and being partless is indeed the apprehension of its distinguishing features.
The sense is that for one whose mind is attentive and who possesses the aforementioned reflection, the self becomes directly perceived by the mind as distinct from the body.
Furthermore, the phrase "when [the mind] is directed" can also be applied to the object of yogic perception.
Thus, by the power of reasoning, it has been established that perception has as its object a self distinct from the body, based on the cognition "I know thus.
The phrase "and there are" (*bhavanti ca*) demonstrates this very point as it is formulated into formal syllogisms (*prayoga*);
the word "syllogisms" (*prayogāḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

What is intended to be demonstrated through the immediate perception of "I know" is that in the first instance there is an absence of having the body as its object, while in the subsequent instance there is the state of having an object distinct from the body.
In both cases, the reason is one and the same: namely, the nature of appearing as a manifestation that does not have the parts of the body as its object.
In both cases, the positive example (*anvayyudāharaṇa*) is "one who is thus";
the manifestation "this" refers to manifestations such as "this is a jar.
In the first case, the negative example (*vyatirekyudāharaṇa*) is demonstrated by the passage beginning with "that which in the body," and so forth.

Having stated the argument based on perception (*pratyakṣa*), he states the positive concomitant (*anvayin*) argument based on the body with the words "tathā-śarīram" (likewise, the body). "This" refers to being perceived; that is, being perceived as external. "Externality" is the resulting logical reason (*hetu*).

Furthermore: For one who perceives his own self as being for the sake of another, and everything else as being for the sake of the self—how can there be the notion of "self" regarding this body, which is for the sake of another, given that it is a composite? (5)

We perceive through direct experience that everything belonging to the category of external and internal objects of enjoyment—such as sound, pleasure, and so forth—exists for the sake of the Self; that the Self, as the enjoyer, exists for no other purpose; and that the Self is the sovereign master of all.
Furthermore, the body does not exist for its own sake;
because it is a composite,
and all composites are observed to exist for the sake of another, such as beds, seats, chariots, and so forth.
Nor should it be argued that since composite objects such as bodies are seen to exist for the sake of others, the self (ātman) must also be a composite;
for if that were the case, it would follow that the self is also for the sake of another.
And it has already been stated that this self is not for the sake of another, as it is directly perceived.
Furthermore, the state of being a composite in the self is sublated by the non-perception of what is suitable [to be so];
and if it were for the sake of another composite, that too would be likewise, and since that too would be likewise for yet another, there would be no finality.
Moreover, when there is an established order, a lack of order is not tenable.
Nor is it the case that for an aggregate to exist for the sake of another, that "other" must itself be an aggregate;
for the Self's status as an "other" with respect to its own-body aggregate is established precisely by virtue of being the enjoyer.

For one who desires inference based merely on a property observed in the example, even if that property is irrelevant to the pervasion (*vyāpti*), there follows the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference.

He introduces a third reason, "the state of being an aggregate" (*saṅghātatva*), in the syllogism whose subject (*pakṣa*) is the body and which aims to prove non-selfhood, with the words "Furthermore...
(*kiṃ ca*). [The phrase] "not for the sake of another" (*aparārtham*)...
"Having another as its purpose" means that which has itself as its primary object;
"itself" refers to the self consisting of the sense of "I" (ahamartha);
"for the sake of the self" means for the sake of the self consisting of the sense of "I" who has become the enjoyer.

Furthermore, for one who knows— that is, perceives— the entire collection of external objects, [it follows that they are non-self] because of their being aggregates, that is, because they possess a configuration of constituent parts.
The meaning of the verse is: how could the notion of "self" arise with respect to this body, which exists for the sake of another— that is, for the sake of an enjoyer who is distinct from it?
Herein is the formal argument (prayoga): the body is not the self, because it exists for the sake of another, like a chariot and so forth.
Nor is there a lack of proof regarding its essential nature;
the point is that the body's existence for the sake of another is established by its being a composite (saṅghāta). //5//

He explains, with the words "of everything," the relationship of pervader and pervaded between selfhood and being-for-the-sake-of-another, as well as between being-for-the-sake-of-another and not being the self—a relationship stated in the first half of the verse.
"Being for the sake of the self" means being a means for the experience of the experiencing self.
"The state of being the principal (śeṣitā) of everything," which results from not being for the sake of another, [is what is meant].
The meaning is that [the self] possesses ownership— that is, primacy— by virtue of being the enjoyer of everything that is to be enjoyed.
He precludes the pervasion of the body by the nature of the self, or its being for no other purpose, with the words "nor is the body [the self]."

He provides an example of the place where the inseparable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) of being a composite (*saṅghātatva*) with being for the sake of another (*pārārthya*) is apprehended, stating: "For composites... (*saṅghātā hi*).
"For the sake of another" means for the sake of an enjoyer who is distinct from them.

Having raised the objection that the self (*ātman*), which is inferred as being for the sake of another because it is seen to be a composite, might itself be a composite, he refutes it by stating: "And [the self] is not a composite. (*na ca saṅghātā*...).

"In that case" (tathā sati) means: here, the intended counter-argument (*pratitarka*) in the inference "the self is a composite because it is composed of others" is as follows: "If the self were a composite, then it would be for the sake of another.
Alternatively, it refers to the counter-inference (*praty-anumāna*): "The self is not a composite because it is not for the sake of another."

He states that there is also perceptual sublation (*pratyakṣabādha*) regarding the claim that the self—inferred as being distinct from the composite body—is itself of the nature of a composite, by saying "due to the non-perception of what is perceptible" (*yogyānupalambhāt*).

Alternatively, he says "due to the non-perception of what is perceptible" to show that even if the status of being a composite were to follow for the self by the force of inference, it will be set aside by its being made the object of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
[The body is a composite for the sake of another.]
In the argument "because it is a composite, like a bedstead and so forth," the fact of being distinct from the body serves as the *upādhi* (limiting condition).
Nor should it be argued that if being distinct from the subject (*pakṣa*) were an *upādhi*, it would lead to the undesirable consequence of the total collapse of inference;

for where the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the subject is established by another means of valid cognition—as in the case of inferring that fire is not hot—it is possible for being distinct from the subject to function as an *upādhi*.

In the present context as well, whether for those who maintain that the body is the self or for those who maintain a self distinct from it, it is accepted that the body lacks the quality of being for the sake of another composite entity; thus, there is no fault in taking its distinctness [from such an entity] as the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).

He states "in another composite" (*saṅghātāntare*) because there is no pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the state of being a composite by the property of being for the sake of another composite, since that would lead to an infinite regress.
Of that [collection] which constitutes the probandum (sādhya) as well—
meaning its being for the sake of another collection—
and of that which is other than it, namely, that which is inferred from the collection constituting the probandum.
The same applies to another aggregate; that is, it has the nature of being for the sake of another aggregate.
And this is not the case in the context of a fixed arrangement.

The point is this: when it is intended that "being a composite" (saṅghātatva) is pervaded by "being for the sake of another" (parārthatva), and when such a systematic relationship is possible, it is not logical to resort to the pervasion of "being for the sake of another through being a composite," because that would entail an infinite regress.
Now, one might object: "The apprehension of pervasion is indeed dependent upon the observation of repeated concomitance."
And that [composite nature] would exist only as being for the sake of another composite, because it is observed to be so in the case of beds and the like; therefore, he says:

"Nor [is there a composite nature] of the composite," meaning that [the composite] exists for the sake of another [self] by virtue of possessing a specific excellence in the form of restricted experience, which is necessitated by the composite.

The meaning is as follows: since "otherness" (paratva)—characterized by being a remainder (śeṣitva)—is possible in the sense of primacy (prādhānya), the rule that [the body] must exist for the sake of another is consistent and logical.

Furthermore, even though "being a composite" (saṃhatatva) is observed in the similar instance (sapakṣa), it is not useful for grasping the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva). This is because, when "being for the sake of another" is the probandum (sādhya) in relation to a composite entity, the reason (hetu) of "being a composite" lacks probative force (aprayojakatva).

He says, "Even those [properties] that are useless for the pervasion (*vyāpti*)," because by the mere observation [of the reason] in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), there would follow the consequence of the invalidity of inference when the probandum (*sādhya*) is inferred in the subject (*pakṣa*) due to the coloring by all properties.

The sense is that if fire were inferred in the subject, the mountain (*parvata*), as being colored by properties such as "belonging to a kitchen" or "being produced by dried cow-dung" which were seen in the similar instance, there would follow the consequence of the invalidity of the inference.
[The term] *dharmamātrasya* means "of the entire property."
"By way of inclusion" means by being included within the scope of the delimitor of pervasion (*vyāpakatāvacchedaka*).
"Inference" refers here to the inference of the probandum (*sādhya*) as colored by that specific form in the subject (*pakṣa*).
"The consequence of the abolition of all inference" means the consequence of the total destruction of the validity of inference as such.

The remainder is clear. Thus, by means of reasoning, it has been established that the "I-notion" (*ahaṃpratyaya*), which is perceptual in nature—as in the thought "I know thus"—has as its object something distinct from the body. Furthermore, since the "I-notion" itself takes the form of the cognition of the body's difference [from other bodies], it was explained that the distinction between selves is also established by perception with respect to the body, which is the sphere of the notion "this."
Even if difference were not clearly manifest, it is impossible for it to exist in the body;
furthermore, because of its dissimilarity to other qualities of that [body], cognition is not a quality thereof. //6//

Since every specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) residing in an effect-substance is preceded by the qualities of its causes, how could the quality of consciousness (caitanya) possibly exist in the body without being preceded by such [prior] qualities?
As for the statement of the Bārhaspatyas: "Earth, water, fire, and air are the principles; from these arises consciousness," [this is untenable].
"Like the intoxicating power [arising] from yeast and so forth";
that is untenable,
because power, being a non-distinct quality, is established in that manner.
In all substances, there exists a common quality called "power" (śakti), which is the counter-correlative of its respective effects;
consciousness is not like this,
because it is admitted to be a quality belonging exclusively to the body.
Because it is an effect and, being established by a uniform type of perception, it possesses the nature of a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*).

Furthermore, it is not untenable that the production of intoxicating power (*madaśakti*) in its own effects—namely, substances—is brought about by atoms which, though themselves non-functional, have acquired the power of intoxication through conjunction with other substances, acting by means of their own qualities.

As for the red dye of betel, however, it is produced by causes consisting of the quality of redness generated through conjunction with another substance following the disjunction of the parts of the previous substance.
For in that case, the quality of redness is indeed perceived in each of the parts individually;
however, the quality of consciousness is neither perceived nor asserted in each of the body's parts individually.
And if that were accepted, since there would be multiple conscious entities within a single body, the relationship of whole and part (between the limbs and the body) would be impossible.
Furthermore, there would be a loss of the conventional practice of recognition,
just as what was seen by Devadatta is not recognized by Yajñadatta and others.
As for the claim that the variegated color on a cloth is not preceded by the qualities of its causes— that is not correct.
For "variegatedness" (*citratā*) is indeed the state of having various forms (*nānārūpatā*).
And since that is produced by threads of various forms, what is there that is untenable?
Although that variegated form does not exist in each individual [thread], it is certainly perceived in the threads when they are combined, as in the cognition: "These threads are variegated."
And these [parts], having come together, possess the quality of being the originators of the cloth;
likewise, this applies to their causes as well, so there is no deviation anywhere.
Nor does the absence of a restriction to a single form imply that the whole (avayavin) is not visible to the eye.
For visual perceptibility is established by the very fact of possessing color (*rūpavattva*), which inheres in the same object as the quality of being large (*mahattva*).
Or, let there be a single specific color called "variegated" (*citra*);
however, it is observed that this is produced by various kinds of colors residing in its causes.
Nor can it be that a specific consciousness is produced in the body as a whole by means of the consciousnesses residing in its parts;
for mere consciousness is impossible in those [parts].
Therefore, consciousness is not a quality of the body.
By this, pleasure and the like are also refuted as being qualities of the body.

Furthermore, consciousness, pleasure, and so forth—which cease even while the body remains firm, provided there is no advent of a contrary quality, like the fragrance of flowers or ointments—cannot be qualities of that [body].
Indeed, its specific qualities such as color and the like do not cease in such a manner.

The qualities of the body belonging to oneself and others are suitable for direct perception and are graspable by the external sense faculties; since knowledge and so forth are not like that, they are not qualities of the body.

Now, even though the distinction between the body and the self is not perceived through direct perception, it will be established by inference that the body is non-self, characterized by insentience; thus he says, "Even though it is not clear.
Alternatively, one might object: "Since parsimony (lāghava) favors it, let the body itself—though it is a composite—be accepted as the self;
let the state of being a composite distinct from the body alone be what is pervaded by being for the sake of another (parārthatva). To this he replies, "Even though it is not clear."
In the first introductory statement, the meaning is: "even though the distinction—that is, the distinction between the self—is not manifest, i.e., not perceptible, in the body.
And in the second, the meaning is: "even though the distinction between the self is not established in the body because it exists for the sake of another.
"Because of its impossibility" (*tadasaṃbhavāt*): impossibility (*asaṃbhava*)—the lack of occurrence—of that [distinction] in that [body] is *tadasaṃbhava*; from that.
Alternatively, the term "in the body" (śarīre) connects with both [the preceding and following clauses] according to the maxim of the central gem (madhyamaṇinyāya).
"Because that is impossible" means because knowledge is impossible.
And in this case, the lack of uniformity between the two uses of the word "that" (tat) is acceptable.
Because in the phrases "in another quality of that" (*tadguṇāntare*) and "in a quality of that" (*tadguṇe*), the word *tat* (that) must refer to the body;

and because the arising of the quality of knowledge in the body is impossible, as well as because of its dissimilarity to other specific qualities of the body, knowledge is not a specific quality of the body—this is the meaning of the verse. //6//
He first establishes the impossibility of knowledge in the body with the words "sarva eva" (all indeed).

[Knowledge] is preceded by the qualities of its cause—that is, it has as its non-inherent cause a quality inherent in that which is co-inherent in the same substratum as itself and belonging to its own genus.
[The phrase] "in the case of its possibility" means...

Since consciousness is absent in the constituent parts of the body, or else— if it were present— since it would follow that there would be multiple conscious beings in a single body, consciousness in the body cannot be preceded by the qualities of its causes.
The point is that because consciousness is a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa), it is impossible for it to exist in the body even without being preceded by the qualities of its causes.
Regarding the word "śakteḥ" (of power):
it is established that power does not have preceding qualities of its cause as its antecedent, because it is a common quality (*sāmānyaguṇa*).
And it is a common quality because it subsists in all substances.

The meaning is as follows: that which is to be inferred by its respective observed effect, whose nature is defined by its respective counter-correlate (pratiyogin), and which exists as a quality called "potency" (*śakti*) acting as the causal agent within every substance—restricted to each specific effect—is understood from the words of the *Purāṇaratna*: "The potencies of all entities are within the scope of inconceivable knowledge. The sense is this: the potency is to be inferred from the various effects perceived; its essential form is determined by its respective correlate; it exists as a quality termed "potency" in every substance as the factor that necessitates action; and it is restricted to each particular effect. Furthermore, this is known from the statement in the *Purāṇaratna* that the potencies of all things are accessible only to the sphere of inconceivable knowledge.
"Not so":
it is not the case that cognition is a general quality;
rather, because it is admitted to exist only in the body, it is a specific quality.
And its true nature is *guṇatva* (the quality-ness) which subsists in a narrower domain than *dravyatva* (substance-ness).
This is according to the method of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). In that established doctrine, *paratva* (priority) and so forth are not distinct qualities.
The intention is that the conventional usage of "priority" (paratva) and so forth is established solely through the addition of the connection with moments (*kṣaṇa*) and the like.
He also states, according to the Vaiśeṣika system, "provided it is an effect" (*kāryatve sati*).
Knowledge is a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa), because, while being an effect, it is the object of a single type of perception, like color and so forth.

The qualification "of a single type" is added to the term "perception" in order to exclude the fallacy [of the probans] in the case of number and other qualities, which are perceptible by two sense organs.
To avoid the fallacy in the case of the conjunction of light with a wall, one must state that [the probans] consists in possessing a genus that is the object of a single type of perception.
There is no fault, because the universal *saṃyogatva* (the nature of conjunction) is perceptible by two sense-faculties.
Since the self (*ātman*) is an object of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), the phrase "provided it is an effect" (*kāryatve sati*) is included to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in that case.
Even so, if the universal *prabhātvam* (the nature of light) is accepted, then in the case of light...

Alternatively, if one accepts that air is perceived through touch, then in order to avoid the fallacy of over-extension (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to air, it must be stated that [the reason] is "because it is a quality belonging to a class perceivable by a single type of perception.
Furthermore, it should be understood that once "being a quality" (*guṇatva*) is included [in the definition], the addition of "while being an effect" (*kāryatve sati*) serves no discernible purpose.

Moreover, the intention is that in the definition of a "specific quality" (*viśeṣaguṇa*), it is impossible to include the clause "distinct from cognition and so forth," provided that cognition and the like are established by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*) to be specific qualities.

Furthermore, regarding the dispute over whether the composite whole is distinct from its parts, it should be considered here that consciousness cannot belong to the body precisely because consciousness is absent in the individual parts.
Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that a specific taste or a specific fragrance, being intoxicating, is what is denoted by the word 'mada' (intoxication)?"

And since that specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) is not preceded by the qualities of its causes, the rule that "the specific quality of an effect-substance is necessarily preceded by the qualities of its causes" is difficult to maintain; to this he says: "Of substances and so forth...

The point is that when substances such as fermenting agents (*kiṇva*) are crushed and so on, there occurs the destruction of everything down to the dyads (*dvyaṇuka*); then, by independent atoms, another substance—wine—is produced through the conjunction of parts possessing intoxication. In that wine-substance, the quality is indeed preceded by the qualities of its causes.
Now, he addresses the lack of invariable concomitance regarding the color of betel-juice with the words "tāmbūle" (in the case of betel). The meaning is clear.
And [he says] "na ca śarīre" (nor in the body).
"It is cognized" means it is perceived;
"it is asserted" means it is established.
Having stated the absence of proof for consciousness in the limbs of the body, he also states the refutation [of that position] with the words "admitting that."
The absence of the relationship between whole and parts—the absence of the relationship of subordinate and principal characterized by the state of being controlled and controller—is the point.
For if the limbs of the body were controlled by a single conscious being, the consistency of worldly activity would be possible.

However, if those very limbs themselves were conscious, then, due to their mutual lack of control and their mutual ignorance of one another's affairs, an inconsistency in worldly activity would necessarily follow; such is the intended meaning.
Regarding "in the case of synthesis" (*pratisandhāne*):
it follows that there would be a collapse of synthesis—such as "what I saw, that I now touch"—as well as the conventional discourse rooted therein;
for, under the view that consciousness resides in the individual parts, the seer and the toucher would be different persons. This is the intended meaning.
By these two stated terms, the occurrence of the undesired and the loss of the desired [consequences] are indicated.
"Possession of manifold forms" (*nānārūpatā*) means being inherent in forms of distinct classes.
Regarding the perception of variegation (*citrapratīti*) when threads of heterogeneous forms are combined, he says: "individually" (*pratyekam*).
"In this way" means: even in its causes— that is, even in the threads which are the causes of the variegated cloth—
there is that same variegated form.
"By the absence of the restriction of a single form" means:
by the absence of a pervadingly existing single form in a variegated cloth, which possesses various forms that do not exist as pervading [the whole]. "In the sense of being one with magnitude" means:

The point is this: since it is possible for the emergent color (*udbhūtarūpa*) qualified by magnitude (*mahattva*) to be the cause of the visual perception of a substance through inherence (*samavāya*) and by way of being in the same locus (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with respect to worldly objects, there is no purpose in including the qualification of "pervasive occurrence" (*vyāpyavṛttitva*) within the scope of the delimiting condition of causality (*hetutāvacchedaka*). Consequently, there is no logical inconsistency in the visual perception of a multicolored cloth.

Even though there is a rule that color must exist as a pervasive property (*vyāpyavṛtti*), he says "Or let it be so. Nor should one suspect that, just as various colors residing in the threads give rise to a variegated color (*citrarūpa*) in the cloth, consciousness (*caitanya*) manifested in the body might arise from unmanifested consciousnesses residing in the parts.
The meaning is as follows: since there is no evidence for consciousness (*caitanya*) as a mere essence (*tanmātra*) or as a universal (*sāmānya*), it cannot exist within the parts of the body;

therefore, the attribution of consciousness to the body's parts presupposes that the body itself possesses consciousness, while the establishment of consciousness in the body depends precisely upon that very attribution—thus there is a circular dependency (*anyonyāśraya*).
"By this [it is meant]"—
the sense is that, just as in the case of cognition, it is impossible for specific qualities (viśeṣaguṇa) such as pleasure and so forth to have the body as their substratum.
Thus, the impossibility of those [qualities] in the body has been explained.
Now, he explains the phrase "because of its difference from other qualities" with the words "api ca" (furthermore).
Without the occurrence of a contrary quality intervening— which would entail the cessation of the previous quality—
the fragrance of flowers and ointments— that is, the fragrance of garlands and sandalwood— [persists].
Indeed, that is not so.
The intended meaning is this: although there is a transformation of form (*rūpa*) through contact with fire, the fact that form persists as long as the substance exists is observed;
however, cognition and the like are not stable in this manner.
Nor should it be said that only each subsequent specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) is the antagonist of each preceding cognition and so forth;
for even if that were so, it would follow that the final [cognition] would persist for a long time.
Thus, it is stated that the fact that cognition and the like do not endure as long as the substance itself constitutes their difference from other specific qualities belonging to the body.
Now, he states another distinction of dissimilarity (vaidharmya) in two ways with the words "of the self" (ātmanaḥ).
It follows that being apprehended by the self alone and being apprehended by the mind alone constitute the dissimilarity of cognition and so forth from other specific qualities of the body.
For qualities such as color (rūpa) and the like, which belong to the body, are apprehended by both oneself and others, and are apprehended by external sense-faculties.
"And knowledge is not [a quality] in that way.

Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): Knowledge is not a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the body, because it does not persist as long as the substance [the body] exists, or because it is perceivable by the mind alone; for whatever is not thus is not thus, like color and so forth (*rūpa*, etc.).
Thus, by proving that knowledge lacks the nature of being a property of the body, the claim that the body is the self (*ātman*) is refuted.
Just as the body is not the self because it is not a knower, like a jar and so forth; furthermore:

because it possesses origination, because it has a specific configuration, because it possesses form and other qualities, and because it is composed of the elements, the body is not the self, like a jar and so forth. (7)
Because it is porous, because it is bodiless, and because it possesses a body—like a dead corpse—the consciousness of the physical frame is to be negated by such valid arguments as these. (8)

Thus, because of this contradiction with direct perception, the negative reasons (*vyatireki-hetu*)— such as "having a sense organ as their locus"— are unable to establish the probandum, as their scope has been removed by the stated proofs which present the probandum through the method of agreement (*anvaya-mukha*). (This concludes the section on the refutation of the doctrine that the body is the self.)
Let it be, then, that the sense-faculties themselves are the self;
yet they do not manifest as "this," in which case [the self] would be like the body.
Nor would those gross [objects] possessing qualities such as manifested color and so forth be excluded from the domain of the letter "ṅ"; for if they were,
it would follow that when the notion of "I" has the sense-faculties as its object— just like the appearance of those [gross objects]— there would be a perception of color-parts and the like.
Furthermore, it is logical that the fruit of your activity—namely, knowledge—should accrue to you, just as the fruits of bathing, Vedic study, and so forth do.
For this very reason, it is said: "of the seer's eye, which is true.
(Thus concludes the section on the prima facie argument for the self being the sense organs.)
That is not so, because it cannot withstand analysis.
For instance: are the sense faculties conscious individually, or do they become so collectively?

If [the self were] distinct for each [sense], there would be no synthesis by one sense of what was seen by another sense; yet such synthesis exists, as in the thought: "That which I saw, that I now touch."
For this very reason, there is no consciousness even when [the senses] are combined;

for it is not the case that a single object is experienced or synthesized by the five sense-faculties acting together. Furthermore, if even one sense-faculty were to perish, it would follow that death would occur.

Furthermore, if consciousness were inherent in the sense organs, then upon the loss of a particular organ, there would be no recollection of the objects of that specific organ. Nor can it be argued that knowledge inheres in the organ because it is the result of its activity;
for even sin and the like, which arise from the activity of weapons and such instruments, inhere in another [the person], not in the instrument itself.
Otherwise, Satyatapas spoke thus after considering the questioner’s impending death and the cruelty inherent in abandoning one who has come for refuge.
(Thus ends the section on the refutation of the doctrine that the senses are the self.
Let it be, then, that the mind alone is conscious.
For if that were the case, the previously mentioned faults would be avoided;
for that [consciousness] is known and asserted to be perceptible by all the sense-faculties,
and its reconnection with another sense-faculty is logically established.
Because the mind, which is the substratum for the connection between perception and subsequent cognition, is a single entity,
recollection is indeed possible even when a particular sense organ has ceased to function, owing to the permanence of the mind.
(Thus ends the section on the prima facie argument that the mind is the Self.
That too is not so; because it is an instrument, like the eye and other senses.
For the mind is postulated precisely as the instrument for the perception of all objects, both external and internal.
Since all objects are not perceived simultaneously, even though the external sense faculties each come into contact with their respective objects,
we understand that there must be some other instrument as well.
Because they lack such assistance, not all [objects] are manifested;
rather, only one is perceived at a time.
Likewise, the cognitions of pleasure and so forth are also possessed of instruments.
Because it is an action, or because it is a cognition, like the cognition of form and so forth.

Thus, since the mind is understood to be an instrument of cognition (*jñāna-karaṇa*), how could it possibly possess agency (*kartṛtva*) in respect to that cognition? For agency is characterized by independence (*svātantrya*);
and that consists in the capacity to procure the necessary instruments conducive to the accomplishment of the goal in accordance with one's own will.

Or rather, its activity proceeds by making another quality inherent within itself the primary factor. However, the state of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) is defined as the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatamatva*), which is invariably restricted to a lack of independence consisting in having an operation that depends upon the direction of another. How then could we admit the connection of these two mutually contradictory properties within a single mind?
Now, if that mind also functions as an agent in acts such as recollection by means of another instrument,
then the dispute is merely over a name;
for he alone who perceives forms and so forth through the eyes and other [senses], and pleasure and so forth through the internal instrument, is the Self.
If the designation "mind" is applied to that very [consciousness], let it be so;
we have nothing lost thereby.
However, in that case, all worldly conventions would be subverted; so, enough of this.
(Thus ends the section on the refutation of the doctrine that the mind is the self.
He asks: what is this so-called "mind"?
But has it not been stated that the internal instrument is a substance?
What, then, is its proof?
Has it not been stated that the non-simultaneity of cognitions is the mark (liṅga) of the mind?

It has indeed been stated; nevertheless, how is the establishment of a distinct entity [the *saṃskāra*] achieved? For even having postulated it, another cause must necessarily be resorted to in order to account for the non-simultaneous arising of memory.
Indeed, there exist in this rememberer latent impressions (*saṃskāras*) produced by the experiences of various objects at different times.
And yet, not all [past objects] are remembered;
rather, only some are remembered at some time.
If it is argued that this is so because of the sequence of the occurrence of causes for the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), [we reply:]...
Even so, it would follow that there is a simultaneity of memories for one whose latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) are to be awakened by mere intention (*praṇidhāna*).
For even when one has withdrawn the mind from all sides through the desire to remember every experienced object and intends them collectively, not all objects enter into memory.
However, if the restriction of memories—whether they be of a pleasant or unpleasant nature—is due to the power of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), [then this difficulty does not arise].

Or, it may be because the self has the nature of sequential cognition; this being so, since external sense organs likewise produce cognitions only when they are respectively in contact with their own objects, the non-simultaneity of cognitions is thus established, rendering a separate [internal] organ unnecessary.

It might be thought: "Since pleasure and so forth, which are occasional and inherent in the self, have external objects, unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), and so on as their efficient causes (*nimitta-kāraṇa*), they must possess an inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*);
and that [inherent cause] is the contact between the self and the mind (*ātma-manaḥ-sannikarṣa*). Thus, the substance of the mind (*manodravya*) is established.
This is incorrect.

Because the knowledge arising from contact with desirable or undesirable objects—which occurs at a time prior to pleasure, pain, and so forth—is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) precisely for that [pleasure or pain] which inheres in the self (*ātman*).
And the non-inherent cause of that [knowledge] is the contact between the sense organ and the object, which itself inheres in the self.

Furthermore, the causal operation of the sense organ, as well as effort and the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), depend upon the contact between the self and the sense organ, which serves as the non-inherent cause.

For effort (*prayatna*), however, the cause is the cognition of what ought to be done (*kartavyatājñāna*) existing in its own preceding moment; and for the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), it is effort itself. Thus, even though the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self—such as cognition, pleasure, pain, desire, and so forth—depend upon non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), it is not logical to postulate another substance [as their substratum].
As for the claim that for a specific quality of an eternal substance, conjunction with another substance is the sole non-inherent cause: [this is rejected].
"The production of color in earth-atoms occurs due to conjunction with fire acting as a non-inherent cause"—
this too is quite gross.
How is it known that color and other qualities arise in earth-atoms from conjunction with fire?

If it is argued that this is because such a thing is observed in the case of an effect-substance (*kāryadravya*), then why is it not observed here as well— that pleasure and so forth arise immediately after the cognition of obtaining the desired or the undesired?
For it is only when there is a deviation from an observed cause that there is occasion for the inference of another cause.
And there is no deviation here;
therefore, among those things that possess the status of well-known causes, that in which the effect inheres is the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa),
while that which is proximate to it is the non-inherent cause (asamavāyi).
It is appropriate to rely on the established principle that whatever else [arises] is caused by that [conjunction];
however, it is not appropriate to rely on its status as a non-inherent cause by accepting a conjunction with another substance that is neither required nor well-established,
because no other cause is perceived.
In the case of color-form (*rūpa*) and so forth, such an admission is made because it follows what is observed;
however, here the opposite has been clearly demonstrated.
Even so, if a conjunction with another substance were to be inferred by the force of pervasion (*vyāpti*), [it would be as follows].

In that case, since it is perceived as being inherent in a substance possessing touch and as being composed of the primary elements (*bhautika*), the inference must conclude with the well-known conjunction with the body and so forth; thus, there is no establishment of a ninth substance.
If it should be argued: "If the mind were composed of the primary elements, it would necessarily be one or another of earth and the rest," [we reply: ...
And that [non-earthiness] is established by other inferences which bring about the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*).
For instance: the mind is not made of earth, because it is a sense organ that serves as the cause for the apprehension of taste, like the tongue;
nor is it made of water.

"Because it is a sense organ (indriya) due to its being the cause for the apprehension of odor, like the nose; likewise, its non-material nature (ataijasa) and so forth can also be determined by its being the cause for the apprehension of objects that are not within the range of those respective [other] sense organs. Thus [it is argued that] the mind is non-physical. This is untenable.

Because it proves the opposite of the specific property of the subject (*dharmiviśeṣaviparītasādhana*), the state of being an organ that causes the apprehension of taste establishes not only non-earthiness but also waterness; likewise, other proofs also bring about the nature of this [specific] element, as if they were intermingling with other elements.
Now, whichever sense organ perceives a particular quality among sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, that very organ is composed of the element possessing that quality.

Alas! In that case, since that [element] is also understood as being distinct from the other elements, its desired distinction is not established merely by its being the means of cognition for that quality.

Moreover, since it is a common means for perceiving qualities such as sound, the mind— like the body— may be composed of the five elements, or consist of one, two, or three, being a mixture of the other elements, as it is stated in scripture:
"For the mind, my dear, consists of food."

That [statement] does not aim to establish that [the mind] has that [water] as its material cause (*prakṛti*), but rather intends merely to demonstrate that its functioning is dependent upon it, just like the statement "breath consists of water" (*āpomayaḥ prāṇaḥ*) and so forth.
For this very reason, the mind continues to persist even in the state of liberation (*apavarga*).

For it has been shown in that very same [text], in the eighth [chapter]: "Beholding these desires with the mind, he rejoices; the mind is his divine eye. Likewise, in the *Mahopaniṣad*: "And he should meditate upon another desire with the mind regarding the supreme deity.
And in the *Purāṇa*: "By the mind alone, the creation of the world [occurs]."
It is said: True, this is so;
it has been stated that resorting to such [a position] is better than postulating a separate substance (*dravyāntara*).
However, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), it is not composed of the primary elements (*bhautika*).
Nor is it a ninth substance. Where, then, does the word "mind" (manas) apply now? It applies to cognition (buddhi) alone.
For this very reason, one is designated as "intelligent" (buddhimān) or "wise" (manasvī);
moreover, the various states of the mind are immediately perceived as direct experience, such as, "My mind is agitated," or "My mind is serene."

And thus, the designation of the mind (*manas*) as an instrument, like those of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), was intended by the predecessors to demonstrate a difference in their functions.
It is said in reply: whether the mind is indeed the intellect, or whether it is a distinct substance;
In either case, it lacks sentience; so what is the use of this investigation into the nature of that which was not even proposed?
(Thus concludes the incidental section on the investigation into the reality of the mind.
Let it be, then, that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) alone is the self (*ātman*).

This being the case, the cognition of the body as possessing a self when it is associated with that [self], and the cognition of it as being devoid of a self when it lacks it, would both be logically established;
furthermore, the soul's departure from the body, its journey to another world, and its transition into another body would be all the more easily accounted for.
This is because the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is to move.

Otherwise, since movement would be impossible for that which is either supremely great or merely great and devoid of touch, the scriptural texts concerning its departure, going, and returning would have to be taken figuratively.
(Thus ends the section on the prima facie view that the self is the vital breath.)
This too is incorrect;
for, precisely because it is air (*vāyu*), consciousness cannot belong to the vital breath (*prāṇa*), just as it does not belong to external air.
Furthermore, even when the self is devoid of mental modifications—as in deep sleep—the vital breath continues to possess activity.
For through its activity, even in one who is asleep, there occurs the digestion of consumed and drunk substances by way of the seven constituent elements (dhātus),
as well as inhalation and exhalation;
for the vital breath (prāṇa) is indeed the internal wind permeated by extremely subtle fire and water.
And that [air], having been exhaled from within the throat, mouth, and nose, and being externally touched by the skin, clearly manifests as non-self (anātman), like a jar or other such objects.
Regarding this very point to be proven, he states further means of proof in the pair of verses beginning with "because it possesses origination" (*utpattimattvāt*).
"Being for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*) means being for the sake of the ear and the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
And that [body] is a composite;
it possesses the nature of being an element (bhūtatva) and the quality of possessing specific qualities perceptible by the external senses.
By these reasons, the state of being distinct from consciousness is to be proven in the body.
By "proper" (nyāyyaiḥ) is meant those endowed with the five forms to be established by the five-membered syllogism beginning with the proposition;
"of the body" (varṣmaṇaḥ) means of the physical frame;
"consciousness" (citiḥ) is knowledge. //7//8//

By this much, the non-selfhood of the body has been established through both perception and inference. He states that those who attempt to prove the selfhood of the body by means of pure negative concomitance (*kevalavyatireki*) are thus sublated.
"By way of positive concomitance" means by means of positive pervasion (*anvayavyāpti*).
"By having the object removed"—that is, by having the probandum sublated; "to establish"—that is, to settle.
Now, he introduces the doctrine that the self consists of the senses with the words, "Let them then be."
He states with the two sentences beginning "And those [objections]" that the refutations mentioned against the position that the body is the self do not apply to this position.
Having stated the absence of subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), he also states the supporting evidence (*sādhaka*) with the words "In this position, in its operation... and so forth.
Knowledge is a property of the sense organ,
because it is the fruit of the operation of the sense organ;
for whatever is the fruit of an operation resides in that [organ] which performs it.

Just as the result of activities such as bathing and Vedic study— namely, purity and the acquisition of a mass of syllables— is inherent in the one who bathes or studies, so too should the application [of the definition] be understood.

The operation of the sense organ (*indriya-vyāpāra*) consists either in the engagement of the sense organ toward the object (*arthendriya-pravṛtti*) for the sake of contact with that object, or simply in the contact itself between the sense organ and the object (*sannikarṣa*).
In the reason, the qualification "being an entity distinct from substance" must be added.

By this, there is no defect even in the case of a staff or similar instruments—which possess an activity conducive to the production or destruction of a jar—even though they lack the property of being a jar.
Having stated the inference regarding the nature of the sense organs, he points out corroborating authoritative testimony as well, saying "for this very reason."
He refutes the selfhood of the sense-faculties with the words "that is not so.

"Inability to withstand conceptual analysis" means that for a subject of conceptualization, even its nature—which is connected to any one of the various possible alternatives among all the conceivable alternatives—is such that it does not deserve [to be] its true form;
in other words, it lacks the capacity to withstand scrutiny.

The underlying intention is that even in the absence of contradiction by perception (*pratyakṣabādhā*), there is contradiction by reasoning (*yauktikabādha*) regarding the view that the self consists of the sense organs.

Having kept in mind the objection that, under the theory that each sense organ is conscious, a single body— like a village with multiple owners— would result in constant strife due to being presided over by multiple conscious entities, he states another refutation beginning with "indriyāntare."

This [objection] applies equally even to the position that the self is a collection of the sense faculties. Thus he says: "For this very reason"—that is, precisely because the aforementioned synthesis (pratisandhāna) is impossible.
He establishes that very point with the words "for not," meaning that the aggregate of the sense faculties is neither the experiencer nor the rememberer.

For instance: if "aggregate" (saṅghāta) means either conjunction (saṃyoga) or the number "plurality" (bahutvasaṅkhyā), then, precisely because it is a quality (guṇatvāt), the possibility of being a knower is not established.
If, on the other hand, the intended meaning is that an aggregate consists of many things that are conjoined, [then the same fault applies].
Even then, it is not the case that many sense organs possess the status of being the locus of vision or the locus of touch.
And thus, because the seer and the toucher would be distinct from one another, the aforementioned recognition would simply be impossible; this is the intended meaning.
He states the further fault in [the theory of] the aggregate of the senses being the self with the words "if there were only one sense organ" (*ekendriye*).
The point is that because the aggregate would perish by that very fact, it follows that the body—being devoid of a self—would undergo death.
He states another defect common to both positions regarding the individual and the aggregate in the verse beginning with "indriye":
if the eye, which is the seer, were to perish, the recollection "this was seen by me" would be untenable.
The meaning is that there is no perception of what is present [by the sense organ],
because it is impossible for one person to remember what was perceived by another; this is the case if the sense organs were sentient.
The subverting arguments have been stated.
Now, he refutes the inference that establishes [the existence of God] with the words "And not in its operation...
The word "etcetera" (ādi) in the phrase "from sin and so forth" (pāpādeḥ) should be understood as including "bifurcation" (dvaidhībhāva) as well.
The meaning is that there is no deviation [from the rule] because the weapon is not inherent in either the cutter or the object to be cut.
Furthermore, it should be understood that the reason is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*) because there is an absence of a subverting argument (*bādhaka*) against the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

Now, he states "otherwise" (*anyathā ca*) to show that the statement of Satyatapas is intended for something else—being applied to the instrument with a metaphorical attribution of agency—and is therefore not a proof for the sentience of the senses.

The speech of Satyatapas—consisting of questions and answers given by him to a hunter who had entered the forest within his hermitage while searching for deer—begins with: "That which sees has no tongue," and so forth.
Regarding this matter, a verse was composed by my venerable teacher: "She who sees does not speak; she who speaks does not see.
O hunter, how can the eye speak? Or how can speech look?"
Thus,
by this it is understood that the questioner is a hunter (*vyādha*). For if he had not spoken, there would have been the consequence of the hunter’s death due to being tormented by hunger.
It should be understood that the Great Sage spoke these words after reflecting upon the great sin incurred by abandoning one who has sought refuge.
Now, he introduces the position that the mind (*manas*) is the self (*ātman*), saying: "Let it be so, then."

The meaning is: "That indeed" [refers to the mind], for it is understood through valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) that the mind is primary and the impeller of all the sense-faculties, and it is likewise designated as such in conventional usage.

He states with the two sentences beginning "And it is possible" that the faults mentioned in the position that the sense-faculties are the self—namely, the impossibility of memory and recollection, the consequence of there being no single self, and so forth—do not apply to this present position.
He refutes the view that the mind is the self with the words "That too is not [the case]," because of its being an instrument;
since the mind is an instrument in every act of cognition, its status as an agent or a substratum is not possible therein.
For the mind is not an object of direct perception;
rather, it is inferred as a specific instrument for all cognitions by means of the mark that cognitions do not arise simultaneously.
And the sense is that its status as a knower is not possible, unlike that of the eye and other [senses].
He establishes this very point with the words "in the external sense-faculties" (*bāhyendriyeṣu*).
"Due to the absence of assistance" (*sāhāyakavirahāt*) means due to the absence of cooperation (*sahakāravirahāt*).
(The term *sāhāyaka* refers to the action of an assistant.)
The meaning is: "due to the absence of contact with that [object]"; the phrase "of the sense organ that grasps each respective object" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Thus, by the mark of the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions regarding external objects, [it is established] that [the soul] is atomic, acting as a co-operative cause for all the sense organs.

Having stated the inference for the mind as a specific instrument, he now states the inference for the mind also as an instrument in the direct perception of internal pleasure and so forth, with the words "likewise, pleasure, etc. [tathā sukhādi].
