Now, one might object: let the mind, which has already been inferred as an instrument, also be the agent in cognition and so forth, on the grounds of parsimony (lāghava).
If this is argued, he says "In that case, thus" (*tadevam*).
The agency of an instrument is not possible;
the point is that there is a contradiction between being an instrument and being an agent, characterized respectively by dependence and independence.
He elucidates the distinction between the essential natures of agency (*kartṛtva*) and instrumentality (*karaṇatva*) with the words beginning "svātantrya" (independence).

Agency is the capacity to assemble the collection of means conducive to the accomplishment of an end solely by one's own will, which is governed by independence consisting in the state of having one's own activity dependent upon one's own desire.

Instrumentality, on the other hand, is characterized by being a preeminent auxiliary in the production of an action desired by another; it is governed by dependence (*pāratantrya*), defined as the state of having one's own operation dependent upon the will and effort of another.
The meaning is that the coexistence of these two [agency and instrumentality] in one and the same thing is not possible.
Even if it were possible for a conscious entity to possess both agency and instrumentality in one instance due to a difference in form,

nevertheless, because there is a lack of firm evidence for the consciousness of the mind, and because it is established by worldly consensus and logical pervasion (*vyāpti*) as being merely the instrument for another conscious being’s experience of pleasure and so forth— just like the eyes and other senses— it is not [the case that the mind is the agent].
The state of being a knower.
In reality, however, with respect to objects that are entirely beyond the senses, the scripture alone is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Therefore, the underlying intention is that the mind is established as merely an instrument for the living self (*jīva*), which consists of consciousness.
One might object: "In the experience of external and internal objects such as form and pleasure, the mind alone is the agent;
however, for the experience of internal pleasure and so forth, another internal instrument must be postulated. To this, he replies: "If that were so... and so on.

This being so, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in our desired position that the knower is a distinct modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). The point is that the designation is merely optional, and thus there is no dispute regarding the underlying reality.
With the words "But... [the author] states the contradiction in common usage that would arise if the Self, the knower, were designated as the mind (*manas*).
The term "mind" (*manas*) is not used by worldly people or Vedic scholars to refer to the Self (*ātman*).
Therefore, the sense is that the designation "mind" applied to the Self is meaningless because it contradicts common usage.
Now, here the Supreme Teacher, adopting the role of an investigator, begins an incidental inquiry into the true nature of the mind, saying: "He says... (*āha*).
"Someone reflects," and so forth.
This reflection is intended to demonstrate that the arguments favored by logicians for proving the existence of the mind lack the capacity to withstand scrutiny.
"What is this? [he asks].
"What is it? is a question regarding its essential nature (*svarūpa*). "What, moreover, is the means of knowledge? is a question regarding the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
By the words beginning with "it has been said, 'the name... and so forth, he raises the issue of the means of knowledge with respect to the mind.
The meaning is that an internal instrument (antaḥkaraṇa) as a distinct substance is not established by the mark of the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions;
for the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions is possible simply through the absence of auxiliary factors such as unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa).

He says this because even if an internal instrument were accepted, one must necessarily resort to the absence of the auxiliary factor of unseen merit/demerit in order to account for the non-arising of simultaneous recollections.
"Even having constructed" means:
cultivated by the experience of various objects—that is, produced by the experience of various objects.
"In the formative predispositions" (saṃskāra) means:
The cause for the manifestation of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is the awakener (*udbodhaka*).
Due to the sequential occurrence of the awakening of latent impressions, there is no simultaneity of memories;
for it is only when a latent impression has been awakened that it serves as the cause of memory.
The meaning is that this is because the awakening [of the latent impressions] occurs sequentially.
"Even so" refers to *praṇidhāna*, which is the mental reflection through focused attention.

The point is this: even when a common activating cause (udbodhaka) in the form of a mental resolve (praṇidhāna) has been made with the desire to remember all the objects experienced, the memories of all those objects do not arise simultaneously;
even though the various causes for remembering multiple objects are present, there is no simultaneity of memory precisely because of the absence of the assistance of unseen merit/demerit (adṛṣṭa).
Rather, it must be accepted that, due to the assistance of adṛṣṭa, the memory of only one object occurs at a time.
"By way of being auspicious or inauspicious" means by way of producing pleasure or pain.

If it is argued that even so, there would be simultaneous recollections of objects that are causes of pleasure due to the power of auspicious unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), he says "in succession" (*krama*) in response.

This is because of the nature of the self, characterized by its possession of successive cognitions, and due to the absence of the auxiliary cause of unseen merit; thus, there is no simultaneity of recollection.

The collective intention is that since it is possible to resolve even the simultaneity of the cognition of external objects, one need not postulate an internal, atomic mental organ (*manas*) as a separate instrument acting in conjunction with the external sense faculties. He introduces another argument regarding the existence of the mind with the words, "It might be thought."
The formal argument here is as follows: pleasure and the like have a non-inherent cause (asamavāyikāraṇa), because they are effects that are positive entities, just like the color-form of an effect.
And the non-inherent cause in the case of pleasure and so forth is precisely the conjunction of the self and the mind, since no other [cause] is possible; this is the essential point.

The two words ending in the genitive case—“of the self” (*ātmanaḥ*) and so forth, and “of the external” (*bāhyasya*) and so forth—are in a *bahuvrīhi* compound and serve as qualifiers for pleasure (*sukha*) and the rest.

By means of these two pairs of words, it is stated that the self is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of pleasure and so forth, while the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) and other factors are the instrumental causes (*nimittahetu*).
He refutes this with the passage beginning “that is not so” (*tadasat*) and so forth.
Regarding "in pleasure":

since it is the cognition itself—whether of a favorable or unfavorable object—that invariably precedes [the experience] within the self, it is logical that this cognition, as the cause of both pleasure and pain, serves as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) therein;
but not the contact between the self and the mind, which is unestablished [as such a cause].
Furthermore, the contact between the self and the sense organ that is in proximity to each respective object is the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for each respective cognition.
Similarly, the knowledge that something is achievable through effort is the cause for volition (*prayatna*) by way of the desire to act (*cikīrṣā*).
And in the case of the knowledge of what is to be done (*kāryatājñāna*), which takes the form of memory, the cause is the awakened latent impression (*udbuddhasaṃskāra*).
In the case of experience, the cognition of the inferential mark (liṅga) and so forth are likewise [non-inherent causes];
in the case of the mental impression (saṃskāra), experience is likewise [a non-inherent cause];
and in the case of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa), effort alone is its non-inherent cause.
This is an illustration:
with respect to desire, the cognition of something as belonging to a desired class or as a means to a desired end is likewise [the cause].
The cognition of something as undesirable or the cognition of it being a means to that [undesirable end] functions similarly with respect to aversion (*dveṣa*).
The author’s underlying intention is that the common claim—that the specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of the self never serve as non-inherent causes (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) anywhere—is not to be trusted.
By the phrase "of desire and so forth" (*icchādīnām*), the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes aversion, effort, unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and mental impressions (*saṃskāra*).

In this context, the mention of the operation of the sense organs—which is the cause for the contact between the object and the sense organ—as having its non-inherent cause (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*) in the conjunction of the self with that which possesses effort, is made by way of incidental discussion (*prasaṅgāt*).
The underlying intention (*hārdam*) is that in no instance—such as cognition or other specific qualities (*viśeṣa-guṇa*) of the self—is there a dependence upon the mind (*manas*).
He raises a doubt regarding another means of proof concerning the mind, beginning with the words "But [it is argued] that in the case of the eternal... (*yattu nitye ti*).

The formal argument (*prayoga*) here is as follows: pleasure and so forth have conjunction with a substance as their non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), because, while being effects, they are specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*) of eternal substances, like the color produced by baking (*pākaja*) in an atom.

The point is that since conjunction with another substance cannot possibly be the non-inherent cause of pleasure and so forth, it remains as a logical residue (*pariśeṣa*) that conjunction with the mind (*manas*) alone must be so; thus, the existence of the mind is established.
He refutes this with the words "that too" (*tadapi*).
"Sthevīyaḥ" means "more gross," that is to say, spoken without due reflection.

This is the intended meaning: for it is only through the observation of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka-sahacāra*) that the determination of causality is established in all cases.

In cases such as the color of an earthen atom, the causality of contact with fire is also postulated solely in accordance with what is observed, since the transformation of color and other qualities in the parts of a body is seen to result from it.
Furthermore, in this context, it is observed that agreeable cognition and the like alone are the causes of pleasure and so forth.

Since these reside in close proximity to the self, which is the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), it is logical that they themselves serve as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*); therefore, there is no occasion to postulate the contact of some other unseen substance as being so.
Regarding the phrase "when the cause is perceived":
for only when one observes the production of an effect even in the absence of a perceived cause is there occasion to postulate another cause;
however, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra) from the perceived cause—this is the meaning.
Regarding the word "therefore":

it is precisely among the observed causes that [causal categories] such as inherent causality (*samavāyi-hetutva*) are to be established, by virtue of their connection with their respective characteristics.

However, if one were to postulate the causality of a conjunction with a distinct substance—which is different from the observed causes such as cognition, which is unnecessary, and which is unestablished—then there would be both the abandonment of what is already established and the conceptualization of what is not established.

The point is that since no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*) has been perceived against knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth being non-inherent causes (*asamavāyi-kāraṇa*), it is pointless to include the condition of "being distinct from those" in the definition of a non-inherent cause. As for the phrase "in this case":

in the case of pleasure (*sukha*) and so forth, however, the opposite is true; that is to say, he has demonstrated the disparity by means of an example consisting in the perception of other [distinct] causes.
By this much, it has been stated that the previously mentioned inference suffers from the fallacies of being non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*) and having an unestablished pervasion (*avyāpyatvāsiddhi*).
Furthermore, he states "even so" (*evamapi*) to show that if pervasion is admitted, there would be the fallacy of proving something irrelevant (*arthāntara*). [He asks] "then what? (*sa tarhi*).
The logical connection is as follows: "In that case, it [is so].

In the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), that conjunction with another substance is observed to be material—that is, originated from the elements (*bhūtārabdha*) and having a material entity as its counter-correlate (*pratiyogika*). Therefore, in the case at hand (*prakṛta*) as well, the conclusion of the inference must be a conjunction whose counter-correlate is the material body and so forth, and whose substratum (*anuyogin*) is the self. Consequently, there is no hope of establishing the mind (*manas*) as a ninth substance that is non-material (*abhautika*), as postulated by the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas). This is the meaning.
The phrase "inhering in a substance possessing touch" is stated with the intention of providing an illustration.
Based on observed experience, it is inferred that conjunction with another substance is a cause only for an effect that is a specific quality of an eternal substance possessing touch;
it is not the case, as indicated by this, that it is a cause for a specific quality of an eternal substance lacking touch.

Thus, it has been stated that the proof of a conjunction with another substance as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*) for pleasure and so forth is not possible. Now, even if one were to accept that proof, he elaborates on how the intended mind (*manas*)—which is non-material and a distinct principle (*tattvāntara*)—will still not be established. Regarding this, the doubt is introduced with the words "Now, if it is argued... (*athocyeta*).
Pratyāsiddha means pratiṣiddha;
pāthasīya means jalīya;
śakyādhyavasāna means śakyaniścaya.
The mind is not composed of earth, nor of fire and so forth, because it is a sense organ whose function is the apprehension of taste, like the tongue.
The mind is not composed of water, because it is a sense organ that perceives odor, like the nose; thus is its elemental nature refuted.
Since its atomicity is established by the mark of the non-simultaneous arising of cognitions, it cannot be included among all-pervading substances.
Therefore, there is the misconception that the mind is established as a ninth substance;
he refutes this with the words "that is untenable," etc.,
[stating] "the locus" (dharmin).

The meaning is that because the stated reasons establish the opposite of that specific quality— namely, the non-material nature (*abhautikatva*)— which is intended as a property of the mind (*manas*), they are fallacious.

The intention is that [the reasons] would prove for the mind the state of being an organ that perceives taste (and thus being composed of water), or the state of being an organ that perceives smell (and thus being composed of earth), and so forth.
Here he raises an objection: "Now, regarding sound," etc. Among [the objects] such as form and so forth, the fact of grasping odor alone is the proof for being composed of earth;
likewise, the fact of grasping taste alone and so forth is the proof for being composed of water and so forth.

And thus, the meaning is that the reason proving the earthiness and so forth of the mind (*manas*) is unestablished (*asiddhi*). To this, the reply is: "Alas, then!"—namely, that whatever sense organ perceives only the qualities of a particular element is itself recognized as being distinct from the other elements.
The meaning is that the mind’s capacity to perceive the qualities of various elements does not, by itself, establish the distinctness of the mind from those respective elements.
Rather, it is the mind’s incapacity to perceive smell and other such qualities that proves it is not composed of earth and the other elements.
The point is that this [incapacity] is unestablished (asiddha) in the subject (pakṣa) of the inference for the non-elemental nature of the mind.

It has also been stated that in the inference [of the mind] being non-terrestrial (*apārthivatva*), "the non-apprehension of the respective qualities of those elements" is a limiting condition (*upādhi*).

Having thus refuted the inference of the mind's non-material nature (*abhautikatva*), he presents the inference of its material nature (*bhautikatva*) with the words: "Moreover, sound, etc."—the mind is composed of the five elements (*pāñcabhautika*), because it is the means for the apprehension of the qualities of the five elements, like the body.
The formulation is "it speaks" (*vadati*).

Because there would be the fault of excessive complexity (*gaurava*) if [the body] were composed of all five elements, and out of fear of a confusion of categories (*jāti-sāṅkarya*), he states another position: "one or two," etc.

The sense is that, just as the body consists of a single element, it is possible for the qualities of other elements to be perceived because it is supported by those other elements; thus, the mind [perceives them].

He cites scripture (*śruti*) in the form of a corroborative statement regarding its being composed of earth (*pārthivatva*), saying "for it consists of food" (*annamayaṃ hi*). He raises the objection that the scripture has another intended meaning (*ānyaparya*), beginning with "that is not so" (*tan na*). This is indicated by the words "but surely" (*nanu*) and so forth.
That is the statement from the Nirukta and the Śruti.
Regarding the phrase "dependent on that":

it is taught in the Śruti that the mind is "consisting of food" (*annamaya*)—characterized by being nourished by the essence of food—because only a mind sustained by the essence of food is capable of functions such as volition (*saṅkalpa*).

The sense is that, just as the specific vital air (prāṇa) consists of water, it is because it is nourished by the essence of water. He also states a presumptive argument (*arthāpatti*) from scripture regarding the non-material nature of the mind: "For this very reason," etc.
If the mind were material, [the following would occur].
"In that case, it would not persist in liberation, just like the body and so forth. To show that the mind does indeed persist in liberation, he cites scripture on that very point:
"In the eighth chapter of the Chāndogya Upaniṣad itself."
Regarding the phrase "consisting of food" (*annamayaṃ hi*), however, in the sixth [chapter],

after having stated the mind's union with the liberated one, he cites the authoritative evidence for the Lord (*īśvara*)— who is by nature eternally liberated— as well, with the words "likewise" (*tathā*).
This is found in the *Śrīvaiṣṇava Purāṇa*, in the fifth section (*aṃśa*).
He refutes the objection stated by the words "tat na" and so forth by partially accepting it, saying "it is said" (ucyate).
"It is true" (satyam) expresses partial acceptance;
it is an admission that the scripture has another intended meaning (ānyaparya).
There is no acceptance of the mind as a distinct ontological principle;
or rather, there is the adoption [of the view] that it is material (bhautika).
The word "or" (vā) indicates a lack of firm adherence [to either position].
For this very reason, he reveals his own intention by means of the passage beginning with "but in reality, regarding the mind" (*paramārthatastu... manoviṣaye*).
"In the intellect alone" (*buddhāveva*) means that the word "mind" (*manas*) functions as a denoter specifically for the intellect.
The expression "possessing a mind" (*samanaska*) is used for both the liberated soul (*mukta*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) precisely because they possess intelligence (*buddhimattva*).
The statement that these two are "without a mind" (*amanaska*), however, intends to negate the fluctuations of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*) produced by karma; this is the underlying sense.

Having explained the worldly convention regarding the mind being identical to the intellect, he now demonstrates worldly perception (*laukikapratyakṣa*) itself with the words "of the mind" (*manasaḥ*).

The meaning is that [the statement] "the mind is serene," and so forth, can only be possible as an object for a perceptual cognition (*pratyakṣabuddhi*), and not as an object for a supersensible mind (*atīndriyamanaḥ*).
By the word "cognition" (*buddhi*), knowledge (*jñāna*) is intended.
One might object: "If the mind (*manas*) is indeed the cognition (*buddhi*), how can its designation as an internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) be consistent? To this he replies: "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).

The point is that even in the theory that the mind is distinct [from cognition], the designation of cognition as an internal organ is for the purpose of demonstrating its possession of activity that serves as the cause of recollection of objects and so forth;

whereas the designation of it as "cognition" and so on is for the purpose of demonstrating its possession of activity that serves as the cause of determination (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth. Thus, the intention is that both designations are justified by their respective functions.

In this regard, the inference of the mind as the instrument for the direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) of pleasure and so forth, as accepted by the logicians (*tārkika*), has not been examined by the investigator.

This is the underlying intention here: since pleasure and pain consist merely in the excellence or impairment of the sense organs, and because these two are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), the mind cannot be inferred as their cause of direct perception.
Alternatively, since those two are of the nature of specific cognitions, their manifestation is established simply through the self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) of cognition itself.

When the investigator has refuted the existence of an additional mind by means of [arguments such as] "it exists," etc., the proponent reveals his own intention with the words "It is said," and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "not having been proposed":
it is precisely the non-selfhood of the mind that has been proposed—that is, it is the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*).
The intention is that since an investigation into the true nature of the mind (*manas*) is not the present subject, we shall not now proceed to establish a mind as a distinct entity.
Or, let it be that for the liberated and for the Lord (*īśvara*), the mind is indeed of the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*).
However, for the bound (*baddha*), the mind must necessarily be accepted as the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) derived from egoism (*ahaṅkārika*), on the strength of scriptural authority.
Furthermore, it is worthy of being accepted as the instrument of mindfulness and so forth;
however, the core intention is that its sentience cannot be established.
He introduces the doctrine that the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the self with the words, "Let it be so, then.

The intention is that because the conventional usage [occurs] such that one is said to "live" when the body possesses the vital breath, and "is dead" when devoid of it, the vital breath itself is the "living being" (*jīva*) due to its being the agent of living.
"Otherwise" means:
[the cognition] of that which is supremely great and that which is not great.
This is the word-division (*padaccheda*).
"Non-greatness" means minuteness (*aṇutva*).
The sense is that, because the self is devoid of tangibility (*niḥsparśatva*), neither action nor omnipresence is possible for it, whether it be minute or [otherwise].
Or one rejects this argument, saying, "This too is incorrect.

In this regard, there are three formal arguments (prayoga): the vital breath (prāṇa) is not the self, because it possesses activity during deep sleep, which is a property contrary to that of the self.
The vital breath (prāṇa) is not the self,
because it is perceivable by tactile perception, like a jar or similar objects;
the vital breath is not the self, because it is air, like the wind from a fan.
"By its function":

the function of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is the cause for the digestion of food and drink that have been consumed. As it is said: "Becoming the Vaiśvānara fire, I abide within the bodies of living beings;
joined with the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, I digest the fourfold food."
Thus it is established by the Gītā-smṛti.
Regarding the term *tanutara*:
the meaning is that it is a specific kind of wind located within the stomach, supported by very small portions of earth, water, and fire.

Moreover, since the doctrine that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the self has already been refuted by the method used to negate consciousness residing in the body, no separate refutation need be applied to it. (9)

Since this self lacks omnipresence and is devoid of touch, its departure, movement, and so forth—though occurring in accordance with the impulsion of effort and unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*)—are possible just as they are for the mind. Therefore, the descriptions of these [movements] do not have a non-literal meaning;
this will also be established in the determination of its size, so let us leave it at that for now.
(Thus ends the section on the refutation of the doctrine that the vital breath is the self.)
Let it be, then, that consciousness alone is the Self, because of its non-inertness.
For non-Selfhood is observed in things such as jars, which are invariably connected with inertness;
and since inertness is absent from consciousness, it also excludes non-Selfhood.
Furthermore, consciousness is non-inert because it manifests by its very existence;
for consciousness, while existing, does not remain unmanifest like a jar or other objects,
such that its establishment would have to depend on something else.
(Thus is the presentation of the position that consciousness is the self.
It might be thought: even when consciousness has arisen, only the object manifests;
for indeed, while cognizing "this is blue," we do not at that very moment perceive a consciousness that is itself non-blue or of a non-"this" nature.
Therefore, by consciousness itself—which exists as its own essential nature—the object is manifested, just as an object is manifested through the contact of the senses.

Consequently, by observing a subsequent adventitious excellence of manifestation residing within that [object], consciousness will be inferred later on. (Thus, by the position that consciousness is inferable, its non-inertness is established.)
That is not so; for even when scrutinized with great care, no illumination as a property of the object distinct from cognition is perceived, just like [the object's] color and other qualities.
Furthermore, since all worldly transactions are established by means of consciousness alone—which is accepted by both parties—the postulation of such [an objective illumination] is untenable.
Moreover, if one were to accept an awareness of an object that is devoid of the appearance of either the awareness itself or the knower, then [one would have to say]: "This is a jar,"...
However, there might occasionally be an appearance such as "I do not know whether [it exists] or not," or "it is not known";
yet this is not the case.
In the grasping of past and future objects and in their recollection, even if verbal expression and conventional usage are absent— or even if they are present—
the object (as a manifestation) is not inferential, because its state of being known is already perceived prior to them.
Success [is not established], much less the establishment of a cognition preceded by that [success] in that case.

For instance, one who is prompted by someone else, having applied his attention and recollected, immediately replies, "I have remembered it today. And this very utterance is not the inferential mark (*liṅga*) for that [recollection].
Because it would be preceded by that [very cognition], and because it would result in the fallacy of mutual dependence (anyonyāśraya),
what shameless person indeed would assert the inference of one's own cognition based on one's own verbal expression?
(Thus ends the refutation of the view that consciousness is inferable.

Furthermore: whatever linguistic usage or distinction of properties occurs in one thing due to its relation with another, when that [usage or distinction] is perceived in the former, it is caused by the very nature of that [former thing].
But it is not based on a relation with that [universal],

as for instance the linguistic usage of "existent" regarding earth and so forth arises from their relation with existence (*sattā*), and the quality of being visible arises from the relation with color (*rūpa*) in both existence and color.

Thus, the conventional usage that "the jar and so forth shine" occurs because they proceed from a connection with consciousness; or rather, the property of being manifest is observed in consciousness itself, yet it does not depend on a connection with [an external] consciousness, but is instead necessitated by its own nature. Therefore, because it is self-luminous, consciousness alone is the Self.
Furthermore, even for one who accepts a knower distinct from consciousness—
He certainly accepts consciousness itself;
for it is not tenable that one "cognizes" when consciousness itself is non-existent.
If this is so, then let that very [consciousness], being admitted by both disputants, be the cognizer—this is preferable.
What is the use of postulating anything else? (Thus is established that consciousness is self-luminous and of the nature of the Self.
But surely, in the cognition "I know," this Self is perceived as the substratum of that knowledge, distinct from the knowledge itself.
True; however, it cannot be maintained that [the object] is directly perceived as a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*),

because [the object] is apprehended as a distinct entity by taking the cognition of difference for granted, and because of the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*) which is non-deviant [in this case],
and because it is impossible for that which is not of the nature of luminosity to be luminous due to a contradiction in its own nature (*svabhāva-virodha*).

Furthermore, by the argument beginning with "and because its nature is luminosity, it is consciousness," the very reality of the "I" aspect, which is of the nature of light, is difficult to establish.
This same method applies even when the conceptualization of an object of cognition (*grāhya*) is refuted.

Therefore, it is consciousness alone that is ultimately real—self-luminous and manifesting the superimposed, unreal conceptualizations of subject and object through the power of the immediately preceding condition known as *vāsanā* and by force of beginningless ignorance.
The manifest and the hidden Buddhists maintain that this very [consciousness] is the self.

As the manifest ones have said: "Though the nature of consciousness is undivided, it appears as if possessed of the distinction between the apprehended object, the apprehending subject, and self-awareness, to those whose vision is distorted."
Or as the *Pracchannas* state: "Pure reality is not the cause of the manifold world (*prapañca*), because it is never ceased;
therefore, Māyā alone is the mother of the distinction between the knower and the known."
(Thus ends the section on the prima facie argument that consciousness is the self.
Here, an objection is raised: consciousness appears as momentary and distinct for each respective object;
if that very [consciousness] were the self, [then the self would likewise be momentary and manifold].
How could one recognize [an object] by thinking, "I saw this yesterday, and today I see it"?

Nor can this be resolved here merely as a difference in appearances lacking an objective basis (*nirālambana*), because the thesis that [cognition] lacks an objective basis has its subject matter contradicted by all forms of perception and other means of valid cognition.

Furthermore, if the means of proof (*sādhana*) were to have an objective referent (*sālambanatva*), then because it would be no different from that [referent], it would follow that all cognitions (*śemuṣī*) are likewise [without an objective basis].

On the other hand, if it were without an objective referent (*nirālambanatva*), the probandum (*sādhya*) could not be established precisely because the means of proof itself would be non-existent. Moreover, the refutation of the absence of an objective referent has been elaborated upon in both the earlier and later portions of the Mīmāṃsā.
And because it is established that [the scripture] is a treatise (*śāstra*) by virtue of its explaining things as they truly are, it is not described [otherwise].
For this very reason, the demonstration of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) by resorting to a continuum (*santāna*) is not more tenable;

for if one were to accept a continuum that is distinct from the momentary cognitions (*vijñānakṣaṇa*), that is stable and performs synthesis, there would be an abandonment of one's own tenet (*svasiddhānta*).
And there is the acceptance of the opponent's established doctrine;
for if it were not accepted, recognition would be impossible,
since it is not possible for one person to reconnect with what has been experienced by another.

Furthermore, it is not tenable that there is an error of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) regarding the cognizer due to the non-apprehension of difference caused by extreme similarity, as in the case of a lamp and the like.

For in that case, a single person perceives both earlier and later manifestations; because the manifestations have identical configurations, he fails to perceive their difference, and thus such an illusion occurs.

However, according to the Sugata’s doctrine, the manifestations of consciousness are mutually unaware of one another and perish without leaving a trace (*niranvaya-vināśin*). Therefore, it is impossible for them to serve either as the substratum or as the object of an illusion of unity.

Furthermore, even if there is perfect similarity, one person is not able to connect an action performed by another as being "done by oneself"; therefore, one must accept a conscious entity that persists through moments of recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*), which rests upon a continuum of cognitions (*saṃvit-santāna*) characterized by appearance and disappearance.
(This concludes the section refuting the doctrine of momentary consciousness as the self.
Someone says: "Cognition is not impermanent."
Because antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the rest are not established; and their non-establishment is due to that [consciousness] being self-established (*svataḥsiddha*),
for antecedent non-existence and the rest cannot belong to that which is self-established, whether by itself or through another.
They are established;
for that which makes its own nature understood must establish it as either existent or non-existent.
If it were existent, there would be no absence at all—how then could it establish [itself]?
Since the means of proof itself is non-existent, it is all the more incapable of being a means of proof in any other alternative; thus, its establishment cannot occur through itself.
Nor can it occur through another, because experience does not have anything else as its object.
Furthermore, if it were something to be experienced, it would follow that it is not an experience itself, like a jar or other objects;
therefore, it is not born.
Precisely because of the absence of birth, the other modifications of existence (*bhāvavikāra*) must also be rejected.
Because they are dependent upon that [consciousness],
multiplicity is likewise refuted in consciousness;
for when the pervader (the state of having an origin) is excluded, the exclusion of its pervaded (multiplicity) is established.
For there is no unborn thing that can be divided;
and because it is an object of cognition (*cetyatva*), difference, mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*), and so forth are not its properties, unlike color and other such qualities.
Therefore, this [consciousness] has no property whatsoever that is an object of measurement (*meyadharma*).

Therefore, consciousness alone—shining as the attributeless, single-flavored essence in which all conceptualizations of duality have been shaken off—is the Self and the Supreme Self; it is eternally immutable.
As it has been said: "That experience which is unborn, unmeasured, and infinite is the Self.
And this very consciousness is the ultimate ground of the purport of the Vedānta texts.
Their formulation is as follows;

as the author of that Vārttika has said: "That very consciousness which is accepted as the fruit with regard to objects of knowledge other than the Supreme (parāg), that same consciousness is here the object of knowledge, according to the authority of the statements of the Vedānta."

"Furthermore, if one were to imagine a meaning other than this [liberation], the consequence would be that the Vedāntas lack authority; therefore, one should not imagine any other meaning for them. Thus it is said.
(Thus ends the section establishing the doctrine that the Self is non-distinct, eternal consciousness.
The knowers of the Self declare that this view is both unworldly and non-Vedic.

For instance, consciousness (*saṃvit*)—which is synonymous with terms such as knowledge (*jñāna*), comprehension (*avagati*), and experience (*anubhūti*)—is an attribute of the conscious Self, the cognizer; it is transitive (having an object), and its nature is to manifest something to its own substrate by its very existence.
It is well-known;
for in this very way, this experience—“I am conscious of this”—is established within each individual among all living beings.
Its arising, persistence, and cessation manifest as directly perceptible, just like those of pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Furthermore, its existence during states such as sleep, intoxication, and fainting cannot be accepted, as it is refuted by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible;
for if consciousness were present even in those states, it would be recollected at the time of awakening.
Nor is it [the object] recollected; for this very reason, upon waking, one reflects: "For such a length of time, I was not aware of anything at all.

Even though there is no rule that everything experienced must be remembered, and even though there is an absence of powerful causes—such as death—that would interrupt the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), this constant non-remembrance establishes nothing other than the absence of experience itself.

Nor does the non-arising of its memory follow from the absence of the delimitation by an object or from the disappearance of the sphere of the *ahaṅkāra*, even though there is the manifestation of consciousness;
for the absence of another object and the non-apprehension of it cannot act as an obstacle to an effect produced by the manifestation of that other object.
This is because, even when all three [the self, the object, and consciousness] appear, each respective manifestation serves as the cause for the recollection of its own specific sphere.
Nor can it be asserted that the referent of the "I," whose stability is secured by the force of recognition, meets its destruction during states such as sleep;
for this very reason, upon waking, there is the reflective awareness: "For so long a time, I slept.
Furthermore, no such thing as consciousness is possible that is devoid of an object or lacks a substratum.
Because [the object] is absolutely non-apprehended;
and those who know the meaning of words maintain that terms such as "consciousness," "experience," "knowledge," and "illumination" are relative terms (*saṃbandhiśabda*).
For in neither common worldly usage nor in the Veda is there any employment of verbs such as "to know" that are either intransitive or without an agent.

As for the argument that, since [the object] exists as self-established, it is impossible for its prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) and so forth to persist at that time due to that very contradiction, and therefore [the object] cannot be established from them— that is quite gross.
For there is no rule that objects are established by consciousness only when they exist at the same time as that consciousness.
Because it would follow that the past and the future could not be cognized.
Now, if you argue that since the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of consciousness and so forth must be established, they must exist simultaneously with it;
has this ever been observed anywhere? Alas, if such were the case—
Since that [object] is established when [the cognition] exists, there is no non-establishment of its prior absence and so forth.
To say that its prior absence is simultaneous with it is the speech of a madman;
for this [cognition], by its very nature as sensory perception, consists in the illumination of objects existing at the same time as itself.
This does not refer to mere cognition (*jñānamātra*) or mere means of valid cognition (*pramāṇamātra*).
By this, the following [position] is also refuted: "If a means of valid cognition exists by itself because it is self-luminous, then it must exist eternally."
And that which is to be measured always exists; for the means of measurement exists only in conjunction with the object to be measured.
Thus [it is said]:
for the connection between the means of knowledge (*māna*) and the object of knowledge (*meyayoga*) is not an inseparable relation with the object at the time of the means' own existence;
rather, it is the state of being opposed to the falsity of that form which appears as having such a place, time, and so forth, as possessed by the object of knowledge.
For this very reason, the claim that "memory does not have an external object because memory is observed even when the object has perished" is mere idle chatter.
Furthermore, since the prior non-existence of consciousness and so forth are not present [in the moment], they cannot be objects of perception.
And because of the absence of indicative marks (*liṅga*) and so forth, there is no establishment [of prior non-existence] through any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
If this is so, then being self-established (*svataḥsiddhatva*) is not the cause [of its establishment], since prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) and the others are not established [by it].
Indeed, it must now be stated that there is simply an absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*);
yet, as has already been said, that absence cannot be asserted,
because the absence [of the object] is established by the very non-perception of what is perceptible (*yogyānupalabdhi*).
Furthermore, direct perception, while establishing the existence of its own object at the time of its own existence, does not establish that object's existence at all times;
from this it is determined that "I exist only now, not otherwise," for it manifests as strictly delimited by a specific time.
Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of even jars and other such things being eternal.
The same applies to cognitions such as inference and so forth.
Furthermore, it has already been stated that a cognition devoid of the distinctions of perception, inference, and the like—which is objectless and without a basis—is impossible.
Nor is it the case that because cognition does not have something else as its object, the prior non-existence of that [object] and so forth cannot be established through other means.
This is because [the cognition] "I knew" is made an object of present consciousness by means of past awareness;
and because the awareness of another is understood through signs such as the avoidance or acquisition of objects determined to be disagreeable or agreeable.

Furthermore, if that [awareness of others] were not admitted, it would follow that all worldly and Vedic transactions would cease to exist, since the apprehension of the meanings of words would be impossible.
Furthermore, there would be the impossibility of approaching a teacher and so forth,
because he is not perceived as possessing knowledge;
nor does being directed toward another object entail a lack of experientiality.
For the nature of experience (*anubhūtitva*) consists either in the fact that its own substratum is manifested by its very existence, or in its being the means of establishing its own object;

and since these two properties are established by self-experience even when consciousness becomes an object for another consciousness, they do not fall away— so how can there be the consequence of it ceasing to be an experience?

However, jars and the like lack the nature of being experience precisely because they do not possess such an intrinsic nature, not because they are objects of experience. Furthermore, even if they were not objects of experience, that same undesirable consequence would apply equally to them.
Like a flower in the sky;
nor does the self possess the nature of experience,
because it is the experiencer.

Nor is it the case that this [consciousness] cannot be experienced, for, just like experience itself which is established intrinsically (*svataḥsiddhi*), it is admitted to be cognizable both by itself and by others. If it were an object of cognition, the consequence of its being non-self (*anātmatva*) would follow; and even if it were not an object of cognition, the same [consequence] as before would apply.
If, however, it is maintained that for a sky-flower, its very non-existence is the cause of its being non-self and its not being an experience,
then let it be granted that for a jar and the like as well, the causes of those [two states] are precisely their not being the locus of consciousness and their not being opposed to ignorance.
If it is argued that these two [properties] would also apply to them insofar as they are objects, [we reply:]...

Even if it is not an object [of cognition], it remains exactly the same; enough of this mockery of ill-founded reasoning. Furthermore, as for the rejection of other modifications on the grounds that experience lacks birth, that too is contradicted by the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).
Because its destruction is observed even in the absence of birth; furthermore,
even if one includes the qualification "being," there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) due to *avidyā* as conceived by you,
for that too, though beginningless, possesses various transformations and is subject to destruction upon the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
If it is argued that those transformations exist as non-ultimate realities, then do those ultimate realities themselves possess transformations,
or are ultimate realities characterized by birth?
By which ultimate reality (*pāramārthya*) the qualification of either the probandum (*sādhya*) or the probans (*sādhana*) might attain its purposefulness?

Such being the case, that which was stated by this person skilled in logic—that "there is no unborn thing to be divided"—is well-supported. Furthermore, as for [the claim]: "nahyajaṃ vibhājyam asti"; [it is refuted as follows:]...
That too is not correct;
for it has been established that the very unborn Self is distinct from the body, senses, and so forth,
and because ignorance— which is admitted to be beginningless— must necessarily be accepted as something separate from the Self.
If it is argued that this distinction is not ultimate,
has a distinction at the level of ultimate reality ever been observed anywhere as being dependent upon origination?
Furthermore, we shall demonstrate immediately hereafter that the distinction between the seer and the seen, established by uncontradicted cognition, is indeed ultimately real.

Furthermore, as for the claim that "there is no cognizable property (dharma) belonging to this [consciousness]," and that "objects of cognition do not possess the nature of consciousness," even that is inconclusive because of properties such as self-luminosity and eternity— which are established by means of valid cognition such as scripture and inference, and which you yourself have accepted.
Nor should it be said that they are mere consciousness (vijñaptimātra), because even when that [consciousness] is established, disagreement regarding them is observed.
For indeed, even while accepting consciousness (*saṃvid*), proponents assert its inferability, momentariness, and so forth;
moreover, because of the difference in their essential natures (*svarūpa*).
For consciousness is the manifestation of something to its own substrate by its very existence (*sattā*).

Self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatā*), however, is the state of being manifested to the self by its very existence (*sattayā*). Furthermore, it has been established in the *Saṃvitsiddhi* itself that "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) is a property common to all things, both conscious and unconscious. If this were not accepted, then the word "manifestation" would merely signify conformity with empirical usage (*vyavahārānuguṇya*).
Eternality (*nityatā*), however, is the state of existing at all times;
and oneness (*ekatva*) is the exclusion of any other number.
Nor is it correct to argue that the aforementioned fault does not apply because those [entities] are of the nature of being devoid of limitations such as insentience, time, space, or plurality.
For even with those properties that are of the nature of consciousness, the fallacy of inconclusiveness (anaikāntya) remains unavoidable;

moreover, since consciousness is devoid of various contradictory properties such as insentience, non-eternality, and manifoldness— which are intended to be negated— the statement of such a negation is mere words.
Furthermore, an object of cognition (cetya) and ignorance are both perceived and accepted by you as residing within the Self.

Moreover, by employing the genitive case in the phrase "of this" (asyāḥ) to express the relationship of this experience, to then assert its qualitylessness would result in a contradictory meaning—like claiming that a mother is barren.
In the doctrine that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the Self, [the author] says "it has been refuted," extending the same line of criticism used against the doctrine that the body is the Self.

For the doctrine that the vital breath (prāṇa) is the self, if it were not rejected and not refuted, but rather remained as a counter-position, would become the motivating factor for applying further arguments for its rejection.
However, the point is that it is not so; for it has already been rendered virtually non-existent by the refutations of the doctrine that the body is the self. //9//
He refutes the impossibility of the self’s movement with the words "by virtue of its non-omnipresence.
It is correct that movement would be impossible if [the self] were omnipresent;
however, if it were atomic, movement would indeed be possible for the self, even though it is intangible, just as it is for the mind.
The meaning is that contact cannot function as a cause for motion without the impulsion of effort, the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "in the [section on] dimension":

this possession of motion by the self will also be established in the section defining the dimension of the self; therefore, the point is that there is no need for further elaboration on its possession of motion at this stage.
"Alam amunā" is an alternative reading.
Here, the proponent of consciousness as the self (saṃvid-ātmavādī) rises up [in objection], saying: "Let it be so, then; let consciousness be the self."
The formal argument is: "because of non-inertness.
He states the negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) with the words "if it were inert" (*jaḍatve*).
"Bound" (*pratibaddha*) means pervaded (*vyāpya*).
"Anātmya" means the state of being without self (*anātmatva*).

This is based on the etymological derivation that "selfhood" (*ātmya*) is the existence of a self, and thus it is the absence of that. Regarding the application of the negative concomitance and the conclusion, he says: "and because of insentience."
"Even that" means even selflessness (*anātmya*).

The point is this: because the cessation of the pervader entails the cessation of the pervaded, the cessation of the pervader—insentience (*jaḍatva*)—establishes the cessation of the pervaded, which is selflessness.
He dispels the objection regarding the unestablished nature of the reason "non-insentience" with the words "And non-insentience... (*ajaḍatvaṃ ca*).

The meaning is that because it manifests by its own mere existence (*svasattāmātrataḥ*), there is an absence of insentience (*jaḍatva*), which is characterized by having a manifestation dependent on another (*parāyattaprakāśatva*).
As for the phrase "not indeed" (*na hi*):
[it refers to] establishment dependent on another—that is, a manifestation contingent upon another.
"Insentient" means up to that point.
Here, he restates the view of the Bhāṭṭas, who maintain that consciousness is to be inferred, with the words "it might be thought.
[The phrase] "the mere object" refers to this.
The point is that in the cognition "this jar is blue," it is not possible for the cognition itself to be the object, just as it is not possible for a cloth or other such things to be so.
[Objection: If that is so, how then is there the manifestation of cognition in the form "I know the jar"?
To this he says: "And therefore... The grammatical connection is: "and after that."
In the sense of "casting" (castva):
this is the meaning—through cognition, a property called "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) arises in the object;
that very thing is what is called "manifestation" (*prakāśa*).
That very excellence of the object produced by cognition is indeed [the means of knowledge],
and it is directly perceived by the knower.
By means of that mark (*liṅga*)— which consists in the manifestation of the object— he infers the cognition, which is its cause, within himself.
And the aforementioned cognition, "I know the pot," has as its object a knowledge derived through inference.

The form of that inference is as follows: this "knownness" (jñātatā) which has "pot-ness" as its qualifier is produced by a cognition that has "pot-ness" as its qualifier, because it possesses the nature of such knownness.
[This applies to] the knownness and the cognition of that property as its qualifier.

And the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established through the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*). He refutes this Bhaṭṭa position with the words "that is not so" (*tan na*). [He says] "in cognition" (*jñāne*).
For "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) is indeed the state of being an object of cognition.

Since it consists in being the object of that [cognition], there is no proof of a specific excellence (*atiśaya-viśeṣa*) as a property of the object that is distinct from the cognition itself which is connected to the object. [As in the thought:
"The cognition of a jar has arisen for me."

The point is that in the cognition "the jar is known by me," there is no experience of a distinct object existing between the reversal of the relationship between the subject (dharmin) and the attribute (dharma).

Having stated the lack of proof through perception, he states the lack of proof through conceptualization regarding a manifestation (*prakāśa*) distinct from the form of "knownness" (*jñātatā*), using the words "in both cases" (*ubhayatra*).

The point is that since the conventional usage of "known" with respect to an object is established by its very being an object of knowledge, the non-establishment of that usage—which is supposed to characterize "knownness"—is unproven as a basis for postulating an additional entity called "knownness."

He supports the view that in the cognitions of objects, there is necessarily the manifestation of the cognition, the knower, and the self as the object of "I" according to the Prābhākara method, by means of the verse beginning with *vitti*.

For if it were admitted that the apprehension of the object occurs without involving the cognition or the knower, then even when the cognition of a jar has arisen, there might occasionally arise a doubt such as "Do I possess that cognition or not?",
or a contrary certainty such as "I am devoid of that cognition," and so forth.
The sense is that since [the self] does not appear as possessing knowledge, it must be admitted that knowledge has all three factors as its object.

Thus, because the self-luminosity of knowledge is established, just as the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the object arises from that very [knowledge], the practical usage regarding "knownness" (*jñātatā*) is also possible; therefore, there is no occasion for postulating a "knownness" that is a distinct entity—this is the underlying intention.

Now, since the production of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) is impossible with respect to objects that are past or future, the cognition of that cognizedness must be established by means of cognition itself; and this same method applies to perception as well—with this intention, he says "atīte" (in the past).
Here, "grasping" (*grahaṇa*) is characterized by inference and so forth.
*Vyāhāra* is speech, which is linguistic expression (*vyavahāra*).
*Vyavahāra* refers to physical actions such as rejecting or accepting.
In this context, both are to be understood as being rooted in the cognition that [the object] is known.

The point is this: since the cognition of "known-ness" arises prior to the linguistic usage of "known-ness" regarding those two [the object and the cognition]—which have known-ness as their root—whether that known-ness exists or not, one does not first infer known-ness there by means of the sign (liṅga) of linguistic usage and subsequently infer the cognition. Rather, the cognition of known-ness occurs solely through the power of self-luminous cognition, and yet linguistic usage based upon it follows. This is the intended meaning.

Regarding the reading "the establishment of the object there is inferential" (*ānumānikī tatra viṣayasiddhiḥ*), the meaning is this: the establishment of the object consists in its manifestation being apprehended through the means of valid cognition that is inference.

However, regarding the reading "the establishment of the manifestation of the object" (*viṣayaprakāśasiddhiḥ*), the meaning is that it is an inference of the manifestation of the object produced by the means of valid cognition that is inference.
He provides an example from the case of memory (*smṛti*) regarding the cognition of "having been known" even prior to linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*), stating: "by someone...
Having understood the state of having been remembered (*smṛtatva*) of an object through the very act of remembering, one declares: "I have remembered it today.
If this cognition of having been remembered were inferential (*laiṅgikī*), [it would not be possible].
In that case, it must be said that by this very linguistic usage as a mark (liṅga), the cognition of [the word] being remembered for its own meaning is inferential;
and therein, a circular dependency (anyonyāśrayaṇa) would result:
the linguistic usage [of the word] would depend upon the cognition of its being remembered, and...
And by that very [cognition], it is [known] as "its own.
Thus, the point is that the cognition of "known-ness" must be accepted as being based solely on the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of cognition.
[This is shown] by its own statement: "by that very [cognition]."
The grammatical construction is "Who [is] like one devoid of shame?
"Devoid of shame" means shameless.
By my own statement—"I... [the sense is completed].

The claim that "I know" constitutes an inference of one's own cognition—meaning an inferential apprehension of a cognition residing within oneself—is utterly untenable; for in any linguistic usage, the cognition of the object to be used is the cause [of that usage], and thus it is impossible to maintain that one infers one's own cognition solely through the linguistic usage of that very cognition. This is the sense.

Since it is possible to infer the knowledge residing in another person's self through that other person's own verbal expression of knowledge, it has been pointed out that one’s own knowledge is inferred by means of one’s own verbal expression.
Thus, the so-called "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) is unestablished;
for the cognition and linguistic usage expressed as "it is known" are accounted for solely by means of self-luminous knowledge.

It has been described that the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of cognition is to be ascertained by the fact that, once cognition has arisen, there is no occurrence of doubt regarding cognition itself or the certainty that cognition is absent. Now, even while conceding that "illumination" (*prakāśa*) is a distinct property residing in the object, he establishes the self-luminosity of cognition on the basis of that very [illumination], in order to refute the theory that cognition is to be inferred from illumination, starting with the words "And another... (*anyaś ca*).

Herein are two formal arguments (*prayoga*): 1. Experience (*anubhūti*) possesses a property that does not depend on anything else, because it is the cause of that same property in another object through its own connection with it, just as color (*rūpa*) is.
For color is the cause of visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) in objects such as a jar through its own connection with them, while possessing that property within itself without depending on any other color.
2. Experience has its own linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) independent of anything else, because it is the cause of linguistic usage in another object through its own connection with it.
For example, existence (sattā).

For it is the cause for the linguistic usage "existent" in relation to a jar and so forth by virtue of its own connection [to them], and it does not depend on another existence for its own usage as "existent."
In this context, the first formulation accepts another property (*dharmāntara*) in the form of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*),
whereas the second does not accept it.
The detailed exposition of the reason (*hetu*) and the probandum (*sādhya*) should be understood from the *Śrutaprakāśikā* and other such works.
By this, since the illumination that culminates in knowledge is established as being independent of any other knowledge, the self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) of knowledge is proven.
And thus, its very nature is that of the Self; so he says, "because of self-luminosity.
Here, the underlying intention is as follows: first of all, the self-luminosity of the Self is established by such scriptural passages as, "In this state, this person becomes his own light."
The self-luminosity of cognition is established by the aforementioned inference; therefore, it is logical that cognition alone possesses the nature of the Self.
Furthermore, he states "moreover" (*kiṃ ca*) to show the parsimony (*lāghava*) in favor of consciousness being the Self.
The term "ātman" means that which has the nature of a knower or experiencer; the word "bhavatu" is in the imperative mood used to grant permission for one's own desire,
and the particle "iti" should be supplied [at the end].
The meaning is that the admission—that consciousness alone is the self—is the best [position].
He raises an objection against consciousness being the self with the words "But [the notion] 'I'...
Because of its predominance, it is perceived that the referent of "I" (ahamartha) alone is the self.
The sense is that this is not the case for consciousness as it appears through its very nature (*dharmatā*).
He offers a rebuttal by accepting half of the point, saying "True.
This is an admission regarding the cognition of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*).
There is no acceptance of its validity.
Regarding its invalidity, he states the reason with the words "But that..."— namely,
that the cognizer is not established by the means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as having a distinct form.
However, [the object] is established through error;

for only non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), which penetrates the mere reality of the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), is a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), on the other hand, which penetrates imagined distinctions such as the relationship between property and its locus (*dharmadharmibhāva*), is not.
The definition of error is "excessive attachment" (atiharḍa).

He also states the logical sublation (yauktikabādha) based on the perception of a distinction between the knower and [the object], beginning with the words "in the cognition of difference" (bhedajñāne).
The phrase "as if it were established" (siddhavatkāreṇa) should be connected with the word "also" (api) that follows later as well.
The reading "apṛthagvastutaye" is likely intended;
alternatively, there is a word-division as "aprakāśātmanaḥ.
And thus the meaning is as follows: even by assuming the existence of the cognition of difference—that is, even by accepting the validity of the cognition of difference in some instances.
Because the Buddhists maintain that the distinction between cognitions is real;
[this is] by means of a probandum consisting in non-distinctness— that is, being not separate entities—
and by a reason whose invariable concomitance has been grasped, meaning its pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been apprehended.
By means of the reason consisting in the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*)—
that is, by the argument that if the cognizer were not of the nature of luminosity, luminosity would be impossible due to a contradiction in its very nature,

whereas if it were of the nature of luminosity, it would necessarily be consciousness itself— and so forth, [this is established] by that which proves the non-difference of consciousness and sublates the difference of consciousness.

The meaning is that the reality—the essential nature—of the self as the "I" (ahamartha), which is a knower distinct from consciousness and not of the nature of luminosity, is difficult to establish—that is, impossible to establish.
The two instrumental endings are to be construed with the word "durupagamam.

Here, the formal argument (*prayoga*) to be understood is: "The knower is non-different from consciousness, because it is perceived only along with consciousness, or because its nature is luminosity."
Alternatively, there may be a reading [of the compound] as "pṛthag-vastu-tayā-anatvāt" (because of not being non-different from a separate entity).
The presentation of the probandum (*sādhya*) in the form of non-difference, which defines non-deviation, follows from the sense of the context.
Furthermore, let the word-division simply be "prakāśātmanaḥ" (of the nature of luminosity).

By means of the reason such as "the rule of simultaneous perception" (*sahopalambhaniyama*) or "consciousness-ness due to having luminosity as its very nature," the Self— which is of the nature of light and non-different from consciousness— is established;
this is done by accepting the cognition of difference as if it were established, that is, by accepting the validity of the cognition of difference as if it were proven.

The meaning is that "reality," in the sense of existence as a distinct entity— that is, as something different from consciousness— is difficult to establish. He extends the aforementioned reasoning, which serves as the cause for refuting the distinction between the subject (grāhaka), to the refutation of the distinction between the object (grāhya) as well, by saying "in the object" (grāhye).

The meaning is that because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*) and because of having the nature of luminosity (*prakāśasvabhāvatva*), the object such as "blue" is non-different from consciousness (*saṃvid*); thus, due to its difference from cognition, the distinction between objects like blue and so forth is also non-existent. Now, if the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*) are non-different from consciousness, how is it that the distinctions between the knower (*jñātṛ*), the known (*jñeya*), and [the act of] knowing appear as distinct from one another? To this he says: "Therefore...
The appearance of the distinction between the apprehended and the apprehender is false, being rooted in a defect (*doṣa*).
The sense is that reality consists merely in the appearance of consciousness (*saṃvid-ābhāsa-mātra*).
In this regard, the view of the manifest Yogācāras, who are followers of the Sugata, is that the defect is *vāsanā* (latent impressions);
whereas that of the hidden Māyāvādins is that the defect is beginningless ignorance (*anādy-avidyā*).

The conceptual construction of the grasped and the grasper— the distinction between the object of knowledge and the knower— characterized by being the objective domain of cognition and the locus of cognition; [the author] demonstrates the agreement of the Buddhists, who are well-known for the aforementioned view, with the words "even though there is no division," meaning that consciousness alone is the self.

And although that [consciousness] is indeed without differentiation, it is perceived as if possessed of distinctions—characterized by the distinctions of objects to be grasped such as blue and so forth, the distinctions of subjects who grasp such as Caitra and Maitra, and the distinctions of cognitions such as perception and inference—due to erroneous cognitions;
this is the meaning of the verse.
He shows the consensus of the Māyāvādins with the words "pure" (*śuddham*).
The pure reality (*tattva*) is not the material cause (*upādāna*) of the manifold of differentiation (*prapañca*);
for if it were so, it would follow that [the reality] could never cease, as it would then entail being the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, for that manifold, it is only *māyā*—being false—that is the cause of the appearance of various and diverse false objects.
The meaning of the verse is that primordial ignorance (*ādyavidyā*) alone is the mother and the material cause (*upādāna*).
Pure Being (*sanmātra*), devoid of distinctions and consisting of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).
The sense is that within that substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the appearance of unreal manifoldness occurs through illusion (*māyā*).
The self-luminosity of the self is established by scripture;
the same for consciousness is established by reasoning.
Therefore, that [consciousness] alone is the self.

However, because everything distinct from that [consciousness] is rooted in defects and is therefore merely an appearance (*ābhāsa*), the position that consciousness alone is the self (*saṃvidātmatva*) was proposed as a prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣita*). Regarding that, there are two opinions: [first,] that the momentary cognition (*kṣaṇika-vijñāna*) is the self;...
And [the view that] "the self is eternal consciousness.
In this regard, he refutes the position of the manifest Buddhists—that the self consists of momentary consciousness—starting with the words "here he says," and so forth.
The meaning is that the proponent of an eternal self states the refutation of the doctrine that the self consists of momentary consciousness.
Regarding the phrase "momentarily perishing":
consciousness, which has the nature of being destroyed at every moment and is manifold according to the distinction of its objects, is perceived as such.
If that [consciousness] were the self, then recognition and so forth would not be possible.
The meaning is that this [recognition] is possible only if the self, which is the investigator, is stable.
Now, he raises the doubt that recognition, like intuition (*pratibhā*), might be without an object, stating: "Nor is it without a basis" (*na ca nirālambane*).
The formal argument (*prayoga*) is: recognition is without an object because it is an intuition, like the playful manifestation of mental construction (*mānasakalpanāvilāsa*).
Regarding this, he states that [the argument] is sublated by the words "if it were without an objective basis" (*nirālambanatve*).

Since there is a rule that all cognition in general must possess an object, and since it would be impossible for something to be cognition if it lacked an object, the proof of objectlessness in a particular instance of cognition has a sublated subject matter—this is the meaning.
Furthermore, even in the case of mental intuition (*pratibhā*), there is no absolute absence of an object.
The point is that [an object appears] elsewhere than where it actually exists;
moreover, it is observed that in some cases there is even correspondence with reality (*yāthārthya*).

Regarding the position that cognition in general is devoid of an object (*nirviṣayaka*), he states "and of the means of proof" (*sādhanasya ca*) to show that this would also involve a contradiction with one's own activity.
The sense is that if the inference proving the absence of an object (*nirviṣayakatva*) itself possesses an object, then by parity of reasoning, all cognitions would possess objects;
whereas if it lacks an object, the probandum in the form of the absence of an object is not established, rendering the undertaking of the proof futile. This has been explained at length.

The meaning is that the refutation of the view that knowledge is without an objective basis (*nirālambanatva*) was carried out by the authors of the sūtras and their commentaries in the first pāda of the first chapter of the *Pūrvamīmāṃsā* and in the second section (*caraṇa*) of the second chapter of the *Uttaramīmāṃsā*,
as well as in the treatise known as the *Nyāyatattva* through the establishment of the correspondence (*yāthārthya*) of all cognitions.

By the phrase "in these two parts of the *Pūrva* and *Uttara Mīmāṃsā*," it is intended that the twenty-lakṣaṇa *Mīmāṃsā* constitutes a single system (*ekaśāstrya*) and that it consists of the *Pūrva* and *Uttara* sections, which are the investigations (*vicāra*) into ritual action (*karman*) and Brahman respectively.
Now, is it not the case that consciousness is twofold—namely, the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) and the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)?
Among these, the former consists of cognitions of blue, yellow, and so forth; the latter has the form of "I" and is of the nature of a self.
To the objection that recognition would be possible even if both types of consciousness were momentary—due to the persistence of the stream of the *ālayavijñāna*—he says: "For this very reason.
Regarding the term "moment of consciousness" (*vijñānakṣaṇa*):
a moment that is itself consciousness is a "moment of consciousness."

The sense is that if one accepts a permanent entity distinct from momentary consciousness as the agent who performs the synthesis (*anusandhāna*) of objects previously experienced, there would be an abandonment of the tenet that "everything is momentary," and furthermore,
it would entail the undesirable consequence of admitting a knower distinct from cognition in another form.
Regarding the phrase "non-acceptance":
if the continuum (*santāna*), characterized as a collection of momentary and successive cognitions, were not distinct from its constituent members (*samudāyin*), then recognition would be impossible,
because the prior experiencer included within that continuum would have already perished.
The meaning is that because the subsequent [moment] is not an experiencer, it is incapable of forming a connection [with the previous one].

In this regard, the following should be considered: even the state of being an aggregate is not possible for momentary things, because in the Buddhist system it is impossible for them to be subsumed under limiting conditions (upādhi) such as a stable, single place or time.
To include [all cognitions] within a single intellect would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasakta*);

for if that were the case, even the cognitions belonging to different mental continua (*bhinnasantāna*) would be so included, resulting in the impossibility of establishing a restriction to a specific continuum (*santānaniyama*).
If it is argued that a "continuum" is a succession of successive cognitions where each subsequent cognition takes the preceding cognition as its material cause (*upādāna*), we say no.
Because that which has perished is non-existent at the time of the effect, it cannot serve as a material cause;
furthermore, since mere anteriority would lead to over-extension,
the restriction to its own specific continuum is simply untenable.

One might object: "Is it not the case that reconnection (pratisandhāna) is established as being of the nature of an error, due to the illusion of unity arising from the extreme similarity of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna)? [The author] replies with the words "na hi" (for it is not so). The meaning is that recognition (pratyabhijñā), being of the nature of an error, is not possible;
the word "is possible" (ghaṭate) is to be supplied [to complete the sentence].
He establishes the disparity between the example [and the case at hand] with the words "it is appropriate.
In the example, there is a well-known, stable, conscious perceiver of two lamp-flames that are very similar but belong to different times; such a person is capable of experiencing error.
Therefore, in that case, recognition in the form of an error is possible.
And in the case at hand, a stable cognizer distinct from the cognitions themselves is not admitted.
Therefore, it must be said that cognition itself, as the self, would effect its own non-difference from another self within itself;
however, because they are unaware of each other's news, cognitions are not capable of apprehending either difference or non-difference from another within themselves.

The collective intention [of the opponent] is that, because of momentary destruction without residue (*niranvayavināśa*), even by virtue of the persistence of prior factors (*dharmānuvṛtti*), the recollection of what was previously experienced and so forth is not possible.
"Mutual ignorance" (*parasparavārtānabhijñatva*) means that one cognition does not grasp another cognition or its object.
"Destruction without residue" (*niranvayavināśitva*) means destruction along with the root—that is, destruction both in terms of essential nature (*svarūpa*) and in terms of attributes (*dharma*).
