Nor is it the case that the occurrence of reconnection [of consciousness] arises from the emergence of latencies (*vāsanā*) from each preceding moment of consciousness in each successive moment, because such a hypothesis—involving the arising and perishing of infinite latencies—is excessively cumbersome. This is the general direction; the remainder is clear.

In this context, the proponent of non-duality (advaitin), unable to tolerate the claim made by a certain proponent of an eternal self (*nityātmavādin*) regarding the arising and passing away of consciousness (*saṃvit*), offers a rebuttal.
This is stated as follows: "Someone says":

because there would be no grasper if the self were non-existent, and because there would be no object of grasp if the self were existent, there can be no apprehension of the prior non-existence of consciousness through itself.
Since consciousness is not the object of another cognition, it is impossible to apprehend the prior non-existence of that consciousness through another cognition;
for it is impossible to apprehend a prior non-existence colored by [the absence of] something without first making that thing itself an object of cognition.
Furthermore, if it were an object of another cognition, it would follow that it is insentient (*jaḍa*), like a jar or other such objects.
The meaning is that because there is no means of valid cognition for it, there is no prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of consciousness.
Therefore—
due to the absence of prior non-existence— there is no origination of consciousness.
The meaning is that prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is also included within "origination. Regarding the phrase "due to the absence of birth":
the other modifications of being (*bhāvavikāra*) are existence, growth, transformation, decline, and destruction.
Existence here is characterized by abiding as delimited by its own material cause,
because it is bound to arising and because it is pervaded by arising.
The meaning is that with the cessation of the pervader, there is the cessation of the pervaded.
"For this very reason" means that precisely because of the absence of origination, even plurality— characterized by the differentiation of cognitions belonging to the same class— is refuted.
Regarding the term *utpattimattvavyāpake*:
this is a *karmadhāraya* compound;
[it means] that which possesses divisions and is manifold, i.e., differentiated.
In this regard, consciousness is neither manifold nor subject to modification;
because it is unborn, that which is not so is not thus, just like a jar— this is the formulation of a negative inference (vyatireki-prayoga).
In the negation of difference and so forth within consciousness, he demonstrates that [consciousness] follows as a subject of attributes by stating "and because it is cognizable.
Differences and the like do not exist in consciousness, because they are objects of experience, just like color and so forth.
Here, the word "difference" (bheda) refers, according to the context, to the various states such as origination, which consist of modification.
Mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is the difference among things of the same class (*sajātīyabheda*).
Difference from things of a different class (*vijātīyabheda*) and internal difference (*svāgatibheda*) are what is denoted by the first word [of the compound].
Alternatively, "difference" (*bheda*) may refer to difference from things of a different class (*vijātīyabheda*).
Mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) is of the nature already described.
The items included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) are states such as origination and so forth, as well as internal distinctions.
The phrase "therefore" (*ataḥ*) encompasses this view.

Consciousness alone—devoid of all attributes such as the existence or non-existence of difference, and free from qualities like luminosity—is the very nature of pure light; it is both the supreme self (paramātman) and the individual self (jīvātman), eternal and immutable.
The sense is that even the distinction between individual selves is merely imagined.
To provide corroboration for this stated meaning, he cites the following verse: "That which is experience... and so forth.
Non-arising is the state of being unproduced;
immeasurability is the state of not being an object of cognition;
and infinity is the state of being devoid of destruction.
The state of being the Self (*ātmatvam*) consists in the nature of both the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*).

The intended meaning is that consciousness alone, which is of the nature described above, is all-pervasive; yet, through the differentiation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) in the form of the supreme self, it takes on the manifold forms of individual selves.
And "that very same [consciousness]" refers to this.
The meaning is that this [reality] is not taught in the Vedāntas by means of the power of verbal expression;
rather, while remaining inexpressible, it is understood in them through the function of *tātparya* (purport). This is a technical definition (*paribhāṣā*).
The word "convention" (saṅketa) means this very thing.
The underlying intention is that the acceptability of this doctrine arises solely through the power of convention.

He corroborates the fact that the Vedāntas have their purport (*tātparya*) precisely upon such consciousness (*saṃvit*) by means of the words of the author of the Advaitavārtika, beginning with "parāgarthe."

That which is produced by the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding external objects such as jars and cloths—which is accepted by the experts in the systems (*tāntrikas*) as being of the nature of a result (*phala*)—is itself considered the object of knowledge (*prameya*) in the Vedāntas.

If one were to assume that the Vedāntas have as their purport (*tātparya*) any other external object, they would simply lack authority (*aprāmāṇya*), because an external object is unreal; such is the meaning of the two verses.

It should be understood that the mere, undifferentiated, eternal consciousness itself is metaphorically designated as the "fruit of the means of knowledge" (pramāṇaphala) because it illuminates various objects by being reflected in the modifications of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇavṛtti) dependent on those respective means of knowledge, or by being delimited by those respective modifications.
He now begins to refute the doctrine of the Māyāvādins in detail, starting with the words "tad idam" and so forth.

The meaning is that those who have directly realized the true nature of the Self say: "This philosophy of the Māyāvādins is *alaukika*—contrary to worldly means of valid cognition such as perception—and *avaidika*—contrary to the Vedas and other authentic scriptures; it is thus inconsistent with both the world and the Vedas."

First, he demonstrates the contradiction with perception regarding the doctrine of the non-duality of consciousness (saṃvidadvaita) favored by the opponent, beginning with the words "tathā hi" (for it is thus).
For the author of the Vārttika stated that the selfhood [of the knower] arises from the cognition of external objects;
he says "saṃvid" (consciousness) to show that such cognition is clearly non-self.

The meaning is as follows: "the word for knowledge" (*jñāna*) and so forth are synonyms denoting a single object; that which is such a property of the self (*ātma-dharma*), illuminating an object and designated by the term "consciousness" (*saṃvit*), is what is intended.
"Of that [consciousness]" (*tasyāḥ*) refers to this.

The point is that it is impossible for this cognition of an object—which is established by perception as having the nature of another entity and as being impermanent—to be of the nature of an eternal self.

He establishes the impermanence of the result of valid cognition (pramāṇaphala), which is an experience involving an object, by means of another method, beginning with the words "In sleep, etc. For if [the cognition] existed during sleep and so forth, there would be the apprehension of the cognition due to its being capable [of being perceived].
The sense is that because it is not perceived, it does not exist at that time.
He further confirms the absence of sensation during the period of deep sleep by means of the recollection of one who has awakened from sleep, using the phrase "for this very reason.
Now, an objection may be raised: since consciousness is self-luminous, there must indeed be its apprehension even during sleep.
Furthermore, because there is no rule that what has been experienced must necessarily be remembered, it is possible for there to be no recollection upon waking.
As for the reflective awareness, "For such a length of time I did not know anything at all," its object is the absence of knowledge characterized by the illumination of objects.
Anticipating the objection that even though consciousness exists during sleep, it lacks the capacity to illuminate objects, he refutes it with the words beginning "yāvat" (as long as).
The section ending with "even in the absence of [the required] restriction" (niyamābhāve ’pi) is a restatement of the objection; the resolution follows later.

That death and so forth cause the interruption of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) was stated in the *Saṃvitsiddhi*: "From death, from the suffering of hell, and even from the calamity of childbirth..."
"Experiences from previous births that have long since passed are not within the range of memory.
Here, *prāyaṇa* means death;
*nityavat* means constant or perpetual.
Alternatively, like a restrictive rule (*niyama*), it means "necessarily.

Even in the absence of the powerful causes of suffering that lead to the loss of all mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), the necessity of non-recollection would prove that consciousness remains unmanifest during sleep.
The sense is that for that [consciousness], which has self-luminosity as its very nature, its non-manifestation at that time would necessarily result in its non-existence.

However, according to our established doctrine (siddhānta), since it is admitted that the knowledge existing as an attribute (dharmabhūtajñāna) is self-luminous precisely at the moment of manifesting an object, its non-manifestation during deep sleep does not cause any logical flaw; this is how it should be understood.
Here, an objection is raised: "And not..."
"Even though it exists" means: because of the absence of delimitation by an object—that is, because of the absence of connection with an object;
and because of the absence of the sphere of the *ahaṃkāra*—that is, because of the dissolution of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*), which is the knower cognized by the notion of "I.
It is only consciousness that is conjoined with the "I-sense" and associated with an object that possesses the capacity to deposit a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).

The sense is this: because of the absence of both [the object and the self] during sleep, even pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra*), though self-luminous, does not deposit a latent impression (*saṃskāra*); therefore, there is no contingency of its being recollected upon waking.
To this, he states the answer: "In the case of another object" (*arthāntare*).
This refers to the non-apprehension of that [object], namely, the non-apprehension of another object.
Regarding the phrase "in the triad":

even when there is the manifestation of the triad of knowledge (*jñāna*), the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and the knower (*jñātṛ*), because the experience of each respective [element] is the cause for its corresponding mental impression (*saṃskāra*) according to its specific nature, if there is an experience of consciousness through one-pointedness, then upon the arising of that impression during sleep, there would follow the consequence of a reflective awareness of pure consciousness alone; for the dissolution of the referent "I" (*aham-artha*) and the non-experience of other objects such as jars and cloths do not act as obstacles to that [awareness].
The sense is that, according to your view, awakening would be impossible; this is the point.
Now, as to the objection that "since the knower has perished during sleep, who could remember [the dream]?", he replies: "And there is no recognition.

The meaning is that because one recognizes on a subsequent day what was done on a previous day, the knower—the referent of the "I"—is established as persisting through both the prior and subsequent days; therefore, its dissolution during the intervening period of sleep is not tenable.
Having thus established the existence of the referent "I" (ahamartha) even during sleep, he establishes that its manifestation also persists at that time with the words "For this very reason.
This recognition of the referent "I" belonging to the period of sleep serves as the proof for the manifestation of that [referent] at that time.

Nor should it be argued that this [recognition] must have as its object the existence of the nature of the self as being one who experienced pleasure during sleep—thereby implying that it does not account for the manifestation of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) during sleep; for although the portion concerning sleep is of the nature of an inference, the "I-sense" is of the nature of a recollective recognition (*pratisandhāna*). Thus, in that regard, there is no [lack of manifestation].
The point is this: just as in cases such as "I existed" (*āsam*), that which is established by its own natural force (*svarasasiddha*) cannot be set aside;

and just as the recognition of the nature of the self experienced during the morning time is logically possible as a form of recollection (*pratisandhāna*) regarding the nature of the self, so too, because it recognizes the nature of the self experienced during deep sleep, it is logically possible for it to be a form of recollection regarding the aspect of the self.

Nor should it be argued that since there is no evidence for the eternal self-luminous consciousness (*nityātmaprakāśa*) producing a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), how can the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) possess the nature of recollection (*pratisandhāna*) with respect to the self;

for we accept that even the eternal experience is a cause of latent impressions, in order to establish its status as a single cause for recollection through its possession of a latent impression produced by itself.
This is clearly stated in the *Siddhāntasiddhāñjana*.
Alternatively, the justification for the term "recollection" (pratisandhāna) is that [the self] consists in the manifestation of its own portion as experienced during sleep;
more on this elsewhere.

Now, one might argue: "Let there be no eternality for cognition possessing an object, but the eternality and other attributes of pure consciousness are indeed established. To this, he says: "And not in the absence of an object," and so forth.

The point is this: the experience of self-luminous consciousness (*svayaṃprakāśasaṃvit*) is known in the world only as consciousness that is conjoined with an object and a substrate, in the form "I know this.
However, the experience of pure consciousness alone is not established for anyone, either by itself or through anything else.
[Objection: But how is it consistent with your own final doctrine (*siddhānta*) to maintain that the Self, whose nature is knowledge, is without an object and without a substrate?
It is said:

since words such as *saṃvit* (consciousness) are conventionally established (*rūḍha*) only for knowledge that possesses an object, the statement denying that its referent is devoid of an object is entirely logical.

Furthermore, for knowledge in its state as a quality (*dharma*), which illuminates objects, there is no lack of a substratum (*anāśrayatva*), because it rests upon the eternal nature of the Self (*ātman*).

Even the knowledge of the self’s own nature (ātmasvarūpajñāna) does not lack an object or possess no attributes, because it illuminates its own nature through the modes (prakāra) of inwardness (pratyaktva), favorability (anukūlatva), and oneness (ekatva).
Furthermore, since doubts regarding the self—such as whether it is one or many, or "I" or "not-I"—never arise, its manifestation must be admitted as being characterized by inwardness.

Moreover, because it is the locus of unconditional love, it is accepted in the established doctrine (siddhānta) that the self is also characterized by happiness (sukhatva); this is the intended distinction.

He establishes that consciousness (*saṃvit*) possesses specific attributes (*saviśeṣatva*) by means of the well-known fact that words such as "consciousness" are relative terms (*saṃbandhiśabda*). To be a relative term means to possess a requirement for a fixed correlative (*niyatasaṃbandhyākāṅkṣāśālitva*).

For when it is said, "knowledge" (*jñāna*) or "consciousness" (*saṃvedana*), there is an invariable expectation regarding its object and locus, such as "whose [is it]? or "of what object? (i.e., whose knowledge, and of what object?).
He confirms this very point by negating its opposite with the words "for not" (*na hi*). [The phrase] "of *jñā* and so forth" refers to the verbal root *jñā* and others.
If it is objected that in expressions such as "the nature of knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpa*), the word is seen used in its isolated form alone, we say no.
For you do not understand the underlying intention here:

the word *jñāna* denoting the subject (*dharmin*), which has "self-luminosity" as its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*), is a distinct word from the word denoting the attribute (*dharma*)— that is, the knowledge that is the property— just as the word *go*, when denoting the four-footed animal, is distinct from the same word when it denotes a ray of light and so forth.
The established usage of our term as a relative (saṃbandhi) word finds its scope in denoting knowledge that has become an attribute (dharma);
for you, however, there is no distinction between the self-nature of the substratum (dharmin), which is knowledge, and the knowledge of objects, which is likewise an attribute.

Because of the established doctrine that consciousness alone, whose nature is the Self, is devoid of distinctions, it is logical that words such as "consciousness" (saṃvit) are merely relative terms [denoting attributes]. Furthermore, it should be understood that since a mere cognition devoid of distinctions cannot serve as a basis for linguistic application (pravṛttinimitta), it is also impossible for it to be denoted by the word "knowledge" (jñāna), which expresses a substantive subject (dharmivācin).

Thus, it has been stated that the result of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*), which others consider to be the self (*ātman*), cannot be the self because it is adventitious (*āgantuka*) and because it is a property of the self (*ātmadharma*).

Now, he restates the opponent's argument regarding the non-establishment of its prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), beginning with the words "But as for [the claim] 'by itself'. The phrase "of that which is established by itself" indicates the absence of establishment through anything else.

The term "of experience" (*anubhavasya*) is to be supplied as the subject (*viśeṣya*). "Precisely because of that contradiction"—that is, precisely because of the contradiction characterized by the impossibility of coexistence with its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). "Of prior non-existence, etc."—that is, of the prior non-existence of consciousness (*saṃvit*), and so forth.

The remainder is clear. He refutes [the opponent's position] with the words beginning "that" (tat), etc. He states the fault in the restriction that cognition in general must grasp an object simultaneous with itself by saying "in the past," etc.
The restatement of the doubt begins with "atha" (now).
Immediately after the word "iti," the word "mataṃ" (the view) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The meaning of the passage expressing the doubt is that there is a rule (niyama) stating that the prior non-existence of consciousness must necessarily be perceived by a cognition that is simultaneous with itself.
Having adopted the restrictive rule (*niyama*), he asked, "How so? [The answer is:

because of its establishment—that is, because of the establishment of the apprehension of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of consciousness—there is no non-establishment of prior non-existence and so forth;
that is, there is no non-establishment of the prior non-existence of consciousness and so forth.

And although this restriction is logical according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), because the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of any existing cognition is apprehended by another existing cognition through inference and so forth— for instance,
the possibility of an inference such as: "I am currently devoid of visual perception, because my eyes are open."
Furthermore, he states "its prior non-existence" (tatprāgabhāvaḥ) because this restriction is untenable according to the opponent's view;
for you maintain that cognition is not apprehended by another cognition.
This being the case, that antecedent absence of knowledge would have to be apprehended by that very [knowledge] which is simultaneous with it, in accordance with the rule stated by you;
and that is untenable—this is the sense.
If it is argued, "For this very reason, we maintain that the antecedent absence of consciousness is unestablished," he replies: "In the case of what is sensory" (*aindriyike*).
The rule that the apprehension of objects existing at the same time belongs only to worldly perception (laukikapratyakṣa) applies,
and not to cognition in general, nor to valid cognition (pramiti) in general.

And thus, there is no logical inconsistency in the apprehension of its own prior absence—which belongs to a previous time—by that very same present cognition; this is the underlying intention (*hārda*). This will become clear further on. He refutes the view that because a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is invariably concomitant with its object (*prameya*), and because the cognition of the means of valid cognition is eternal due to its self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*), its object must also be eternal, by saying "by this" (*etena*).
By this— namely, by the absence of a rule that valid cognition in general must apprehend an object existing at the same time as itself—
the restatement of the view to be refuted is [concluded]:
"It is a means of knowledge because it is self-luminous."
Valid cognition (*pramiti*) is self-existent; its existence is independent of anything else and it always exists.
If this is so, then for the reason that will be stated hereafter, the object to be cognized (*meyavastu*) also always exists.
For this reason: "mānam" means valid cognition (*pramāṇajñāna*); "meyayug eva" means it is necessarily concomitant with its object of cognition (*prameya*).
Even though valid cognition is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*), it is nevertheless non-eternal precisely because it is produced by a cause.
Your [position] that the apprehension of the prior non-existence of that [object] may indeed occur either by itself or through another [means of knowledge] is untenable.

Therefore, it is improper to establish the permanence of the object (meya) by depending upon the permanence of the means of knowledge (miti). Furthermore, this method of refutation should be understood as being based on the absence of a rule that a cognition of a means of knowledge must necessarily grasp its object at the same time.
[Objection: But if cognition apprehends a non-existent object, how can its invariable concomitance with the object of cognition (*prameya*) be established?
To this, he says: "Not so" (*na hi*).
It is not the case that there is an invariable concomitance of cognition with the object of cognition in the sense that "when there is cognition, then there is the object of cognition."

However, insofar as something appears in a cognition by virtue of its connection with a particular place and time and by possessing a particular form, its relation to the object of knowledge (*prameya*) consists in the absence of the non-existence of that specific mode;
[this is] the non-apprehension of anything other than that form within the object.
The intended meaning is that "it" (the cognition) is precisely the state of having that [object] as its qualifier in that which possesses it.
By the phrase "for this very reason," he incidentally rejects the view that memory lacks validity;
[the term] "pralāpaḥ" means mere idle chatter.
This means that [memory] is not a meaningless statement.

Furthermore, even with respect to a past external object, memory— which penetrates that very object as it truly is— is neither devoid of an object nor does it deviate from its object of cognition (*meyavyabhicāra*).
The meaning is that this is precisely because being "connected with the object of cognition" (prameyayogitva) consists in the fact of apprehending a particular qualifier in that which possesses it.
The phrase beginning with "atha tu" is a restatement of an objection; or alternatively, [the reading] is "ucyeta."
Or rather, the word "is held" (*matam*) should be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence].
The rebuttal begins with "If it is so," and so forth.

For one who asserts that because consciousness is self-established, its prior non-existence and other such states are unestablished, to now state the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) as the cause for that [non-existence] constitutes a different reason (*hetvantara*).
The meaning is that the absence of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇābhāva*) is also unestablished. This is because it has already been established;

for it was stated previously that "in states such as sleep, intoxication, and fainting, the existence of [the self] cannot be accepted, as its presence is excluded by the non-perception of a suitable object."

In this regard, the following should be understood: although the perception of its absence— namely, "I do not know"— is not possible with respect to the self during deep sleep even though consciousness is unmanifest (due to the contradiction of sleep itself),
for that [perception] consists in the absence of all knowledge whatsoever, including that which possesses an object.

Furthermore, since consciousness—which is by nature self-luminous—is not manifest during sleep, its non-existence at that time is established. This cognition of its absence is inferential, based on the mark (liṅga) of the non-apprehension of consciousness during sleep, which is characterized as a "non-perception of the capable" (yogyānupalabdhi), inferred from the rule of non-remembrance upon awakening.

And it is this very inference, through the universal property of being a cognition (jñānatva), which takes as its object one's own non-existence even during sleep; thus, it is established that the apprehension of its own prior non-existence occurs by itself.
He establishes the impermanence of cognitions by another method as well, with the words "api ca" (furthermore). "Na sādhayati" means it does not establish;
"tat" means therefore.
It is indeed delimited by a specific time—that is, it is merely occasional.
Through this occasional nature, there is a dramatic representation (*abhinaya*) of the manifestation of perception, such as: "I exist only now, not at other times.
Such a designation occurs precisely through the superimposition (*samādhyāropa*) of consciousness.

Alternatively, since others accept that the very fruit of valid cognition (*pramāṇaphala*) possesses both selfhood (*ātmatva*) and self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), the intention is that, according to their own view, the manifestation of the object of cognition would occur in this very manner.

As for the phrase "otherwise": because perception has the inherent nature of manifesting an object that is simultaneous with itself, if that [perception] were eternal, it would follow as a logical consequence that its objects, such as a jar, would also be eternal. This is the meaning.
As long as a jar or the like is not perceived, it is not because it does not exist,
but rather because, even though it exists, it is only at certain times; thus, the occasional nature of the perception of a jar or the like is not caused by the non-existence of the object.
However, the intended meaning is that [the cognition] is indeed characterized by its own occasional nature (*kādācitkatva*).

Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): perceptual consciousness does not pervade the time of its own object, because, while manifesting an object existing at the same time as itself, it does not manifest that object for as long as the object exists.
The word "thus" establishes the impermanence of cognitions such as inference and so forth, just like that of perception;
the ellipsis is "shining forth only as occasional.
For it is not possible for those [cognitions] which depend upon the consideration of a logical mark (*liṅga*) and so on to be eternal.
Furthermore, cognitions such as "I inferred" and "I remembered" indicate their own occasional nature;

for even though these cognitions lack the restriction of grasping an object at the same time [as its existence], their established occasional character is not conditioned by the non-existence of the object.
However, the sense is that [the permanence] is due solely to its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
Now, if it is argued that although cognitions possessing objects are impermanent, pure cognition devoid of an object is eternal, he says "nor" (*na ca*) in response.
In the terms *pratyakṣa* and *anumāna*, the suffix denotes the abstract state (*bhāvapradhāna*).
The natural usage of terms such as *dhī* (intellect) and *saṃvit* (consciousness) refers exclusively to knowledge that possesses an object (*saviṣayaka-jñāna*),
and it is a rule that their referent must necessarily have a substratum (*sāśrayatva*).
The underlying point is that, both by the force of perception and by the authority of scripture, even the knowledge of one's own nature (*svarūpa-jñāna*) is not devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣa*).
By this it is shown that pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra*) exists as eternal, devoid of distinctions, and self-luminous by nature.
It is precisely that [consciousness], when delimited by a modification of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇavṛtti*), which acts as the illuminator of objects.
Because the delimiting modification is occasional, there arises the perception of that [consciousness] as qualified [by it] as being non-eternal.
The view that "that very [consciousness] as delimited by the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is the knower" is also refuted.
Is the function (vṛtti) of the internal organ characterized by activity (vyāpāra), or is it characterized by modification (pariṇāma)?
It cannot be the first, because there is no manifestation of an object without the operation of cognition (jñāna-vyāpāra) based on that alone.
For in such passages as, "When the mind follows after the wandering senses,

it carries away one's wisdom; therefore, one's wisdom flows away," the establishment of the manifestation of objects is determined solely through the extension of cognition by way of the mind and the sense-faculties.

In some instances, the teaching regarding the non-difference between wisdom (*prajñā*) and the mind (*manas*) should be understood as figurative, because the mind possesses an activity that conforms to the activity of knowledge.
It is not the second [case],
for there is no very firm evidence for the mind having the same dimensions as the form of the object.

Furthermore, there is no evidence for the claim that consciousness is devoid of distinctions, by which one might more convincingly postulate that the knower and so forth are merely forms of adventitious difference. Moreover, this [position] is sublated by uncontradicted means of valid cognition such as perception and scripture, which establish the distinction between the unconditioned knower, the object of knowledge, and the act of knowing; therefore, enough of this for now.
Having thus stated that the proof of its own prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) is established by itself, he states it from another perspective as well with the words "nor by another" (*na cānya*).

Having stated that one's own past cognition is apprehended through memory and so forth, he states that even the cognition of another is apprehended by another cognition with the words "in the contrary" (*pratikūle*).

This means that the cognition of favorability or unfavorability regarding a specific object belonging to another person is inferable from the observation of their activity in the form of avoidance (*hāna*), acquisition (*upādāna*), and so forth.
He states the refutation regarding the non-acceptance of the fact that one cognition is graspable by another cognition with the words, "And if that is not accepted.

The meaning is that if the cognition of another [person] were not accepted, then since the apprehension of linguistic capacity (*śaktigraha*)—which occurs through linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*)—depends upon the inference of another's cognition, the very apprehension of capacity would be impossible; consequently, there would follow the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the total disappearance of linguistic usage, which is rooted in that [apprehension].

Alternatively, since the relationship between word and meaning—the relation of signifier and signified—is constituted by cognition, if one does not accept that a cognition is graspable by another cognition, then [the relationship] could not be established through grammar and so forth.
The meaning is that because demonstration would be impossible, there would follow the consequence of the total collapse of all verbal communication.
"By the impossibility of grasping word and meaning" means by the impossibility of grasping the relationship between word and meaning.
He says "approaching a teacher" (gurūpasarpaṇa) to show that even such things as approaching a teacher would be untenable if the inference of another's cognition were not admitted.
Of that teacher.
Now, he refutes the claim that being an object of experience is incompatible with being an experience itself, by stating: "Nor [is it] the state of having another as its object.
The term "of its own substratum" (svāśrayasya) is to be construed with both [parts of the compound].
At the time of its own existence, consciousness certainly possesses either the quality of manifesting itself to its own substrate or the quality of illuminating its own object for its own substrate.
This twofold nature of being an experience would not be possible at the time of its own existence if it were not manifesting itself to its own substrate or if it were not illuminating its own object.
That is not the case;

for even though [the experience] appears to its own substrate in its past state, or to another person in its present state by means of another cognition, the consequence of its losing the aforementioned nature of being an experience does not follow—this is the point.
Furthermore, he states that being an object of experience (*anubhāvyatva*) is not a decisive factor in its not being an experience (*ananubhūtitva*) by means of the phrase "of the jar and so forth."
Precisely because of the absence of such an intrinsic nature— that is, precisely because of the lack of the aforementioned two-fold character of being an experience—
it follows that it is "non-experience," meaning either its distinctness from experience or its non-denotability by the term "experience."

The introduction of a counter-objection (*pratibandī*) regarding the claim that being an object of experience (*anubhāvyatva*) alone is the cause for something not being an experience (*ananubhūtitva*) is expressed by the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).
The consequence of that (*tat-prasaṅga*) refers to the consequence of it not being an experience.
Its presentation as an example of what is non-existent is according to the opponent's own system (*paraprakriyayā*).
Thus, by establishing that consciousness is an object of experience, he also establishes that the self is likewise [an object of experience] and that it is distinct from consciousness;
"the state of being an experience" means having the nature of a cognition whose object is the [self].
Because it is the experiencer— that is, because its locus is the object—
it is not the case that "it [is not perceived] either.
For even though its own essential nature has a manifestation independent of another cognition, it is nevertheless graspable by cognitions such as hearing and so forth.

The meaning is that since even another person’s self can be inferred through such things as the movements occurring in their body, the claim that the self is not an object of experience is contrary to scripture and reasoning, and is therefore untenable.
Regarding the phrase "let it be accepted":

the point is that for objects like a jar, the fact that they are not the locus of knowledge is precisely what constitutes their being non-self; and let it be accepted that the sole determinant of their not being an experience (ananubhūtitva) is simply their non-opposition to ignorance (ajñāna), rather than their being an object of experience (anubhāvyatva).
The doubt here concerns the phrase "atha" (now/if): [it arises] because [the self] is not the substratum of those cognitions and is not opposed to cognition;
and [it concerns] its being an object, that is, its being something to be experienced.

The rebuttal is: "Even if they are not objects [of cognition], they would be just like that—like flowers in the sky. If it is argued that their non-existence alone is the cause [of their being non-existent] and not their unperceivability, then by that same logic, non-existence would also follow for [the self] insofar as it is unperceivable.

If it is argued that [the reason] lacks probative force (*aprayojakatva*), the underlying intention is that this is equally true even regarding the state of being an object of experience (*anubhāvyatva*).
Enough of this;
because it is rooted in a fallacy of pervasion (*vyāptyābhāsa*), it constitutes a mere fallacious argument (*kutarka*).
Therefore, it should be understood that "non-abiding" (apratiṣṭhitatva) means the absence of a culmination in the establishment of the intended object.
Thus, by establishing the nature of being an object of experience (anubhāvyatva), the proof of the prior non-existence of consciousness even from the perspective of the opponent is intended.

It should be noted that, although in our own system (siddhānta) knowledge as a quality (dharmabhūtajñāna) is eternal, its state characterized by specific conditions conducive to the illumination of objects is indeed non-eternal; thus, [the opponent's objection] is precisely what we accept.
Because consciousness is self-luminous, its prior non-existence (prāgabhāva) cannot be established;
and due to the absence of prior non-existence, it is unproduced, and for that very reason,
others have stated that it is devoid of the modifications of being (bhāvavikāra).

In that context, having taken for granted— as if already established— the fact that the reason "because it has not arisen" is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*) by means of supporting the proof of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of consciousness, he states that [the reason] is "inconstant" (*vyabhicarati*) in the inference that excludes other modifications.
The meaning of the locative case here is "delimiting factor" (*avacchedakatva*).
Its [the non-existence’s] connection is with the term "deviation" (*vyabhicāra*).
The meaning is that "unproducedness" deviates from the probandum (*sādhya*)—which consists in non-perishability—by way of being delimited by antecedent non-existence (*prāgabhāva*).

Since the locus of that [non-existence] itself serves as the delimiter of the property residing therein, it is established that the antecedent non-existence, which delimits the deviation residing in the reason, possesses both the state of having the reason (*hetumattva*) and the state of lacking the probandum (*sādhyābhāvavattva*).
Regarding the word *bhāve*:

even if "being a function of existence" (*bhāvavṭṭittva*) is used as a qualification of the reason (*hetu*)—namely, its being unarisen—the meaning is that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of beginningless ignorance (*anādi-avidyā*) as conceived by the opponent.

Since there is such a deviation, the instrumental case in *avidyayā* is intended to express that ignorance is the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) for the desire to state that [non-arising] is the cause of that [existence].
He raises a doubt in order to avoid the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) with the words "non-ultimate" (*aparamārtha*). The probandum (*sādhya*) is the absence of ultimate transformation;
and since that absence—namely, the ultimate transformation—is not present in ignorance (*avidyā*), there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*). This is the intended meaning.
"He replies, 'And [regarding] the ultimate realities'":
"of you" (*te*)—
the word "in your view" (*mate*) is to be supplied.

One would perceive the meaningfulness— i.e., the state of having a connected meaning— either of the probandum (sādhya), such as the modification (vikāra) that constitutes it, or of the means of proof (sādhana),
such as the origination (utpatti) that constitutes it.
Or rather, it is purposeful as a means of excluding deviation (*vyabhicāra*).

It was stated [in the text] that "or [it is for the sake of] the probans," in order to prevent the fallacy of the unestablished nature of the essential character (*svarūpāsiddhi*) by virtue of the possibility of even consciousness having an imagined origination.

This is the intended meaning: since you do not admit real modification or real origination, the qualification of "ultimate reality" (*pāramārthika*) applied to both the probandum and the reason is untenable.
Because it would follow that the negative concomitance (*vyatireka-vyāpti*) between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*) would be unestablished;
and because, in the absence of such qualification, there would be no possibility of avoiding either deviation (*vyabhicāra*) or the lack of essential proof (*svarūpāsiddhi*).
Thus it is said: "And this being so... (*tathā ca sati*).
This is a statement of censure containing irony;

for it means that even when a qualification is provided, the intention of one who wishes to employ a qualification as a precluder of deviation is not fulfilled, and thus no valid observation is established. This is the underlying sense.
Having restated the claim that "consciousness is undifferentiated because it is unarisen," he refutes it with the words "even that [is not so].

The meaning is that even that [refutation] is not [valid], because differences—whether of the same kind, of a different kind, or internal—are established by uncontradicted perception and other means of knowledge; therefore, the inference that negates them has a contradicted object.

[Vasubandhu] states "of that which is unborn" (*ajasyaiva*) to point out the inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) [of the reason] when one wishes to prove non-arising in the negation of a distinction from heterogeneous things (*vijātīya-bheda*).
He states "by virtue of being beginningless" (*anāditvena*) with respect to the ignorance (*ajñāna*) accepted by the opponent as well.

With the conceit that since the distinction between self and non-self is not ultimately real, there is no lack of pervasion (*anaikāntya*) when negating ultimate difference, he raises an objection with the words "not ultimately real.
He refutes this conceit with the words "ultimate difference.
"Bound to birth" means being pervaded by the state of having an origin (*utpattimatva*).
For it must be stated that there is a negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) such that "whatever possesses ultimate difference has arisen";
yet this is not the case, because in your system, ultimate difference itself is unestablished (*aprasiddha*).
Thus, if you were to provide such a qualification, it would result in the fallacy of the reason being unestablished (*asiddhi*).
The sense is that if the qualification is not included, the fallacy of inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) is difficult to avoid.

Nor should it be argued that the probandum (*sādhya*) is established as the absence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) resides in a difference qualified by a property residing in a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇadharma*), such as "ultimate reality" (*paramārthatva*), and thus there is no fault.

Even so, in your view, since there is no other instance apart from the subject (*pakṣa*) for grasping the concomitance (*sāhacarya*) between the reason and the probandum, there is simply a failure to establish pervasion (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*).

This is because, given that an absence whose counter-positive is delimited by a property residing in a different locus is a purely positive (*kevalānvayi*) phenomenon, it is impossible even to state a negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*).
Nor should it be said that the eternality and non-differentiation of pure consciousness (saṃvinmātra) are established by scripture alone;
for even scripture contradicts your position.
For it is described in detail elsewhere that in the scriptures, the ultimate difference between the eternal categories of consciousness, matter, and the Lord is indeed taught.
And this will become clear later.

When the negation of internal difference within consciousness (*saṃvit*) is being established, he states that there is sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) with the words "unsublated" (*nirbādhe*).
[This refers to] the difference between the seer and the seen (*dṛgdṛśyabheda*), [which is perceived] by the various acts of seeing (*dṛśām*).
There is a mutual distinction between objects of sight and that which is both the seer and the seen.
He states the refutation even regarding the inference that denies internal differentiation within consciousness with the words "tadapi" (that too).

By stating that the properties of consciousness (*saṃvid*) are established by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it follows that the proof for the negation of properties within consciousness is vitiated by the fallacy of "missing the time" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*).

For this very reason, it is appropriate to point out a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the subject itself (*pakṣa*) regarding the inference that negates the properties of consciousness—whether that inference be a negative one (*vyatirekin*) having consciousness as its subject, or a positive one (*anvayin*) having the properties as its subject.

To the objection that there is no harm in an inference negating distinct properties because the properties of consciousness are non-different from consciousness itself, he replies: "Even though that [consciousness] is established... (*tatsiddhāv api*).
The meaning is that it is not possible for the objects of dispute—the various phenomena (*dharmas*)—to have the nature of a single, common consciousness (*saṃvit*).

Furthermore, he states "and because of the difference in essential nature" (*svarūpabhedāt ca*), asserting that there is no identity between consciousness and its attributes due to their difference in form (*ākāra*), just as there is none between a jar and a cloth.
He then establishes this very difference in essential nature with the words beginning "its own substrate" (*svāśrayam*).
The manifestation of some particular object—
that is, the bringing about of its illumination— is what is meant by "cognition" (*saṃvedana*); this is an expression where the abstract state is emphasized.
That is to say, the state of being consciousness;
or rather, illumination— that which illuminates—
for itself, for its own sake.
Or [it may be] for its own substratum.

The nature of cognition (*saṃvedana*) consists in its being the illuminator of its own object with respect to its own substratum; and the self-luminosity of cognition consists in its being manifest by itself. Thus, one should understand the difference in the essential natures (*svarūpa-bheda*) of these two properties.
He states the meaning of the term "manifestation" (*prakāśa*), which is included within the very nature of being a consciousness and self-luminosity, with the words: "And manifestation...
This manifestation is a specific property (*dharma*) synonymous with "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*).
Furthermore, this does not belong to that which is merely insentient (*jaḍa*).
But this applies even to conscious objects;
thus it is said [in the *Saṃvitsiddhi*]: "It is common to all objects, both conscious and unconscious. This is stated in the *Saṃvitsiddhi* itself.
The meaning is that this is for the purpose of establishing the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of consciousness;
or rather, the meaning is that it is specifically within the treatise titled *Saṃvitsiddhi*.
By this, it is understood that the *Saṃvitsiddhi* was composed prior to the *Ātmasiddhi*.
Although the definition of the category of "manifestation" (prakāśa) is not found in the extant portion of the *Saṃvitsiddhi* text currently available,
it should nevertheless be understood that this is possible, given that many portions of the *Saṃvitsiddhi*— at the beginning, the end, and the middle— are lost.
Even when one does not accept the manifestation of a distinct entity (dharmanantara), he says: "the non-acceptance of that.
What is designated by the word "manifestation" is simply conformity with linguistic usage (vyavahāra), which is dependent upon cognition.
The point is that even for that which is not currently being used in linguistic discourse, its fitness for linguistic usage through cognition remains entirely unimpaired.
The delimitation by the number one is the state of possessing the number one. He raises an objection: "And not [if there were] insentience," meaning the absence of insentience in its own...
Luminosity is its nature; omnipresence and eternity consist in being unconditioned by space and time;
and unity is the absence of multiplicity.
However, these are not positive entities.

The point is that since non-existence (abhāva) consists of its locus (adhikaraṇa), it does not follow that consciousness (saṃvid) possesses properties [of non-existence]. He refutes this with the words "even by those of such a nature.
This means that non-existences are either not distinct [from their loci] or consist of other properties residing in the locus.

The meaning is that, because the natural intuition of the relationship between the locus and the located (ādhārādheya-bhāva) arises, it is unavoidable that [consciousness] shares the same properties even as non-existence.
That alone is of the nature of non-existence upon whose cognition the notion of the object to be negated does not arise;
and since doubts regarding impermanence and so forth arise even while consciousness is being cognized, it cannot be of the nature of non-existence.

However, the intended meaning is that eternality and so forth are characterized precisely by other opposing attributes, such as being connected with all times. Regarding the phrase "in consciousness" (*saṃvidi*):
without the cognition of the possession of opposing attributes, it would be impossible for the proposition to negate insentience (*jaḍatva*) and the like.
And the sense is that, upon the cognition of that [consciousness], the establishment of its possessing common properties (sadharmatva) is unavoidable.
Nor should it be argued that the proposition makes known only the nature of consciousness as being opposed to qualities such as insentience (jaḍatva), and not its possession of opposing attributes;
for it is not established that consciousness—which serves as the substratum (adhiṣṭhāna) for all superimpositions—is opposed to everything.

Nor should it be said that "it is pure in that way," because if one accepts that it is the opposite of all specific qualities (*viśeṣa*), then just as it is the opposite of insentience (*jaḍatva*) and so forth, it must also be the opposite of non-insentience (*ajaḍatva*) and so forth; consequently, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) follows that it would be distinct from both the insentient and the sentient, and so on. If you argue that even in the absence of non-insentience and the like, it is by its very nature (*svarūpa*) non-insentient and so forth, then why should it not also be by its very nature a property (*dharma*) even in the absence of being a property? This is the direction of the argument.

He also states that there is "inconclusiveness" (*anaikāntya*) in proving the absence of connection with consciousness for the subject of properties such as difference, by saying "the object of cognition" (*cetyam*).
"The object of cognition" means that which is experienced.
"In the self" means in the self that is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).
Furthermore, the proof for the absence of the property of consciousness (*ciddharmatva*) is untenable,
because the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is not established. Nor is the statement "properties are not of consciousness" particularly sound.
The phrase "api ca" (furthermore) is stated because the meaning of the genitive case—namely, the relation (*saṃbandha*)—cannot be construed with the term *cit*.

The intention is that since it is a linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) that suffixes convey their own meaning as connected to the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*), the connection of *cit* with the meaning of the case-ending is established; therefore, the proposition denying both the particular and the universal in that regard has a contradictory meaning.
If the establishment [of consciousness] were accepted, consciousness would possess attributes;
if not, its utter non-existence would be asserted, like that of a rabbit's horn. //10//
Is it not indeed an accomplishment?
Of what, sir? If it is of nothing, then it is not an accomplishment at all.
If it is argued that it [the self] indeed belongs to someone in a certain way, as if it were their sonhood,
then what is the meaning of the genitive case?

Thus, if the nature [of the self] were like that of a sky-lotus according to the aforementioned view, the description of the purport of the Vedānta would result in nothing but the Vedānta itself [as a mere fiction].
Moreover, even if experience were eternal, the impossibility of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) would remain exactly as it was;
for recognition establishes an experiencer who persists through prior and subsequent times, in the form: "I experienced this."
Experience, however, is simply experience for you; with respect to that [experience], it is neither an agent nor an object.
(This concludes the section refuting the nature of the self as eternal consciousness, as maintained by the proponents of Māyā.)

If it should be argued: "Even though [the self] is such [non-existent] from the perspective of ultimate reality, it appears as an experiencer due to delusion, just as mother-of-pearl appears as silver;
for a false appearance cannot arise without depending upon something real," that is not so.
For if that were the case, the referent of the "I" (the self) would appear as co-referential with the experience itself, such that the experience would manifest as "I am the experience."
Just as the form of a luminous object standing before one—such as a conch, the moon, or the like—is perceived as being silver, yellow, or located in a mirror, or as having a dual nature;

so too this experience, appearing as something distinct, is observed to qualify the "I-sense" (the *ahamartha*) as a separate entity, just as a staff qualifies Devadatta, in the cognition "I experience.

Therefore, since this notion of "I" manifests the "I-sense" as qualified by such an experience, how could it be asserted that its objective support is merely the experience itself acting as a qualifier?
The cognition is like that of "Devadatta is a staff-bearer" [where the staff is distinct from the person].
And from what source is this certainty derived—that the state of being a knower is superimposed?
If it is argued that it is because it appears to one who possesses the conceit of identity with the body, just as in the thought "I am fat";
But surely, even the experience that is considered to be the self appears as something distinct from it; therefore, that too should be [non-self] in the same way.
If you argue that it is not so because it persists even after the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), then tell me:
is this self merely an object of cognition subsequent to the knowledge of reality?
Ah, in that case, it would be better not to know reality at all;
for even through delusion, one perceives much that is auspicious therein.
But surely, the state of being a knower is the agency of the act of knowing; it is subject to modification, insentient, and resides within the knot of the ego.

The Self is the enjoyer of that fruit, yet it is a non-agent, changeless, a witness, and pure luminosity. For agency and the like, being objects of perception, are not attributes of the Self— just as color and other qualities are not—

because if the Self were an agent, then even though it were the object of the notion of "I," it would unavoidably follow that it is non-self, subservient to another, and insentient, just like the body.

Moreover, it is observed in worldly and Vedic actions that there is a distinction between the body—which is well-known as the agent—and the cognizer who experiences the fruits of those actions and possesses the sense of "I.
Likewise, here too, it is logical that the witness, the inner self (*pratyagātman*), is distinct from the cognizer whose nature is the "I.
This is not, however, correct.
For apart from the inner self (pratyagātman), which is established as the knower through the thought "I know," no other self consisting of mere luminosity called the "knower" is perceived.

Indeed, when one distinguishes [the self] from the body, senses, mind, vital breath, and cognition as the substratum of knowledge, it is the very state of "I-ness" (ahambhāva)—which appears as if facing inward—that constitutes what is called "inner-directedness" (pratyaktva).
Its status as a witness (sākṣitva) likewise consists in its being an immediate knower.
For one who does not know is not designated as a "knower.
And it is established by personal experience that everything which is manifest shines forth to the knower as "I am," appearing thus: "I know" and "it manifests to me."
(Thus concludes the determination of the nature of the inner self as the "I" which is the knower.
Nor can that which is called the ego (ahaṅkāra)—whether designated as the intellect (buddhi) or as a particular transformation of the undifferentiated (avyākṛta)—be the knower;
for, like the body, it is untenable as such due to reasons such as its being insentient, subject to transformation, inert, and existing for the sake of another.
Nor can that [consciousness] arise for those two through the falling of a reflection of consciousness,
because no shadow is observed of that which is not visible to the eye; nor, moreover, does knowership exist in reality even in consciousness according to you.

By means of which [contact], just as heat arises in a lump [of iron] through contact with fire, so too would the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) arise or be known in another entity through contact with that [Self].
(This concludes the examination of the impossibility of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) being the knower and the cognition thereof.
If it were argued: "The ego-sense, though insentient, manifests the Self—which is merely the capacity for knowing—as its own substrate."

For this is the nature of manifestors: that they manifest what is to be manifested by being situated within themselves, just as a mirror, water, a fragment of rock, or a head manifest the face, the solar orb, or the universal "cowness" (gotva), respectively.
And it is due to this [nature] that the delusion arises: "I know."
For this very reason, indeed, when the mental representation (*ullekha*) has vanished, the Self shines forth in deep sleep and liberation as nothing other than its own natural, lucid experience;
and for that same reason, the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) is non-self (*anātman*).
Thus says the Lord of the Sun:
“If the self were my nature, it would persist in liberation and deep sleep;
since it does not persist there, this ‘I’ must belong to something else.
(Thus concludes the preliminary argument establishing that the ego-sense is the manifestor of consciousness.)
He establishes that consciousness possesses attributes by another method as well, with the words "and if [its] establishment...
Here, "establishment" (siddhi) means manifestation (prakāśa).
If that is accepted, then by that very fact, consciousness would possess attributes.

However, if that [nature] is not admitted, then because it would be unmanifest—like the horn of a hare—and thus unestablished, its sheer non-existence (tucchatva) would follow; such is the meaning of the verse. //10//
Here an objection is raised: "But surely it is [simply] establishment.
[The reply is: Consciousness is not that which has manifestation as its substrate, but rather consciousness is of the very nature of manifestation itself.
The meaning is that it is neither a state of non-existence (tucchatva) nor a state of possessing real properties (sadharmakatva).
[The opponent] challenges this by asking, "Of what, sir?
Fearing the consequence of [the object] having specific qualities (saviśeṣatva), the other says, "Of nothing."
The proponent replies, "In that case, it is not so.
The meaning is that a property (*dharma*), such as manifestation (*prakāśa*), cannot exist without a substratum (*dharmin*).
He demonstrates that proof (*siddhi*) possesses a relational nature by stating, "For that... and so forth.
For a son belongs to a father;
the point is that the establishment [of a relationship] is dependent upon a correlative and a counter-correlative, just like the state of being a son.
He says "of the self" because there is no other possible recourse.
The meaning is that the establishment of consciousness is such that its substrate is the self and its counter-correlate is also the self.
Here, the word "self" (ātman) denotes one's own nature (svarūpa). If this is so, then consciousness would indeed possess attributes; to this he says: "What [is there]? (ka iti).

The meaning is that, just as a son possesses "sonship" in relation to his father, so too does consciousness (saṃvit) possess the attribute of luminosity (prakāśa) in relation to itself; thus the nature of the conscious self is established. In this way, the meaning of the verse has been explained through several steps consisting of objections and their refutations. Having thus refuted the claim that consciousness is devoid of distinctions (nirviśeṣatva), he says "tadevam" [therefore, thus], stating that describing the purport of the Vedāntas as being directed toward a consciousness devoid of distinctions results ultimately in the invalidation of the authority of the Vedāntas.
"For the sake of the destruction of the Vedānta," that is to say, "for the eradication of the authority of the Vedas";

for when the doctrine of a self consisting of momentary consciousness has been refuted on the grounds that recollection and other such phenomena would be untenable, those who maintain the doctrine of a self consisting of eternal consciousness arise.
Even in this view, he states that [the proof] is "api ca" (furthermore).
The meaning is that the validity of such [cognitions] as "I experienced this" is possible only if the knower is eternal,
and not merely by the eternity of cognition itself.
He explains this very point with the words "experience" (*anubhūtiḥ*).
He states the meaning of the particle *eva* (only) with the words "not that" (*na tām*).
Even though, according to our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), experience does not possess the status of being an experiencer; [nevertheless, it is so designated].
Furthermore, if it is maintained that there is the state of being experienced,
and that the self, which is the knower and the referent of "I," is eternal,
then the recollection of previous experiences and so forth becomes logically possible.

In the view of the opponent, however, because consciousness and the self are neither objects of experience nor subjects of experience, the aforementioned unification of cognitions is simply untenable; this is the intended meaning.
Thus, by the force of this unification, it is established in the mind that the nature of the self belongs to the knower alone, and not to mere cognition.
This very point will be further supported by the subsequent body of the text.
In this regard, he first restates the opponent's position regarding the erroneous nature of the cognition of being a knower, beginning with the words "yadi ucyeta" (if it is said).
Pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*) is the ultimate reality;
that alone is the self (*ātman*).
In this substrate, the error of the knower regarding the object "I" is like that of silver in mother-of-pearl.

The intention of the opponents is that, for the sake of accounting for such delusion, the ultimate reality must be accepted as the mere consciousness of the substrate. He refutes this, saying: "That is not so."

"If that were so" means the following intention: when one property is superimposed upon a substratum that possesses another property, there would be an appearance of the superimposed object and its locus as being co-referential (that is, non-different), just as in the case of "this is silver."

Furthermore, when there is the superimposition of one property upon another, it is observed that the object appears as possessing that superimposed property, as in the cases: "the conch is yellow," "the face is in the mirror," and "there are two moons."
Furthermore, in this case, there is no such manifestation of experience as "I" or "possessing-I-ness.
Therefore, it is not logical that the referent of "I" (ahamartha) is superimposed upon consciousness.
On the other hand, the acceptance by the opponents that consciousness is superimposed upon the referent of "I" is untenable, because of the rule that a superimposition must have a real substratum.
And it should be understood that this is because the referent of the "I" (ahamartha) is unreal.
Regarding the word "separately" (pṛthak): appearing separately means appearing as a qualifier (prakāra) distinct from the qualified (prakārī).

The meaning is that because the cognition "I am a staff-bearer" is equivalent [in structure] to the cognition "I know," the cognition "I know" must likewise involve the apprehension of the quality of knowledge (jñāna-dharmavattā) residing in the referent of the "I" (ahamartha).
Thus, in the phrase "tadevam," the locative case in "daṇḍamātre" denotes the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*).
The meaning is that [the self] has the mere staff as its objective support.

Just as in the case of "the man with the staff," there is neither the reality of the mere staff nor the falsity of the man, so too in the case of "I know," there is neither the reality of the mere cognition nor the falsity of the knower.

However, the intention [of the author] is that it is more reasonable to accept the reality of the "I-sense" (ahamartha) as the knower, because no subverting evidence is perceived. To the question, "If the cognition of being a knower is an error, what is the determining factor?"— that is, "on what grounds?"—
the proponent (pūrvapakṣin) replies to that:
He says, "It is called gross," meaning that because it is apprehended by those under delusion, its status as a knower is characterized by superimposition (adhyāsa).

Keeping in mind the intention that this does not prove superimposition—since it is fallacious due to being overqualified (sopādhika) by the fact of being sublated—he states a counter-argument: "But [if you say] 'as the Self'... and so forth.

He states the resolution through the mouth of the opponent—that consciousness is not false because it remains unsublated even when apprehended by one who has the delusion that the body is the self—by saying, "Because of the arising of the knowledge of reality.
He says, "What [is this]? meaning that this same non-superimposed nature of being a knower applies equally.
His intention is that since the state of being a knower persists even in liberation, which is the fruit of the knowledge of reality, it is therefore unsublated.
With the words "Alas, if this were so," he introduces the undesirable consequence that would follow if the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) were to cease in liberation.

The sense is this: if it is argued that liberation is the human goal because it consists in the cessation of suffering, then it follows as an unwanted consequence that it is not a human goal because of the cessation of the experience of bliss and the cessation of the experiencer. He raises an objection, suggesting that liberation does not suffer a loss of its status as a human goal even upon the cessation of being a knower and so forth, on the grounds that these are not properties of the Self: "But [what of] the state of being a knower? etc.
Ego (ahaṅkāra) is the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa);
that very thing is a "knot" (granthi) because it is difficult to untie.

The state of being a knower (jñātṛtva) is based solely upon that [ego]; its meaning is that it consists of transformation characterized by the nature of knowledge, is of the nature of change, and is insentient because it is a transformation of the insentient.
He states the true nature of the self with regard to its fruit:
it is the enjoyer of the fruit of agency,
yet it is not an agent because of its changelessness.

The meaning is that the Self exists as a witness by virtue of having the nature of pure luminosity (*prakāśamātra*). That which has luminosity alone as its measure is "pure luminosity" (*prakāśamātra*).
Regarding the phrase "in the state of being an agent" (*kartṛtve*): [it refers to the following].

The self (ātman) is neither the agent nor the referent of "I" (ahamartha), because it possesses the nature of being the self, because it exists for its own sake, because it is non-inert, or because it is changeless; for whatever does not possess these [qualities] is not thus, just like the body—these logical arguments are implied here. How can there be the state of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva) for that which is distinct from the agent?
Regarding this, he says, "It is seen. He refutes this with "Not so.

Having stated that the self, as a mere luminosity distinct from the knower, is sublated by its non-perception, he says, "The body and the senses," etc., asserting that the status of the self as the referent of "I" must be accepted precisely on the strength of its own inwardness (*pratyaktva*).
Since knowledge is impossible in the body and so forth, the distinctness of the Self from them has indeed been established;
therefore, the status of being the knower must be attributed to the Self. If the body and so forth were the object of the notion of "I," [then they would be the knower].
In that context, the *ahaṃkāra* (I-maker) is indeed of the nature of self-conceit (*ābhimānika*).

The opposition—that is, the contrariety—of that state of "I-ness" (*ahaṃbhāva*) consists in its being contrary to the sense of "mine-ness" (*mambhāva*) residing in the body and so forth. And because it moves toward what is opposite (*pratīpam añcati*), it is "pratyak," the object of the *ahaṃkāra*.
Because of that inwardness (*pratyaktva*), the state of "I-ness" (*ahantva*) accrues to the Self.

There is a poetic conceit (*utprekṣā*) that [the ego] seems to move along a contrary or opposite path toward the Self, the Seer, which is opposed to the body and other objects of perception that fall within the scope of the notion of "this" (*idaṅkāra*).
In the root [of the word *pratyañc*], the form *añcati* ends in the locative case.
The phrase "when the self is present" is the ellipsis [to be supplied].
As for the term "witnesshood," the sense is that it is based on the grammatical rule: "The term *sākṣin* is used in the sense of one who sees directly."
And all that is to be known shines forth from the knower himself, not from mere cognition alone;
therefore, the selfhood belongs to the knower alone and not to mere cognition—this he states with the word "all.
The word "cakāsate" ends in the dative case.

Therefore, the status of being a witness is not possible for mere consciousness alone, but only for the knower; thus, the intended meaning is that the nature of the Self belongs to that [knower] alone, and not to mere consciousness.
As for the claim that the state of being a knower consists of modification—that is not so.
For those who know the heart of the Upaniṣads do not accept, as the followers of Kapila do, that "knowership" consists in being subject to the transformation of knowledge;
rather, it is simply the state of being the substratum of *dharmabhūtajñāna* (knowledge as an attribute), which possesses the activity necessary for the manifestation of objects.
This applies to [the self] when it has an object.
This is because, in the sense of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), agency consists in being a substratum (*āśrayatva*),
just as objecthood (*karmatva*) consists in being an objective domain (*viṣayatā*).
As for the claim that the state of being an enjoyer belongs to someone other than the agent:
That too is incorrect;

for primary agency—consisting in being the substratum of an internal effort preceded by knowledge and desire that are conducive to bodily actions such as grasping—is logically possible only in the self (ātman). Indeed, those who know the heart of the Vedas and Upaniṣads hold that "the fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer; the agent [is the one entitled to the fruit], because the scripture must have a purpose."
As for the claim that agency and so forth are not attributes of the self because they are objects of perception, that too is weak;

for if "being an object of perception" means being graspable by the external senses, then that is unestablished with respect to the subject, which is characterized as the substratum of internal effort.
If that [property] is "being an object of experience," then the reason is unproving (*aprayojaka*).
As for the application of "non-selfhood" (*anātmatva*) and so forth to agency (*kartṛtva*) and the rest, [it is likewise unproving].
That too has its root shattered;

for it is only that which is non-primary [the intellect] which is pervaded by "non-selfhood" and so forth, whereas since "non-selfhood" and the like cannot possibly apply to the Self—which is the primary locus of agency and the substrate of the notion of "I"—this is the summary. Having thus stated that knowership, "I-ness," and so forth belong primarily to the Self alone, he says that knowership is untenable in the intellect (buddhi)—known as the Great Principle (mahat-tattva)—which is a specific transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti), or in the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), which is its effect.
And as for the phrase "nor in the indeterminate":
this refers to the state of being insentient— that is, the absence of a self— but not the absence of being a knower.
Because it would entail the undesirable consequence that the probandum and the reason are identical.

Alternatively, the syllogism is: "The Great Principle (mahān) or the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) is not a knower, because it is non-self, or because it is subject to transformation, or because it is insentient, or because it exists for the sake of another, like the body.

Now, one might object: even if the status of being a knower is impossible [in the primary sense], let there be the perception of being a knower therein through the falling of a reflection of consciousness (cicchāyā), or through contact with consciousness; to this, he says: "And not consciousness... (naca citīti).

Because consciousness is formless, a reflection of it cannot occur within the intellect (*buddhi*) or other such faculties; otherwise, there would be an appearance of consciousness therein, just as there is an appearance of redness in a crystal. Furthermore, the status of being a knower does not exist in consciousness itself.

The sense is that through contact with that [consciousness], there might arise in it either the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) or the manifestation thereof, just as iron acquires heat and its manifestation through contact with fire.
The expression "it would arise or be known" means that a quality or a defect produced by such contact arises and is perceived therein.

Now, in order to account for the cognition of the state of being a knower, he restates the position favored by the opponent—that the *ahaṅkāra* manifests consciousness—beginning with the words "If it is said... and so forth.
Manifesting means making manifest;
[it is so called] by virtue of being its own substratum— that is, by virtue of being supported by it—
[the suffix] *tal* being applied to a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
The various individual cows, such as Khaṇḍa, Muṇḍa, and others;
the orb of Mihira—the solar disc;
the remainder is clear.

"And caused by that" means that the appearance of the ego (ahaṅkāra) as the substratum of consciousness is due to its being the manifestor of consciousness; just as the appearance of a mirror as possessing a face is due to its being the manifestor of the face. This is the meaning.
He states "for this very reason" to show that the sense of "I-ness" (ahaṃbhāva) belongs only to a specific transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti), and not to the Self (ātman);
for the perception of being a knower is an illusion.
For this very reason, the Self appears as pure consciousness alone during deep sleep and liberation;
the point is that at those times, there is no appearance of the sense of "I.
This is the meaning of the phrase "for this very reason."

The meaning is that the "I-object" (ahamartha) is non-self precisely because of the absence of any mention of the "I-sense" (ahambhāva) in the experience of the self whose nature is the pearl of deep sleep;
in this regard, he cites the words of Sureśvarācārya as a corroborative authority, beginning with "of the Self."
If the sense of "I" (ahambhāva) were a property of the Self (ātmadharma), it would persist—meaning it would follow—during deep sleep and liberation;
since it does not so follow, the meaning is that this [sense of "I"] is indeed not a property of the Self.
This [argument] is incoherent, because:
It is not logical to say that egoity, which is insentient by nature and like extinguished embers, reveals the Self, which is self-luminous, as if it were the sun. (11)
"For it is intended that the manifestation of all objects depends upon the non-inert experience (anubhava) which is regarded as the Self.

That the insentient ego (ahaṅkāra)—whose own establishment depends upon that experience—should manifest such an experience, which accomplishes all objects and whose nature is a light devoid of the fluctuations of rising and setting; this is a laughingstock for the knowers of the Self.
With these words, he rejects this position [of the opponent] with the phrase "this, therefore" (tad idam).
He states "In the case of the tranquil [fire]" (*śānte*) because it is illogical and untenable for the insentient ego (*ahaṅkāra*) to illuminate self-luminous consciousness.
