"Tranquil embers" (*śāntāṅgāra*) refers to a mass of fire extinguished by water.

The meaning is that just as it is impossible for something of a non-luminous nature to illuminate the sun, which consists of light, so too it is impossible for the insentient ego—a specific transformation of *prakṛti*—which is itself non-luminous by nature, to illuminate the essential nature of the self, which is self-luminous consciousness.
He elaborates on this very point with the words beginning "ātmatve" and so forth:

[the opponent argues that] the illuminator of all objects sometimes illuminates and at other times does not; however, the self, whose nature is experience, is a constant illumination, devoid of the alternating states of rising and setting.

The meaning is that this contradictory statement— that the insentient *ahaṅkāra*, whose manifestation is invariably dependent upon that [consciousness], manifests it— is a source of ridicule even for those who know the reality of the Self and stand nearby;
for indeed, there is no need for another illuminator for that which accomplishes everything, which is self-established, and which is the nature of the ever-present experience.
Furthermore, the insentient ego (ahaṅkāra), which is necessarily manifested by that [consciousness], lacks the capacity to illuminate it;
thus, the claim that experience is manifested by the ego would be untenable—this is the sense.
Moreover: "The relationship of the manifested and the manifestor cannot exist between them due to their mutual opposition."
If [the self] were something manifested, it would lack the nature of experience, just as a jar does. //12//
Do not say that the palm of the hand, which is manifested by the rays of the sun, is seen as the manifestor [of those rays];
for the palm is merely the cause of their increased intensity.
Since the solar rays are clearly perceived in such a state, they cannot be said to be manifested by the palm.
Moreover, what is this "manifestation" (abhivyakti) which is said to be produced by the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) for the Self whose nature is experience? That [manifestation] is not established.
This is because it is accepted as being established by itself, and thus its establishment does not depend on anything else;
nor is there a cognition having that [self] as its object, because it cannot be experienced by another cognition.
For if it were an object of experience, it would follow that it lacks the nature of experience, just like a jar or other such objects;
for this very reason, it cannot be an auxiliary to the instrument of knowledge.
For that [knowledge] functions either by removing the obstacles to the arising of knowledge regarding the object of cognition, like a lamp which dispels deep darkness for the eye;

or by acting as a limiting condition for the contact with the object of cognition, like a manifesting mirror or the like for the eye and other senses which perceive universals, one's own face, and so forth;
or by washing away the blemishes residing in the knower, like tranquility, self-restraint, and so forth, for the scriptures and other means of knowing the reality of the higher and lower Self.
There is nothing within the scope of experience that can be removed by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) which acts as an obstacle to the arising of knowledge.

However, ignorance (*ajñāna*), because it shares the same locus and object as knowledge, cannot be attributed to the Witness (*sākṣin*) you propose, for that Witness is devoid of both [knowledge and its opposite].
Indeed, a jar or similar object, being devoid of the possibility of knowledge, is not said to be "ignorant."
In the same way, since the status of being a knower never belongs to pure consciousness alone, it too could not possess ignorance; or,
even if such ignorance were to exist, it cannot be accepted as something removable by the sense of "I" (ahaṅkāra), because ignorance is to be removed solely by knowledge.
Furthermore, because of such an admission:
knowledge removes ignorance only with respect to its own object;

and since it is not accepted that the experience (anubhava) which is considered to be the Self has that [knowledge] as its object, the ignorance pertaining to that [Self] would never be destroyed by anything at any time.
Furthermore, it cannot be asserted that ignorance, in the form of the prior non-existence of knowledge, acts as an obstacle to the arising of knowledge.

That ignorance is a positive entity (*bhāva-rūpa*), indeterminable (*anirvacanīya*), and the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world, and so forth, is mere verbiage; this will be demonstrated in the examination of relations (*saṃbandha-nirūpaṇa*).
Therefore, the manifestation of experience through the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) does not consist in the removal of defects from the object of cognition.
Let it be that experience is manifested by something, or let it be that the ego (ahaṅkāra) possesses some power of manifestation;
however, it is untenable for the ego—which has as its sole nature being manifested by that [experience]—to possess the capacity to manifest that [experience]. Thus he says, "Furthermore" (kiñca).
Regarding the term "vyaṅgye" (in the case of the manifested):
the relationship of mutual manifestation between the nature of experience (*anubhavātman*) and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is untenable.
This is because of their opposition; that is to say, due to their state of antagonism, characterized as a contradiction of essential natures (*svabhāvavirodha*), as previously stated.
It has been stated that it is indeed contradictory for that which is manifested by something to be the very means of manifesting it.
For the ego (ahaṅkāra), its manifestation must depend upon consciousness (saṃvit) alone for it to be the manifester of that [consciousness];
because a false object, whose existence depends upon its appearance, cannot even have existence when its appearance is absent.
Furthermore, consciousness itself, while manifesting, must manifest the ego-sense;
otherwise, it would follow that it is insentient.
And thus, it would be stated that the manifestation of consciousness is dependent upon the ego-sense, whose own manifestation is dependent upon self-luminous consciousness.

Furthermore, there would be a mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*): the manifestation of the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) would depend upon the manifestation of consciousness (*saṃvit*), and the manifestation of consciousness would depend upon the manifestation of the ego. Moreover, another interpretation has been described by the venerable Nigamānta-guru in his *Tattvaṭīkā*, stating that because of the opposition to the previously stated definition and due to the occurrence of subverting arguments, the relationship of the manifested and the manifester cannot possibly exist between consciousness and the ego. Regarding the view of the opponent that consciousness is manifested by the ego, he states another refutation [beginning with] "If it were manifested": *Vyaṅgyatve...* [and so forth].
The meaning is that if experience were to have its manifestation dependent on something else, it would follow that it is not an experience, just like a jar or other such objects. //12//

He dispels the doubt that there is no contradiction even if that which is manifested (the suggested meaning) also acts as a manifestor (of something else), because such a thing is observed, by the words "in the case of the sun" (*dinakare*).
For the palm of the hand serves merely as a cause for the concentration [of light] by obstructing the movement of the sun's rays that have entered through the opening of a window.
And he says "of the palm of the hand" (*karatalasya*) to show that for those [elements] when combined, there is a clear manifestation by their own nature.

The underlying intention is that it is as difficult to establish—as it is for the palm of the hand—that the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), being formless, can be the cause of the clear manifestation of consciousness even by obstructing its movement;
thus, it has been stated that the manifestability of the conscious self by means of the ego is both unnecessary and untenable.
He states "Moreover, etc. because even among the possible modes of manifestation, none are applicable in this context; thus, the ego (ahaṅkāra) cannot be its manifestor.
Its establishment refers to the self-luminosity of consciousness (*saṃvid*).
Since it is admitted that consciousness is self-luminous and lacks dependence on any other light for its manifestation, the ego cannot be the cause of the manifestation of consciousness.

Since consciousness (*saṃvit*) is not an object of another cognition, it cannot produce a cognition that has it as its object; thus, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) does not possess the quality of being a manifestor (*abhivyañjaka*) in that sense. Consequently, both modes of being a manifestor—namely, [the mode of] illuminating and the mode of producing the cognition that illuminates—are refuted.
This is why [it is said]: "for this very reason."

The meaning is that because experience itself cannot be experienced, and because no instrument for experiencing that [experience] is established, even the mode of manifestation characterized by its assistance is impossible.
Alternatively, let there be some instrument for the knowledge of that [experience];
however, stating that the modes of its assistance are not possible in the present case, he analyzes that assistance, beginning with "For that... (tāvat sa hi).

That favor toward the perceiver is characterized by the provision of auxiliary causes (*sahakāri*). Regarding the phrase "pertaining to the object" (*vedyagate*): the first alternative is that there is favor toward the instrument of that cognition by means of removing obstacles to the arising of the cognition pertaining to the object.
He states the second [reason] with the words "in the object" (*vedye*).
This means that because the sense organ is the cause for bringing about contact with the apprehended object.
For the individual (*vyakti*) brings about, by way of itself, contact between the eye and other senses and the universals (*jāti*) and so forth residing in the object.
And in the case of mirrors and the like, there is contact of the eye with the face and so forth through the reflection of the path of the visual rays.
He states the third [type of contact] as "residing in the knower" (*vettṛgata*).
A "blemish" (*kalaṅka*) refers to sin and the like, which are obstacles to the arising of knowledge.

Furthermore, by the passage beginning with "Not one who has not desisted from misconduct," it is understood that tranquility (*śama*) and the other [disciplines] act as auxiliary factors for the scripture in generating the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).

For it is only in one whose mind is purified—whose defects such as sin and passion have been removed by desireless action (*niṣkāma-karman*) and by tranquility and the rest—that the knowledge of reality arises through the scripture.
Regarding the present context, I shall first address the impossibility of the first type of assistance, stating: "Not, first of all... and so forth.

If it is argued that ignorance itself, which exists within the object of knowledge—the self that is of the nature of experience—is what opposes the arising of knowledge, he says "ignorance" [in response].
This means that ignorance is such that its locus and object are identical to those of knowledge;
that is to say, it has the same locus as knowledge and the same object as knowledge.
In that which is devoid of the existence of both— that is, lacking both being the locus of cognition and being the object of cognition—
there is a "placement," meaning a setting down of a footstep, or in other words, a connection.

The point is this: ignorance—whether it be of the nature of the prior non-existence of knowledge (*jñānaprāgabhāva*) or something else sharing the same status as that—is not possible in the nature of "experience" (*anubhava*) as you conceive it, since that [nature] is devoid of the possibility of being a knower, just as it is not possible in the case of a jar or similar objects.
This argument is advanced even while provisionally accepting your position.

Furthermore, even if ignorance were to reside in the Self (*ātman*), it could not be removed by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*); therefore, the ego-sense does not possess the character of a "manifestor" (*abhivyañjaka*), which consists in removing defects from an object of cognition. This is the intended meaning.
Regarding the acceptance of ignorance as residing in the nature of experience—which is [according to you] other than the Self—he states the undesirable consequence: "And if it were knowledge...

The point is that if ignorance were to reside in the Self and have the Self as its object, then because the Self is not an object of experience, that ignorance would be incapable of being removed by knowledge and would thus follow as eternal; for knowledge and ignorance stand in the relation of sublater and sublated only when they possess the same locus and the same object.
Furthermore, the admission of knowledge having the self as its object is contradicted by one's own established tenets.
By this it is intended that the self is merely pervaded by a modification (*vṛtti*) of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*),
and not that it is pervaded by the consciousness delimited (*avacchinna*) by that [modification].
By which [means] would insentience and other such defects follow?

The claim that the cessation of ignorance regarding the Self occurs solely through a modification (vṛtti) of the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) bearing the form of the Self is also refuted; for it is impossible for a modification, being itself insentient, to bring about the cessation of ignorance.
For knowledge alone is the remover of ignorance.

However, if [ignorance] were removable by the consciousness delimited by that [knowledge], then being an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) and so forth would be unavoidable for the Self (*ātman*); this is the general direction [of the argument].
Furthermore, is ignorance of the nature of the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of knowledge?
Having raised the alternative that [the self] might be of the nature of an existent entity, he refutes it with the two verses beginning with "In knowledge... [and so forth]:
"Because the sense organs are not its locus, they cannot be the cause of its connection [with objects];
because the referent of 'I' is the knower, it is not purified by that very [knowledge]. (13)
Furthermore, it is not the nature of a manifestor to illuminate that which is to be manifested by means of its own substrate,
as this is not observed in the case of lamps and the like;
moreover, knowledge, its instruments, and their auxiliaries possess a nature conducive to illuminating objects exactly as they exist.

And that [self-cognition] follows from the logic of intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*); for if that were not accepted, there would be the undesirable consequence of a lack of certainty in all cases.
As for the individual, the universal (*jāti*) is its very form, and thus it is communicated as such.
It is not caused by being a manifestor;
for, as already stated, there is deviation [from this rule].
Furthermore, mirrors and the like are causes of defects characterized by the reflection of visual light, rather than being manifestors of the face and so forth.
The manifestor, however, is simply light and so forth.
Even though it is a manifestor, the appearance there [of the object] otherwise is caused by the defect of moving against the direction of the light.
But in this case, it is not the nature of the "I-sense" (ahamartha) to produce such a defect.
If that were the case, it would follow that all means of valid cognition, such as perception, would be invalid, and thus nothing would be true.
Therefore, the inner self (pratyagātman) is none other than the referent of "I" established as the knower; it is not mere consciousness alone.
(Thus ends the section refuting the view that the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) is the manifestor of consciousness.
As for the claim that during deep sleep and liberation there is a manifestation as pure cognition alone,
yet the "I" does not appear;

In that regard, the claim that the Self exists in such a state during deep sleep has already been refuted previously. For even there, the Self shines forth in the singular form of "I" until one awakens;
at most, it does not shine clearly or distinctly because of the non-experience of external objects and the suppression of the quality of *tamas*.
It must be said that even the experience favored by you manifests in exactly that same way at that time;

for no one who has awakened from sleep is ever observed to reflect upon an experience occurring during the period of sleep such as, "I am not the 'I', nor am I another object, but rather I abide as pure experience alone as the witness of ignorance."
If it is argued that such a state is obtained simply from the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)—"For all this time, I was not aware of anything"—then how so?
If it is argued that it is because of the designation "nothing whatsoever" (*na kiñcit*), [we reply:
in that case, even the manifestation of the experience itself would be denied.

Moreover, having apprehended the self established at the time of deep sleep as "I," when one negates its cognition by saying "I did not know anything," the fool (devānāṃ priyaḥ) does not even realize that he is contradicting his own experience by asserting the non-existence of the consciousness established at that time and the non-establishment of the referent "I. It has already been stated that there is no consciousness that is devoid of an object and devoid of a substratum.

[Objection: But surely there is the conviction upon awakening that "even me, while asleep, I did not know. [Reply: True; however, that [conviction] proclaims the non-knowing of the *aham-artha* (the self-sense) in its specific form—though that *aham-artha* is entirely absorbed in the clear self-experience well-known from the state of deep sleep—by taking up the embodied self as "me" and so forth, which is perceived at the time of awakening as qualified by caste, stage of life (*āśrama*), and the like. It does not, however, proclaim the non-knowing of the pure *aham-artha* itself.
But this is not the case for the self (ahamartha) which has cognition as its intrinsic nature.
Indeed, such is the experience: "While sleeping here, I was like this," and even, "I did not know myself.
Furthermore, it is your own established position that the Self exists during deep sleep as the witness of ignorance.

And it has been stated that being a witness (*sākṣitva*) consists in being a direct knower (*sākṣājjñātṛtva*). Since this [witness] appears as "I know," it is precisely the referent of the word "I" (*asmadartha*); how then could the referent of "I" not manifest at that time?
For that which shines for itself shines only as "I."

Thus it is established that even in states such as deep sleep, the self, while manifesting, manifests precisely as "I. (This concludes the section on the demonstration that the referent of "I" is present even in sleep.
As for the claim that the referent of "I" does not persist in liberation—that is mere idle talk.

For if that were the case, liberation would effectively be the destruction of the self under another guise, as in the doctrine of the Nihilists (vaināśika). Indeed, "I" is not a mere attribute (*dharma*),
such that it could be said that even upon its disappearance— just as in the cessation of ignorance— the self remains in its own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
For its very nature is "I" alone;
even knowledge manifests as belonging to that [Self] as its attribute, as in the thought, "knowledge has arisen for me.
What, then, need be said regarding the selfhood of something else?

Furthermore, another person—who, whether through delusion or by way of reality, perceives himself as suffering due to the miseries of saṃsāra, thinking "I am miserable"—develops a desire for liberation (*mumukṣu*), thinking: "How might I, having dispelled all this collection of undesirable things so that they never arise again, become undisturbed and established in my own true state? He then engages in the means to achieve that.
If, through the performance of those means, he realizes: "I myself shall no longer exist," [he abandons them].

He would depart even from the context of discourse concerning liberation; consequently, because the qualification [for such discourse] would be impossible, all Vedāntic injunctions and all treatises on liberation would lose their very authority. If it is argued that "the light characterized as 'I' will remain in the state of liberation," what follows from this?
For no discerning person would exert themselves with the thought, "Even if I am destroyed, some light will remain.
By this, the following view is also refuted: "The Self is that light which, within our cognition, is the non-objective (anidam) portion consisting of the single essence of consciousness."
Because it is manifested by that power, it is established by its very definition that the object "I" who knows is indeed the referent of *yuṣmad* (the second person).

This is because it contradicts direct perception. To claim that the conscious being who is established as "I know" is the referent of *yuṣmad* is a statement of contradictory meaning, like saying "the mother is barren."
Furthermore, this [Self] does not have its manifestation dependent on anything else, because it is self-luminous by virtue of having consciousness as its very nature.
Moreover, that which is luminous must be the illumination of something else simply because it is luminous, like the light of a lamp; therefore, it cannot be the Self.
Therefore, that which is established as "I" by virtue of being the knower is indeed the object, the Self;
and even in liberation, it manifests to the Self precisely as "I," because it manifests for itself.

Whatever manifests to itself is observed to manifest precisely as "I," just like the transmigrating self (*saṃsāryātman*), which is accepted by both disputants as appearing in that manner. Furthermore, whatever does not shine forth as "I" does not manifest to itself.
Just as a jar or similar object [is perceived],
this liberated self shines for itself;
therefore, it shines precisely as "I am that."
Nor should it be argued that if [the Self] were thus manifest, it would follow that the liberated one is ignorant, a transmigrator, and so forth;
for that would contradict his state of liberation,
and the notion of such states does not have that [Self] as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
For the notion of "I" is not conditioned by ignorance,
since it is observed even in Vāmadeva and others, for whom all ignorance has been entirely destroyed by the direct knowledge of Brahman as the Self.
For it is taught [in scripture]: "Seeing this very thing, the seer Vāmadeva realized: 'I was Manu and the Sun; I alone exist now and I shall be in the future,'" and so forth.

Likewise, even for the Supreme Person—who is never, in any way, touched by even a trace of the afflictions such as ignorance—the self-identification as "I" is recognized [in the texts]: "I, indeed, [became] these three deities," "May I become many, may I procreate," and "He thought: 'Shall I create the worlds?'"
Likewise: "Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable, therefore I am celebrated in this world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama (the Supreme Person)."
By such statements as "I am their deliverer," "I am the seed-bestowing father," and "I know all that has passed away," [it is shown].

Thus, although the body is directly distinct from the Self which is the referent of "I," there is nevertheless the delusion of "I" with respect to the body due to a certain modification of the unmanifest (avyaktika-pariṇāma);
it is with this intention that the Blessed One taught the inclusion of egoism (ahaṅkāra) within the field (kṣetra), stating, "the great elements and egoism."

Furthermore, this [notion], which is synonymous with pride, is the cause for disregarding those persons worthy of respect; it is therefore generally taught in various treatises as something to be abandoned.

Consequently, the cognition "I" that is free from sublation must have the self (*ātman*) itself as its direct object. However, when it occurs with respect to the body, which is not the self, it is rightly termed ignorance (*avidyā*).
And it has been said by the great seer Vasiṣṭhanandana: "Listen also, O delighter of your lineage, to the true nature of ignorance: it is the notion of a self in that which is not the self.
Furthermore, there is no manifestation of mere consciousness alone in anyone's body.
By this [explanation], even for those who maintain that the self consists of nothing more than those [aggregates], the cognition of "self" would be logically possible.
Regarding the second alternative, the refutation concerns the instruments [of perception].

The meaning is that because the self is not an object— due to its being beyond the scope [of the senses] and not being graspable by the sense organs— it is impossible for the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) to manifest it by serving as the condition for the contact between the self and the sense organs.

Regarding the third [alternative], the refutation is "of the sense of 'I'": the meaning is that even the third hypothesis is not tenable, because it is impossible for the impurity inherent within oneself to be removed by oneself alone. //13//
Having thus refuted the state of being a manifestor (*vyañjakatva*), he now refutes the nature of a manifestor as it is conceived by the opponent, beginning with the words "And not...
For a lamp is the illuminator of a jar and so forth, but it does not illuminate that [jar] by means of its own occurrence [within it].
Indeed, there is no such cognition as "the jar is in the lamp."
Or [one might say], "The lamp possesses the jar.
However, the point is that there is an "inconstancy" (anaikāntya) in the rule stated by you—that "the jar is on the ground"—precisely because it exists in its actual state.
He states the reasoning for why cognition and so forth have as their very cause the illumination of the object as it actually exists, with the words "And that... (tac ca).
The meaning is: by means of the reasoning consisting of the intrinsic validity (*prāmāṇya-svatastva*) [of knowledge].

Intrinsic validity (*svatastva*) regarding both the production (*utpatti*) and the apprehension (*jñapti*) of validity consists in being produced by the causal complex of knowledge (*jñāna-sāmagrī-prayojyatva*) and being manifested by the causal complex that manifests knowledge (*jñāna-bhāsaka-sāmagrī-bhāsyatva*).
[Objection: But if validity is intrinsic, how can there be an apprehension of a contrary form in some cognition?
It should be understood that [the apprehension of falsity] occurs precisely due to the addition of an extraneous defect (*doṣa*) to the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of cognition;

and even when intrinsic validity (*svataḥprāmāṇya*) is apprehended, the doubt regarding the validity of a cognition occurring in a state of non-habituation arises solely from the doubt that it is rooted in a defect.
He states the refutation against not accepting the intrinsic nature of validity with the words "tadanabhyupagame" (if that is not accepted).

The point is this: since the suspicion of invalidity (aprāmāṇya-śaṅkā) could arise even regarding the cognitions of an omniscient being, if one does not accept the intrinsic nature (svatastva) of validity, then intrinsic validity must indeed be accepted.

Otherwise, even when certainty regarding validity has arisen, the suspicion of invalidity would continue to spread without restraint, and consequently, unshakable action (niṣkampapravṛtti) toward anything would be impossible.
Regarding the term "manifestation" (*vyakti*): the manifestation of the universal (*jāti*) by virtue of residing within it is not caused by the manifestor's power of manifestation;
rather, it arises solely from the very nature of the thing itself, insofar as it constitutes a mode that is inseparably established with the individual (*vyakti*).
However, light and so forth are indeed the manifestors;
the point is that even the manifestation's status as a manifester is not universally accepted.
"Mirror and so forth" refers to this.

The cause for the perception of the face otherwise is simply the expansion of the ocular light—whose movement is obstructed by a mirror or similar object—after it has turned back and spread toward the face; this [expansion] constitutes the defect.

Whether the mirror and such, which act as the manifesting agents (*vyañjaka*) through the defect consisting of a reverse motion, actually possess the status of a manifesting agent or not, the point is that the appearance otherwise is not necessitated by their status as manifesting agents.
"Na cehe" means:
the induction of such a defect—that is, the induction of a defect consisting in the operation of the instruments of knowledge being employed for the apprehension of what is contrary [to reality].
"Tathā sati" means: if that were the case.

The meaning is that since the "I-object" (ahamartha) is also a cause for the cognition dependent upon the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa), if it were to produce defects in those means of valid knowledge, no cognition produced by a pramāṇa could possibly be true. Therefore, because the perception of being a knower cannot be an error according to the aforementioned reasoning, the "I-object," which is established as the knower, is indeed the Self (ātman).
The intended meaning is that it is not mere cognition alone.
Herein is the formal argument: cognition is not the self, because it is established as a phenomenon (dharma), like form and so forth.
In this way, the status of the self as the "I-sense" (ahamartha) which is the knower has been established.

Now, having restated the opponent's view— that since the "I-sense" (ahamartha) does not manifest during deep sleep or liberation, it is therefore not logical for that "I-sense" to be the Self— the author refutes it with the words beginning "yattu suṣuptau" and so forth.
In this context, "therein" refers to deep sleep and liberation.
The meaning of the locative case is "being contained within" (ghaṭakatva).
Its connection is with deep sleep (suṣupti). Such a state of abiding means the self’s abiding as pure consciousness alone through the disappearance of the sense of "I" (ahaṃbhāva).

The meaning is that [the existence of the "I-sense" during sleep] has already been refuted previously by the force of reconnection (*pratisandhāna*), and by the force of establishing the existence and cognition of the "I-sense" during sleep.
As for the word "yadi": [it introduces a hypothetical objection].
The word "it might be said" (*ucyeta*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

The meaning is: if it were further argued that in deep sleep there is no manifestation of the self as clearly distinguished from knowledge and the object of knowledge by way of being the experiencer of various external objects (*parāgartha*).
[However,] there is no manifestation [of the self] as distinguished from the non-experience of external objects.
Furthermore, it should be clearly understood that "it is not so" because of the suppression by the quality of *tamas*.
This is equally true even in the opponent's view; thus [the author] says, "in what you yourself accept.

The underlying intention is that even in the absence of clear manifestation, the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) persists in a subtle state during deep sleep, just like the consciousness (*saṃvit*) accepted by the opponent.
"Not 'I am I'":
the meaning is that the self, which now appears as "I-ness," does not exist in that way during deep sleep.
[The reading] "ekamaham" is either redundant or a corruption.

The meaning is that the synthesis expressed as "for so long" and so forth is consistent with the existence of the *aham-artha* (the "I-principle") alone during deep sleep, by virtue of its being the witness (*sākṣin*) to ignorance.
He raises an objection: "for so long.
"Being such" (*tathātva*) means the manifestation of pure consciousness (*saṃvin-mātra*) alone.
The proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) objects, asking "How so?
The skeptic replies, "Nothing at all.
The proponent then challenges him, saying, "If that were so..."

The meaning is this: since the term "something" (kiñcit) encompasses consciousness (saṃvid) as well—just as it does the referent "I" (ahamartha)—without any restriction, then even the manifestation of pure consciousness (saṃvinmātra), which you intend [to establish], would not be proven.

Now, if it is argued that "something" is a reference to mere insentient matter (jaḍamātra), then the referent "I" is likewise not excluded, because it is non-insentient by virtue of being the self (pratyaktva); this is the sense.

Alternatively, if it is argued that "something" is a reference to the object of knowledge alone and not to knowledge itself, then by the same logic, there is no reference to the knower either; this is the sense.
With the words "api ca" (furthermore), he states the contradiction regarding the reconnection [of consciousness] in the opponent's position;
"devānāṃ priyaḥ" means a fool,
for such is the etymological derivation.
And ignorance is the lack of knowledge regarding the specific modes of experience.
For it is not the opinion of anyone that the statement "there is no jar on the ground" has as its object the negation of the ground while affirming the existence of the jar;
rather, it has precisely as its object the negation of the jar and the existence of the ground.
The meaning is that the cognition "it is of such a duration" is directed solely toward the existence of the knower who negates the [object's] cognition.

Now, one might object: "Even if there is a negation of consciousness possessing an object, there is no contradiction in the manifestation of featureless (nirviśeṣa) consciousness. To this, he says: "even when objectless," and so on.
Even in deep sleep, knowledge is held to be possessed of a substrate (sāśraya), even if it is without an object.
Furthermore, the proponents of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) maintain that when [the self] has become the object of cognition (dharma-bhūta), it is not manifested at all.
Regarding the non-experience of the "I-principle" (ahamartha) during deep sleep, the opponent raises an objection as a proof for its existence by saying, "But [I remember], 'Oh, me!
The author refutes this by partially conceding the point, saying, "True."
Acceptance [of the self] occurs when it is perceived;
non-acceptance occurs when the referent "I" is not experienced in any way during deep sleep.
Regarding the phrase "in deep sleep":
The meaning is: "of that which has as its sole substratum an indistinct self-luminosity existing at the time of sleep.
"In that form" means in the guise distinguished by caste, stage of life, and so forth.
"Of the nature of a knower" means of the essential character of a cognizer.
This was stated in order to demonstrate that during sleep there is no manifestation of cognition, but rather of the very nature of the knower;
thus he expresses the meaning of the experience with the words "as it were."
The word *iva* is used in the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).

Even according to the position of the opponent—that the Self shines forth during deep sleep as the witness of ignorance—he states "moreover" (*api ca*) that the manifestation of the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) at that time is unavoidable.
This is because [the rule] *sākṣāddraṣṭari saṃjñāyām* applies specifically to one who perceives directly.
The word "witness" (sākṣin) has been etymologically derived [as one who knows].

And since that [witness] is understood as the very referent of "I" (ahamartha) by virtue of being a knower, the point is that the manifestation of the referent of "I" during deep sleep will indeed be established as the witness of ignorance, in the form "I am ignorant."
He states "svasmai" (for oneself) because the self's status as the "I" must necessarily be accepted, since subjectivity is established by the notion of "I.
He concludes the demonstration that the referent of "I" (ahamartha) is manifest even during deep sleep with the words "tatsiddham" (that is established).
By the word "ādi" (and so forth) in the phrase "svāpādi," states such as delusion (moha) and others are to be understood.
Now, having restated the cessation of the notion of "I" in liberation, he refutes it with the words "But that which... and so on.
"That is *vārtam*":
*vārtam* means trivial or insignificant.
The meaning is that this view is trivial; "since" refers to the Vaināśika system, which is the Buddhist philosophy.
By another way, namely by way of stating the non-continuation of the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*);
[the word] *yena* [is used],
and after *ātmanaḥ*, the word *ātmā* should be supplied as a supplement.
If the referent of "I" were merely a property (dharma), then your statement that the self persists even upon the cessation of that [referent] in liberation would be more tenable;
however, it is not merely a property,
but rather that very [referent] is the self— this is the summarized meaning.
The phrase "knowledge also" rejects the view that mere knowledge is the self;
the intended meaning is that for knowledge, which is cognized as a property (*dharma*), it is impossible for it to possess an independent selfhood.

Since it is impossible for the internal factor of knowledge itself to be the self, he says "what talk [of the external]" regarding the external factors such as the sense organs, which are even less likely to be the self.

The point is that it is not logical for anything other than the "I-sense" (ahamartha), which is cognized as the knower, to possess the nature of the Self. He states another objection regarding the cessation of the sense of "I" in liberation with the words "anyaśca" (and if it were other).
For the state of being an enjoyer of pleasure and pain, as well as the desire for liberation arising from the affliction by the threefold suffering, belong only to the knower, the "I-sense."

If he were to perceive his own destruction in liberation, he would not desire it; and thus, it would follow that liberation is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*). Furthermore, one who knows this would certainly not engage in the knowledge or the practice that are the means to liberation.

The sense is that, in such a case, the authority of the scriptures of liberation—which possess authority both as sources of knowledge (*jñāpaka*) and as motivators of action (*anuṣṭhāpaka*)—would be undermined.
"Not so," [he says];

for just as a discerning person would not, upon the destruction of his own body or house, fail to act [to preserve it], thinking that a portion of the earth characterized by his body or house will remain.
The sense is that the knower, as the "I-sense" (ahamartha), would not proceed toward liberation through the thought, "In this way, the light characterized by the I-sense shall endure";
for, due to its being consciousness (cittva), it is self-luminous (svayaṃprakāśatva), and from that, it possesses inwardness (pratyaktva).

Then, with the words "by this," he rejects the position that selfhood belongs only to consciousness (*cit*) or knowledge (*jñāna*), and not to the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) which is distinct from it:
in the cognition "I know," that which is cognized as "I know"— which is of the single nature of consciousness, inward-turned (*pratyak*), and distinct from the external— is [the self].
That very Self is pure luminosity.

The referent of "I" (ahamartha), which appears upon that substratum and whose manifestation is dependent upon it, is characterized solely by the category of "you" (yuṣmadartha); its nature is that of the extrinsic object (parāgartha) alone, and thus it is not the Self—this is the meaning.
By the phrase "in that [consciousness]," its difference from consciousness is stated;

by the phrase "as being manifested by its power," its lack of self-luminosity is stated; and by the phrase "by definition it is precisely the object of the second person (yuṣmad-artha)," its extroversion is stated—these are the marks indicating that the "I-notion" (ahamartha) is not the Self. "By definition" means by way of its essential nature (svarūpataḥ).
Or else, from the mark (liṅga) of its not being self-luminous:
cognition is self-luminous because it is cognition;
cognition is direct because it is self-luminous.
"Knowledge is the self because it is inwardness"— this constitutes three formal arguments:
"The referent of 'I' is not self-luminous because it is distinct from consciousness," and "The referent of 'I' is outward because its manifestation depends on another."
The three arguments contained herein are: "The referent of 'I' is not the self because it is external";
and the reasoning for its refutation is that this contradicts direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
If consciousness (*cit*) were the self (*ātman*), there would be a sublation by the means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha*);
for it is cognized by perception precisely as a property (*dharma*).
In the proposition "the referent of 'I' (*ahamartha*) is the referent of 'you' (*yuṣmadartha*)," he states the contradiction with the word "I."
This amounts to saying that the proposition is equivalent to the claim that "the mother is barren.
Now, in the phrase "yuṣmad-artha" (the referent of the second person pronoun), the suffix *ḷ* is used figuratively to signify "otherness";
therefore, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the point that the "I-sense" (ahamartha) possesses extrinsic luminosity because its manifestation depends upon consciousness, he says: "And not that [latter].
Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): The "I-sense" has a manifestation that does not depend on anything else, because it has consciousness as its essential attribute;
for whatever does not have this [attribute] does not have such [manifestation], just like a jar.

The direct perception of consciousness as the self, which was previously stated to be a sublater [of the opponent's view] regarding the nature of *dharma*, is now stated to be inferential in that same manner in the verse beginning with "prakāśaśca" (and luminosity). Furthermore,
the reasoning previously stated for the existence of the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) in the state of liberation is here presented.
Now, he elaborates upon the inference regarding the manifestation of the liberated one as "I" by means of the method of the complete syllogism, beginning with the words "And that...
and "Nor is it thus...":
If the liberated one were to manifest in this way—as manifesting as "I"—then it would not be possible to attribute ignorance and other such qualities to him, as one does to a transmigrating being.

The meaning is: "because it contradicts the state of liberation"—that is, because it contradicts the cessation of ignorance and so forth that occurs in the state of liberation established by the scriptures.

The intention is that the inference—"the liberated self possesses ignorance or the attributes of transmigratory existence, because it appears as 'I', like a transmigrating self"—is sublated by the scriptures which teach the specific nature of the liberated one. [Objection:
But surely we do not seek to prove that the liberated one possesses ignorance and so forth.

If it is argued that "if the liberated self were to appear as 'I', then it would follow that it possesses ignorance and so forth," and that this is merely a reductio ad absurdum (prasaṅga), [the author] says in response to that: "because it does not have that as its limiting adjunct" (atadupādhitvāt). "That cognition" (tatpratyayasya) refers to the cognition "I" (ahaṃ-pratyaya).
"And because it does not have that as its limiting condition" means because it lacks ignorance as its cause.

For a reductio ad absurdum (āpādana) is only appropriate when there is a relationship of pervaded and pervader (vyāpya-vyāpaka-bhāva) between the consequence to be established (āpādya) and that which establishes it (āpādaka).
The point is that such a relationship does not exist here, because the causal relation (hetu-hetumadbhāva) and other factors that determine it are absent.
"Ajñānopādhi" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, meaning "that for which ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), that is, the instrumental cause.
In the phrase "of Vāmadeva and others," the word "others" (*ādi*) is intended to include Mahādeva and so forth.
Furthermore, the reading "atatpratyaye" found in older printed editions is incorrect.
The reading "etad-pratyaya" or "ahaṃ-pratyaya" is possible;
furthermore, "ahameva ca" is the statement of Rudra in the Atharvaśiras.

The point is that since the notion of "I" (ahaṃpratyaya) is observed even in those whose defects of ignorance along with its latent impressions (*savāsanā-avidyā*) have ceased, it is impossible for this [notion] to have ignorance as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*).
In this regard, the scriptural passage concerning the recollection of the liberated, such as "I am food," etc., should also be considered.
Now, if it is argued that for these [liberated ones], the notion of "I" is merely a persistence of what has been sublated (*bādhitānuvṛtti*), to this he replies: "In the same way."
Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live are the five afflictions (*kleśa*).
The mention of "afflictions" is an elliptical expression intended to include karma, its maturation, and their latent impressions (*āśaya*).
For it is well-established in the Yoga-tantra that the Lord (*īśvara*) is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions, karma, their maturation, and their latent impressions.

The underlying intention is that for the Lord, who is at all times and in every way free from ignorance (*avidyā*), the cognition "I" regarding His own self cannot possibly have its root in ignorance or similar factors.

The citation of the passage concerning the volition of creation is intended to demonstrate that because the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) were absent prior to the time of creation, the "I"-cognition belonging to the Lord at that time was not caused by any external adjunct, but was caused solely by His own essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The word "I" (*aham*) in the phrase "Alas, I [am He]" refers to the self-nature that perceives the inner controller of both the conscious and the unconscious.
Because it denotes the supreme self-nature to be attained by the liberated, the word "I" belongs to the Blessed Lord in the verses of the *Gītā*.
The sense is that the Lord, if possessed of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), cannot be the inner controller (*antaryāmī*) nor the goal attained by the liberated.

Likewise, in the passage "For them, I am the Self" (*teṣām aham*), it is the Lord's pure essential nature alone—which enables one to cross the ocean of death and transmigratory existence—that is indicated as "I.
The underlying idea is that one who is oneself possessed of limiting adjuncts is not capable of liberating others from their adjuncts.
And with the intention of [emphasizing] His being the father, the protector, and so forth, He says, "I am the seed-giving father.
That which is denoted by the word "I" is the essential nature of the cause of the universe; it is neither that which is conditioned by ignorance (ajñāna), nor is it mere consciousness (jñāna) alone.
However, the statement "I know" (*vedāham*) was employed for the purpose of making known that [the Self] is omniscient.
It is not logical that these many instances of the word "I" (*ahaṃśabda*), which have as their object the extracted essential nature [of the Self], should be considered secondary;

rather, the sense is that they are primary because "I-ness" (*ahantva*) is their basis of application (*pravṛttinimitta*), and precisely because the manifestation of the essential nature occurs through that "I-ness."

Now, if the state of "I-ness" (ahambhāva) is indeed the very nature of the Self, how is it that the statement in the *Gītā* regarding the inclusion of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*) within the field (*kṣetra*), as well as its teaching on the necessity of abandoning it, is to be understood? To this he says: "And thus...

By means of the specific transformation of the unmanifest—namely, by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), which is a transformation of the Great Principle (*mahat*), itself a transformation of primordial matter (*pradhāna*)—that which is not the "I" is made to appear as the "I"; hence it is called the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
And the instrument is the mind (*mānasa*).

Thus, it follows that *ahaṅkāra*—which is the cause of the conceit "I" (*ahaṃ-abhimāna*) regarding the body which is not the Self, and the cause of the delusion of Selfhood (*ātmabhrama*) regarding what is not the Self—is taught as being included within the field (*kṣetra*).

Now, he explains that this *ahaṅkāra*, which was stated to be something to be abandoned in the verse "egoism, power, and pride," consists essentially of arrogance rooted in false conceits based on birth and other such factors, by saying "in that which is to be highly esteemed," etc.

Furthermore, the etymological derivation here is "that which is made into 'I' by me" (an-ahaṃ-mahaṃ-kriyate). The meaning is the conceit of self (*ātma-abhimāna*) regarding a body born of a noble family.

And the sense is that this very [conceit] is called "pride" (*garva*) because it is the cause of arrogance, being the basis for both the disparagement of those worthy of honor and the elevation of oneself.
The derivation [of the term *ahaṅkāra*] occurs in both cases by including the sense of the suffix *cv-*;
however, when the sense of *cv-* is not included, it is derived as *ahaṅkāra*, meaning "the notion of 'I' regarding the Self. This is the distinction. Therefore... [it is said].
The meaning is this: the uncontradicted notion of "I" has the primary Self as its object, whereas in relation to the body and so forth, that notion is characterized solely by error.
In this regard, let the words of the jewel-like *Saṃvādi Purāṇa* be heard.
O twice-born one, this word "I" is not a fault when applied to the Self;
however, the cognition or the word that takes what is not the Self to be the Self is characterized by delusion.
And this point should be investigated there as follows:
"knowledge of the self" refers to the notion of "I";
"sound" refers to the word "I."
By the venerable Parāśara, the son of Śakti and grandson of Vasiṣṭha (the delight of the lineage of Vasiṣṭha),

it is stated that "nor in cognition" (*na ca jñaptau*), because even from the examination of the form of the delusion that the body is the self, the nature of the self as the referent of "I" must be accepted.
"The notion of non-self" (*anātmabuddhiḥ*) means the notion of a self in what is not the self.
It is probable that the reading should be exactly as such;
for if the self were merely cognition (*jñapti-mātra*), the form of the delusion identifying the body with the self would be "I am unconscious of gross objects" (*sthūlāsaṃvit*),
and not "I am gross" (*sthūlo 'ham*).
For this reason also, the self is precisely the referent of "I";
for when it is present, the cognition "I" arises with respect to the body,
and when it has departed, it does not.
The sense is that it is logical to accept that this very self is the referent of "I.

Therefore: Because it is established by perception, because it conforms to the previously stated reasoning and scripture, and because of its association with ignorance, the self appears as the knower and as "I. (14)
Thus concludes the section establishing that the sense of "I" (ahambhāva) always manifests for the knowing self even in states such as liberation.
Regarding what was stated—that consciousness alone is the self because it is non-inert (ajaḍatva)—it must be asked here: what indeed is this so-called non-inertness?
If it were argued that "that which, though existent, does not manifest is insentient (jaḍa),

whereas its opposite— possessing an existence characterized by non-deviating manifestation— is non-insentient (ajaḍa)"; then, in that case, the reason (hetu) would be inconclusive due to its deviation from pleasure (sukha) and so forth.
Indeed, pleasure, pain, desire, and so forth, though existing, are never non-manifest;
furthermore, the property of having manifestation as concomitant with their own existence is inconclusive due to the case of lamps and the like.
Moreover, because a manifestation distinct from cognition is not admitted, [the reason] is unestablished (*asiddha*).
And there is contradiction [in your position].
If it is thought that pleasure and so forth, although their manifestation is non-deviant, manifest to another and therefore do not transcend insentience like a jar,
and for that reason are not the Self;
Or does knowledge manifest to itself?
For even that [knowledge] manifests only to another— the "I-sense" (ahamartha) which knows it— as "I know," just as in the case of "I am happy."
Therefore, the reason "non-insentience" (*ajaḍatva*), being employed with the intention that [the self] is manifest to itself, is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of consciousness (*saṃvit*).
Consequently, the "I-sense" (*ahamartha*) alone is the Self, which is non-insentient because it establishes its own nature by its very existence;
the luminosity of cognition, however, is dependent upon its relation to that [Self].
For this very reason, knowledge is manifest to its own substrate-consciousness and unmanifest to others, just like pleasure, pain, and so forth.
And in this way, this self does not shine forth to itself by depending on another self or any other distinct entity.
This will be demonstrated immediately hereafter. Thus ends the refutation of non-insentience as a proof for the self being of the nature of knowledge.
Furthermore, the rule of the simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*) with knowledge does not preclude the fact that the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*) is a distinct entity from knowledge.
Otherwise, it would follow that knowledge itself possesses that same nature;

for since that [knowledge] too is invariably perceived together with that [object], it would result in being non-different from the referent of "I" (the self) and thus fall into the state of being merely illusory.
Furthermore, the rule of invariable co-perception with specific cognitions is unestablished.
Because deviation is observed in each individual case,
and there exists no mere consciousness (*vittimātra*) that is devoid of all connection with specific objects or consists of mere particulars,
by virtue of which a rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambha-niyama*) would hold.
It might be argued that [the self] is designated as the "experiencer.
However, even though the universal (sāmānya) exists, it is not accepted by the followers of the Sugata as a real entity (vastu).
Furthermore, we shall explain that this Self remains as its own light even when all mental functions have ceased.
And there would be a contradiction of one's own words because of the instruction "one, two";
for the word "together" (saha) is used when two things enter into a single action, as in the example: "The teacher goes together with the student."

Moreover, by taking as two the blue object and its cognition, the rule of identity— that they are non-different— is like the rule that the sun is barren; furthermore, there is inconclusiveness (anekānta) regarding consciousness with respect to insentience and other properties being denied [of it],
as well as with respect to the cognitions of transmigrating beings which share the necessity of being perceived simultaneously with the cognition of an omniscient one.
If their non-difference were accepted, it would follow that cognition possesses insentience, materiality, and so forth, and that the Buddha is bound.
Furthermore, the fact that they are necessarily established within a single cognition is also refuted by the manner already described.
It has been stated: "The absence [of the reason] in the counter-example is unestablished.
Let it be that the cognizer, the object of cognition, and the cognition are necessarily established by a single cognition, yet let there be no identity between them."
What is the contradiction?
He concludes that the referent of "I" (ahamartha) is the self with the word "therefore":
because the referent of "I" is established by direct perception as the substratum of the cognition "I know," it is precisely this referent of "I" that is the self.
The inference and the scripture have been stated regarding its manifestation as "I" even in liberation;
furthermore, the reasoning characterized by the impossibility of selfhood otherwise has been stated to establish that the Self is the referent of "I.
Moreover, because of the connection with ignorance in the form of the delusion of identifying the body with the Self—as in "I am stout"—the Self is indeed the knower who is the referent of "I."
And the meaning of the verse is that it always appears as "I.
It is also implied here that with respect to the self being known, there exists perception and so forth;
and perception such as "I know" is indeed well-established.
By negating that knowledge is a property of the body and so forth, the inference by elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*) is also established.
Furthermore, scriptural statements will be cited later in the root text itself.
Since ignorance shares the same locus as knowledge, the argument—that it would be impossible for the Self to be associated with nescience if it were not the knower—is also essentially stated here.
Thus, the selfhood of the "I-sense," which is the knower, has been established. //14//

Now, he refutes by means of an alternative analysis even "non-inertness" (ajaḍatva), which has been proposed by others as the proof for the selfhood of cognition, beginning with the words "as it has been said. The explanation of the phrase "contrary to that" begins with "unerringly," and so forth.
"Unerringly" (avyabhicarita) means that whose manifestation is constant or necessary.
The meaning is that that which possesses such an existence is non-inert (*ajaḍa*).
In other words, non-inertness consists in having a luminosity that pervades its own existence.
"If that were so" means:

since the state of being non-inert (ajaḍatva) exists even in pleasure and other [qualities] which are not-self, there would be a logical deviation (vyabhicāra); this is what is being stated. He refutes another mode of "non-inertness" with the words "by its own existence" (svasattayā).
That which has manifestation by its very own existence is "that whose manifestation is occasioned by its own existence";
and the claim that this constitutes insentience (*jaḍatva*) is also fallacious, as it overextends to things such as lamps.
For indeed, when there is the light of a lamp, there is no dependence upon another lamp.
If it is argued that there is nonetheless a dependence upon the eye and so forth in that case, let it be so.
For to that extent, the state of being necessitated by its own existence remains unimpaired;
however, the intention to express that it is necessitated by its own existence alone is not possible, because such a thing is not established in experience.
Because the manifestation of that [object] depends upon a nature that is of a different kind;
this will become clear immediately hereafter.
He states another refutation as well, beginning with "jñāne" (in cognition).
Dharma is not intended to be something distinct from cognition, namely "illumination";
rather, cognition itself is of the nature of illumination.
Therefore, the reason—"having the nature of illumination contingent upon its own existence"—is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the subject (*pakṣa*), which is cognition.

For one who accepts that [consciousness] is eternally luminous, its description as being "dependent upon its own existence" is contradictory. Alternatively, the sense is that if luminosity is admitted in the case of consciousness (*saṃvit*), it contradicts the intended quality of being devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣatva*). He states, "If it is thought," [referring to the opponent's view], that non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*), consisting in appearing to itself by itself, is the proof for its being the Self (*ātmatva*); however, this is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*).
He states that the manifestation of knowledge is dependent upon its substrate with the words "tatsambandhe.
Manifestness (*prakāśatā*) means either the nature of knowledge (*jñānarūpatā*) or the state of being manifest (*prakāśamānatā*).

The nature of cognition (*jñānatva*), which consists in the illumination of its own object for its own substratum, as well as the state of being illuminated, are both caused solely by the attributes of the self (*ātman*).
For cognition does not illuminate its own object for anyone other than its own substratum.
The sense is that it manifests by itself;
"therefore" means because it shines for itself.
The meaning is that "I-ness" belongs to the object denoted by "I" alone, and therefore that [object] is the self (*ātman*).
"Manifestness" (*prakaṭatā*) means the state of being luminous (*prakāśamānatā*). "Connection with another self" means connection with another substratum.
"Another thing" refers to cognition and so forth.
"And this" means that it is an explanation of the phrase "having no other means of proof"— this is the intended sense.

Having refuted "non-inertness" as the proof for consciousness being the Self, [the author] now refutes the "rule of simultaneous apprehension" (sahopalambhaniyama)—favored by the manifest followers of the Sugata—which seeks to prove the non-difference of the knower and so forth from consciousness, with the words "And not by cognition...
and "of cognition also...".

The underlying sense is that, because the rule of simultaneous apprehension is equally applicable to the false object "I" (ahamartha), it follows that consciousness would be non-different from that [false object], and thus consciousness itself would be subject to falsity.
Because your reason brings about what is contrary to what is intended, the fallacy of the reason (*viruddha-hetu*) has been pointed out.
Furthermore, he establishes that consciousness is perceived only together with the object "I" (*ahamartha*).
[The term] "by a fixed [perceiver]" means by one whose light is pervasive and self-luminous.
By that [notion of] "I" (*ahaṃkāra*).

That which is perceived together [with something else] is "simultaneous perception" (*sahopalambha*). Furthermore, the restriction of simultaneous perception—consisting in the fact that the perception of one thing is pervaded by the perception of the other—is held by others to be a proof of their non-difference.

And this [reason] for proving the non-difference of the "I-sense" (ahamartha) from consciousness is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the subject (*pakṣa*); thus he says, "and it is unestablished.
Here there is a dilemma (*vikalpa*): is the necessary co-perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) of the "I-sense" intended with each specific instance of cognition, or rather with cognition in general?
Or is it by mere cognition?

Regarding the first [alternative], there is a lack of proof (*asiddhi*); for it has been stated that even in the absence of the illumination of visual or other cognitions, the referent "I" (*ahamartha*) is manifested when illuminated by another cognition, as such a deviation is observed in each individual case.
Regarding the second and third alternatives, he states the fault: "And not in a particular," etc.

According to the principle that "there is no universal without a particular," there exists no mere cognition—whether as a specific cognition distinct from visual perception and so forth, or as cognition in general.

Furthermore, the non-deviation of the manifestation of those respective particulars has already been stated in the case of the manifestation of the "I-sense" (ahamartha); the point is that even in the absence of the manifestation of those respective particulars, the "I-sense" continues to manifest.

"Even so, there is indeed no deviation from the manifestation delimited by 'cognition-ness' (*jñānatva*), because in the manifestation of the object 'I', the manifestation delimited by 'cognition-ness' is constant. To this, he replies with the word "sāmānya" (universal).
The sense is that for the Saugatas, such a reason is difficult to state, because they do not admit a persisting universal (*anuvṛtta-sāmānya*).

He states, "even without the manifestation of cognition" (*vināpi jñānaprakāśena*), that there is a manifestation of the referent "I" (*ahamartha*); and according to the established tenet (*siddhānta*), he says "in all cases" (*samaste*).

Regarding the phrase "by its own word" (*svavācā*): since concomitance (*sāhitya*) is necessarily restricted to difference, the very designation of the reason—that it is perceived only together—is itself a form of the designation of difference.

Thus, his intention is that there is a contradiction between the proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) in his proof for the identity of consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the object "I" (*ahamartha*), just as in the case of saying "one is two.

Having stated the contradiction between the words constituting the reason and the proposition, he states the contradiction between the words constituting the proposition itself with the words "Moreover" (*api ca*).
For their proposition is indeed this: "Because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension (*sahopalambhaniyama*), there is non-difference (*abheda*) between blue and the cognition thereof."
The meaning is that here, the prescription of oneness regarding that which is qualified by duality is contradictory, like the prescription of barrenness for one’s own mother.

It should be understood that in this context—wherein the proof of the non-difference between cognition and the cognizer is being refuted—the same method of refutation applies to the proof of the non-difference between cognition and the cognizable, due to the similarity of the types of arguments used.
Having stated the defect in the words, he states another defect in the object [of the inference] with the words "and it is inconclusive" (*anekāntaśca*).
Because consciousness is self-luminous, at the time when insentience and other such qualities are manifested, the manifestation of the cognition itself is also necessarily established.

Thus, for insentience, corporeality, and so forth— which are subject to the rule of being perceived simultaneously with consciousness— there would follow the consequence that consciousness itself is insentient and corporeal,
since no distinction between the attribute (dharma) and the substratum (dharmin) is admitted.

Furthermore, because it is accepted that the relationship of locus and located (ādhārādheyabhāva) can be perceived even when there is no difference [between the two], so too, upon the perception of the cognitions of bound beings by one who knows all, the cognition of the Buddha is necessarily perceived as well. If those perceptions of the cognitions of bound beings were not different from the cognition of the Buddha, it would follow that the Buddha himself is a bound being.
The sense is that if one does not admit non-difference in each respective case, the reason (hetu) is inconclusive (anaikāntya).
He likewise refutes another reason intended to prove non-difference by the same method with the words "niyamenaike" (by necessity, as one).
"Establishment through a single cognition" means the manifestation of both [the object and its cognition] within a single act of consciousness.

And the manner of refutation is as follows: if one attempts to prove the non-difference of consciousness from the object "I" on the grounds that they are the objects of a single cognition, then by the same logic, the non-difference of the "I" from consciousness would also follow as a consequence. Furthermore, it is unproven that the object "I" is established solely through specific cognitions such as visual perception, since it is also established through other forms of cognition.
"And because [the state of] sleep is established by itself"—
thus he states the lack of a probans (*aprayojakatva*) with the words "in the case of the counter-example" (*vipakṣe*).
"Exclusion from the counter-example" (*vipakṣavyatireka*) means sublation in the counter-example (*vipakṣe bādhaḥ*).
He demonstrates that very non-establishment [of the reason] with the words "Let it be so.
The sense is that there is no subverting argument (*bādhaka-tarka*) when the presence of the reason in that which lacks the probandum is being posited;
therefore, the reason is non-conclusive (*aprayojaka*).
Does blue and so forth depend upon illumination for the sake of conventional usage because it is non-luminous by nature, or rather because it is non-different from it? (15)
Thus, because it remains a matter of doubt, non-difference cannot be definitively established; furthermore, this rule pertains to the object of cognition, not to the intellect and the cognizer. (16)

Moreover, there is a clear contradiction with direct perception (*pratyakṣabādha*), because in all cognitions, the difference between the cognition and the cognizer is as directly evident as the object of cognition itself.
Furthermore, neither the perceptibility of the counter-correlative nor its visibility need be required for the direct manifestation of the difference.
Since mere establishment [of a relation] is insufficient as a logical reason (*aprayojaka*), it does not entail its specific qualification.
Furthermore, it is a matter witnessed by everyone’s own experience that entities are perceived as distinct from their own nature even when the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is not manifest.

Now, one might object: since the concomitance of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*) is grasped as being pervaded (*pratibandha*) by non-difference—just as placing one's foot upon the head of the perception of difference in a living person—how could sublation of that [non-difference] possibly arise from it?
For if that were the case, even the inference of a difference between flames would be sublated by the recognition of their identity.
Your "beloved of the gods" (the fool) is ignorant of the distinction [between types of cognition].

For in that instance, since the presence of defects in the established causes persists, the immediate appearance (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*) arising therefrom cannot sublate an inference preceded by a flawless perception.

For instance, it is observed that when many lamps are lit in close succession with a single wick, those who do not perceive their difference form the memory-conviction "this is that very same one" due to their extreme similarity.

Therefore, it is determined that in other cases as well, because of the uninterrupted occurrence of abundant causes in succession and the separation of parts, such a cognition has as its object a continuous stream of lamps that function in extreme similarity.

Likewise, a cognition of oneness-and-manifoldness, which is occasioned by a reversal of the functioning of the sense organs occurring spontaneously and whose object is rejected by multiple, faultless perceptions arising at the same time— as seen in the case of a double moon—
is not capable of overcoming the inference of oneness there. However,

since in this case [of the Self] there is no such cognition that directly perceives the distinction between the knower, the knowledge, and the known, this [inference of oneness] certainly prevents the possibility of the emergence of an inference of non-difference here.
Nor is it correct to say that their suchness (tathātva) is to be inferred here solely from the rule of the concomitance of apprehension,
because no subverting argument (bādhaka) has been found against the contrary case;
for such a rule is also logically possible on the grounds that [the objects'] establishment is dependent upon consciousness.
Furthermore, because it is non-sensory, the contrary of its occurrence is irrelevant;
and because any subverting cognition is refuted by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible.
Moreover, consciousness is indeed the establishment of an object.
And it is undisputed that this [consciousness] is self-luminous;

therefore, such a rule is unavoidable. Furthermore, it is not reasonable for one who is not insane to suggest that even difference could be established without [the establishment of] existence itself. Enough, then, with this excessive agitation caused by a doctrine contradicted by experience.
(Thus concludes the refutation of the Buddhist assertion regarding the conceptual construction of the apprehended object and the apprehending subject.
Furthermore, since the manifestation of blue and other such objects—which are not themselves of the nature of luminosity—is established by direct experience, it does not require further proof;
the self, however, is indeed of the very nature of luminosity.
And yet, it does not follow from this that [the cognition] is non-cognition,
because it is independent.

We have already stated previously that cognition is that which, being dependent on others and adventitious, remains as long as the causes such as the contact between the object and the sense organ are present, and which has a form delimited by the object.

The self, however, is independent and the knower; it manifests within each individual as "I. If, moreover, such a self is designated as "knowledge" because its establishment does not depend on anything else, let it be so designated at will.
Nevertheless, this knowledge is like other forms of knowledge; it is not merely the act of cognition itself.
(This concludes the refutation of the Advaitin's preferred view regarding the conceptualization of the grasped and the grasper.)
For this very reason, the Chandogas record in their tradition: "Now, he who knows 'let me smell this,' he is the Self," and so forth.

Likewise, the Vājasaneyins, following the question "Which one is the Self?", record this very definition: "He who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart, the Person.

For here, he who is established as the impeller among the vital breaths—well-known through the experience of all people, abundant in the perception of various objects, the inner light within the abode of the heart—is [the Self] as the "I," by way of inwardness.
"That person" (sa puruṣaḥ) refers to the very nature of the Self as previously described.
For the followers of the Atharva Veda state: "He indeed is the seer, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower, the doer, the conscious self, the person.
Likewise: "O, by what means could one know the Knower? and "The seer sees neither death, nor disease, nor even suffering."

"He is the Supreme Person; remembering this body, he does not come back into birth"; "In this very way, these sixteen parts of the observer, which have the person as their goal, dissolve upon reaching the person"; "Therefore, different from this one consisting of mind is the inner Self consisting of consciousness"—and so forth.
Even in the definition of Brahman given in the passage "Truth, Knowledge," the word *jñāna* does not denote mere knowledge; rather, it denotes that which possesses knowledge [as an attribute].
For if it were to denote that [knowledge] itself, it would follow that the word would have the acute accent on its first syllable according to the rule "ati."
Furthermore, this word "jñāna" is udātta on its final syllable;

such a quality is consistent with it being formed by adding the possessive suffix *ac*, and not otherwise. We shall demonstrate this very point with great precision in the exposition of the Supreme Self.

The Aitareya Upaniṣad also, having stated "Brahman is consciousness" (prajñānam brahma), shows that the Lord is indeed possessed of supreme knowledge by saying "He, by means of this conscious self" (sa etena prājñenātmanā).
Thus it is established that this Self is indeed the Knower.
(Thus concludes the section defining the nature of the inner self as distinct from the body and other such things.

But what, then, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for this conscious inner self that is distinct from the body and so forth? Akṣapāda, who is skilled in logic, maintains that it is inference (*anumāna*).
As it has been said: "Desire, aversion, effort, pleasure, pain, and cognition are the marks (liṅga) of the self.

Is the invariable concomitance (avinābhāva) of these with the self observed, as the specific concomitance of smoke with a particular fire is observed? Alas, if that were so, since the self would be cognized from those very [marks], what is the use of inference?
Let there be no perception of it through its specific characteristics;
however, there will be perception of it in a general sense.
For instance, desire and so forth—because they possess the properties of being effects, non-eternal, and qualities—are inferred to be dependent, just like sound and other such phenomena.
And that which is their substratum is the self (ātman).
Its status as a quality (guṇatva) follows by the method of elimination (pariśeṣa);
it is not a generality (sāmānya), a particularity (viśeṣa), or inherence (samavāya), because it is impermanent.
It is neither a substance nor an action,
because it inheres in a pervasive substance;

and its status as a specific quality (viśeṣaguṇa) follows from the rule that, while being non-eternal, it is perceivable by only one sense organ among those belonging to beings such as ourselves, just like color and other such qualities.

Thus, while establishing [the self] as a mere substratum through reasons characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatirekin*), [these reasons] are restricted to having the self as their object by means of purely negative proofs (*kevalavyatireki-sādhana*) that refute its being a quality of a distinct substance.
For instance: "Desire and so forth are not qualities of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), because they are directly perceived by the self alone."
Or rather, because they are not perceivable by the external sense organs;
for those qualities that belong to the elements are perceptible to both oneself and others and are perceptible by the external instruments,
just like color and so forth.
Desire and the others are not such [qualities], and thus they are not qualities of that [soul].
Furthermore, space, time, and the internal organ do not possess specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*);
nor are their qualities perceptible, and thus they too do not possess [such] qualities.

The previously mentioned reasons for negating [desire and so forth] as being specific qualities of the body—such as "because they do not have preceding qualities as their cause" and "because they do not persist as long as the body exists"—should be cited here as well.
Therefore, desire and the rest are not qualities of the body, because, while possessing the evidence that refutes their status as its qualities, they are nonetheless qualities;
