for those things which do not possess the aforementioned probandum [of being qualities of the body] are not like this.
Even though they possess the aforementioned means of proof, they do not exist [as such],
just like form and so forth;
whereas desire and the rest, which do possess the aforementioned means of proof, are indeed exactly as described in the aforementioned thesis.
Alternatively, the thesis may be that desire and the other qualities are distinct from the body and so forth, which are the loci of doubt;
the reason is exactly as previously stated,
and an example must also be adduced.

Alternatively, the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) may be demonstrated in a general manner: whatever quality, while being accompanied by a means of valid cognition that sublates its existence as a subordinate attribute of something else, is a quality, it must be the quality of something other than that [substratum];
just as sound [is the quality] of ether (*ākāśa*) in contrast to earth and the rest, so too is the self (*ātman*) established.
(Thus concludes the examination of the position that the self of distinct characteristics is known through inference.
Some maintain that this too is not correct;
for instance, by means of reasons characterized by positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), only a substrate in general, common to the body and so forth, is understood.
Nor is the self established by that much alone;
for a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) argument never even reaches the stage of being a valid proof, because it lacks positive concomitance with similar instances (sapakṣa).
It is like the uncommon [reason].
Nor does it follow that the purely positive reason (*kevalānvayin*) is non-probative—
like the common [reason]— due to its lack of observation of exclusion from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*).

This is because [the nature of the reason] is ascertained as being essentially concomitant with the probandum through the observation of positive concomitance (*anvaya*), even when adventitious conditions (*upādhi*) suspected on account of place, time, and so forth, have been eliminated.
Furthermore, the essential nature of being concomitant with the probandum cannot be ascertained merely by observing the absence of the probandum when the probans is absent;
for since non-existence pervades infinite locations, it is inherently difficult to grasp it in its entirety.
Because if it were to occur even partially elsewhere, a necessary connection would be impossible,
and because it would be seized by doubt— namely, whether the absence of the probandum is caused by the absence of the probans, or rather caused by some other cause.

The proposition that [pleasure and so forth] are qualities belonging to an entity distinct from earth and the other elements is also one whose qualification is unestablished, because no other substance is established [as their locus].
(Thus ends the refutation of the Naiyāyika’s inference for the self.
By this, the various proofs propounded by the Sāṃkhya, such as "being for the sake of another" on account of being composite, should also be understood as refuted.

And so, we shall first explain those very points: "The Puruṣa exists because [the body] is a composite, for the sake of another, because it is the reverse of that which possesses the three guṇas and so forth, because it presides [over the guṇas], because there is the state of being an enjoyer, and because of activity for the sake of isolation (kaivalya)."
The meaning is this: the body, the sense organs, and so forth exist for the sake of another, because they are composite entities, like a bed, a seat, or a shelter;
and the compositeness of the body and of the elements is directly perceived.

The fact that the unmanifest, the mahat, the ego, and the senses possess the nature of pleasure, pain, and delusion is likewise to be inferred from that very [scriptural authority]. Nor is the reason subject to the fallacy of contradicting both specific qualities (*ubhaya-viśeṣa-viruddha*), because while the origin of the senses from the ego (*āhaṅkārika*) is accepted, the property intended to be proven—namely, "being for the sake of another" (*pārārthya*)—is established as "being for the sake of an uncomposite other" (*asaṃhata-pārārthya*); thus, the reason does not result in a contrary conclusion regarding either of these specific qualities.

Because the fact that the sense organs originate from the *vaikārika*—that is, the *sāttvika*—subdivision of ego (*ahaṅkāra*) is established by valid means of knowledge through the positive and negative concomitance with ego, by the force of scriptures such as "The gods are remembered as *vaikārika*," and by the presence of the qualities of luminosity and lightness; therefore, it is untenable to refute this.

Furthermore, if the self were a composite, it would follow that it too must exist for the sake of another composite, leading to an infinite regress and the undesirable consequence of postulating numerous entities for which there is no evidence.

Furthermore, since being a composite (saṅghātatva) is not a necessary reason for being subordinate (śeṣitva), it would follow that the validity of inference itself becomes impossible, as it could not establish all the properties observed in the example; moreover, its non-composite nature (asaṅghātatva) is unshakable.

Nor is it the case that, when non-egoistic nature and being for the sake of another composite are sublated by the force of other means of knowledge, the property of being for the sake of another composite must also be sublated simply because it remains unsublated [by those specific means].
And thus, the Self is established as being non-composite, devoid of the three qualities (traiguṇya) and other attributes that pervade and exclude compositeness.

Likewise, the body and so forth are presided over by another because they consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion, just as chariots and the like are [presided over] by means of machines and so on. Moreover—

Furthermore, pleasure and pain, which are experienced as favorable and unfavorable, possess that which is to be favored and that which is to be opposed, like a servant and an enemy; and because they are visible, the body and so forth have a distinct perceiver, just like jars and other such objects.

The reversal of the qualities of the three constituents (traiguṇya) and so forth in the case of the presiding subject—the observer who experiences the agreeable and the disagreeable—must be determined as previously explained.

Likewise, since everything from the body up to the unmanifest (avyakta) consists of the three constituents, the state of liberation characterized by the absolute cessation of suffering would be impossible;

yet, because the scriptures and the great-minded sages exert themselves for that purpose, there exists a Puruṣa distinct from the body and other such things, non-composite, and untouched by the three constituents and their like.
(Thus concludes the examination of the inference for the Self as asserted by the Sāṅkhyas.
Here too, although some supreme supervisor and observer is established by means of such arguments as "being for the sake of another" due to being a composite,
nevertheless, his specific intended characteristics— such as being non-composite and being devoid of the three guṇas— cannot be definitively ascertained.

For instance, the successive postulation of further composites, which follows from the force of observing the rule that one composite necessarily exists for the sake of another composite, does not constitute a fault—just as the postulation of an infinite succession of causes follows from their being effects. Nor is this [postulation] lacking in justification; for:

Since it is impossible for the Puruṣa— who is non-composite, unattached, devoid of all modifications, incapable of receiving any addition, and whose nature is immutable pure consciousness— to be subordinate to a composite aggregate,
that [aggregate] must be subservient to him, and it must exist for his sake.
If that which is benefited or acted upon, and that which benefits or acts, [are mutually dependent],
and the Sāṅkhya Puruṣa is not like that, then how can he possess otherness (paratva) with respect to the aggregate?
And how can there be the "being-for-that" (tādarthya) of the aggregate?
If it is argued that even though it is not actually benefited, the [self] conceives itself as being benefited, let it conceive so at will.
What follows for the status of being an object of assistance (*upakāryatva*)?
It is certainly not the case that because the ignorant perceive the sky as possessing a surface or impurity, it thereby becomes so.
Furthermore, it must be investigated: whose such an error is it, and how does it arise?
It cannot belong to the power of consciousness (citiśakti),

because it is utterly pure due to being devoid of all modification, and thus the transformation of delusion— which is the cause of hundreds of impurities— is impossible for it. As for the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), which is designated by various synonyms such as "intellect" (buddhi), it does not undergo delusion because, being insentient, it is like a physical body.

If it is argued that even though it is insentient (*acid*), it becomes conscious because it has received the reflection (*chāyā*) of consciousness (*cit*) due to its transparency; we say no, because it is impossible for a formless consciousness (*cit*) and the intellect (*buddhi*) to have a reflection or for such a reflection to be grasped.
If it is argued that "reflection" means "like a reflection"; [we reply:]...

What indeed is the meaning of "as it were" (*iva*)? If you say it means "having the same nature as consciousness" (*cit-sarūpatva*), then alas! if the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) were to attain a state of having the same nature as consciousness—which is devoid of all modifications—then it would follow that the internal organ has its entire range of functions (*vṛtti*) completely subsided; thus, this connection with modifications such as delusion, pleasure, and pain would be even more difficult to establish.

If it is argued that there is similarity by virtue of being conscious, established through individual self-realization (*pratyātmasiddha*), we say no; for according to you, the person (*puruṣa*) is nothing but consciousness itself.
There is no cognizer.
As the venerable Patañjali said: "Since consciousness itself is the person (puruṣa), what is designated here by what?
If it is argued that the meaning is simply the state of not being insentient;
It has already been stated that non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*) is nothing other than the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*); therefore,
to explain it by means of that very same term is of no consequence.
Moreover, how could one who asserts that the establishment of cognition is dependent upon the proximity of consciousness (citi) maintain its non-material nature (ajaḍimāna)?

Furthermore, it is impossible for a distinct attribute characterized by the state of being a knower—colored by specific objects—to exist as a reflection, since such an attribute does not exist in either of the two substrata of the original and the reflection, namely consciousness and the internal organ (svānta);
and this theory of reflection has already been refuted in the critique of the disguised external (Buddhist) doctrine.

As for what is said— that even though the Self (puṃs) is changeless, its own internal organ (svānta) alone manifests its own various modifications, such as valid cognition, error, and so forth, which arise through the power of proximity to that [Self], as well as specific objects, just as a powerful king displays to his master the activities of his vassal circle, such as the agitation of opposing forces; therefore, the Self is designated as both the witness and the enjoyer— [This is the translation of the provided text.]
"King" means one who is valorous and victorious;
that [definition] is untenable,
for it is only when there is a seer that the object of sight is seen.

Furthermore, for the Sāṃkhyas who maintain that the self is pure consciousness (*dṛśimātra*), and for those disguised followers who rely upon them, the status of being a "seer" (*draṣṭṛtva*) is not real.
Nor is it possible for there to be the status of being a "remnant" (*śeṣitva*) based on something merely conceptual;
indeed, it has already been stated that even such a conceptual construction is impossible.

But a king who appoints ministers to those tasks either generally or specifically, and who enjoys their fruits such as sovereignty and so forth, is engaged in activities such as purchase, acceptance, or procreation based on the relationship of master and servant; therefore, he is not an illustration of a person who is inactive and incapable of receiving any new qualities— this [objection] is trivial.
(Thus ends the refutation of the inference for the self as favored by the followers of Kapila.

Since the objects of such inferences are already sublated by direct perceptions such as "I am fat" and "I am walking," the temporal lapse [of these inferences] is well-established; therefore, those who do not trust even the inferential proof of the self, the Vedic scholars, assert that its proof is solely based on scripture.
For the Śrutis directly demonstrate the Self's distinction from the body and so forth:

"This one is 'not this, not this'; "bodiless, woundless, without sinews, pure, untouched by evil; "some embodied beings enter a womb for the sake of a body, while others enter a stationary object; "it is never born, nor does it ever die; "for when the living self has departed, this [body] indeed dies; "for indeed, as long as one possesses a body... [and so on].
There are scriptural passages such as, "There is the removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant; indeed, pleasure and pain do not touch one who is bodiless.

Furthermore, injunctions prescribing means for attaining heaven and other results that occur at a later time imply a conscious entity that is eternal and distinct from the body and its adjuncts. Thus, this inner self (pratyagātman) is established by the authority of scripture and by the logical necessity of those [scriptural] statements.
(Thus concludes the exposition of the position that the self, being of a unique nature, has scripture alone as its means of valid cognition.
Now, one might object: why is such a great burden placed upon the head of the Veda, which is concerned solely with the attainment of the beneficial and the avoidance of the harmful?
For we actually apprehend this [self] through perception itself, which is the very foundation of all means of valid cognition, including inference and scripture.

Just as [the self] is distinct from visible objects such as a jar, so too this seer clearly manifests through direct perception as distinct even from the body, [thinking], "This is my body" and "I know this.
(Thus is the proposal of the position that the self is perceptible.)
Do not speak thus.
For perception is indeed cognition born from the contact of the sense organs with their objects.

And the sense organs are not capable of producing cognition through contact with the inner Self—which is distinct from form and the other [objects], which is unsurpassed and subtle—just as they do with external objects such as form.
As it is handed down in scripture: "The Self-existent pierced the openings for the senses.
He establishes the lack of necessity [for an external object] with the half-verse beginning with "Why," and so forth:
Does the object, such as blue and the like, require cognition—which is self-luminous and its own illuminator—for its own manifestation, because it is not self-luminous?

Alternatively, because of the doubt that "it conforms to the manifestation due to non-difference from consciousness"—that is, because of its non-distinction from *saṃvit*—the meaning is that the non-difference between blue and its cognition cannot be definitively determined.
The conformity of blue and so forth to consciousness is characterized by their being perceived simultaneously with consciousness.

And regarding the question of whether this [conformity] is caused by non-difference from consciousness, or whether it is caused by the dependence of insentient (jaḍa) blue and so forth upon self-luminous consciousness for its own manifestation, as long as there is no determination that it is caused by non-difference, [the non-difference remains unproven].
The meaning is that, for the time being, this [reason] does not establish non-difference,
nor is there any means of determining that it is necessitated by non-difference;
thus, the point is that it is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).

He says "residing in the object" (*bodhyastha*) to show that the rule of simultaneous perception establishes non-difference only between two objects of cognition, but not between the cognition and its object, nor between the cognizer and the cognition.
There is no non-difference among cognitions or among cognizers, even when they are perceived simultaneously.
Otherwise, it would follow that the Buddha himself is bound;

nor [can it be] between cognition and the object of cognition, or between two cognitions, because that would entail the consequence that cognition is insentient and so forth, and because it would entail the consequence of the identity of true and false objects.

However, the meaning is that one should accept the non-difference of the two objects of cognition (*bodhya*)—which exist in such a state—in some respect, such as between a quality and its possessor (*guṇa-guṇin*);
the phrase "the intellect and the cognizer" (*buddhi-boddhṛgau*), on the other hand, is used with reference to the subject at hand.
Alternatively, it is possible that the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*) applies only to the two objects of cognition themselves.
But [this is not the case] for the intellect and the knower;
for even in the absence of the intellect, the knower is manifest, as in states such as deep sleep—this is the meaning. //15//16//
He also states that the proof of the non-difference between knowledge and the knower is contradicted by perception (*pratyakṣabādhitatva*) with the words "and it is clear" (*spaṣṭaśca*).
For in the cognition "I know the jar," there is a distinct manifestation of the difference between the object of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing;
this is the meaning of "contradiction thereof."
He raises the doubt with the words "na ceti" (if it is not so):

either being an object of perceptual knowledge or being an object of knowledge in general is required as a cause for the perception of that difference, insofar as it pertains to the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).
The opponent’s intention is that, since consciousness (*saṃvit*) is self-luminous because it is not the object of another cognition, the perception of its difference cannot occur within the knower.
He refutes this with the words "by the mere establishment" (*siddhimātreṇa*);
that is, by the mere establishment—or the mere manifestation—of the counter-correlate, which is consciousness.
In the case of its establishment—that is, in the establishment of the perception of a difference in consciousness—the meaning is as follows:

because it is not a necessary factor (*aprayojakatva*), since the manifestation of that [consciousness] dependent on another cognition such as perception cannot be the cause for the perception of difference; and because there is no implication (*anākṣepa*)—meaning an impossibility of implication—of a specific feature of that [manifestation], namely a specific manifestation dependent on another cognition such as perception.

The meaning is this: for the perception of mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*), only the perception of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) is required, as well as the mere manifestation of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*); however, the perception of the counter-positive itself is not required.
Otherwise, in the case of a pillar, there would result the impossibility of perceiving its distinction from a *piśāca*.
However, in the present context, the manifestation of the counter-correlate—the cognition—exists by its own nature;
therefore, there is no inconsistency in the perception of that distinction in the cognizer.
In reality, each specific form (*asādhāraṇākāra*) itself constitutes the nature of the difference from others, by virtue of being opposed to the cognition of identity with anything else.
And since that [specific form] shines forth even when the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is not manifest, he says "even though not manifest.
Thus, the point is that the apprehension of the distinction between cognitions is simply the manifestation to the knower as "I-ness" (*ahantva*).

Furthermore, it should be understood that in the conventional usage of "difference from that," the cause is the cognition of its unique form (asādhāraṇākāra), assisted by the recollection of the counter-correlate (pratiyogin).
By the phrase "in all the world," it is indicated that the perception of difference is not possible [without such factors].
Since momentary perception cannot persist until the apprehension of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) is followed by the apprehension of the difference,

and since the simultaneous apprehension of both the absence of the counter-correlate and its locus would result in a failure to establish a specific connection— much like a mere collective mental grasping (*samūhālambana*)— the view that the apprehension of difference is essentially of the nature of error is thereby refuted.

Since each unique property (*asādhāraṇadharma*) itself consists in the exclusion of others (*itarabhedatva*), and since that [property] is apprehended in the very first moment the substratum (*dharmin*) is perceived; for this very reason, when one sees an object never before seen, the cognition of difference—namely, "this is some distinct entity"—is universally accepted by the world and established by one's own experience, and thus it is not fit to be denied. Therefore, it is said to be "attested by the direct witness of all people."
He raises an objection with the words "nanu jīvataḥ" (surely, of one who is living).
By the phrase "placing the foot on the head," he means by way of refutation.
"Grasping the connection" refers to grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*).
From that—namely, from the perception of difference—the possibility of its sublation arises;
that is, the possibility of the sublation of the inference of non-difference. This being the case—that is, when perception is the sublater of inference.
It would be refuted—that is, sublated.

The point is this: the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*) has been grasped as being pervaded by non-difference (*abheda*) only in the case of two things that are actually apprehended as distinct.
Therefore, when inferring non-difference on that basis, it is determined that the aspect of perceiving distinction within direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is characterized as an error.
Nor is there a contradiction with the foundational authority [of scripture],
because we accept the nature of things established by perception— which is useful for grasping pervasion—
whereas difference is not useful for grasping pervasion.
"He avoids [the argument] because he does not know the distinction" means that you do not understand the disparity between the example (dṛṣṭānta) and the subject of the example (dārṣṭāntika).
He demonstrates this very point as follows:
Regarding this: neither being perception (*pratyakṣatva*) nor being inference (*anumānatva*) is the determining factor for being sublated (*bādhyatva*) or being a sublater (*bādhakatva*).

Rather, it is precisely being rooted in defects (*doṣamūlatva*) or being rooted in the absence of defects (*adoṣamūlatva*) that functions as such. And so, just as the inference regarding the difference in flames—which is rooted in the absence of defects—is a sublater, [so too is the case here].

The perception of the oneness of the flame-flame, however, is sublated because it is rooted in the defect of similarity; the collective intention is that, in the present case, the apprehension of the distinction between the knower, the known, and the knowledge is not rooted in such a defect.
He establishes the persistence of the admitted causal defect in the perception of the oneness of the flame with the words beginning "tathā hi" (for instance).
By the statement that the two flames have been recently extinguished and rekindled, their actual difference is made known.
It is thus stated that the non-perception of this difference and the cognition that they reside in the same wick are the causes for the error of identity between them.

Furthermore, for the observer of the extinguishing and rekindling, there exists a direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the difference between the two flames; therefore, the identity-perception of the flames residing in the observer who did not witness the extinguishing and so forth is also sublated by that [direct perception].
The [author] establishes, by the word "ataḥ" (therefore), that even in a case where [the lamp] has not been extinguished, there is a cause for the illusion as explained in the *Nirukta*.

Even in a situation where [the lamp] is not extinguished, one must admit a distinction between the flames due to the successive difference of the conjunctions of the oil, the wick-parts, and fire—which are the causes of the lamp.
Furthermore, the continuity of the effect-series follows from the force of the continuity of the cause-series.
However, the cessation of each preceding flame follows precisely from the cessation of its cause.
For its cause is the contact of fire with the specific parts of the wick and the oil;
since fire requires a substratum to consume, the destruction of those specific parts of the wick necessarily entails the destruction of that contact with fire.

Thus, once the difference between the preceding and succeeding flames of a lamp is established, the sense is that there arises an illusion of unity due to the non-apprehension of difference within the continuum of similar lamps and the perception of a defect in the form of similarity.

Having cited as an example of an illusion of unity regarding things that are actually manifold a case of direct perception, he now cites as an example of an illusion of multiplicity regarding what is actually one, also in the form of direct perception, with the words "likewise some.
In the illusion of two moons caused by pressing the eye with a finger and so forth, the defect is the reversal of the natural outward radiation of the visual rays, resulting in their bifurcation.

And its being sublated by the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of the identity between the person who points it out and the moon is stated in the passage beginning with "at the same time" (*samasamaye*).
He demonstrates the disparity between the example (*dṛṣṭānta*) and the subject of the example (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "but not so" (*na caivam*).

The direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) in the form "I know the jar," which possesses worldly objectivity (*laukikaviṣayitā*) as determined by the distinction between the knower, the act of knowing, and the known, is rooted in error (*doṣamūla*).
The meaning is that [the difference] is not seen at all as being sublated by the perception of non-difference;
thus, its capacity to sublate the inference of non-difference is well-established.
To the question "Why is it not the other way around? he says: "And not through perception... and so forth.
The identity (*tathātva*) of the knower and the known consists in their non-difference from knowledge.
The phrase "in the counter-example" (*vipakṣe*) serves as a reminder of the previously stated lack of probative force (*aprayojakatva*).

The meaning is that because there is an absence of a subverting argument (*bādhakatarka*) against the counter-example, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not established; thus, the inference of non-difference (*abheda-anumāna*) remains unproven and cannot be suspected of subverting the perception of the difference between knowledge, the knower, and the known.

He says "by virtue of being non-sensory" (*anaindriyikatvena*) because the apprehension of a distinction between cognition and its cognizer would have to be rooted in a defect consisting of the differentiation of the outward extension of sensory functions.

The meaning is that, since cognition and its cognizer are not objects of the external senses, it is impossible for the apprehension of their distinction to be caused by a differentiation in the functioning of the senses.

Furthermore, he says "due to the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible" (*yogyānupalambhena*) to show that there is no subverting cognition here, as there is in the case of the illusion of two moons.
The intended meaning of the statement "and it is not so here" has been elucidated by these two sentences.
With the words "api ca," he elaborates on what was stated in the sentence beginning with "saṃvidadhīne":
namely, the restriction that there is a necessary concomitance in being perceived together with consciousness (*saṃvid*).
"Inevitable" means that it is difficult to avoid even if one does not accept non-difference.
To the objection, "Surely the object and so forth may be established even without consciousness," he says: "Nor even difference.
"Difference" refers to the difference between the grasped and the grasper.

The meaning is that "attainment" refers to knowledge, and thus speaking in this manner constitutes a departure from one's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*). Alternatively, it refers to [the argument] regarding the rule of simultaneous perception as a proof for non-difference.
He states the self-contradiction as well with the words, "nor even difference.

The meaning is that since even the appearance of difference must be denoted by consciousness alone, according to the previously stated reason, if difference is non-different from consciousness, then the reason consisting of difference would also not be established.
Alternatively, the sense is that even the difference between cognitions, which you yourself accept, would not be established.

Having thus refuted the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambhaniyama*)— which is favored by the manifest Sugatas and serves to establish the non-difference of consciousness— he now also refutes the nature of luminosity (*prakāśasvabhāvatva*) favored by the hidden Sugatas, with the words "in the absence of luminosity" (*aprakāśe*).
This refers to that which is of a non-luminous nature— that is, having a non-luminous essence— and which is distinct from cognition (*jñāna*).

By this, it has been demonstrated that the inference of the non-difference between the object of knowledge and its cognition is sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) and that the logical reason (*hetu*) is unestablished in the subject (*pakṣāsiddhi*).
Even though the object of knowledge does not have luminosity as its intrinsic nature because it is insentient (*jaḍatva*), [the following applies].

Furthermore, the sense is that the occasional manifestation of jars and other objects is possible through their connection with self-luminous cognition (*svayaṃprakāśajñāna*). However, he says "but not by that much alone" (*na ca tāvatā*) to indicate that while the reason— "the knower is non-different from cognition because its nature is manifestation"— is accepted, the probandum [itself] is not thereby established.

The nature of cognition (*jñānatva*) consists in being a consciousness that illuminates an object. For the meaning of the verbal root *jñā* (to know) has the property of being a quality of the agent, which is cognition;
however, since the self (*ātman*) is the substratum (*dharmin*), it does not possess that same nature—this is the intended sense.
First, he describes the nature of cognition as being "dependent" (paratantra):
its nature consists solely in its various modes,
and its occurrence is occasional.

And "penetrating the object" (viṣayāvagāhitva) are the attributes of cognition. Regarding the view that "a stream-cognition (dhārāvāhika-vijñāna) is considered by us to be a single cognition," the distinction is this: [in that case] it persists—that is, continues—in the form of a stream; whereas in the alternative position, it continues in its own essential nature (svarūpataḥ) as long as there is no transition to another object. This is the differentiation.
He states the self’s intrinsic nature with the words "the self.
Being the substratum (*dharmitva*), being the knower (*jñātṛtva*), and appearing as "I" (*ahantvena bhāna*) are the attributes (*dharmāḥ*) of the self.
Now, one might ask: if the self is distinct from cognition in this way, how can the designation "the self's cognition" (*jñānam iti*) be justified? To this, he says "if" (*yadi*).
It is non-different from itself.
The term "knowledge" (jñāna) is applied to the self because of its similarity to knowledge.

And that [similarity] consists in self-luminosity, which has the nature of being independent of another for its manifestation; the sense is that it is characterized by being qualified by something through both relations: having an objectivity determined by itself and identity [with that qualification].
"Even so" means that the nature of the self, when expressed by the word "knowledge," is indeed equal to knowledge;
however, it is not the primary knowledge consisting of mere cognition (*jñapti*). This is the meaning.

Alternatively, it should be understood that [the self] is the very locus of cognition (*jñānāyatana*), and not merely the act of cognizing (*jñaptimātra*); the word "should be understood" (*mantavyam*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Consequently, the intended inference of the opponent—that the cognizer, the self, is non-different from cognition—is sublated by powerful direct perception; this is the underlying sense.
The phrase "for this very reason" establishes that the self's status as a knower—which is established through perception and inference—is also confirmed by scripture.
The sentence beginning with "Now then" (atheti) has as its purport the nature of the self as the "I," which is the knower.

The phrase "this which... has as its purport the self's abiding within the heart and its self-luminosity, referring to the self that presides over the senses and is characterized by an abundance of sensory cognition.

The passage beginning with "For this [Self]" (eṣa hi) and so forth establishes that the Self— designated by the word "knowledge" because it is self-luminous— possesses both agency, which is obtained through a presiding presence consisting of volition and effort conducive to the operation of the senses and other faculties, and the state of being a knower.
The passage "the knower" (vijñātāram) establishes that the nature of the Self to be known by those seeking liberation is characterized by the quality of being a knower.
The meaning is: the Supreme Self, whose body is the living self (jīvātman) as the knower.
"In liberation, one does not see another who possesses knowledge"—here, "the seer" (paśyaḥ) refers to the liberated self, who perceives all.

The scriptural statement regarding the absence of knowledge during the state of liberation is intended to mean the absence of the perception of that which is to be abandoned; thus it establishes [the verse] beginning with "Do not see.

For at that time, because everything is seen as being in accordance with one's own nature through the Lord’s sovereign power (*vibhūti*), there is no disagreeableness toward any object whatsoever. This is the state of suffering (*duḥkhatā*).
The second half-verse, "The seer sees everything," should also be cited here;
its explanatory form begins with "He is the highest" and so forth.
The passage beginning with "He moves about there" and ending with "not remembering what was added" should likewise be cited here.

The distinction is as follows: even upon the cessation of the sixteen parts (*kalā*) in liberation, the phrase "in this very way" refers specifically to the non-cessation of the knowledge that constitutes the defining attribute of one's true nature;

furthermore, the phrase "therefore, [it is] two-fold" aims to establish the self's distinction from the body, senses, mind, vital breath, and [empirical] cognition by virtue of its possessing knowledge.
Having thus established the self's status as a knower, he establishes it for the Supreme Self as well with the words "It is true."
"Tadvad-vacana" means expressing that which possesses knowledge;

"tadvacanatve" means in the state of expressing that which possesses knowledge. If the word "jñāna" were expressive of that which possesses knowledge (i.e., a possessive), then as a word ending in the abstract suffix *lyuṭ*, it would be udātta on its first syllable by virtue of the *lit-svara* rule.
But this [word] has its accent on the penultimate syllable (*antodātta*).
The intention is that this word, ending in the *ac* suffix, must be accepted as denoting a knower (*jñātṛ*). Thus it says, "in the Aitareya."
The intention is that, by the force of the context, the word *prajñāna* refers to one who possesses wisdom (*prajñānavat*).
[The term] *prājña* means "one who is wise" (*prajña eva prājñaḥ*);
the suffix *aṇ* is used here in its own sense (to form a synonym).
By that—

meaning by the omniscient Supreme Self. He concludes the definition of the nature of the self, which was proposed as being "other than the body, senses, mind, vital breath, and intellect," with the words "that is established."

Now, in order to establish the self-luminosity of the self—which was asserted as being "provable by no other means"—he begins the examination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) with the words "But what... and so forth.
Regarding the term "inference":
although direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), such as the cognition "I know," is indeed possible as a means of valid cognition in that regard.
Because it is impossible for that [cognition] to have the body and so forth as its object; furthermore,

the intention is that even if perception has a distinct self as its object, this means of valid cognition must be established by reasoning (*tarka*) itself— consisting of the investigation of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*) such as "this [means of knowledge] ought to function toward this [object] in this way"— as expressed in the words "as he says."

The intention is as follows: since he stated that [the self] which is distinct from desire and so forth is inferred [from them], it is understood that Akṣapāda’s view is that inference alone is the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) in that regard. He raises an objection: "What of these? [i.e., what is the status of these other means of knowledge?]
Dhūmadhvaja says: [The word] "fire" [refers to] *agni*.

The point is this: since the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is rooted in the observation of concomitance (*sahacāra*), and since that [concomitance] is established through perception itself—given that it possesses a distinct nature when there is an observation of concomitance involving desire and so forth—what is the use of inference?
Furthermore, if there is no observation of concomitance, how could pervasion be grasped by means of it?
"If [the pervasion] has not been grasped by desire and so forth, how could there be an inference from them?
He answers with the words "Let it not be" and so on:
let there be no grasping of the concomitance between the specific desire and so forth and the specific probandum (sādhya) that one wishes to prove.
The inference of the self proceeds precisely from the observation of concomitance by virtue of its being a substratum and a quality;
this is what is meant by "inference based on general observation" (sāmānyato dṛṣṭa).
He establishes this very point with the words "for instance" (tathā hi).
Being an effect (kāryatva) is the state of having an origin (utpattimattva).
Impermanence (anityatva) is the state of being subject to destruction (vināśitva).
Being a quality (guṇatva) is the possession of the universal (jāti) "quality-ness" (guṇatvatva).
Or [it may mean] having as its sole nature the state of being a qualifier.
These [qualities] are pervaded by the state of being dependent (*āśritatva*).
The intended inference here is: "Desire and the rest are dependent because they are qualities, like color."

Here, he establishes the reason with the words "and because it is a quality" (*guṇatvam ca*). The meaning is as follows: since being a category (*padārthatva*) entails being one or another among substance and the rest, once substance-ness and the other [categories] have been excluded by means of an inference that differentiates it from substance and so forth, the category-ness that remains—qualified by its distinction from substance and the rest—is established as being precisely "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*).
He states the other inferences for differentiation with the words "not in the universal" (*na sāmānye*).
In establishing the differentiation of non-existence (*abhāva*), impermanence (*anityatva*)—in the form of possessing origination and destruction—must be stated.
Therefore, there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in the case of prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) or posterior non-existence (*pradhvaṃsa*).
"In the pervasive" means "because of being inherent in the omnipresent [Self]";
this reason is established according to the view of the Naiyāyikas.
It is not action (*karman*), because it lacks the status of being an independent cause of conjunction and disjunction;
nor is it substance (*dravya*), for which the reason may be stated as "because it is not conjoined.
Having established its nature as a quality (*guṇatva*), he establishes its nature as a specific quality (*viśeṣaguṇatva*) in the verse beginning with "viśeṣe."
The phrase "while being impermanent" (*anityatve sati*) is included to exclude deviation (*vyabhicāra*) with respect to "form-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth;
the qualifying portion (*viśeṣya-dala*) is included to exclude such deviation with respect to "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) and so forth.
Even so, there would be a deviation in the case of light, because that is perceptible by the eye alone;
therefore, one must state "provided it is a quality."
Even so, that same consequence would apply to the contact with a wall of light;
therefore, one must specify the definition as "possessing a genus that is perceptible by a single sense-faculty alone.
And in that case, the qualification "impermanent" would be redundant.
The same applies to the property of being a quality (*guṇatva*);
for there is no evidence for a genus "luminosity" (*prabhātva*), and since "fire-ness" (*tejastva*) and the like are perceptible by two sense-faculties.

However, it should be understood that if the genus *prabhātvaja* (the state of being born from light) is established as valid, or if the tactile perception of air is accepted, then the inclusion of the property "being a quality" (*guṇatva*) is indeed necessary.

The qualification "for those like us" (*asmadādīnām*) is intended to refer to those who are incapable [of perceiving objects with the mind], since for yogis, even by means of the mind, there is the apprehension of color and other qualities.

He states the inferences by way of elimination (*pariśeṣānumāna*) with the words "In this way" (*evam*), in order to establish the determination of the specific substratum for the inference based on general observation (*sāmānyato-dṛṣṭānumāna*).
By those who reject [this view], it is said:

one position is that inference based on general observation (*sāmānyatodṛṣṭa*), which is essentially positive inference (*anvayin*), leads to the inference of a specific [property] when assisted by the inference of its difference from others. Another position is that a specific reason, established subsequently through the inference of its difference from others—which is based on general observation—functions as a purely negative (*kevalavyatirekin*) inference.
And by this statement, the first position is suggested:
"those which are the qualities of the elements.
Here, it should also be understood that the word "suitable" (*yogyāḥ*) is to be supplied.
The application and conclusion in the negative inference (*vyatirekin*) are not like that.
Regarding "space and time":
desire and the rest are not qualities of space, time, or the mind.
Because they are specific qualities (*viśeṣaguṇa*),
or because they are perceptible (*pratyakṣatva*);
whereas those which are the qualities of space and so forth, such as number (*saṅkhyā*) and the rest, [are not].
They are not perceptible, nor are they specific qualities; [this is so] because there is no cause.
"Anukraṣṭavyāḥ" means those to be drawn forth or included.
He states the general application, which is the fruit of various inferences, with the words "by that" (tena).
He also sets forth another alternative position with the words "in the point of dispute" (vimatipade).
The term *vimatipada* means the locus or cause of disagreement—that is, the various conflicting doctrines; "from those" means from those things which are their objects.

Herein is the formal argument (*prayoga*): desire and the rest are qualities belonging to something distinct from the body and so forth, which are the subjects of disagreement regarding their substratum, because they possess the nature of being qualities that fall within the scope of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that negates [their being qualities] of those [body and so forth].
"And as for the example" refers to the one based on negative concomitance (*vyatirekin*) and so forth.

Even if a non-substance distinct from well-known substances were established, an example based on positive concomitance (*anvayin*) would not be possible, because its being a quality (*tadguṇatva*) is not established.

Nor should it be argued that, since the absence of the probandum (*sādhyavyatireka*) is likewise unestablished prior to the inference, how can an example of negative concomitance (*vyatireki-udāharaṇa*) be possible? The point is this: the probandum is simply "inherence in something distinct from established substances," and thus its absence in things such as color (*rūpa*) can indeed be established. Alternatively, he states "or generally" (*sāmānyataḥ vā*) because a positive pervasion (*anvaya-vyāpti*) based on generality is also possible.
This [argument] depends upon the establishment of the substratum of the term "distinct" (*vilakṣaṇa*).
The intention is that in the inference of that [substratum], the apprehension of pervasion (*vyāpti*) occurs through the inclusion of odor and so forth.
And thus, it should be understood that there is no harm even if one does not accept the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*).
The Vedic scholars (śrotriyas) reject the inferential proof of a distinct self as favored by the Naiyāyikas with the words "this too.

Even if the mere locus is established by a positive concomitant (anvayin) [reason], they argue that a specific locus cannot be established by a purely negative reason (kevalavyatirekin); to this, he replies with the word "kevala" [referring to the state of being a mere negative].
This refers to the stage of the means of proof, that is, the state of being an inferent.

It does not find [the probandum] and does not attain it, because of the absence of positive concomitance with similar instances (*sapakṣa*); that is to say, because there is no connection with a locus where the co-occurrence with the probandum is observed.
"Like the 'uncommon' (*asādhāraṇa*) [reason]" means:

The point is this: just as a reason that is "uncommon" (asādhāraṇa)— because it occurs in only one side [of the debate]— lacks the capacity to prove [the conclusion], since it lacks the apprehension of concomitance with the probandum due to the absence of grasping its co-presence,
so too a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) reason lacks the capacity to prove [the conclusion], because it is impossible to grasp its pervasion (vyāpti).

If it is argued that the uncommon (asādhāraṇa) reason is indeed defective because it does not occur in a similar instance (sapakṣa) when one exists, whereas there is no such defect in the purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) reason because of the very absence of a similar instance,
this is not so.
In the case of a purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*), does the probandum (*sādhya*) have prior ascertainment or not?

If it exists, then where that ascertainment occurs, if the reason (*hetu*) is present there, it would be a positive concomitant (*anvayin*); if, however, it is absent, it would simply be an uncommon (*asādhāraṇa*) reason.

If [the probandum] does not exist, then because the absence of the probandum is likewise unestablished, even the status of being a *kevalavyatirekin* (purely negative reason) is difficult to maintain; this is the general direction [of the argument]. The detailed exposition, however, should be sought in works such as the *Nyāyapariśuddhi*.
He raises an objection with the words, "And it is not thus."
The absence from the dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*)— that is, non-existence in the dissimilar instance—

is like the "common" [inconclusive reason], which functions across all three positions. Just as in the case of the common [reason], the reason is non-probative because it does not exist in the dissimilar instance.

The meaning is that even in the case of a purely positive (kevalānvayin) reason, since a counter-example (vipakṣa) is unestablished, the absence of its existence there is likewise unestablished; thus, it would follow that such a reason lacks probative power. If it is intended that a purely negative (kevalavyatirekin) reason is not a prover because the apprehension of pervasion is seen to depend on observing both types of concomitance in a positive-negative (anvayavyatirekin) reason—due to the non-observation of concomitance between the probandum and the reason—then the implication is that a purely positive reason would also lack probative power, since one does not observe the concomitance between the absence of the probandum and the absence of the reason.
"He excludes [the possibility of] place, time, and so forth" means:

since a probans (*hetu*) might exist even in the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) due to some other causal factor in a particular place or time, once the suspected *upādhi* has been removed by a favorable counter-argument (*anukūlatarka*) that includes the specific place and time, [the probans is established] even from the mere observation of the concomitance (*sahacāra*) between the probandum and the probans.

The meaning is that positive concomitance (*anvayavyāpti*) is ascertained. The particle *api* is displaced; it should be construed immediately after "by the observation of positive concomitance" (*anvayadarśanena*).
The meaning is that [the reason] possesses the nature of being concomitant with the probandum—that is, it is pervaded by the probandum.

The point is that since the apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatireka-sahacāra*) is required only for the apprehension of negative pervasion (*vyatireka-vyāpti*), there is no logical inconsistency in the apprehension of positive pervasion (*anvaya-vyāpti*) in the case of a purely positive inference (*kevalānvayin*), even though negative instances are unestablished.

Furthermore, this is the intention of the proponents of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*): that the fulfillment of the five characteristics of a valid reason is achieved in a purely positive inference simply because the existence of a counter-example (*vipakṣa*) is itself unestablished.

One might object: "In that case, the apprehension of negative concomitance (*vyatirekavyāpti*) is established simply by observing the co-occurrence of the absence of the probandum (*sādhya*) and the absence of the probans (*sādhana*). To this, he says: "And not the absence of the probans... The nature of the probans as being conjoined with the probandum consists in its possessing negative concomitance as defined by the probandum; that is, it is characterized by being the counter-positive of an absence that pervades the absence of the probandum. He states the reason why the ascertainment of such concomitance is impossible with the words: "of the absence... (*abhāvasya*).

The meaning is this: because the loci of the absence of the probandum and the probans—which are negative (vyatirekin)—are infinite in relation to their respective substrates, it is impossible for there to be a negative concomitance (vyatireka-vyāpti), defined as the rule of coexistence in the absence of the probandum, even in some single instance (*kalayā*), since the probans would have to occur somewhere where the probandum is absent.
This is because that which possesses the negative probandum and probans is limited, and thus [the probans] could occur entirely (*kārtsnyena*) in some place where the probandum is absent.
The underlying intention is that apprehension [of the pervasion] is also possible.

Now, one might object: "In as many perceptual instances as there are, the pervasion should be ascertained simply by observing the co-occurrence of the two absences. To this, he says: "In case of doubt" (*sandeha*). For negative pervasion (*vyatirekavyāpti*) consists in the pervasion of the absence of the reason by the absence of the probandum.

And when there is the doubt, "Let the absence of the probandum (sādhya) exist, but let there not be an absence of the reason (hetu)," the pervasion by the absence of the means of proof (sādhana) would not be apprehended in the absence of the probandum, provided there is a lack of a supporting argument (anukūlatarka). The removal of such doubt occurs through the force of an argument characterized as "otherwise-unaccountability" (anyathānupapatti), such as the fact that the probandum is necessarily contingent upon the means of proof or possesses a nature invariably tied to the means of proof.

The underlying intention is that [the inference] is not possible without the determination of the causal relationship (hetu-hetumadbhāva) rooted in the observation of the concomitance (sahacāra) between the probandum and the probans; thus, the purely negative inference (kevalavyatirekin) is unestablished.

Furthermore, regarding the inference of "being a quality distinct from earth and so forth" by means of a specific reason, he states the non-establishment of the probandum (sādhyāprasiddhi) with the words "from earth and so forth."

Even if the existence of another entity, such as a quality (*guṇa*), is well-established, the property to be proven— namely, its being characterized by "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) as residing therein— is indeed unestablished.
Nor should it be argued that what is being proven is merely the state of being inherent in another entity such as earth,
for that [inherence] is already established in the case of "form-ness" (*rūpatva*) and so forth.

The meaning is as follows: since the property of "inherence in that which is denoted by a word" (niruktasamavetatva) is well-established only in things distinct from qualities and actions, its application to prove [the existence of] a quality such as cognition is untenable.
Furthermore, the property of "inherence in a substance that is a different entity" is itself unestablished prior to the inference; this is the underlying intention.
With the words "by this," [the author] extends the refutations of the Naiyāyika’s inferences for the self to the inferences for the self proposed by the Sāṅkhya as well.

"And so it is": the intention is that we shall first explain precisely those reasons favored by the Sāṅkhya—which establish a self of a different character—for the sake of the students' clarity and for the ease of refutation.
"Because they exist for the sake of another who is a composite," and so forth, is a verse from the *Sāṅkhyakārikā*.
He explains this with the words "this is the meaning," and so forth.
"Sharaṇa" means a house.
"Sanghātatva" (the state of being an aggregate) means having the nature of a collection of parts.
“Of the elements” means of the five great elements (*mahābhūta*).
“In the unmanifest” means that its nature consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion; that is, its essential character is that of pleasure and so forth.

Or [it may mean] having the nature of being the producer of pleasure and so forth. By that, its "being such"—that is, its consisting of an aggregate of the three qualities (guṇas) in the form of sattva, rajas, and tamas—is to be inferred through its effect, just like the body and so forth; this is the meaning. He raises the objection that the reason "being an aggregate" is contradictory [with the conclusion] by saying, "Nor [is it so] of the sense organs."

Contradiction regarding both specificities (*ubhayaviśeṣaviruddhatva*) means that [the reason] brings about a form that contradicts the intended specificities of both the subject (*pakṣa*) and the probandum (*sādhya*).

This is because, through the observation of frequent co-occurrence—namely, that "being an aggregate" (*saṅghātatva*) exists in the primary elements and their derivatives by virtue of "not being derived from the *ahaṅkāra*," and that "being for the sake of another who is an aggregate" (*saṃhataparārthatva*) exists in houses, beds, and so forth—the pervasion (*vyāpti*) has been grasped; consequently, in the case of the sense organs included within the subject, there arises the non-*ahaṅkārika* nature, which contradicts the intended *ahaṅkārika* nature.

The meaning is that the reason (*hetu*), "being a composite" (*saṅghātatva*), is contradictory because it entails "compositeness," which is the opposite of the "non-composite nature" intended for the other term that constitutes the probandum (*sādhya*).
Furthermore, the logical connection is that the reason is not contradictory to either of the two specific qualities [of the subject].
He establishes its non-contradictory nature with the words beginning, "In the case of the *ahaṅkāra*... and so forth.

Since the functioning of the organs, ending with the mind, is observed only when the function of the ego (ahaṅkāra) is present, and is not observed in its absence—as during deep sleep—it is determined that they are derived from the ego. Furthermore, because they possess the qualities of buoyancy and illumination characteristic of the effect of *sattva*, the sense is that they are the products of the *sāttvika* ego. And there is scriptural authority as well: "The ten gods are the *vaikārika* [products]."
"And the eleventh is the mind"—this is the form of the Smṛti (tradition).

The "gods" are the sense-faculties (*indriya*), so called because of their connection with light (*prakāśa*) or because they are presided over by the gods. They are called "Vaikārika" because they are the effects produced from the Vaikārika, which is the Sāttvika ego (*ahaṅkāra*).

The meaning is as follows: because an exception (apavāda) is untenable—that is, because sublation (bādhana) is untenable—there is no pervasion (vyāpti) between the state of being a composite (saṅghātatva) and not being derived from the ego-principle (anahaṅkārikatva).

This is because the class of sense organs, which consists of the three guṇas, is established by valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa) as being derived from the ego-principle; thus, the reason is inconclusive (anaikāntika).

Having set aside the contradiction regarding the specific qualification of the subject (*pakṣa*), he sets aside the contradiction regarding the specific qualification of the probandum (*sādhya*) with the words "But as for the self...
and "And because it is not a decisive reason (*aprayojaka*)."

The meaning is this: since the status of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) is possible for the uncomposite Self precisely because it is conscious, the state of being a composite (*saṅghātatva*) is irrelevant to its supremacy (*paratva*) or primacy.
If being a composite were the determining factor for supremacy, then there might indeed be a pervasion (*vyāpti*) such that "whatever is a composite is for the sake of another";
and by the force of that pervasion, one would have to accept the postulation of many composites.
But this is not the case;

thus, the underlying intention is that when "being for the sake of another" is taken as the probandum (saṃhataparārthatva), the pervasion (vyāpti) of "being a composite" (saṅghātatva) is unestablished (asiddha).

Furthermore, it should be understood that the "compositeness" of the self—inferred on the grounds of its being for the sake of a composite—is sublated by the non-perception of what is otherwise perceptible (yogyānupalabdhi).

He states, "And not by another means of valid cognition," because the pervasion of being a composite with being for the sake of another will be established due to the absence of contradiction by other means of valid cognition.

He concludes the proof of the Self through the inference that composites exist for the sake of another with the words, "And thus. The meaning of the passage beginning with "if there were compositeness" is that [the Self] is devoid of the three qualities—sattva and so forth—and their effects, just as it is devoid of being-for-the-sake-of-another, which is the pervader of compositeness.

It has been stated that because the consequence of an infinite regress would follow if another [cause] were composite, the "reversal of the three qualities" (traiguṇyaviparyaya) must be understood as having the nature of being non-composite (atraiguṇyātmakatva); thus, the portion of the verse ending with "asaṃhataḥ" has been explained. Now, he explains the portion beginning with "adhiṣṭhānāt" by saying, "likewise, the body and so forth."
By virtue of consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion— that is, by way of being an aggregate composed of the constituents such as *sattva* which have pleasure and so forth as their nature—
they are presided over; that is, they are impelled toward conformity with their effects by another conscious being who is distinct from them.
"By means of the machine and so forth, such as the charioteer and others.
He explains this [point] regarding "the state of being an enjoyer" with the words "Moreover, when it is favorable":
that which is to be made favorable is that which possesses a favorable cognition.
*Anukūlavedanīya* means the object of a cognition characterized by the mode of being favorable.
Similarly, *pratikūlanīya* and *pratikūlavedanīya* are to be understood [as the objects of cognitions characterized by the modes of being unfavorable].
*Bhrātṛvya* means an enemy.
An alternative interpretation of the phrase "because of being an enjoyer" (bhoktṛbhāvāt) is that it refers to being a seer (draṣṭṛtva).

Regarding the passage beginning with "because of being a controller" (adhiṣṭhātuḥ): since the activity of an aggregate depends upon another controller, if that controller were itself an aggregate, then its activity would likewise depend upon yet another controller.
In the same way, since this would apply to what follows as well, it would lead to the fallacy of infinite regress; therefore, the sustainer must be admitted to be non-composite (*asaṃghāta*).

Likewise, if the enjoyer—who is to be gratified by pleasure or repelled by pain—were composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), then that [enjoyer] too would necessarily be subject to being experienced as agreeable or disagreeable. Consequently, because it would necessitate further things to be agreed upon or disagreed with, the fallacy of infinite regress would follow.
Thus, its being composed of the three *guṇas* must be accepted.
The sense is that by means of the inference of a distinct observer—whose subject is the body and so forth—the self’s distinction from the body and other such things is also established.
He explains the portion "and because of activity for the sake of isolation" with the words "likewise, from the body and so forth."

Here is the formal argument (*prayoga*): The engagement in the means for achieving isolation (*kaivalya*) is preceded by the knowledge of the true nature of the self that is capable of attaining the state of isolation, because it is an engagement in the means for achieving isolation.

Whatever engagement of a discerning person is directed toward the means for a specific result is preceded by the knowledge of the true nature of the self that is capable of attaining that particular result.

The meaning is as follows: just as there is activity directed toward the means for attaining heaven, so too, from the knowledge that liberation is impossible for anything composed of the three *guṇas*—from the body up to *pradhāna*—which is by nature subject to transformation, the existence of a distinct Self (*ātman*) is established.
First, he refutes the inference put forward by the Sāṅkhyas to establish a self distinct from the aggregates— namely, that "the composite is for the sake of another"—
with the words beginning "In this case too," etc.,
[and] the words "prior and posterior," etc.
The meaning is "one after another" (anyānya); or it may be "existing in a sequence of before and after" (pūrvāparībhūta);
or the complete reading may be "a collection of prior and posterior [moments]" (parāparasaṅghāta).
"By being an effect alone," etc.:
from an effect the cause is to be inferred;
since the cause itself is occasional, it is also an effect, and thus its cause must be something else.

The meaning is this: just as the postulation of a causal series proceeding higher and higher is not a fault because it is based on valid authority (*prāmāṇika*), so too is the postulation of a series of composite bodies resulting from the force of invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*).

To the objection that—since "being for the sake of another" (*parārthatva*) is defined by "being an enjoyer" (*bhoktṛtva*), and since being a composite body is not the cause of that—it is impossible to grasp a pervasion (*vyāpti*) between "being a composite body" and "being for the sake of another," he says: "And not... (*na ca*).
The status of being the master of an aggregate can only exist in that which possesses an excellence dependent upon it.

Furthermore, such dependence on an excellence for the purpose of conferring excellence is impossible in the case of the *puruṣa* (Spirit) postulated by the Sāṅkhya, who is non-composite, untainted, immutable, and therefore incapable of having excellence conferred upon him. Thus, through inference, it is established that there must be some composite entity that presides over the aggregate, and not a non-composite one.
The meaning is that this applies to the *puruṣa* according to the Sāṃkhya doctrine;
the underlying intention is that even an excellence in the form of experience could not possibly belong to the Sāṃkhya *puruṣa*.
By this, the argument that "the *puruṣa* exists because there is the state of being an experiencer" is also refuted.
Furthermore, it is observed that a bed and the like serve the purpose of the body,
and the body serves the purpose of another body.

Therefore, since being a composite (saṅghātatva) is the motivator for "being-for-another" in the sense of participating in an excellence dependent upon that [body], it is indeed intended that the apprehension of the pervasion (vyāpti) is possible through the state of being for another as delimited by that [composite nature].

Regarding the phrase "taddhi" (for that [is so]): if something is benefited by another or is produced by it, that [latter] is its *śeṣin* (the principal), becoming the primary (*pradhāna*) or the *aṅgin* (the whole);
whereas that which benefits or produces it exists for the sake of the former, being its *śeṣa* (subordinate) or *aṅga* (part). This is the meaning of the logical connection (*anvaya*).
It is assisted— that is, it is rendered possessed of an excellence—
just as the body and so forth are by means of garlands, sandalwood, and the like, or just as a sacrifice and the like are by means of the *prayāja* offerings and so forth.

It is "made" (kriyate), meaning it is produced, just as a jar and the like are produced by means of a staff and so forth, or a sacrifice and the like by means of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) and so forth.
In this context, the distinction is that that which is being assisted or being acted upon is the principal (aṅgin), while that which assists or acts is the subordinate member (aṅga);
and it is not so [in the case of the self].
Likewise, [the Sāṃkhya puruṣa] is one capable of receiving an excellence.
The "Sāṃkhya puruṣa" is the self (ātman) as conceived by the followers of Kapila.

Now, if it is argued that even though the self cannot be assisted, the assistance provided by the body and so forth is accomplished for its sake—characterized by the delusion "I have been assisted"—and thus its being directed toward that [body] is logical, to this he says:
"And moreover" (*api ca*):

this is said with the intention of non-difference between power and the possessor of power, regarding the *puruṣa*, whose nature is consciousness (*caitanya*), as the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*).
The statement regarding the alternative designation "intellect" (buddhi) means that it is another name for that which is conventionally designated within its own system.
"It does not wander" means that the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is not the locus of error because it is insentient, just like a jar or similar objects.
"Even though it is non-acid" means that even though it is insentient (*acetana*), it appears as if sentient because it serves as the substratum for the reflection of sentience (*caitanya*).
Here, the words *cit* and *cetana* intend the sense of self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśa*).
Regarding the phrase "of that which is formless":

the meaning is that since shadow—which is characterized by luster and possesses the property of having a brilliant form—is impossible in consciousness (*caitanya*), which is formless, and since a transfer characterized by reflection is impossible in the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), which is also formless;
for it is observed that only in things possessing form, such as crystal, is there a reflection of the redness of a hibiscus flower or similar colors. This is the intended sense.
He suspects that [the word] "shadow" (*chāyā*) is used;
however, by the word "shadow," the primary sense of "luster" is not intended,
but rather "similarity."
The meaning is: "If it is argued that 'becoming like consciousness' means 'acting like a conscious being,'" he replies with "Who indeed?"—the sense of which is:
"In what form does this similarity [consist]?"
Regarding this, it is said:
"the nature of being consciousness" (citisarūpatva).
The meaning is that similarity consists in possessing the common absence of transformation into a mental modification (vṛttipariṇāma).
"Alas, [the opponent] thus refutes [our position]"—
the meaning is that the functions (vṛtti) such as error and so forth are not possible if the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) were devoid of activity.
Indeed, the quality of being conscious (cetanāyamānatva) is refined [by us] precisely for the purpose of accounting for error.
If that [nature] consists in being devoid of activity,
then there is no possibility at all for the arising of error and so forth;
and thus, the very purpose for which this undertaking was begun has been accomplished— this is the intended meaning.
He raises another alternative with the words "by way of being conscious" (*cetanatvena*);
the meaning is "by way of being a knower" (*jñātṛtvena*).
Another alternative is "not being insentient" (*ajaḍāyamānatvam*).
"He avoids [the charge of] insentience (*ajaḍatvam*).

This means that it was stated during the demonstration of the knowing self (*jñātṛātman*) that insentience—characterized by being a luminosity independent of anything else—is possible only for the self, which is the "I" (*aham-artha*) that is the knower.

And thus, since such insentience has the same substratum as knowing (*jñātṛtva*), the demonstration of knowing would effectively have been accomplished simply by the demonstration of knowing; this is the intended meaning.
"By that very [nature]" means by non-insentience (ajaḍatva) alone, which has the knower as its sole locus. This is the state of appearing as non-insentient.
Nothing whatsoever is incapable of establishing the intended error;
that is to say, what is unestablished is established by means of the unestablished.
Or rather, this is nothing at all; the sense is that [the opponent's position] is difficult to establish, as it neither avoids over-extension nor supports the subject at hand.
Furthermore, he states "api ca" (moreover) to point out the Sāṅkhya’s deviation from their own tenets regarding the admission that the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is non-insentient.

To the objection—namely, that even if the internal organ cannot possess similarity with consciousness (*cit*), let there simply be a reflection of consciousness within it which possesses the status of a knower and so forth—he replies "na ca citi" (nor in consciousness).
The consciousness is intended as the "original" (bimba), and the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is intended as the "substratum of the reflection" (pratibimbādhāra).
In this dvandva compound, the word "intended" (abhimata) forms a karmadhāraya with each member.

The superimposition of curvature and the like residing in the original object (*bimba*), or of impurity and the like residing in the substratum of the reflection (*pratibimbādhāra*), is possible upon the reflection.

However, the point is that neither the state of being a knower nor error exists in either of these two factors under discussion, such that they could be superimposed upon the reflection of consciousness (*cit*).
"And it has been answered" means that the remainder [of the sentence] is "in the *Nyāyatattva-śāstra* and other works. Now,

since it is accepted that the modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of cognition in the form of an object occurs precisely within the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), the claim that there is no occurrence in either one [of the two] is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Then, one might raise the objection with the words "As for what is said," etc., that the appearance of consciousness as a knower is indeed logical because of the non-apprehension of the distinction between consciousness and the intellect (*buddhi*).

Even though the power of consciousness (*cit-śakti*) is changeless, various modifications (*vṛtti-bhedāḥ*)—characterized by perception through the means of knowledge such as direct perception, as well as error and so forth—arise in the internal organ (*antaḥ-karaṇa*) solely by the force of its proximity.
Due to its predominance, consciousness serves as the witness (*sākṣitva*) and the enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) of these modifications.

The intention of the objector is as follows: "Just as even an inactive universal monarch (sārvabhauma) possesses the state of being a victor through the valorous battle waged by a circle of powerful vassals due to his preeminence, so it is here. [The author] refutes this, saying: "That is untenable. "Parākramīya" means possessing excessive valor. He refutes it, stating that it is illogical.
For witness-hood is not mere consciousness, but rather the state of being a direct perceiver;
that [witness-hood] does not belong to the intellect (citi).

If it is argued that "the state of being a seer (draṣṭṛtva) is imagined," it has already been stated that even the delusion of being a seer is impossible in the case of consciousness (caitanya), which is changeless, devoid of attributes (nirdharmaka), and immutable (kūṭastha).
However, in the illustrative example [of the king], there is no lack of activity nor is there a lack of attributes for the sovereign;
moreover, the causes for the relationship between property and owner—such as purchase, acceptance, production, and maintenance—are well known.
The intention is that lordship is established for the king on account of his supporting [the subjects] and so forth,
but not for the *puruṣa* as conceived by the Sāṅkhyas.

If it is argued: "Granted that inference is impossible for the Self as conceived by the Sāṅkhyas, nevertheless, the proof of the Self as intended by the Naiyāyikas and others—characterized by the capacity to receive excellence (*ādheyātiśaya*) and as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*)—might be established through the inference that 'a composite exists for the sake of another'"; we reply: no. This is because the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is that "a composite exists for the sake of another who is not itself a composite," and thus it is impossible to establish a "non-composite other" [in this manner]. Nor is it the case that...
One might argue: "Let there be a pervasion of the state of being a composite by the very fact of being for the sake of an enjoyer;

thus, the establishment of an uncomposite self follows without obstacle. But this must be rejected, because even in the case of the body, the proof would merely result in establishing that it is for the sake of an enjoyer in the form of another body, and thus the intended [self] would not be established.

Furthermore, because an enjoyer distinct from the body and so forth is unestablished prior to inference, and because the pervasion (vyāpti) cannot be grasped as having for its purpose an enjoyer of a different nature, it is impossible to prove a self of a different nature; this is the general direction [of the argument].
He also states that the inferences proving the distinction of the self from the body and so forth are sublated by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) with the words "I am fat.
This is because the subject matter has been crushed by perception—that is, because the probandum (*sādhya*) is sublated by perception.
The fallacy of the reason consists in its being sublated by the fact that [the subject] belongs to a past time.

Regarding the various types of negative inference (*vyatirekānumāna*)—that is, inferences of a distinct nature as maintained by the followers of Kapila and the Naiyāyikas—the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) cite scripture itself as the authority for the existence of the self despite the difference of the body and so forth, stating: "This is He."
"Not this, not this" (*neti neti*) is the negation of all attributes pertaining to the body and so forth belonging to the Self.

The meaning of "bodiless" (*akāya*) and the following terms is that the true nature of the Self is distinct from the body and free from bodily attributes such as wounds. Regarding the word "womb" (*yoni*): [it refers to the source of birth].
In this context, by demonstrating the connection with a womb that brings about a body, the soul's distinctness from the body is established.
"Body" (*śarīra*) is so called because it is subject to decay (*śīryamāṇatva*); and this [decay] does not occur in its own essential nature.
However, this is by way of qualifying the body;
thus, since birth and so forth belong only to the body and not to the self,
the scripture states "it is not born," thereby declaring the self's distinctness from the body.

The state of being conjoined with a body is also merely adventitious (aupādhika), whereas in liberation there is indeed bodilessness; regarding this point, he cites scripture with the words "na ha vai.
