Having stated scripture as the authority, he further states the argument from presumptive testimony (arthāpatti) based on scripture concerning the distinct nature of the Self with the words "kālāntare."
"Non-occurrence of that" means non-occurrence of the literal meaning of the Vedic text otherwise,
or non-occurrence of the injunction otherwise.

The performance of rituals that serve as the means for attaining heaven and other such states following the destruction of the body, or the injunctions for such performance, would indeed not be possible without the enjoyer—the self—being distinct from the body and being eternal.

Now, if it is argued that even if the distinction of the self from the body is established, the distinction from the senses and so forth is not yet proven, we reply: even the existence of a sense-faculty distinct from its physical seat (golaka) cannot be established without scripture.

According to the treatises (śāstra), however, the proof of that [self] occurs solely as an instrument for the sake of a distinct self; thus, the proof of a distinct self is established from the treatises without obstacle.

Having demonstrated, according to different views, that the distinct self is known either through inference alone or through scripture alone, he begins to describe its perceptibility according to the Mīmāṃsaka view, starting with the words:
"Now, [regarding] the beneficial and the harmful..."

The beneficial is that which is powerful, not followed by undesirable consequences, and is a means to achieve the desired, being accessible solely through the scripture (*śāstra*). The harmful is that which is followed by powerful undesirable consequences.

For a scripture whose sole purpose is to incite one toward the beneficial and turn one away from the harmful, even to imagine it has another aim than [the teaching of] reality (*tattva*) is merely a way of casting a great burden upon it.
One may assume the purport (*tātparya*) of a scripture even regarding a portion of reality that is useful for the task at hand, provided it cannot be obtained from other sources;
however, this does not apply to what can be obtained elsewhere.
Furthermore, the self (*ātman*) is distinct from the body and its like.

Since [the self] is clearly apprehended by perception itself, the authority of the scripture characterized by its being a "prior statement" (purovāda) is not possible here; this is the Mīmāṃsaka’s counter-argument directed against the Vedic scholar (śrotriya). Here, the Vedic scholar raises the doubt that the self is not graspable by the senses, [to which the author replies] with the words "Do not say so," etc., [referring to the self as] distinct from form and the like, and devoid of color and touch.
For in the case of the perception of a substance, either manifested color or manifested touch must serve as the cause.
Due to the absence of these, the perception of the self is not possible.
By the phrase "supremely subtle," the intention is to express its unfitness for apprehension by the sense organs.
The sense is that perception is effective only with respect to what is suitable [for it], not what is unsuitable.
Regarding the fact that the self is not graspable by the senses, he cites scripture: "parāñci" and so forth.
The meaning is that the senses are capable of grasping only external objects.
Moreover, every object of the senses is independent of the mind;
therefore, sensory cognition is not capable of contacting the self. (17)
It might be thought: "Since the external sense-faculties are composed of material elements, let them not function with respect to the self;
however, the mind will so function because it is not composed of material elements.
That is not so.
For even if that [mind] were considered a sense organ, its material nature (bhautikatva) would be unavoidable;
as it is stated in scripture: "For the mind, my dear, consists of food" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.5.4). This has been explained in detail in the investigation [of the mind].
(Thus, the doubt regarding the non-perceptibility of the self:
Now, it might be argued—there certainly exists the cognition "I," which has a direct manifestation;
and this is not possible without [the self] being an object of the senses.

Furthermore, since independence of the internal mind (*svāntasvātantrya*) is established even with respect to pleasure and the like—which are not within the range of the external senses—it is logical that this notion of "I" (*ahaṃpratyaya*) has that [internal mind] alone as its cause.

The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: the self (*ātman*) is graspable by mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), because, while being imperceptible to the external senses, it is nonetheless perceptible, just like pleasure and the like.
(Thus is the introduction of the inference for the mental perceptibility of the self from the perspective of the Bhāṭṭa school.)
That is not so; for there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of self-awareness (*saṃvedana*).
Nor is that non-perceptual, because it manifests as "I know" without any other limiting condition (*upādhi*).
Furthermore, it has already been stated that if cognition were not directly perceived, its very existence would be unestablished.
Nor can that [cognition] be included among the similar instances (sapakṣa) on the grounds of being mental perception (mānasapratyakṣa), because it cannot withstand critical scrutiny.
Indeed, when the cognition of an object arises from some conjunction of the self and the mind,
it must be stated whether the awareness of that object is produced from that very same [conjunction] at that same time, or at another time by means of something else.
Moreover, the simultaneous production of both is not possible;
for if that were the case,
there would result at that very moment an infinite multitude of cognitions directed toward various successive objects.
And that [simultaneous arising] does not exist;

furthermore, if they were to arise simultaneously, the restriction of the relationship between object and subject would be without foundation. If it were to be cognized by a cognition produced at a different time, it would not possess the nature of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Because consciousness is momentary, the preceding cognition does not persist until the arising of the subsequent apprehending cognition; for if it did persist, it would follow that all cognitions would persist at all times. Furthermore, since it is opposed by its effect, the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) arises immediately after, and thus there is no persistence over time. Therefore, consciousness is not an object of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, since consciousness is not imperceptible, there is a clear instance of deviation (*vyabhicāra*);
moreover, because being perceived by the senses is invariably concomitant with non-selfhood (*anātmatva*), there is a contradiction (*viruddhatā*).
Finally, the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*) is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*).
This is because pleasure and pain are not admitted to be perceptible.
They are not so admitted because pleasure and pain consist solely in the excellence or impairment of the sense organs;
for when that [excellence or impairment] is imperceptible, its excellence or deficiency cannot be perceptible either.
Due to the proficiency gained through practice, there arises in those two the conceit of direct perception, as if they were the very nature of the sense faculties;
this is similar to how, for those who maintain that the mind is inferable, there is such a conceit regarding the various states of the mind.
However, he who follows the doctrine of the Sugata considers even those two to be included within consciousness itself, because they arise from causes non-different from consciousness.
Alternatively, by resorting to the position of Kaṇabhakṣa (the Vaiśeṣika), one might assert that those two are specific qualities of the self;
or, through those two, one might explain the substratum of pleasure and pain; or else, one might consider here the reflection [of the opponent] that "one is inherently happy."

Attachment, aversion, and so forth, however, are merely specific states of consciousness itself; since they are perceived in that very same way [as consciousness], no inference can arise based on them as examples.
Attachment is consciousness whose objective apprehension is prompted by pleasure;
that same consciousness, when its objective apprehension is prompted by opposition to that [pleasure], is aversion.

The agitation of the mind through the cognition of existing suffering is sorrow (*śoka*); the agitation of the mind through the cognition of future [suffering] is fear (*bhaya*), and so forth; this should be understood from the very texts on definitions (*lakṣaṇagrantha*). Enough with this elaboration. (Thus ends the refutation of the inference that the self is an object of mental perception based on the testimony of the Guru.)
Furthermore, it has already been stated that for a single, partless self, there can be no relationship of subject and object with respect to itself, because of the contradiction involved. Moreover,
if one resorts to a distinction of parts to establish that [relationship], yet another part must be resorted to for the sake of establishing those [parts].
Likewise, there would be an infinite regress in each respective case, and the self would possess the nature of a composite;
(thus is the contradiction pointed out regarding the self existing in the state of subject and object).
But is it not the case that the appearance of a grasper has been asserted by those whose intellects are deluded by faith in their own tenets on the basis of scripture;
for there is merely the manifestation of various objects in proximity to the sense organs and so forth?
"Let such a cognition indeed exist in some cases;

however, it is based on the self as established by mental perception (*mānasa-pratyakṣa*) qualified by a knowledge inferred from an objective property (*dharma*)—such as *prākaṭya* (manifestation) or *prakāśa* (illumination)—which has as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) the adventitious nature [of that property].
(Thus ends the Bhaṭṭa's rebuttal against the Prābhākara position.)

It is said: Oh, how indeed the very experience of the investigators themselves is a delusion, in that at the time of experiencing an object, they do not perceive in themselves any distinction from their previous state!
For it has been stated that this matter is exactly as follows:
We do not know whether it is known or not,
nor do we know whether it appears to me or to another; such a cognition never exists at all.
If there were no manifestation of both the cognition and the cognizer, even such an apprehension would result [in error];

thus, this excellence of one's own conscious experience over that of another's, which is clearly manifest in all cases, would not be possible in the absence of the manifestation of a grasper (*grāhaka*).
Furthermore, if the object were a cognition inferred [by another], the manifestation would necessarily be "I have known" (*ajñāsiṣam*).
"I do not know";

for at the time when the inference arises—consisting in the observation of a specific excellence in the object produced by knowledge and the subsequent consideration of its pervasion—the knowledge intended to be inferred has already passed away.
That the inference of knowledge is impossible has been stated previously.
Furthermore, the theory that mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) apprehends the self has been refuted;
for if that were the case, there would be no distinction between what is known by oneself and what is known by another. (Thus concludes the Prābhākara proof of their own position.)
Now, one might ask: how can it follow that there is no distinction between what is cognized by oneself and what is cognized by another if the apprehending subject (*grāhaka*) does not appear?
For the distinction between what is cognized by oneself and by another is certainly not dependent upon the establishment of an apprehending subject;
rather, that distinction is logically established by the arising of a cognition of an object inherent in oneself and the arising of a cognition of an object inherent in another.

Even the distinction between cognitions related to oneself and those related to others is based on the difference in the causal complexes (*sāmagrī*)— such as the contact of one's own or another's sense organs with their objects— that give rise to knowledge. Furthermore, the establishment of the self (*ātman*) need not enter into that causal complex,
because it can function as a cause while remaining unmanifested, just like the sense organs and other such factors.
Nor is it correct to say that the cognition of an object is itself the cognition of the self;
for the establishment of one thing does not constitute the establishment of another thing,
as that would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga).
Moreover, that upon which the differentiation of the forms of entities depends—

namely, consciousness— is at that time itself of a concealed form, just like the sense organs and so forth. How, then, could there be any possibility of the appearance of the self, which is the substratum of that [consciousness]?
As for what they say— that the manifestation of a triad, namely "I know this"— is universal—
that too has not been established by experience and has just been refuted immediately [above].
(Thus ends the Bhaṭṭa critique of the Prābhākara position.)
Let it be, then, that the self is established precisely as the grasper at all times of grasping objects.
For the self-establishment of consciousness must indeed be admitted, because all other means of proof have been refuted in every respect.
And because that [consciousness] is real, it is never observed not to manifest;
just as consciousness is invariably concomitant with manifestation.
Since this has already been elaborated upon in the first section (*adhikaraṇa*), it need not be introduced and refuted here.

Even though the entire class of objects of cognition (*prameya*) is not perceived at times such as deep sleep, the fact that consciousness (*saṃvit*) is the means of establishing them is nonetheless accepted.
Therefore, it is logical to accept that the self (*ātman*) is also established by that very same consciousness, which has already been established as the instrument for proving other entities.
(Thus the Prābhākara again establishes his own position:
As for the claim that even during the time of sleep, when the cognition of objects has ceased, this self shines forth— that,
although it may be logically consistent, does not satisfy the minds of those who conduct their worldly affairs according to actual experience.
He also presents a logical argument: "In the case of being non-mental" (*acittve*). "Bound to non-mentality" means "pervaded by non-mentality.
The self is not perceptible by the senses because it possesses consciousness (*cetanatvāt*).
And the formal argument (prayoga) here is: "That which is not thus is not thus, just like a jar and so forth. //17//
Here, he introduces the Bhāṭṭa position with the words "syān matam" (it might be thought).
The learned scholar refutes it with "tan na" (that is not so);
for it is precisely because they possess odor and other qualities that the olfactory organ and the others are established as the perceivers of odor and the rest.
And thus, the material nature of the sense of smell and the others is established;
by that illustration, the material nature of the mind (manas) will also be proven.
The implication is that, just as in the case of the sense of smell and the others, the mind would likewise not be the grasper of a non-material self.
Regarding the material nature of the mind, he also cites scripture, saying "consisting of food" (*annamaya*).
The Bhāṭṭa replies with the words beginning "Now, it might be argued," etc.
"Direct manifestation" (*aparokṣāvabhāsa*) means that which is distinct from indirect cognition (*parokṣapratīti*).
This means possessing ordinary objectivity (*laukika-viṣayatā*).
Furthermore, the independence of the mind (*manas*) with respect to pleasure and so forth consists in its capacity to produce perception without depending on the external sense-faculties.
"Graspable by mental perception" means possessing ordinary objectivity as determined by mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
The remainder is clear.
He refutes the inference under discussion through the voice of the Guru with the words beginning "That is not so" (tan na) and so forth.
For deviation (vyabhicāra) consists in the presence of the reason (hetu) in that which lacks the probandum (sādhyābhāvavat).
In that regard, since the qualifying portion of the cause— the cognition— is already established, [the author] first establishes the qualified portion with the words "na ca tat" (and not that).
This is because it appears— that is, it is manifest— by virtue of being free from other conditions, meaning it does not depend on causes such as logical marks (*liṅga*), words, or knowledge.

To the objection that the inference of knowledge is based solely on "knownness" (*jñātatā*), and thus the appearance of knowledge lacks the status of being free from any other condition (*ananyopādhikatva*), he replies with the words "And if it were not perceptible" (*apratyakṣatve ca*).
This is because there is no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) for a "knownness" distinct from knowledge that could be intended as the inferential mark (*liṅga*) of knowledge;
and even if such a thing existed, since it would be beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), it would be impossible to grasp its invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) with knowledge.

The point is that since the causal complex (sāmagrī) that produces knowledge can directly produce "cognizedness" (jñātatā) itself, the postulation of an intermediate cognition would be purposeless; thus, the non-perceptibility of knowledge remains unestablished.
He raises the objection that even in the case of self-awareness (saṃvedana), the probandum [non-perceptibility] might exist, with the words "And not even that.
He then refutes the perceptibility of consciousness as mental perception (mānasapratyakṣa) by showing its inability to withstand analysis, with the words "In the crushing [of the object]."
"When one conceptualizes" means:
if it were so— that is,

if one accepts that at the very moment the cognition of the object arises, the cognition of that [object-cognition] also arises by the force of its cause, namely the contact between the self and the mind.

The meaning is that there would follow the consequence of the simultaneity of the collection of cognitions, beginning with the cognition of the object and continuing through the subsequent cognitions of those cognitions.
"Nikurumba" means a collection.
He states another refutation regarding the simultaneity of the cognition of the object and the cognition of that cognition, beginning with the words "yugapat" (simultaneously).

The meaning is that because the object is a cause in the case of perception, it is possible for a subsequent cognition in the form of an after-cognition (*anuvyavasāya*)—which is produced by a preceding cognition—to have the preceding cognition as its object; however, this is possible if they occur sequentially, not simultaneously. To the objection, "Let them then be successive," he replies with the word "asama" (unequal).

The meaning is that because cognition is momentary, at the time when a subsequent cognition arises, the preceding cognition no longer exists; therefore, its status as an object of direct perception (pratyakṣatva) would be impossible, even if one were to admit that the preceding cognition is cognizable by another cognition.
He states the fault in the case where the momentariness of cognition is not admitted with the words "and if it exists" (bhāve ca).
[Objection: But surely there is no momentariness!
Nor is there permanence;
rather, if it is argued that the cessation of cognition is desired through its own effect alone, he says in response: "In the case of the effect," [referring to] the contradiction of the effect.
If contradiction were characterized by the capacity for destruction, then cognition would have to persist for two moments;
if it were characterized by non-coexistence, then it would exist for only a single moment.
However, in this context, it is precisely contradiction characterized by non-coexistence that is intended.

It should be understood that if [the cognition] were to persist for two moments, then—according to the Nyāya method—a mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) would be established, and thus its denial would be untenable.

Furthermore, even in the Nyāya system, it should be noted that there is the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the persistence of the substratum of the cognition that takes as its object the second, third, and subsequent cognitions.
He also states an objection against the inference of the self’s being an object of mental perception, beginning with the words "of being sensory" (*aindriyikatvasya*).
Since being perceivable by the senses is pervaded by non-selfhood, the exclusion of the pervader necessarily entails the exclusion [of the pervaded] from the self;
thus, the intended meaning is that the probandum is contradictory to "selfhood," which is the delimiting condition of the subject (*pakṣatāvacchedaka*).
Even if one maintains that only being graspable by the external senses is pervaded by non-selfhood, he states another refutation: "and it is devoid of the probandum."

The meaning is that the positive example (anvayadṛṣṭānta) is devoid of the probandum (sādhyaśūnya). Although the deficiency of the probans (sādhanavikalatva) also results [as a fault] through the method of demonstration,

nevertheless, according to the established system (siddhāntaprakriyā), because pleasure and so forth are of the nature of states of cognition and cognition is self-luminous, one should keep in mind the self-luminosity of pleasure and so forth, and thus [the example] is indeed deficient in the probandum.
It has been stated:

since it is impossible to grasp the pervasion of the probandum by the reason—delimited by that [reason]—due to the absence of either the probandum or the probans in the concordant example (*anvayadṛṣṭānta*), "unestablished pervasion" (*vyāpyatvāsiddhi*) is what is intended.
Now, if pleasure and pain are not perceptible, how can they appear as if they were perceptible?
Regarding this, he says: "In the case of the sense-faculties (*indriya*).

Just as, even though the sense-faculties are beyond the reach of the senses (*atīndriya*), there occurs at times—during the operation of the visual faculty or others—an appearance as if they were directly perceived, such as "this is my eye" or "I, possessing the eye, see. This appearance belongs to a conscious being who synthesizes the various operations of the eyes and other faculties; it is produced by the abundance of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) of the sense-faculties and their objects.

In the same way, the conceptualization (*parāmarśa*) of pleasure and pain in the state of the sense faculties also possesses a form identical to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) due to the abundance of its repeated practice; this is the meaning. Here, the illustration is "the state of the mind" (*manovasthā*).
This refers to those who maintain that the mind is inferable (*anumeyamanovādinaḥ*), who seek to establish the mind as distinct from cognition (*buddhi*) through inference.
The fact that desire, volition, and so forth are modifications of the mind is understood from the scriptural text, "Desire, volition—all this is indeed the mind.

Furthermore, it must be stated that their appearance as objects of direct perception occurs solely due to the abundance of repeated experience regarding those objects, just as is maintained by those who argue for the inference of the mind;
such is the sense.

The identity of pleasure and pain with the self, as well as the fact that the self consists of adventitious attributes, are well-known according to different philosophical views; this is restated [in the verse] beginning with "yas tu sugate.
To this, he replies with the words "tābhyām" (by those two).

The dual form of the fourth case [is used here]. This refers to the substratum of pleasure and pain as established in the *Nyāyatattva* treatise by two thinkers— one following the Buddhist system and the other following the Kaṇāda (Vaiśeṣika) system— who respectively maintain that the self is non-different from momentary states, or that the eternal self consists of adventitious attributes.
The meaning is that one should proclaim this investigation into inherent happiness found within this context.

Now, if it is argued that even though there may be dispute regarding the mental perceptibility of pleasure and pain, passion and aversion themselves will serve as the illustrations, he says "In pleasure" (*sukhe*).

Since the apprehension of an object prompted by its quality of being pleasant is the manifestation of its desirability, that very cognition is passion; that is to say, it is characterized by the cognition of desirability directed toward pleasure.
The contradiction or impairment of that pleasure is that very cognition which reveals its state of being an object to be abandoned, and this is indeed aversion (*dveṣa*).
Since both of these [aversion and the cognition] are manifest in the same way as the cognition itself, there is no positive concomitance with the probandum; such is the intended meaning.
Furthermore, sorrow and fear do not serve as examples either.
He says "it does not arise" (bhūte) to show that you [do not exist].
As for the reading "that movement" (taccalanam), it is not correct;
rather, grief (śoka) is the agitation of the mind caused by the recollection of past suffering.
Fear is the agitation of the mind dependent upon the grasping of the causes of future suffering.

Since both of these are properties of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), they lack direct perceptibility (*pratyakṣatva*); thus, the point is that they are unfit to serve as an illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
Having stated the impossibility of a proof for the mental perception of the self, he now states a refutation (*bādhaka*) as well, beginning with "of one" (*ekasya*).
What is intended here is the contradiction characterized by the impossibility of a single entity simultaneously being both agent and object in a single action.
To show the fault in resorting to a distinction of parts within the self in order to avoid the aforementioned contradiction, he says: "If there were no division into parts" (*aṃśabhede*).

Since the existence of another part consisting of the apprehending self must necessarily be established by valid cognition, yet another part to apprehend that [apprehending part] would have to be postulated.
The meaning is that there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) by proceeding higher and higher in this manner.

If it is argued that there is no infinite regress because the apprehension of one part occurs at one time and the apprehension of that part by another part occurs at another time— thus being possible through a difference in time— the author says "and [the state of] being an aggregate" (*saṅghātatvaṃ ca*) in response to that as well.
The meaning is that, this being the case, having parts—which is contradictory to the partlessness of the self—would necessarily follow as a consequence.
Furthermore, if there were parts, one would have to infer impermanence and other such defects.
Here, it should be understood that the Guru does not accept that the self, which is the knower, can be an object of knowledge.
However, at the time of the cognition of objects, by virtue of its status as a knower, one considers it to be mere luminosity;
and the same applies to the cognition itself.
When his own position has been thus refuted by the Prābhākara, the Bhāṭṭa refutes that view as well, beginning with "But surely... (nanu ca).
Immediately after "śrutya," the words "tanna, sa tu" are to be supplied;
here, the reading "na ca grāhakābhāsaḥ" is possible.
The word "is established" (*siddhyati*) is to be supplied after "by scripture" (*śrutyā*).
The word "but that" (*sa tu*) is to be connected before "his own tenet" (*svasiddhānta*).

The sense is that the doctrine of the appearance of the grasper (*grāhakāvabhāsavāda*), which is rooted in the conceit of those whose minds are dominated by attachment to their own tenets, is not established by the authority of scripture.
The "appearance as subject" (*grāhakāvabhāsa*) refers to the manifestation of the self (*ātman*) as the substratum in all cognitions.
Intending to show that experience contradicts the reason for the non-establishment of this [self] through scripture, he states the mode of experience [beginning with] "the sense organs," etc.
The underlying intention is that scripture would not establish what is contradicted by experience.
Regarding the word "śrutyā," there might otherwise be a different reading.

The proponents of the Prābhākara school, who take pride in their own tenets, maintain that the appearance of a cognizer (grāhakāvabhāsa) should not be accepted because it contradicts direct experience.
For the collective intention is that experience illuminates only those various objects (padārtha).
[Objection: But surely, in the perception of a jar and so forth, in the absence of a manifestation of a grasper (*grāhakābhāsa*), how can there be the experience "I see the jar" and so on?
To this, he replies with the two statements beginning with "tādṛśo 'pi" [even such a one].

For whichever person a cognition has arisen regarding a certain object, that object manifests only to him; thus, the property of "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*)—which is a quality of the object—is related to the self as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).
Furthermore, the inference of knowledge possessing that [specific] mark is itself occasional;
consequently, the aforementioned experience— consisting of the mental perception of the self as colored by the inferred knowledge— is also strictly occasional,
and it is not of the nature of a visual perception of a jar.
The sense is that by means of this [self], the self would appear within the cognitions of objects.

And here, regarding mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*), the Bhaṭṭas intend to resolve the contradiction between the object and the agent by asserting that the self is the object (*viṣayatva*) by virtue of possessing cognition, while it is the locus (*āśrayatva*) by virtue of possessing a body and so forth.
The objection of the Prābhākara against this is stated in the passage beginning with "it is said... and so on.
"It is indeed one's own experience" means that once knowledge has arisen,

the perception of the self as possessing that [knowledge] is also established by experience; the point is that there is no delusion regarding that very [self], namely, no delusion of its non-existence.
This is a reproach stating that it is "excellent" for one who does not even know their own experience to be an investigator.

With the words "it has been said," etc., he recalls the previously mentioned fault regarding the absence of the manifestation of both the cognition and the knower at the time of the perception of an object:
if there were no manifestation of the cognition, there would follow the undesirable consequence of doubt and so forth as to whether it is known or not.
The sense is that, in the absence of a knower who provides illumination, there would follow the possibility of doubt and other such states, such as "is this known by me or by another?
This is what is meant by "so 'yam" (this is that):
"saṃcetita" means "known."

The "excess" (atiśaya) is experienced as being characterized by manifestation to one's own self. Regarding the phrase "in the case of inference": if the mental perception of the self—consisting in the manifestation brought about by the cognition inferred from the mark of "cognizedness" (jñātatā) based on such cognitions as "I know"—had the past cognition as its objective support, then the verbal expression would necessarily be "I knew," and not [the current "I know"].
The meaning is that there is no mention of "existing in the present" (*vartamānatva*) in the cognition "I know.

Now, one might raise the objection that the cognition "I know" is actually an error regarding the aspect of presentness, caused by the failure to perceive the difference between moments due to extreme rapidity; in response to this doubt, he sets forth another refutation of that view as well, beginning with the words "jñāne ti" (in the cognition).

It has already been stated previously that it is impossible for the inference of one's own cognition to have as its cause merely the linguistic usage based on that cognition. Furthermore, the inference of cognition based on the mark of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) is extremely precarious; for it is impossible to grasp the invariable concomitance (*avinābhāva*) between cognition and cognizedness, and because cognizedness is otherwise established by the causal complex of cognition itself—this is the underlying intention.

Moreover, [the author] refutes the possibility of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) in order to establish that the knower’s manifestation occurs only within the cognition of the object, using the words "In the case of mental [perception]" (*mānase*).
The phrase beginning with "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*) and so forth:

in the expression "the state of being mental perception" (*mānasapratyakṣatvam*), the suffix *tva* is applied to a bahuvrīhi compound. The state of being graspable by the self (*ātmagrāhyatvam*) is the self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatvam*) of cognition.
And that [non-perception] is established by the demonstration that cognition lacks the possibility of being either mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) or inference (*anumāna*).
Furthermore, the mental perceptibility of the self is refuted because the intended probans is fallacious; the meaning is that it is refuted due to the absence of a valid proof.
"Refuted by cognition" (*dhīnirastam*) means refuted by the cognition that investigates its fallacy.
The qualification "cognized by the self" (*ātmagrāhya*) is intended to establish that there is no deviation (*vyabhicāra*) [in the cognition of the object].

Here, one might expect the root text to read either *ātmagrāhyadhīvyabhicāranirastam* ("excluded by the deviation of the cognition cognized by the self") or some other variant. Having thus established through another method the impossibility of the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*) appearing [as distinct], he concludes that if they do not appear, the previously mentioned excellence (*atiśaya*) in the cognition of the object is impossible, stating: "that being so" (*tathā sati*).

"Non-distinction" (anatiśaya) means "absence of difference. The meaning is that if, in the cognition of an object, there were no manifestation of the knowledge and the knower, it would follow that there is no distinction between what is cognized by oneself and what is cognized by another; for [in that case] the object would appear as being known to itself, while its non-appearance [to others] would not be established.
The Bhāṭṭa refutes this, asking: "But how so?"

The specific quality of an object consisting in its "manifesting to itself" is established precisely because that quality resides in the cognition of that object, even though the cognition itself does not manifest to itself.

The intended meaning is that the excellence of the self consists simply in being the substratum for the awareness of the object; thus, at the time of the cognition of the object, it is something unprecedented.
Nor should it be argued that the aforementioned doubt remains in force if neither the cognition nor the cognizer is apprehended.

Because the manifestation of the object and its properties through one's own cognition is itself directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) with respect to oneself, there is no room for doubt as to whether "it manifests to me" or not.
Furthermore, since cognition is immediately inferred from the manifestation that is its fruit, such questions as "Has my cognition arisen, or that of another? do not even arise.

However, according to the Nyāya method, because cognition is destroyed by its effect and thus lasts for only two moments, [the certainty of the object] occurs solely through the force of *anuvyavasāya* (subsequent reflective awareness).

It should also be understood that there is no contingency of [the need for] etymological definition (*nirukta*), doubt (*saṃśaya*), and so forth, even when the cognition and the cognizer do not appear, provided that the object is known.
In this context, he incidentally refutes the claim that the arising of consciousness in the self is the cause of the self's manifestation by stating, "Nor the self...

Now, one might object: "Let the causal complex for the cognition of an object, even if it does not include the establishment of the self, be the cause for the manifestation of the self as well. To this, he replies: "Nor in the object..."

The meaning is that the causal complex for the cognition of an object—consisting of the contact between the sense faculty and its object, the suitability [of the object], and so forth—is not capable of producing the cognition of a self that is unsuitable [for such a process].
This is because it would lead to an over-extension (atiprasaṅga), namely, the consequence that the causal complex for the cognition of a cloth would result in the cognition of a jar and other things.
Furthermore, he says "api ca" (moreover) to show that even when there is cognition of an object, the cognition itself remains unmanifest.
For the establishment of the object of knowledge (*meyasiddhi*) is dependent upon the means of knowledge (*māna*).

The meaning is this: that consciousness by which the determination of the specific qualities such as genus (*jāti*) and attribute (*guṇa*) of objects depends, even if its own nature is not manifest at the time of illuminating the object, exists as a real entity (*svarūpasat*) just like the eye and other sense organs.

The point is that just as the specific qualities of an object are established by a cognition existing in its own right (*svarūpasaj-jñāna*), so too the excellence of the object to be known is established by a knower existing in his own right (*svarūpasaj-jñātṛ*).
He restates the view of the Prābhākaras with the words "As they say," and so forth.
"Universal" (*sārvatrika*) means pervading all objects of knowledge, such as perception, inference, and the like. He refutes that [view] with the words "That too," and so forth.
The statement "it does not ascend to experience" expresses the absence of a means of proof (*sādhaka*);
and the fact that it was immediately refuted [by the opponent] constitutes the sublation (*bādhaka*).

The Prābhākara objects again: "Let this be so; for this is the very nature of cognition—that it is the cause of the manifestation of its own substratum, just as it is of its own object. Thus he says: "Let it be then."

The meaning is as follows: by the very fact of being the apprehender—that is, by the very fact of being the substratum of cognition—the cognition of the object itself arises through the totality of conditions for the awareness of the object.
And that cognition, by its own inherent capacity alone, illuminates both itself and its own substratum, even though they are not its objects.
He first establishes the self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) of cognition with the words "must be admitted" (*abhyupagantavye*).
With the phrase "in every way" (*sarvaprakāre*),
he means that this follows from the refutation of both mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*) and inference based on the mark of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*) and so forth.
The meaning is that it is because there is a necessary rule that whatever exists must be manifest; this has been explained in detail.
The phrase "in the *Nyāyatattva-śāstra*" is to be understood as the ellipsis [of the sentence]. Regarding the words "not here," etc.:
having introduced the view that [the object] is non-deviant from manifestation, the meaning is that this [view] regarding cognition is not to be refuted here.
Having thus stated that cognition is self-luminous, he establishes that it is also the cause for the manifestation of objects with the words "sato 'pi" (even though existing).

The meaning is that since an object, even though it exists, does not manifest during deep sleep due to the cessation of cognition, it is thereby established that cognition possesses the capacity to manifest objects.
Therefore... [ata iti].

The point is that since consciousness (saṃvit), which is intended as the illuminator of others, is itself capable of illuminating the subject (pramātṛ), it is not necessary to postulate that the Self (ātman) possesses self-luminosity (svayaṃprakāśatva). He refutes the view that "consciousness exists even during deep sleep" by restating it with the words "As for that which... (yattu... tat). Regarding "that": [it refers to the aforementioned position].

The meaning is this: although the self's luminosity during sleep is supported by reasoning—namely, that the retrospective recognition, "I slept happily," would otherwise be inexplicable without the illumination of the self during sleep—this luminosity of the self during sleep does not sit well with those who rely solely on direct experience (*anubhava*).
The word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even though it is logically established" (*upapadyamānam api*) implies that there is no logical justification whatsoever for it.
It is clarified that the reconnection [of the series] occurs in quite another way;
this alternative proof will be elaborated upon later in the root text itself.
However, for one who has been liberated, knowledge is not possible due to the absence of its cause;
if [the self] were eternal, there would be eternal liberation, and thus such statements are merely explanatory praises (arthavāda). //18//

For one who has shaken off all connection with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of knowledge and action pertaining to the sense organs and the body, and who is thus liberated (*apavṛkta*), no basis whatsoever for the arising of cognition of self or other can be conceived.
Nor is it logical to claim that, because the mind is a permanent sense organ, cognition is produced at that time solely from its conjunction [with the soul];

for although the mind is eternal in its own nature like space, its capacity to produce cognition by functioning as a sense organ is dependent upon the constraints of merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*).
Having denied the self's illumination during sleep, he denies it even in liberation with the words "of the one who is liberated" (*apavṛktasya*).
[The term] *apavṛktasya* means "of the liberated one.
If it is argued that the knowledge of the liberated one may be eternal, he says in response: "If it were eternal," etc.
The consequence that there would be an absence of saṃsāra has thus been established here.
[Objection: In that case, what is the status of the supreme scriptural texts concerning omniscience in liberation?
To this, he says: "They are arthavādas."

The meaning is that the scriptural passages concerning omniscience and so forth are intended to praise the means to liberation, having as their cause the non-existence of the effects of ignorance. //18//
He elaborates on the very meaning of the verse with the words beginning "nirdhūte" (when shaken off), etc.
The "continuity" (*anubandha*) consists of the latent impressions of knowledge (*jñāna-vāsanā*) and the latent impressions of karma (*karma-vāsanā*).
The meaning is: "of one for whom all connections with the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of the body and the senses have been cast away.
Regarding the phrase "one's own and others":
the meaning is that it is the producer of knowledge whose object is either one's own essential nature (*svarūpa*) or some other object (*arthāntara*).
"Regarding 'dharma and adharma'":
the meaning is that [the mind] is dependent upon the cooperation of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
Being constrained by dharma and adharma, the mind is the instrument for cognition.
Even though the sense organs are eternal, [the self] is [distinct] because of its being an instrument, like the ear. //19//

Nor can that conjunction [of the self and the mind] assisted by *dharma* born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*) be the means [to liberation], because this contradicts scriptural passages such as "his actions are exhausted" and "then the wise one, having shaken off merit and demerit, becomes stainless," which teach the destruction of all karma, both white and other. Furthermore, if liberation were the fruit of *dharma*, there would be the undesirable consequence of returning [to transmigratory existence].

This is also because of scriptural passages such as, "There is nothing uncreated [attained] by means of what is created," and "Just as here the world acquired through action perishes, even so there the world acquired through merit perishes.
Nor can it be argued that the very existence of the Self at that time is the cause for the knowledge of That;
for that would entail the abandonment of what is already established and the postulation of what is not.

Furthermore, if that [liberation] were caused solely by those [elements], it would exist at all times just as the nature of the self exists; this would entail the consequence that transmigration never begins, and it would result in there being no distinction between the states of bondage and liberation.
Nor can it be argued that its absence now is due to its being obstructed by the body, senses, and so forth.
That indeed is an impediment which, while the complete cause is present, obstructs the arising of the effect;
and yet, even now, the status of the self as that complete cause has not been established.
Since knowledge and perception belong only to those possessing a body and sense organs,
it is the talk of a madman to claim that the very same thing— which has been established as the cause of knowledge— is the binder of the soul.
Therefore, there is no knowledge in the state of liberation.
The doctrines concerning momentary cognition, pleasure, and so forth, must be interpreted as figurative descriptions (*guṇavāda*) subordinate to the injunction for the knowledge of the Self.

Therefore, since the establishment of the Self is necessarily concomitant with the very time of the cognition of an object, according to the aforementioned principle, the Self is established as the cognizer precisely within the cognitions of objects.
(Thus concludes the demonstration of the Guru’s position that the Self manifests only at the times of the cognition of objects.)
The knowers of the Vedanta do not approve of this either, as it is merely the prattle of a limited intellect arising from a failure to understand the true nature of the Self.
For the cognition of an object is simply the cognition of an object;
it cannot, by itself, establish the cognition of the Self or its own essential nature.
Because it does not have that as its object.
For whatever is not the object of a particular consciousness is not established by that consciousness, just as taste is not established by the consciousness of form.
Furthermore, since the intellect (*buddhi*) and the knower (*boddhṛ*) are not objects for the cognition of their own objects, they too are not established by that [cognition].
But is it not the case that this is the very nature of being an object— that it is established by the consciousness of its own object?
For consciousness is indeed consciousness alone, and the knower is indeed the knower alone; how, then, could there be for these two any entry into the nature of the object of knowledge?
For it has been stated that they fall within the scope of mental perception (*mānasapratyakṣa*).
Furthermore, there is the impossibility of consciousness being an object of inference.
From what, then, is the establishment of consciousness [known]? From itself alone; for consciousness is self-luminous.
Not so; for that [cognition] also, like its object, is established only through being manifested to another, and not by itself.
And if it were established by itself, why would it appear only to someone specific and not to everyone?
If it is argued that "it is because of inherence in that"— for whatever consciousness inheres in a particular thing, that [consciousness] manifests only for that thing and not for another,
because of its non-inherence in the latter— if this is so, then:
In that case, the manifestation of consciousness would depend solely on its connection with a self,
because it follows the presence or absence of that [self].
If it were argued that, although consciousness is by nature luminous, it depends on that [self] merely for the purpose of delimiting it from specific counter-correlates;
"Not for the sake of establishing its own nature";
from what, indeed, does this certainty arise?
For if consciousness were ever to manifest independently of a counter-correlate (pratiyogin), just like the nature of the self, [then it would be established].
Therefore, one might conclude it is so;
yet it is not thus.

For its existence as an intrinsic nature (svarūpasattā) depends precisely upon a substratum and a counter-correlative, just like conjunction or sonship; thus, there is no room for the conjecture of its separate establishment (pṛthaksiddhi).
If it is argued that because true cognitions never deviate from manifestation, their manifestation is inherent to their own nature,
then does that [nature] ever deviate from its connection with the self?
Furthermore, if this were so, then according to your view, pleasure, pain, and the like would also be self-established.
For it is not the case that even those [external objects], being existent, do not manifest.
Rather, self-luminosity is attributed solely to consciousness (*saṃvit*) itself, which is accepted by all disputants as the establisher of other objects;
since the establishment of all other internal and external entities is possible through such consciousness alone, what is the use of postulating many [luminous principles]?
The sense is: "by the acceptance of its nature as luminosity.
He establishes this very point with the verse beginning *dharmādharmāvaruddham*.

[The body] is characterized by being restricted by merit and demerit (*dharma* and *adharma*), meaning it is distinguished by a particular state due to its dependence on the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*) defined as merit and demerit.
Regarding the statement "the auditory organ is like the ear": the auditory organ (*śrotra*) is precisely the space delimited by the ear-canal (*karṇaśaṣkulī*).
And it functions as the instrument for the apprehension of sound only when accompanied by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
"Not in its absence" means that the status of the ear as a sense organ is based on what is observed; that is to say, it is just like that.
Thus, the point is that because of the absence of *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit) in liberation, the mind does not possess the status of a sense organ. //19//
And [the author] does not fear [this objection], as stated in "nor in that born of yoga" (*na ca yogaje*).
The meaning is as follows: the mind’s conjunction [with the self] is "aided by the dharma born of yoga," which is to say, it is assisted by the dharma born of yoga.

Due to the power of the dharma born of yoga, the status of the mind as a sense organ persists even in liberation; thus, the idea is that knowledge of the self through the mental [sense organ] is possible at that time.
Regarding the persistence of merit born of yoga (*yogaja-dharma*) in liberation (*mukti*), he states the contradiction with scripture in the words "they are exhausted" (*kṣīyante*).
"White and other" means having the nature of merit and demerit. Now, [an objection]:

If it is argued that the meaning of the scripture is intended to indicate the cessation of all actions other than those produced by yoga-dharma, the author replies to that with the words "And if [liberation] were the fruit of dharma.

The meaning is this: if, at the time of liberation, knowledge—whether having the self as its object or being omniscient—were produced by dharma, then because it is a rule that whatever is a produced entity is subject to destruction, there would follow the undesirable consequence of ignorance and so forth arising once again.
To illustrate with scripture that the fruit of action is non-eternal, he cites: "There is no uncreated [fruit]."
[Objection: But surely liberation itself, being the very Self, may be the cause of knowledge. To this he replies: "And not the Self" (*na cātmeti*).
Or rather, the root text might read "the Self by its mere existence" (*ātmā sattayaiva*).
Regarding the phrase "kḷpte":
the meaning is that there follows the abandonment of the sense organs and so forth, which are accepted as the causes of cognition,
and the postulation of the solitary self alone— which has not been so postulated— as the cause of cognition.
He states another defect as well with the words "tanmātre" (in that alone).

If [the cause] were the mere nature of the Self, then the knowledge belonging to the time of liberation would exist at all times; thus, there would be the undesirable consequence of the non-occurrence of saṃsāra, because knowledge is the obstacle to ignorance and to the saṃsāra rooted in it—this is the sense.

He states the fault in the case of bondage (*bandhe*) even when there is the existence of knowledge in the form of the clear realization of reality (*viśadatattvasākṣātkāra*), as well as in the occurrence of *saṃsāra*.
The meaning is that if the knowledge of the time of liberation were present even during the period of *saṃsāra*, there would be no distinction between *mokṣa* and *saṃsāra*.
[The opponent objects: "But surely, the very destruction of suffering and so forth constitutes the specific nature of *mokṣa*."
The point is this: if that were the case, liberation would consist merely in that [absence of suffering], and thus knowledge and the like would be useless.

One might object: "Even if the self, which is the cause of the knowledge existing at the time of liberation, is eternal, it does not follow that such knowledge must exist during transmigratory existence, because the body and so forth act as obstructions. To this, he says: "And not... (na ca).
"He indeed avoids that" means:
having established the impossibility of [the body's] being an obstructer, he states the contradiction in that regard as well with the words "in the case of the established cognition.
"Of that very thing" refers to the body, the sense organs, and so forth.

He explains what was stated as "these are explanatory passages (arthavādas) and similar utterances" with the words "at that time," etc.: in liberation, which consists in the cessation of suffering, there are statements regarding happiness;
and the statements regarding knowledge have the intention of referring to the non-existence of the prior absence of knowledge.

The meaning is that those [scriptures] are merely for the purpose of praising self-knowledge and are indeed subordinate to its injunction. This concludes the Prābhākara position; "therefore" means according to the stated principle—that by the logic already explained, it is only reasonable for cognition, which illuminates its object, to also illuminate its own substrate.
The proponent of the final view (siddhāntin) refutes the Prābhākara position with the words "This too is the self," and so forth.
[The opponents are] those for whom there exist various types of erroneous cognitions regarding the modes of the self, which are the effects of ignorance concerning the true nature of the self.
The meaning is that their statement is purposeless.
How is the teaching of the Guru purposeless?
To this he says: "In the object" (viṣaye).
"No," [he replies].
Self-awareness (*ātmavitti*) is knowledge that has become a property of the self (*ātmadharma*).
Its own nature (*svarūpa*) is the nature of the self (*ātmasvarūpa*).
In this context, the reading might be "the self" (ātmā) or "the nature of cognition" (vittisvarūpam). [The verb] *siddhum* means "to manifest.
[The phrase] "because they do not have that as their object" means because those two lack the status of being objects for either the subject-object relation or for cognition.
The Guru raises an objection, [saying]: "But surely, even though cognition and the cognizer are not objects, their establishment occurs solely through the power of cognition. [He replies:
It is cognition itself, and not the object of cognition, nor is it insentient like an object.
It is indeed the knower (*veditṛ*), but not the object of knowledge (*vedya*), nor is it unknown like an object of knowledge.

Thus, because their intrinsic natures are distinct from [ordinary] entities, the establishment of those two—even though they are not objects—will be accomplished through the power of the knower; therefore, the claim that they are unestablished due to being non-objects is difficult to maintain, as they possess the status of being objects [in this specific sense]. This is the intended meaning.
To the objection that "let the manifestation of those two [cognition and its object] occur simply by being objects of another cognition," he replies with the words "for it has been said.
He states the proof of the establishment of cognition through its own power by way of raising an objection and providing a resolution, asking "Why?
and answering "Because it is established through itself alone."
It must be accepted as a matter of necessity that at the time of the cognition of an object, that cognition itself is also manifested even though it is not an object;
and the underlying intention is that the Self is [manifested] as its substratum.
Regarding this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) challenges the self-luminosity of consciousness as stated by the Guru with the words "Not so," and so forth.

The point is that because consciousness has a manifestation dependent solely on its own substrate (the self), it is possible for it to be manifest only to that [self]; thus, its self-established nature remains unproven.
To this, the opponent offers a rebuttal, suggesting: "If you say it is due to inherence in that [self]. He himself then explains his own statement: "That in which it inheres," and so forth.
The sense is that, although consciousness is self-luminous, it manifests as the Self alone because it is not established as separate from the Self.
The objector rejects this with the words "if it were so," meaning "in the absence of that [Self]."

The meaning is that the fact that the manifestation of consciousness has its cause in its connection with the self is established, because its positive and negative concomitance follows the positive and negative concomitance of the connection with the self.
Again, the opponent raises an objection: "If it is said...
Here, *pratiyogin* means the object (*viṣaya*).
That very thing is the "particular" (viśeṣa)— that is, the qualifier (viśeṣaṇa); it serves solely for its delimitation— that is, for its connection [with the object]—
which amounts to saying it serves solely for the illumination of the object.
"Dependent on that" means dependent on a connection with a self;
it does not mean for the sake of its own self-luminosity. He asks: "Why? and provides the answer.
Thus, it means that such certainty is not possible.
He demonstrates the impossibility of certainty itself with the words "yadi hi" (for if).
[The cognition] is independent of a counter-positive and independent of an object.
Thus, consciousness requires a connection with the self (*ātman*) solely for the purpose of manifesting the object, not for its own manifestation; such is the meaning.
And it is not the case that [consciousness is self-manifesting] in that way;

the point is that at the very time of manifesting the object, since consciousness is already manifesting to its own substrate, one must admit that its self-manifestation does not depend on a connection between the object and the self.

The underlying intention is that even in the case of knowledge whose object is past or future, there certainly exists a distinct relationship between the knowledge and its object, characterized as the relation of subject and object (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), which is a specific type of essential relationship (*svarūpa-sambandha*).

Now, one might object: "Cognition (*saṃvit*) is indeed without an object and without a substratum; its mere appearance as having a substratum and so forth is solely due to the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and its modifications (*vṛtti*). To this, he replies with the words "in the substratum" (*āśraye*).
On the ground, the locus of the contact with the jar is the ground, and the counter-correlative is the jar;
the locus of sonship is the son,
and the counter-correlative is the father.
The object is the counter-correlate of knowledge, and the self is its substratum.
Accomplishment consists of both persistence and manifestation.
Neither a state of being nor a manifestation of consciousness exists without an object and without a substratum;
furthermore, the experience of mere consciousness is sublated by non-perception.
Thus, the point is that even the requirement for a connection with a self is unavoidable regarding the manifestation of consciousness.
He raises the objection again that consciousness must be self-luminous because its luminosity pervades its own existence; he answers with the word "satyā" (if it were real).
The meaning is that, since the connection with the Self necessarily precedes [consciousness] and is required, it must indeed be accepted as the cause for the manifestation of consciousness.

He also states the flaw in proving self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) by means of the aforementioned reason: "Moreover, in this way," meaning that the reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntya*) with respect to pleasure and so forth.
That being the case:
"The witness of every object and its cognition is accepted in all cases."
Let the Self alone be self-established; what is the use of many such [entities]? //20//
Furthermore: The establishment of a thing occurs through its very witness, not by means of worldly [instruments];
for the self is observed to be the witness of both the object and the cognition of that object. (21)
Granted that the cognitions of objects may be self-established,
nevertheless, this Self does not become perceptible through them,
because it is their witness.
Indeed, this person is the witness; he is not perceived by that [object], just as one who directly perceives a jar is not perceived by the jar.
And since consciousness is the direct perceiver of cognitions of objects, it too does not become manifest through them.
(Thus the proponent of the established doctrine refutes the view of the Guru.
But surely, let the relation with the self also be a cause for the manifestation of cognition, just like the relation with the object.
To that extent, there is no loss of self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*),
because its establishment follows from the fact that it is manifest without depending on another cognition of the same class.
However, self-luminosity should not be attributed to the Self (*ātman*) in the same way as it is to an object (*viṣaya*).

But the Guru raises the objection again, [saying] "Or else, regarding another object," [arguing that] since cognition— which is accepted as illuminating external objects— must also be assumed to illuminate itself for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*). He refutes this, saying "If that were so" and "of everything."

Since it would involve excessive complexity (gaurava) to postulate that each [object] is self-luminous, it is more appropriate to postulate that the Self alone—which directly perceives all objects and all cognitions—is self-luminous, rather than the cognitions themselves.
This means that, just as objects appear to the Self, so too do cognitions; therefore, let the Self alone be self-luminous.
The sense is that all others should have their manifestation dependent solely upon that [consciousness]. //20//
Thus it has been stated that even consciousness (*saṃvit*) does not possess primary self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*), because its manifestation is dependent upon itself.
Let it be granted that knowledge (*jñāna*) possesses such [self-luminosity] in some sense by virtue of its manifestation being independent of another cognition;
nevertheless, the Self (*ātman*) does not have a manifestation dependent on knowledge. To this he says:
"Kiñce" means "whatever"; "yo yasya" means "whoever belongs to whom";
"sākṣī" means a witness, one who sees, a revealer.
Success is illumination;
it is not worldly—that is, it is not established by ordinary experience.
It is characterized, meaning it is perceived. //21//
He himself explains the verse with the words "Let them be so named," etc.

The sense is that, according to the reasoning already stated, since the manifestation of consciousness as its own self is untenable, the self must necessarily be accepted as self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśa*).
[Thus,] they are established in their own nature independently of any object of their own kind or any external goal to be accomplished.
Therefore, all things [are established by themselves], and the self is established independently [of anything else]. //22//
For no category of object is ever observed to require another entity of its own kind for its own manifestation.
Indeed, a jar does not require another jar for its establishment;
rather, it requires something of a different class, such as light.
In this way, light, while manifesting itself, does not depend on another light,
nor does it depend on objects such as a jar whose manifestation depends upon it;
rather, it depends on a sense faculty, which is of a different genus.
In this way, a sense faculty (*indriya*) also does not depend, for its own manifestation, upon another sense faculty, nor upon light and so forth, nor upon a jar;
rather, it depends upon a consciousness (*saṃvedana*) of a different genus.
Likewise, consciousness also does not depend, for its own establishment, upon another consciousness whose establishment is dependent on itself, nor upon a sense faculty and so forth.
But [the self] depends upon its own substrate, which is of a different class and independent;

likewise, the self does not depend on another self, nor on consciousness, the sense organs, and so forth, for its own manifestation. Thus, the establishment of the self’s essential nature is indeed independent of anything else. (This concludes the proponent's demonstration of the self-luminosity of the self.)

Having stated the refutation against the view that consciousness depends on something else for its manifestation, he also states the proof for the self’s self-luminosity with the words "sajātīye" and so forth.

For all manifest objects manifest without depending upon another object that is of the same class (*sajātīya*), or absolutely similar to themselves, or that is to be established by them, or whose manifestation is dependent upon them; thus, the self, while manifesting, manifests without depending on another self whose manifestation would depend on it, nor on cognition (*jñāna*) and the like.
Thus it must be inferred; and in this way, its self-luminosity follows as a result—this is the intended meaning. //22//
The expansion of the meaning of the verse begins with "Indeed, no one... and so forth.
Here is the essential point: self-luminosity, characterized by being manifest without depending on another cognition whose object is itself, is common to both cognition and the Self;
however, self-luminosity characterized by being manifest independently of everything other than itself belongs to the nature of the Self alone.

On this point, those who know the reality of the Self say that consciousness belongs to the Self by its very nature, because it is a property of its own essential form, just as luminosity is a property of fire. (24)
Apart from being the substratum of consciousness, the self has no other essential nature;
for that which is devoid of consciousness is not the self, just like a jar or similar objects. //25//

The power of consciousness does not constitute the selfhood [of the puruṣa], because that would entail its destruction upon liberation; and if it were distinct from consciousness due to some other factor, the postulation of that power would be redundant. (26)
For in the system of Kaṇāda and Akṣapāda, liberation is characterized by the absolute cessation of all specific qualities of the self, such as cognition, pleasure, pain, and so forth.
And there is no evidence whatsoever that a thing whose effects have been absolutely destroyed is still capable of producing those effects.

Since the effects of pleasure, pain, cognition, and the like are observed to belong to a self specifically associated with a body and other attributes, they lead one to postulate a productive capacity residing only in that specific [conditioned] self.
Just as smoke has the capacity to produce itself when connected with moist fuel in the presence of fire,
and just as the rice-sprout [arises] from the grain with its husk;
furthermore, since the self's exclusion of what is non-self is possible only when there is cognition, there is no need to resort to that [inherent] capacity.

And this being the case, it is not tenable that consciousness alone is the Supreme Self, because consciousness has a nature that is dependent upon a substratum and a counter-correlate, whereas the Self possesses a nature contrary to that;
furthermore, because the "I"-sense, which is the conscious subject, manifests directly.
Furthermore, because the nature of the conscious self has just been elaborated upon by the force of experience, reasoning, and scripture;

nor is it a sound argument to maintain the status of being a knower in the doctrine of the self as pure consciousness alone by superimposing the quality of awareness upon its adventitious connection with objects—
since a relation resides in both relata, it would follow that the object itself must also be a knower.
Nor is there a fixed relationship like that between cause and effect; for in that case, there is a connection characterized by a rule of mutual dependence between the produced and the producer.
If it is argued that the same [relationship] exists here as well, we say no.
Because there is no cause for dependence:
for what purpose does the object depend on consciousness, or consciousness on the object?
If it is argued that this is for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*), what is the meaning of "accomplishment"?
It cannot be origination (*utpatti*).
This is because its cause has been definitively ascertained to be something else;

for jars and the like possess well-known alternative causes consisting of clay, staffs, the rotation of the wheel, and so forth, and they do not depend even upon consciousness for their own production.
Furthermore, the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñānamātravāda*) has already been refuted.
To say that the eternal self requires an object for the sake of its arising is a most ill-spoken statement.
If you argue that "arising" means "manifestation," then,
my friend, is the self— which is indeed self-luminous— nevertheless dependent on an object for its manifestation?
Since this [consciousness] requires an object for that purpose,
this self-knowledge is indeed magnificent;
furthermore, it has been demonstrated that luminosity cannot possibly be some property of an object that exists apart from consciousness itself.
Even if this [cognition] were to arise, it could not have the mere nature of consciousness alone as its cause, because that would entail the consequence of all objects being manifested at all times;
for an effect whose complete causes are always present does not only occasionally occur.

Or, if one resorts to adventitious excellence, then knowledge itself has been accepted under another name; thus, it follows that the self is indeed possessed of that [knowledge]. (This concludes the proof for the eternality of knowledge as an attribute of the self.)
But if knowledge is accepted as being adventitious and of the nature of an action, because it establishes the attainment of an object, how can it be the very essence (*svabhāva*) of the self?

For instance, when something is distinct from another entity, it is observed that its specific [result], such as the reaching of a destination to be reached— which exists in relation to another generative substance by way of being an effect and so forth— is produced by an adventitious and specific action, such as "going," inherent (*samaveta*) in that [substance].
It might be argued that such an accomplishment of purpose (*arthasiddhi*), which is unique to a particular person, can be inferred as being produced by an action inherent in that person.
This is not so;

for there is an inconclusive fallacy (*anaikāntya*) due to the ownership of fields and the like acquired through non-action—which is unique to the owner of the field—and due to the ownership of rice and other crops belonging to the cultivator, which is also unique to him.
Nor can it be argued that the possessor of the field (kṣetrin) is not a producer therein because of being devoid of activity;

for this would lead to a fallacy due to the deviation [of the reason] in cases such as time and so forth, and because there is no difference in the principle of "the effect occurring when the cause is present."

If it is argued that the very existence of that [consciousness] is the causal operation (*janakavyāpāra*) in that case, then surely that [existence] is common to the preservation of crops and so forth; how, then, can it be produced by an uncommon operation?
Moreover, if this were so, let that same [existence] be the causal operation even in the illumination of an object.
What is the use of this assumption of what has not been established?
If it is argued that even when that [self] exists, the object does not manifest, then why does "one's own-ness" (svatva) necessarily arise simply because life exists, as previously described?
If it is argued that the existence of rice and so forth is also required [as a cause], then here too the proximity of the sense organs and so forth is required; thus the analysis is the same.
Therefore, it is simply this: that which possesses the aforementioned uncommon property in relation to a particular object has its cognition caused by that very uncommon property of that object.
It is indeed intended that consciousness belongs to the self, just as luminosity belongs to the sun.

Nor can it be inferred that knowledge is adventitious— like motion and so forth— on the grounds that it conforms to a variety of causes, for we perceive its limitation by time through such cognitions as "I know" and "I knew."
Because [the reason] is inconclusive due to the light of the sun (*ādityaprakāśa*).
For even in that case, there is the cognition: "The sun illuminates this place," "it illuminated it," and "it will illuminate it.
If it is argued that, although the light of the sun is natural, the cognition of a delimitation (*avaccheda*) is possible because its connection with the place being illuminated is occasional;

In this case as well, then, a particular object of experience—having acquired a state of fitness through its proximity to the sense organs and other factors—delimits the innate quality of consciousness belonging to the self; it is in dependence upon that [object] alone that conformity to the sense organs, as well as the application of the cognitions of past, future, and present, become possible.
But how, in this regard, is the determination made?
Is this distinction merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), like that between the light of a jewel and the light of the sun, and not inherent (*svābhāvika*) like that between going and cooking?
No, because it is perceived as being of that very nature through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For this self has never been observed to be formless like a clod of earth or similar objects;
and whatever is perceived directly as possessing a particular quality has that very quality as its intrinsic nature.
Just as the wind is perceived solely by way of its quality of touch,
whatever does not possess a certain intrinsic nature is not perceived in its own form even in the absence of that [quality].
If it is argued that [the self] is like Devadatta and others because of being devoid of movement and so forth,
just like the body, we say no, because that reason is unestablished (*asiddha*).
It might be argued that just as this conscious being appears conjoined with the body, which is devoid of its own intrinsic nature (*asvabhāva*), so too it appears conjoined with consciousness.
That is not so, because [the premise] is unestablished (*asiddha*).
For this conscious entity does not manifest as being qualified by the body alone;
for even in the absence of any mental connection with the body, yogis whose minds are focused and whose external senses have ceased [their activity] clearly experience it as "I.
Furthermore, I have already stated that the cognition "I know" has as its object a distinct reality, since it is devoid of any appearance of the body's color or configuration.

Because it is impossible for a single body—just like the mind—to be inherently and persistently connected [to the self], given that bodies such as those of gods and humans differ according to karma and are subject to appearance and disappearance;
furthermore, even though the *liṅga* (the subtle body) persists, it lacks perceptibility and thus cannot be a point of deviation [from the self].
(Thus is established that knowledge is the very nature of the self.)

If it is argued that there would be the consequence of manifestation for a person whose nature is consciousness even during sleep and fainting, we say no, because this [argument] cannot withstand analysis.

For instance, does this consequence refer to a property common to all things, produced by consciousness, synonymous with terms such as "manifestness" (*prakaṭatā*), which is intended by the word "manifestation"? Or...
Now, is it to awakening itself, or to that which is not remote from it?
In the first case, there is no such contingency precisely because of its absence.

Furthermore, non-existence was already demonstrated at the time of establishing the self-evidence of consciousness (*saṃvit-svatassiddhi*). Even regarding existence, its non-arising is possible due to the obstruction of darkness; as for the other two [alternatives], they result in exactly what is desired [by the opponent]. Thus, this is merely the pointing out of a non-fault.

Since it is indeed accepted that the person (puruṣa) possesses this same nature of consciousness even during states such as sleep, its presence at those times does not constitute a fault. Now, if it is thought that if self-experience exists even in sleep and so forth, then there would be the consequence of worldly activity (vyavahāra) just as in the waking state— this is not so,
because [that experience] is not within the scope of worldly activity.
