What indeed is the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the self? For it is not possible to take it up, cast it off, or remain indifferent toward it.
If you argue that verbal expression (*vyāhāra*) would follow [as a consequence], then what of it?
Is it not the case that the object of the non-conceptual cognition of infants, the mute, and others is indeed subject to linguistic usage?

If you argue that because of the absence of auxiliary factors such as proficiency of the organs and the desire to communicate, no verbal expression arises in those cases, then this same rule applies elsewhere as well; thus, your objection is a "reproach of the irreproachable."
If it is argued that this leads to the undesirable consequence of memory, we say no, because [the self] does not possess mental modifications (*avṛttitvāt*).

If it were said: "Since one accepts the experience of the self during states such as fainting, there would follow, just as in the case of experiencing another object, a subsequent memory in the form 'I experienced thus'; that is not so.
Because they are not modifications [of the intellect].
For fainting or deep sleep are not specific modifications of the intellect like seeing, touching, and so forth, by which they could deposit a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) as the seed of memory.

However, when the instruments (karaṇas) have their functions ceased due to the arising of darkness (tamas), there is for the Self merely an abiding in its own nature as consciousness, which is effortless and innate.
Nor does it possess the capacity to deposit latent impressions (saṃskāra) simply because its nature is consciousness;
for if that were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of no liberation, since impressions would be incessantly accumulating.

Furthermore, when an experience has ceased after depositing a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) corresponding to itself, recollection arises in accordance with its own seed, which has been awakened by such things as the sight of something similar or related.
However, in this case, there is never any cessation or birth of the cognition of the self's own nature,
because it is perpetually connected to the existence of the eternal self.
Furthermore, the absence of any other causal sign (*nimitta*) will be explained immediately hereafter.
Thus, while the experience itself is still persisting, how could memory arise?
Even the unified cognition, "I who existed yesterday am the very same I today," has as its object a self-nature delimited by time.
It does not [arise] from the mere intrinsic nature [of the object]. Furthermore, the self-experience during sleep and similar states is both indistinct and non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*).
Moreover, since the seed of memory is deposited by a more intense conceptual cognition (*savikalpaka*), how could that undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) possibly follow?
And due to that state of equilibrium, there arises the conceit of non-experience, just as there is a lack of conscious attention toward the body and the effort required to sustain it.
Nor does the objection apply that if one were to remain in mere unmodified, natural consciousness, there would be no distinction between deep sleep and liberation;
for in one case (deep sleep), the latent impressions of the afflictions (*kleśavāsanā*) and the suppression of the *guṇas* are present.
In other cases, there is the absolute cessation of that [cognition].

Even in the case of asamprajñāta-samādhi, there is a distinction for one who possesses supreme dispassion, whose latent impressions of cessation are most potent, who has fulfilled his duty, and who is destined for liberation. (Thus ends the resolution of objections raised regarding the eternity of knowledge.)
But how is it that, even though there is no functioning of the mind during sleep, there arise for one who has awakened such retrospective reflections as "I slept happily" and so forth?
For memories do not occur whose objects have not been previously experienced.
Indeed, the reflection "I slept happily" has its source in the mental impression (*bhāvanā*) formed by the experience of the quality of *tamas* arising with the assistance of the quality of *sattva*.
The reflection "my mind is serene,
my limbs are light" occurs when there is an abundance of sattva; however, when rajas and tamas predominate, one reflects, "I slept in pain."
"My mind wanders about, unsettled";
yet when sattva and rajas have been overcome and tamas has become intensely predominant, I am deeply deluded and asleep,
and my limbs are heavy.
"The mind is as if robbed, as if closed"—
this is indeed so.
This has already been answered:
these conditions do not have their origin in latent predispositions (*vāsanā*);
rather, they are caused by the consideration of specific states of the body, sense-faculties, and mind at that particular time.
Regarding the term "those who rely on inference":
for these [feelings] are of such a nature, namely— because my mind is serene and my limbs are light due to the proper digestion of food.
Therefore, the recollection "I slept happily" is possible;

for even during the state of sleep, due to the varying degrees of cessation of the sense organs, there occurs a faint recollection based on the immediate connection with various favorable or unfavorable objects at that time. Thus, it does not constitute a distinct mental modification (*vṛttyantara*).
Regarding sleep:
how then is the aphorism of the Great Sage [to be understood], namely, "Sleep is a fluctuation having non-existence as its causal condition"?
Because the context is focused on cessation (*nirodha*), there is no intention to define the essential nature of the fluctuation itself, just as in the case of the [other] distortions (*viparyaya*).
For there is no such thing as false cognition that is not established upon the nature of that [object], since all cognitions are non-deviant from their objects;
and that [nature] is established by the very context of the argument (*adhikaraṇasiddha*).
This will be established further below.
That consciousness which partakes in isolation (*kaivalya*) is taught as being subject to suppression—such as sleep and so forth—by virtue of its opposition thereto.
(Thus ends the refutation of sleep as being a form of mental modification.)

Or let it be that sleep is simply a mental modification (*vṛtti*) based on the quality of darkness (*tamas*) in its most intensified state, which serves as the cause for the absence of the aforementioned modifications such as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
and let there also be recollections (*smaraṇa*) consisting of the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of one who has awakened.
Even so, [the objection remains].
The fact that the self has consciousness as its inherent nature is established by the persistence of cognition throughout the nine states.
One might object: "Even if cognition persists due to the persistence of its causes, how can there be a certainty regarding such an intrinsic nature? It is answered thus:
because the manifestation of objects is merely occasional, the knowledge that constitutes an attribute of the self is indeed adventitious.

The manifestation of the self's own nature is not constant, but occurs only at the time of the cognition of an object through [the mediation of] knowledge, and not by itself; thus, in response to the objection raised here, the author first establishes the permanence of knowledge with the words "here they say."
Knowledge is that which is inherent to the very nature of the self (*ātman*).

And because the self is eternal, that knowledge is likewise eternal. Furthermore, since knowledge is a quality that defines the nature of the self, the self's essential form could not be established as devoid of knowledge, just as light cannot be established as devoid of luminosity.
Therefore, even in liberation, the possession of knowledge must be accepted, because that which is devoid of knowledge is not the Self; such is the meaning of the two verses.

Now, one might object: "Even in the absence of knowledge, the nature of the Self at the time of liberation possesses the power of knowledge. To this, he says: "To the power of consciousness" (citiśaktyai).
The second half of this [verse] is missing;
in its place, our own supplement has been inserted within these parentheses.

The meaning is as follows: if the eternal [self] possesses the inherent capacity [for cognition], there is a rule that the fruit [of that capacity] must necessarily occur; thus, if it possessed the power of knowledge, knowledge would arise in the liberated one at some time. Since no knowledge ever arises in liberation, that power too must have perished then, which would amount to asserting the very destruction of the self, because the cessation of the attributes that define the nature of a thing necessarily entails the cessation of its nature itself.

If it is argued that knowledge or the power of knowledge does not define the essential nature of the self, but rather—though adventitious—is accepted as a quality (*dharma*) belonging specifically to the self and not to things like a jar, and thus the distinction between one self and another is established; we say:
not so, because it will be established later that knowledge is indeed a quality that defines the essential nature of the self.
The underlying intention is that the doctrine of an insentient self (jaḍātmavāda) is to be disregarded by the wise because it contradicts the Upanishads (trayyanta). // 24 // 25 // 26 //
He explains the passage beginning with "citiśaktyā" by means of the passage beginning with "buddhyā".
He says "api ca" (furthermore) because it would be useless for one who is like a stone—a liberated self—to rely upon a conscious power (*cicchakti*) that distinguishes him from the insentient.
This [sentence] would be an explanation of a portion that has been omitted.
[The author] restates and refutes the objection: "In that case, if cognition is eternal, let its very nature be admitted as the Self," by saying, "But this being so... and "Of that...
[and] "At best... and "Of that...".

The meaning is that it is illogical for cognition— which is dependent upon objects and their substrates— to possess the nature of a self that is independent and does not depend on them. Furthermore, he says "and directly" (sākṣācca), meaning that the discussion regarding parsimony and complexity (lāghava-gaurava) applies only to conceptual constructions, but not to the cognizing self which is clearly perceived.
If it is argued that the direct perception of the self as the knower— expressed in the thought "I know"— is an error, he replies to that with the words "in experience" (*anubhave*).
This means immediately prior— that is, without any interval—
precisely at the point where the selfhood of the knower is being established.
The point is that, because it is supported by valid means of knowledge and sound reasoning, the non-erroneous nature of the knower’s self-perception must indeed be accepted.
Now, one might object: consciousness alone is the self;
its so-called "cognition" is merely its connection with an object.
Therefore, one might object that the status of being a knower is possible for the Self; to this, [the author] says, "Nor in mere consciousness.

If the connection between the object and consciousness—which is intended as "knowing"—were of the nature of *saṃyoga* (conjunction), then because such a relation resides in both relata, it would follow that the object also possesses the status of being a knower; thus he says, "Because of the relation. One might further object, "Nor in the effect... [i.e., the cognition].

The intention of the objector is as follows: just as the relationship of cause and effect, although determined by both the cause and the effect, still allows for the distinction between them— namely, "this is the cause of that" and "this is the effect of that"— so too, although the connection between consciousness and its object is determined by both the object and the subject, the distinction between the knower and the knowable is nonetheless possible.
He avoids that [objection] there as follows:

although the relation between effect and cause is called the "causal relation" (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*), nevertheless, being-an-effect (*kāryatva*)— as determined by the cause, residing in the effect, and characterized by dependence upon a cause that precedes it— culminates in the state of having a cause that pervades the effect at the time delimited by its own prior moment.

The meaning is that the definition of causality— which is determined by the effect, resides in the cause, is characterized by dependence on an effect occurring subsequent to itself, and ultimately results in the state of existing at a time strictly prior to the effect—

is necessarily distinct in each case; however, in this [case of conjunction], the established position that there is only one single conjunction inherent in both [the two relata] is difficult to maintain.

Even though conjunction resides in both its relata, because it resides in consciousness (cit) through the relation of being the locus (anuyogitā), it is established that consciousness alone possesses the status of the knower (boddhṛtva), while its counter-correlate, the object, possesses the status of the known (bodhyatva); nevertheless,
the Self is not mere consciousness (cinmātratva).
However, it should be understood that the fact of consciousness (cit) having the mental content (cityā) as its substrate must also be accepted precisely because it is based on scripture.

One might object: "In this case as well, let the relationship between consciousness and the mental content be defined simply by the rule of mutual dependence. To this, he replies: "No, there is no dependence."

The meaning is that there is no object in the form of a purpose (*prayojana*) which could serve as the cause for dependence. This is further explained by the words "for what purpose" (*kimartham*), and so forth.

An objection is raised: "But since objects are imagined within consciousness itself due to the defect of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), there must indeed be a dependence on consciousness as their substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*"; to this he replies: "And it has been refuted... (*nirastaśca*)."

Thus, having rejected the dependence of consciousness (*cit*) upon an object for its arising, he now rejects the dependence of consciousness upon an object for its arising by means of the words "of that which is eternal" (*nityasya*).
The sense is that it is even more contradictory to assert that eternal consciousness arises in dependence upon an object.
The phrase "Why [is it]? rejects the dependence of that manifestation upon an object; the words "O venerable one," and so forth, are spoken with reproach.
Thus, the speaker's very lack of self-knowledge results in this consequence.

The sense is that because the self-luminosity of the light of the Self—which illuminates objects—is self-evident. [An objection: "Granted that there is a dependence on consciousness (cit) for the illumination of objects. To this, he says: "And illumination... and so forth.
Consciousness alone is the illumination.
If it is argued that consciousness depends upon itself for that purpose, the implication is that this results in the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).
He states "even if possible" (*saṃbhavan*) even regarding the position that illumination is distinct from consciousness.

The meaning is that if the manifestation of objects depended solely upon consciousness (*caitanya*), it would follow that this manifestation is eternal. Furthermore, if it were dependent upon consciousness as if it possessed adventitious attributes (*āgantuka-dharma*), then its status as the knower-self (*jñātṛ-ātman*) would be established beyond doubt; thus he says "adventitious" (*āgantuka*).
And this adventitious excellence consists precisely in the expansion of knowledge, which is its own inherent attribute (*svadharma*).

The meaning is this: cognition (*bodha*) is knowledge qualified by that [object]; the self is the substratum of that [cognition]. Therefore, it is not tenable to claim that the self is mere cognition.

Now, one might object: "In this way, just as the self has cognition as its form (*svarūpa*), it cannot also have cognition as its nature (*svabhāva*), because it is impossible for impermanent cognition to be the nature of an eternal self."

He raises the objection with the words "But if this were so," because one must consider that the occasional nature of the cognizer itself is what accounts for the occasional nature of the manifestation of the object.
In order to establish that cognition is an action and is adventitious, he teaches the general pervasion (sāmānyavyāpti) with the words "in another object" (*arthāntare*).
"Another object" refers to a village and the like.
The "other substance" (janakadravyāntara) is the goer (*gantṛ*).

The attainment of the destination to be reached is the conjunction with the village or the person. Although this [attainment] resides in both [the village and the person], its meaning is that it is observed to be unique to the person (*puruṣāsādhāraṇa*) because it is rooted in the activity of the person, and it is produced by the adventitious action of going (*gamana*) which resides in the person.

It follows that, by virtue of its dependence on that [agent] and so forth, "being produced by an adventitious action residing in that [agent]" pervades "the state of being a property residing in something other than that which is unique to it.
Having stated the example, he demonstrates the application (*upanaya*) and conclusion (*nigamana*) with the words "tādṛśī" (such).
The proposition (*pratijñā*) and the reason (*hetu*) are established through their meaning.
Alternatively, one may employ three members [of a syllogism] according to one's preference.

Here, what is intended to be proven is that manifestation (prakāśa), which has the object of knowledge as its locus, is unique to each respective person and is produced by the adventitious cognitive activity belonging to that specific person.
He refutes the very notion of pervasion (vyāpti) with the words "Not so," and so forth.

"Without action" means that ownership over fields and so forth, acquired through family lineage, belongs to one from birth alone because there is no other claimant, or because, if there were one, they would have obtained it through inheritance.

The meaning is that there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) because, in the case of ownership over another's field or other property—which is not one's own unique [cause]—there is no production by an action residing in that [owner].

Regarding the reading *abhāvaprāpta*, it is possible that the text was originally *bhāvaprāpta* or *svabhāvaprāpta*, or some other variant. Furthermore, he demonstrates another instance of deviation: in the case of seeds sown in one's own field by another person or by fate (*daiva*), once they have sprouted, the resulting ownership is unique to oneself; yet, this ownership is not produced by any action of one's own that has newly arrived [to cause it]. Thus, he shows the deviation as well.
Regarding the term "the owner of the field" (*kṣetrin*):
it means "in its presence.
Just as even that which is devoid of activity is established as a cause through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), such as in the case of [a field] and the act of cultivation.

Likewise, since the ownership of the field and so forth is established in the owner (*kṣetrin*) only by means of that [act], it follows that the status of the owner as a causal agent will be established therein, even though he is devoid of activity; this is the intended meaning. One might object: "The owner is not devoid of activity, for his very living is itself the activity. Thus, the author raises this doubt with the words, "That very living... (*tajjīvanam eva*).
He refutes this, saying "Is it not so?
For the livelihood of the landowner is indeed a common cause for the protection of crops and so forth;
however, it is not an uncommon cause for ownership of the field and such. Likewise...
The point is that the inference [of] being produced by uncommon adventitious activity is indeed inconclusive (*anaikāntya*).
Now, it might be argued: "It is precisely the state of being produced by its operation (*tadvyāpāra*) that is being proved, not the state of being produced by uncommon activity."
If it is argued that there is therefore no deviation [from the rule], then he says "Moreover, in this way" (*api caivam*), meaning that it is simply the continued existence of the cognizer.
Why? Because...
The sense is that the postulation of adventitious cognition is useless.
Regarding the phrase "here too":

the sense is that when the collection of auxiliary conditions—such as the contact between the sense organ and the object—is present, let the very life of the cognizer be the generator of the manifestation of the object.

Since even life, characterized by existence at successive moments of time, does not possess the nature of an action, it cannot be established that [the body] is produced by its operation either; rather, it must be established that it is produced by its unique properties (asādhāraṇadharma). He concludes with the words "Therefore" (ataḥ). Let this be so.
What gain is there for you from that? To this he replies: "That very thing is desired.
The sense is that our gain is simply the refutation of you, who have set out to establish what is undesirable to us, by means of a different point (arthāntara).

Furthermore, it should be considered that because there is deviation even in the case of ownership of fields and so forth acquired through one's own nature (*svabhāva*), it is impossible to prove that [ownership] is produced by adventitious factors (*āgantuka-dharma*).
Thus, the proof for the adventitious nature of cognition based on its occasional manifestation of objects has been refuted.
He now restates another way of proving that [adventitious nature] in order to refute it: "And not when there is a difference in causes," and so forth.
Knowledge is adventitious because it is perceived as being delimited by time,
like movement and so forth;

and knowledge is produced by the contact of the sense organs with their objects because its presence and absence follow the presence and absence of that contact, like cooking and so forth produced by fuel and so forth— these two formal arguments are implicit here.
He refutes [the opponent's position] precisely by means of an inconsistency (*vyabhicāra*), stating "In the case of the sun" (*āditye*).

For even in the case of the solar light, which is intrinsic, its connection with various locations to be illuminated is delimited by the three periods of time; thus, the cognition of being delimited by time—which has that [connection] as its qualified object—does not prove the occasional nature (*kādācitkatva*) of the essential nature of the light itself.
He raises an objection with the words "even if it were natural" (*svārasikatve 'pi*).
"Naturalness" (*svārasikatva*) means being inherent (*svābhāvikatva*).

According to the maxim that "affirmations and negations regarding a qualified entity descend to the qualifier when there is a contradiction regarding the qualified," the cognition of temporal limitation regarding the qualified entity culminates in the qualifier.
Furthermore, the inference of impermanence has a qualified object as its domain, not merely the essential nature (svarūpa) alone.

Thus, the meaning is that impermanence belongs precisely to that which is perceived as delimited by time when qualified by a certain form; since there is no perception of temporal delimitation for the essential nature alone, there is no deviation (vyabhicāra).
He refutes [the objection] by stating "here too," [arguing] that the perception of the limitation by time of the mere essential nature (*svarūpamātra*) is unestablished even in the subject (*pakṣa*).
"Capability" (*yogyabhāva*) means the capacity for manifestation.
The meaning is that consciousness (*caitanya*) qualifies itself through its own relation in such a way that it becomes delimited by time—that is, it possesses the state of being limited by time.
He states that even the conformity to a specific cause is established otherwise by saying "precisely with reference to that.
This means precisely with reference to the connection with the object.
And thus, the underlying intention is that the first inference is not probative (*aprayojaka*).

The fact that temporal limitation and so forth are adventitious (*aupādhika*) or intrinsic (*svābhāvika*) has been observed in various instances. One might again raise the doubt: "How then can there be a certain determination of its adventitious nature in the case of cognition? To this, it is said:
"This [cognition] is adventitious..."
The distinction—the distinction of cognition as past, future, and so forth—is conditioned by its relation to objects.
Regarding the phrase "precisely as such [form]":

since cognition has the nature of the eternal self, it is eternal; thus, the intention is that it is easily ascertainable that the perception of its being delimited by time is merely conditional (aupādhika).
The meaning is that the Self has knowledge as its intrinsic nature because it is directly realized precisely as possessing knowledge.
Direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) is a particular modification (*vṛtti*); and that [realization] occurs of the Self precisely as possessing knowledge—this is the sense.
Therefore, there is no deficiency even if the self, which shines by its very nature, does not appear as possessing cognition during deep sleep;
nor is it the case that, even so, one would [erroneously] think, "I am happy," or "I am suffering."
It should not be argued that the reason [for the self's existence] is unestablished because, in the direct intuition of the self as "I desire" or "I hate," it does not appear as possessing knowledge;
for even there, the expression "I" implies the possession of knowledge regarding objects that are either agreeable or disagreeable.
Furthermore, since pleasure and the like are also particular states of cognition,

and because at the time of the direct perception of desire and so forth, the self appears as possessing the experience of desire and the like due to the self-luminosity of cognition, it should be understood that the apprehension of the self will be established precisely as possessing cognition—
even though scripture alone remains awake regarding such matters as cognition being the very nature of the self.
Furthermore, because this treatise is primarily concerned with reasoning, it is reasoning alone that has been demonstrated here;
the scripture will be presented later.
This is indicated by the words "na hi" (for not).
That which has the nature of being insentient is that which is not a substratum for consciousness.
The remainder is clear.
Here, an objection is raised: "Like the body."
The fact of being perceived solely as possessing that [quality] is not pervaded by having that as one's own nature;
the meaning is that even though the self is perceived solely as possessing a body, it lacks the nature of the body.
He refutes this by stating, "Because it is unestablished."
The explanation of the passage concerning the doubt begins with "syād etad" and so forth;
"sadhrīcīna" means precisely "accompanied.
The explanation of the passage constituting the refutation begins with "tan naivam" and so forth.
The apprehension of the self as being necessarily accompanied by a body is unestablished;
for even in the state of yoga, in the state of focused attention, and even in the state of mental experience, the self appears without the body.
Thus, the sense is that there is no deviation [from the rule].
Having stated that in yogic perception and in the contemplation of the self, the self appears even without the body, he says "I know" with regard to ordinary perception as well.
He confirms the absence of the body's nature as the self with the word "karma.
And his inner intention is that the self is not established merely by its being perceived as possessing specific bodies such as those of various humans and so forth.
"Like the mind" is an example by way of dissimilarity (vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta).
That is to say, the body does not follow [the self] in the same manner as the mind does.
This is stated with the intention that even in the state of liberation, the mind continues to function.

One might raise the weak objection: "Even when the gross body has ceased, the subtle body persists at all times; and since that [subtle body] does not have the nature of the Self, there is a deviation [from the rule] in that case. He dispels this doubt with the words "of the *liṅga*.
By the word "also" (*api*), it is indicated that even its persistence does not exist during the dissolution (*pralaya*) or in liberation (*mokṣa*).
The intention is that because the subtle body (*liṅgaśarīra*) is beyond the reach of the senses, there is no deviation [from the rule] due to the absence of a cause.
Here, this should be understood: the nature of knowledge, which is an attribute of the self, is indeed eternal;
however, its capacity to illuminate objects arises from its expansion through the doors of the senses and so forth, as it possesses the qualities of contraction and expansion.
Furthermore, impermanence is asserted with respect to that which is qualified by the quality of illuminating an object;
therefore, by means of this specific qualification, its impermanence is established while its nature is established as permanent.
Now, having raised a fourfold objection regarding the permanence of cognition, he refutes it with the words beginning "bodhasvābhāvye" (if it has the nature of awareness).

The first objection is that if the person (*pums*) has consciousness as its intrinsic nature (*jñānasvabhāvatva*), then there would be the manifestation of its own form even during sleep and fainting.
He refutes this by means of an analysis of the meaning of the term "manifestation" (*prakāśa*), beginning with the words "In the case of the alternative... (*vikalpe*).

Even if there exists a manifestation produced by knowledge that is distinct from knowledge itself, it is not produced in the self during sleep because of the obstruction of the quality of darkness (*tamas*); just as visual perception is not produced when obstructed by dense darkness.
"Existence" (bhāva) means "being thus" (tathābhāva); that is to say, the state of possessing cognition (bodhavattva).

The second objection is that if consciousness were to exist, there would be the undesirable consequence of the self being in a state of wakefulness during sleep; he restates this as "Now, if it is thought... and refutes it with "Not so."
A physical or verbal conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) is being proposed;
[the author] states "Who indeed... (*kaḥ khalu...*) because the first [possibility] is not possible.
The word *kim* is used in the sense of censure (*kṣepa*).
For it is not [the case that] "this does not exist," because the nature of the self is eternally attained; this is the intended meaning.
He restates the second [position] with the words "discourse" (*vyāhāra*).
"What does he avoid? means:

even when there exists that non-conceptual cognition—which does not register specific qualifiers such as expressive words and so forth—belonging to infants, the mute, and others, no verbal expression of its object is observed. This is the meaning.
Thus, the point is that since knowledge lacks the pervasion (vyāpti) by verbal expression regarding its own object, the [unwanted] consequence (prasaṅga) is misplaced.
The third objection is that if there were experience, there would be the consequence of memory upon the self's awakening from sleep;
he restates this with the words "smṛtau" (in memory).
"He avoids it because it is not a function" refers to the explanation of the doubt, beginning with "If it is said... and so forth.
"He avoids it" refers to the explanation of the rebuttal, beginning with "That is not so" and so forth.
"No," [it is replied].

A particular modification of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti-viśeṣa)—that is, a particular state of knowledge that has become an attribute (dharma-bhūta-jñāna)—is the experience of the self during sleep and so forth; it is characterized solely by its own nature (svabhāva-lakṣaṇa).
The meaning is that it is not characterized by a specific state of knowledge that has become a dharma (dharmabhūtajñāna).
By the phrase "by which," the intention is that the very activity of cognition (*jñānavṛtti*) alone produces the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) which is the seed of memory.

"But this is so": the meaning is that during sleep and other such states, the self simply exists as possessing its natural, inherent attribute of knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), but there are no mental modifications (*vṛtti*) of that knowledge.
"And not in [the case of] awakening" means that its nature is an eternal cognition whose own object is itself;
for knowledge that has become a property (dharmabhūtajñāna) is indeed eternal and has the self as its object.
This is according to the view of some that [the cognition] again grasps the object through the attainment of auxiliary conditions such as the contact between the sense organ and its object;
or else, "awareness" (*bodha*) itself is its own state, its essential nature (*svarūpa*).
The doubt arises: "Since this Self is, by its very nature, of the form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), why should it not produce a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) regarding itself?
However, by virtue of the context, the meaning here is properly understood exactly according to the manner previously stated:
[it refers] to this eternal consciousness.
He dispels the suspicion that eternal consciousness (*nityabodha*) could produce mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) by stating "in the case of the uninterrupted" (*anavarate*).

This being so, since impressions would arise every moment due to the power of the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the stream of impressions never coming to rest; and thus, liberation (*mokṣa*), characterized by the absolute cessation of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, maturation (*vipāka*), and latent dispositions (*āśaya*), would fail to be established—this is the meaning.

Having stated the defect in [the view that] the nature of eternal consciousness (*nityabodhasvarūpa*) produces mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), he also states its lack of purpose with the words "And in the case of experience" (*anubhave ca*).
For the postulation of mental impressions is for the sake of cognizing what was previously experienced but is no longer being experienced.
The sense is: since there is an eternal experience while one is awake, what is the point of postulating mental impressions?
"Correspondence with itself" means having the same object as the original experience.
"Its own seed" refers to the seed of memory, namely the latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
To the objection that memory is indeed observed to have the self as its object, he replies: "I who... and so forth.

A cognition consisting of a mixture of memory and direct experience (*smṛtisaṃbhinnapratyaya*) is a cognition whose object is the nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*), being of the nature of memory with respect to the aspect delimited by past time and of the nature of direct experience with respect to the aspect delimited by present time.
Regarding the phrase "delimited by time":

although the mere nature of the Self is always manifest, because that which is delimited by various times and so forth is grasped by a mental modification (*vṛtti*), and because such a modification generates a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), the aforementioned cognition is logically established; this is the meaning.
"Not merely its own nature" means not having its own nature alone as its object.

Having stated that there is a sublation [of the idea] and an absence of purpose regarding the production of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) by the cognition of an eternal self, he further states that it is impossible for such a cognition— occurring during sleep and so forth— to produce a latent impression, by saying "and it is indistinct."
The meaning is that it is "indistinct" due to being overwhelmed by the quality of *tamas*,
and "non-conceptual" because it does not penetrate the distinctions between external and internal objects;
[this occurs] when [the intellect] is not overwhelmed by a more powerful [quality].
The seed of memory is the *saṃskāra* (latent impression);
it is deposited—that is, produced.

Here, this should be understood: although, by the force of the retrospective recognition of one who has awakened from sleep—such as "I slept happily"—the experience of the self's own nature during the time of sleep must also be admitted as a generator of a *saṃskāra*.
Moreover, this is a statement based on the view of a certain school of thought;
for this very reason, the author will later state another position with the words "Or let it be," and so forth.

Even if it is impossible for a memory whose object is limited to that alone to arise while the experience is still present, there is no harm in the arising of a reflective cognition (*pratyavamarśa*) with an augmented object through the power of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*).
[This will be] explained further ahead.
Now, is it not the case that the experience of the self's own nature is impossible at all times?

For it is established by experience that the manifestation of the "I-sense" (ahamartha) through pleasure and so forth occurs precisely at the time of experiencing objects; to this, he says: "And because of its constancy" (sāmyāt ca).
When an object is experienced in a single general form, because its specific features do not manifest, there arises the illusion that it was not experienced at all.
An illustration of this is the body and so forth.

For example, although the body—characterized by hands, feet, and other limbs—is constantly experienced during the waking state, it is only at the time when adventitious specific features manifest that it is specifically cognized; at other times, it is as if it were not being experienced.

The sense is that, just as during wakefulness, although the effort to sustain the body continues at all times, it appears clearly only at the moment of intentionally lifting the hand or other limbs— seeming as though it were not experienced at other times—
even so it is in the present case. This is the point, even though the effort to sustain the body...
Logicians maintain that what is termed the "source of life" (jīvanayoni) is beyond the reach of the senses.
Nevertheless, since the maintenance of life can be accounted for by the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) alone, the postulation of a supersensuous effort (prayatna) is unnecessarily cumbersome.
For it is observed that even during wakefulness, the holding together of the body and its limbs occurs through effort.
And that effort is indeed capable of being perceived.
However, the intention of the venerable teachers is that during sleep, the maintenance of the body occurs solely through the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*).
Therefore, it should be understood that there is no inconsistency in this illustrative example.

Having restated another objection— that if consciousness persists even during sleep, then there would be no distinction between that state and the states of meditative absorption (samādhi) and liberation (mukti)— he refutes it with the words "na cāvikṛte" (and not when unmodified).
In sleep, there are the afflictions such as ignorance (avidyā) and so forth, as well as a state of extreme contraction of knowledge due to the predominance of the quality of darkness (tamas).
For at that time, even the illumination of its own self does not occur through cognition;

however, in liberation (mokṣa), there is the absolute cessation of afflictions (kleśa) and, through the removal of obstructions, the state of possessing eternal, uncontracted knowledge of all objects— this is the distinction.
Regarding the term *asaṃprajñāte*:

in some places the reading is *saṃprajñāte*. The sense is that there is a great distinction between [the state of] sleep and [the state of] meditative absorption (*samādhi*) for a person; this distinction is brought about by the accomplishment of the means to liberation, which consists in the mind being directed solely toward the Self due to the intensity of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of supreme dispassion and cessation (*nirodha*).
However, "caritādhikāreṇa" is the correct reading; it means "by one who has fulfilled his duty. "Apavargiṇā" means "by one who brings about liberation."
The phrase "by means of the mind" (*manasā*) requires the addition of a substantive meaning "capable of directly realizing the Self in the state of isolation" (*kaivalyāvasthātmasākṣātkaraṇayogya*).
However, if the reading is *caritādhikāriṇā*, it means "one who has fulfilled his duties" (*kṛtātman*).
Or [it may be said]: "by one who has accomplished what was to be done.

Thus, the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpatva*) and the essential nature of consciousness (*citsvabhāvatva*) have been established by refuting the objections that arose. Now, it might be argued that even during deep sleep, the manifestation of the Self will be accomplished through a mental modification (*vṛtti*) that does not arise [as a distinct cognition].

Having set aside the argument that [the self] is self-luminous, he raises the objection, "But how [is this known]? even regarding deep sleep, by suggesting that a mental modification (*buddhi-vṛtti*) must be admitted there as well.
Here, the collective intention is as follows: so-called "deep sleep" is the experience of the quality of *tamas*.
Its nature as pleasure arises when that *tamas* has the slightly awakened *sattva* as its auxiliary and serves as its objective support.

The function of *sattva* consists of lightness and so forth. When *tamas* is accompanied by slightly awakened *rajas*, its state as an object of cognition is characterized by suffering, instability, and so on. And when *tamas* is intensely awakened, completely overwhelming both *sattva* and *rajas*, its state as an object of cognition is characterized by profound delusion and so forth.

Only when there is the experience of darkness during sleep can the subsequent recollection at awakening—such as "I slept happily"—be accounted for through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) produced by that [experience], and not otherwise. He answers by partial acceptance with the words, "It is true, so it is. This signifies agreement regarding the aforementioned cognition.
If sleep were of the nature of a mental modification (vṛtti) supported by the quality of darkness (tamas),
or if it were of the nature of memory (smṛti), then the aforementioned cognition would not be admitted in cases such as deep sleep;
thus he says, "the answer has already been given."
Regarding the term "inferential":
sleep is simply the absence of the common occurrence of mental activity (*vṛtti*).

And because of the mark (*liṅga*) of the non-recollection of what is otherwise capable of being remembered, there is an inference at that time of the absence of mental activity, which is by nature luminous.
Furthermore, because of signs such as lightness of the body and the sense organs, there is an inference of pleasure and so forth in that state. The point is that,

by the force of recognition on a subsequent day of what was done on a previous day, this very cognition— even regarding the existence of the self during the time of sleep— is essentially inferential in nature.

"Not another mode of functioning" means that one should not accept that sleep is of the nature of a mental modification (buddhi-vṛtti) directed toward the quality of darkness (tamas). The meaning is that the aforementioned cognition is accounted for simply by the inference of sleep itself.
One raises the objection: "If sleep does not have the nature of a mental modification (*vṛtti*), what then is the status of the Patañjali Sūtra? He answers with the words "in cessation" (*nirodhe*).
The intended meaning is that sleep is the general absence of modifications that have positive objects as their support.

The intention is that, because it shares the common property of being suppressible (*niroddhatva*) with the other mental states (*vṛtti*), sleep is metaphorically designated as a state (*vṛtti*). Here, "like error" (*viparyayavat*) serves as the illustration. This is because, in the absence of any theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), it is precisely the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*)—which is designated as "error" and is what must be suppressed—that is intended [as the model]; thus, just as [error] is a state, sleep is also a state.
The meaning is that it is "proclaimed. And as for the phrase "that [is]":

the non-deviation of all cognitions from their objects—characterized by the manifestation of things exactly as they are—is established as a settled point (*adhikaraṇasiddha*) in the treatise on the *Nyāyatattva*; such is the sense.
And he states that these [distractions] must be suppressed because they are obstacles to the means for achieving isolation (*kaivalya*), by saying "in isolation.

The meaning is that the nature of the Self, which pertains to isolation—that is, the Self qualified for liberation—is opposed to them; thus, because they obstruct the accomplishment of the means desired by that [Self], they must be suppressed.

Even if one accepts that the cognition "I slept happily" is of the nature of a retrospective synthesis (*pratisaṃdhāna*), [the author] says "let it be so. Since the self is perceived precisely as possessing consciousness, its nature as awareness has been stated. Furthermore, by demonstrating through the aforementioned method that awareness persists even during sleep, that very point will be established; thus, there is no loss for us.

The sense is that the claim— that the heart is the manifestation of the self only through its function (vṛtti) and not by its own nature— will be thoroughly established by what precedes and follows as being like a sweetmeat promised by a liar;
furthermore, "remembrances" are those consisting of the form of synthesis (pratisandhāna).

For, since there is no consciousness inherent in the person as previously described, darkness existing during sleep and other such states cannot be established, due to the non-establishment of its cause. //27//
For at the time of deep sleep, all the sense-faculties together with the mind have indeed ceased to function;
moreover, a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) has no capacity other than that of memory,
and darkness is not self-luminous.
Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that even objects existing elsewhere would be constantly manifest.

Furthermore, since cognition is established as the means for accomplishing all objects, one must necessarily admit— by the force of logic— that it is by this very cognition, which exists as an inherent nature and is devoid of any external instrument, that there occurs the manifestation of either darkness (*tamas*) or some other quality residing in the self, which has emerged through its own natural activity.
The self is eternally luminous because it is a cognizer.
For non-eternal luminosity, which is pervaded by non-cognizership, finds no room within the self that possesses cognizership—a state opposed to its pervader.
Even if one were to admit that sleep is a mental modification (*vṛtti*), the permanence of cognition is not thereby established.
He restates the opponent's objection—that activity is produced by instruments—with the words "he says.
He refutes it with the word "thus" (*ittham*);
the meaning is that the determination of its nature as cognition occurs in the manner about to be described immediately hereafter.
Regarding the phrase "yataḥ" (since):
the meaning is that because a causal agent is impossible during deep sleep, one must accept that consciousness, which illuminates both darkness and light, is established by its very nature. //27//

He explains the verse himself with the words "uparatāni" (they have ceased). Because the activity of other [faculties], such as pleasure and so forth, has ceased, there is no occasion for the operation of cognition during sleep due to the cessation of the functioning of the instruments.

Therefore, if deep sleep is accepted as the experience of darkness (*tamas*), one must necessarily admit that the manifestation of the quality of darkness occurs through consciousness itself by its own nature.
The point is that, consequently, the fact of having consciousness as its intrinsic nature (*bodhasvabhāvatva*) is established.

In reality, knowledge does not possess the nature of illuminating darkness during sleep, because its function is extremely contracted. Rather, the established conclusion is that "awakening" is simply the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the self—which appears at that time as pleasure—by virtue of the power of the experience of its own nature. As for the cognition "I slept," this aforementioned perception regarding the portions of time belonging to the period of sleep is indeed of the nature of inference.

However, if constant experience were not to produce a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), then it must be understood that the experience of the nature of the Self during the time of sleep is itself the direct cause of the aforementioned recognition (*pratisandhāna*), and that the portion consisting of the immersion into the Self occurs as bliss (*sukha*).

Furthermore, regarding the objection that even though the Self is of the nature of consciousness (*bodhasvabhāva*), its manifestation should occur only at the time of a mental modification (*vṛtti*) and not at all times—the author establishes its eternal luminosity with the words "And [the Self] is eternally luminous.
Regarding the phrase "in the state of being a non-knower" (*apramātṛtve*): [it refers to the state where the Self is not functioning as a subject].
The meaning is that whatever is the pervader in the form of non-measurership is the pervaded.
Furthermore, its self-established luminosity also arises from the state of being a knower.
For the state of having a manifestation dependent on another is pervaded by the quality of being a non-knower. //28//
(Thus is established the eternal self-luminosity of the Self, whose nature is consciousness.
But what is this "luminosity" (prakāśa) that is accepted as its eternal and inherent property?
And what is the relationship between this [knowledge] and the self?
If it is knowledge itself;
and the relationship is that of the locus and the located;

Therefore, in order to demonstrate the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the absence of the probandum by the absence of the reason, one must employ a pot or the like as an example: "Whatever has non-eternal luminosity, or whose luminosity is dependent on another, is not a cognizer (*apramātṛ*), just like a pot or the like.
And since a negation of a particular implies the admission of a general [possibility], it would follow that adventitious knowledge is admitted in the case of pots and such things.

Now, if it were thought that this [undesirable consequence] should not occur, and the relationship itself were proclaimed to be the relation between object and subject (*viṣaya-viṣayibhāva*), then it would follow that the self is an object of knowledge eternally;
and since being made an object of knowledge is necessarily dependent upon specific means [of cognition], [the self could not be known at all].
If it is argued that there is the possibility of inherent nature,
and that such a restriction applies only to the domain of the insentient, we say no;
for we observe that such a state exists even when something becomes an object for another sentient being.
Nor should it be said that the rule of dependence upon means of proof applies only to objects that are not the self (*anātman*);

for even in the case of the self, when it is made an object of inferential, scriptural, or yogic knowledge, such dependence is observed. Furthermore, it is contradictory for a single entity to simultaneously function as both the object and the agent in a single action.

Just as in the case of a needle’s point, which acts both as the piercer and the pierced, the inner self (pratyagartha) is known either through scriptural instruction or through inference by way of its attributes— such as eternality, unsurpassed subtlety, all-pervasiveness, and the nature of consciousness—
but not in its essential form (svarūpataḥ).
If self-establishment is accepted only with respect to its own nature (*svarūpa*), then the contradiction remains unresolved.

On the alternative view that the relationship of being the object of cognition and the means of cognition is admitted through a distinction of aspects (*rūpabheda*), then, just as in the case of a non-thesis, words and so forth would not possess self-establishment.
(This concludes the enumeration of faults regarding the claim that the state of being the locus of cognition and the state of being an object consist in the nature of being manifest.)
Now, it might be argued: "Luminosity is not cognition;

rather, it is a quality common to all things—both sentient and insentient—that is caused by that [cognition], by virtue of which things are said to 'shine forth,' and through which both manifest and latent states are extended without distinction across all objects."
Furthermore, the relationship between all entities and that [Self] is characterized by the nature of the substratum and the dependent;
and that [relationship], being innate and eternal for the Self, exists solely through the power of the aforementioned proof.
This position has been refuted.
There is no such thing as "illumination" that is distinct from cognition.
That cognition which is conducive to the production of linguistic usage is said to be "illuminated."

Since knowledge arises in accordance with the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the object of knowledge, the knower, and one's own self, it is logical that a uniform linguistic usage manifests across all three. If one accepts that manifestation is their inherent nature (*svābhāvya*), then what further purpose is served by resorting to consciousness (*caitanya*)?
Nor should it be said that manifestation itself is that [consciousness].
Otherwise, it would follow that even objects such as jars must be conscious, since they too possess luminosity.
If it should be argued that a person's state of being manifest occurs only when he possesses consciousness, then what is the status of consciousness itself at this point?
For that [cognition] is indeed volition itself; it does not cognize.
Now, if it is argued that this property [of cognition] depends upon its relation to that [object];
What is the connection that serves as its basis? It is not the relationship of locus and located.
Otherwise, it would follow that objects such as jars would lack that [nature];
nor is there a relationship of object and subject, because that very relationship cannot be established.
This non-determination should be investigated in the *Bhrāntyadhikaraṇasiddhānta* and in the *Saṃvitsiddhi*.
Furthermore, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that both the self and that [object] would not be manifest.
Establishment consists precisely in being the locus of manifestation dependent upon cognition.
Furthermore, the position that cognition is to be inferred by that [object] has already been refuted.
Even for one who maintains the doctrine of self-luminous consciousness (*svaprakāśa-saṃvit*), the discrepancy regarding conformity with worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is impossible to avoid.
One must also consider this: how could a cognition inherent in the self (*ātman*) produce illumination or transactional usage with respect to an object with which it has no connection?
Do not say that this is due to the proximity of its own causes, such as the sense organs or the inferential marks;

for an effect that has already acquired its own nature does not, while being produced, depend upon its instrumental cause [for the sake of its own commencement]. Otherwise, it would follow that the fetching of water and other functions of a jar and the like would require the presence of the potter and others in the same locus.
Furthermore, the destruction of an effect does not necessarily follow from the destruction of its instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).
Yet, when the contact of the sense organs and so forth is destroyed, the cognition of form and other objects perishes.
Therefore, consciousness also issues forth along with the sense organ and comes into contact with this or that object.
Just as the tactile sense-organ [is affected] by the hand and so forth, so it is in this case;
for since that cognition has that [organ] as its limiting condition (*upādhi*), it is logical that it follows the presence or absence of that organ.
Otherwise, why would a cognition that has already arisen cease when the contact between the sense-organ and the object ceases?
This same fault applies even to those who maintain that the manifestation of the object is a property produced by cognition. For cognition is merely an instrumental cause;
why, then, should the manifestation of the object cease when that [instrumental cause] ceases?
Or from where [could it arise], since it remains as long as that state exists?
To the objection—“Could it not be that its eternal luminosity is produced by its own inherent nature of consciousness?”—he says: "established by itself" (*svataḥsiddhe*).
[This refers to] the pervader and the pervaded.
The meaning is: "From the absence of the pervader follows the absence of the pervaded.
The intended sense is that the establishment of the quality of having a manifestation independent of anything else follows precisely from the very nature of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*).

[Objection: Even if the manifestation of a cognition does not depend on another cognition, it still depends upon its relation to a self; therefore, the property to be proven—the characteristic of having a manifestation independent of anything else—is absent in the case of cognition.

Therefore, since there is knowledge in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), the objection that "knowership" (*jñātṛtva*)— which exists only in the subject (*pakṣa*)— is an "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*) reason has no room to arise. Although, according to our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*), the purely negative inference (*kevalavyatirekin*) does not possess the status of a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*),
nevertheless, it is indeed possible to establish this [point] against opponents by following their own methodological framework.
In the final system (siddhānta), however, the self-luminosity of the self is established precisely through the aforementioned positive concomitance (anvaya).
Furthermore, by the force of the means of valid cognition that apprehends the self’s eternity, the eternity of its luminosity is also established as a matter of course.
And the intention of the Supreme Teachers is that the foundation of all objects is established by the scriptures (śruti). //28//
Now, as an incidental digression, he introduces an inquiry in order to determine the nature of the category of "manifestation" (prakāśa) with the words, "But what [is it]?
Even though cognition is eternal, this inquiry is relevant to the present subject because it establishes the specific determination of cognition according to each respective object.
He says, "If... [yadīti].

The meaning is: if it is asserted that in the expression "it shines" (*prakāśate*), the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is illumination or cognition (*jñāna*), and the meaning of the suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is the state of being a substratum (*āśrayatva*). He refutes this with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*).
Regarding the phrase "tatra ca":

since the negation of a specific quality— namely, eternal luminosity— in the negative example (*vyatireka-udāharaṇa*) necessarily results in the acceptance of luminosity in general, the meaning is that one would thereby have to accept that things such as jars possess adventitious knowledge.
Nor should it be said that, this being the case, there would be no absence of a knower (*ajñātṛtva*) due to the absence of a cause therein;

for what is intended here by the term "non-knower-ship" is "selflessness" (*anātmatva*). Furthermore, it should be understood that the mere state of being the locus of illumination cannot be established as the probandum, because it is already established.
In order to avoid the aforementioned fault, he raises another alternative, thinking, "Now let that not be the case.
That is to say, if it is argued that "being manifest" means "being an object of cognition," he refutes this as well with the words "therefore" (*tataḥ*).
The meaning is that by proving the self to possess eternal luminosity, it follows as a consequence that it must be an object of knowledge at all times.
If it is argued, "This is indeed accepted," he replies with the words "In [the case of] knowledge" (jñāne).
For the operation of knowledge in illuminating an object is mediated by the sense organs and other such means.
Therefore, the meaning is that the status of the self as an object of knowledge, being independent of anything else and eternal, is difficult to establish;
likewise, there is no such restriction.
The meaning is that there is a rule that making something an object occurs only in dependence upon an instrument (*karaṇa*).
Likewise, regarding the word "bhāve" (in the sense of a state of being),
the meaning is that it is observed to be dependent upon the operation of an instrument.
"Nor indeed" means that one should not say that the dependence on an instrument for the act of making an object belongs only to that which makes its own self a distinct object;
for [this applies] even to the Self.

The meaning is that since we observe even the manifestation of one's own self to be dependent on instruments such as words and logical marks (*liṅga*), one must not restrict the rule [that knowledge is independent].

Now, it might be argued: "It is precisely an eternal cognition whose object is the essential nature alone that you wish to establish; and this [cognition] does not require an instrument when taking the self as its object. To this, he says: "In the case of what is contradictory" (*viruddhe*).
The acceptance of both agency and objecthood for that which is mere self-nature (*svarūpa-mātra*) is contradictory.

Furthermore, it is impossible to maintain that there is no contradiction in the cognition of mere self-nature by means of a difference in forms (*ākāra-bheda*); this he states with the two verses beginning with "If [it were] eternal" (*nityatve*).

Now, one might object: even if the self-nature alone is what is known, its status as the knower (*gamaka*) is possible through a distinction between general and particular properties (*sāmānya-viśeṣa-dharma-bheda*); to this, he replies:
Regarding the phrase "by way of a difference in form":
just as, although the word "word" (śabda-śabda) is itself denotable by the word "word," its state of being denoted is by way of the form of being a quality perceivable by the ear,
while its state of being a denoter is by way of a specific sequence [of phonemes], the self-luminosity of the word is not thereby compromised.

The meaning is that, in this way, even for the self which has been made the subject of the thesis, self-luminosity would not be established if there were a difference in the properties that delimit the status of being the grasped and the grasper.
Thus, the investigator has refuted both positions.
Now, he restates the Bhaṭṭa method with the words "Now it might be said."
Manifestness (*prākaṭya*) is illumination (*prakāśa*),

and its substratum-ness (*āśrayatva*) is the relation. Furthermore, the cognition and linguistic usage expressed as "it is manifested" (*prakāśate*) predominantly function with the meaning of being the substratum of manifestness.

The meaning of the objection is as follows: "Luminosity produced by cognition is common to all things, whether sentient or insentient; that very luminosity is eternal and inherent to the self, which is to be established through the power of its being a knower.
He refutes this position through the mouth of the Prābhākara, stating, "This has already been rejected."

The method of refutation is as follows: since the conventional usage of "known-ness" (*jñātatā*) is established through self-luminous cognition itself, there is no evidence whatsoever for a distinct property called "known-ness" produced by cognition.
Regarding the phrase "one in all three," "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) means cognition (*jñāna*).

The meaning is this: in the position that "the relation—which is conducive to the linguistic usage dependent upon those [three]—manifests as the meaning of the verb," it is only in this way that the linguistic usage of "the oneness of purpose manifests among the object, the cognition, and the cognizer" becomes possible.
The underlying intention is that the production of a state conducive to the linguistic usage of this triad is the very nature (*svabhāva*) of the cognition of a jar or other objects.

He states that "if a permanent luminosity distinct from cognition were admitted in the self, then cognition would be useless" (*tattvāntare*). He raises an objection, saying "if it is argued," (*yady ucyeta*), on the grounds that since the self's manifestation occurs only when there is cognition whose object is itself, cognition is not useless for the self because it serves as a common causal factor for its preservation (*kṣemasādhāraṇaprayojakatā*). He then refutes this, saying "in consciousness," (*saṃvidi*).
Consciousness (*saṃvit*) is indeed knowledge itself,

not the substratum of knowledge. Thus, the point is that if the inherence of consciousness were the cause of being manifest, then because that [inherence] is absent in consciousness itself, its own manifestation would not be possible.

If it is argued that the very connection with consciousness is accepted as the cause of manifestation, the author replies to that with the words "What [is this] by her? Here, a refutation is made through an analysis of the possible types of connection with that consciousness.
If the relation of consciousness consists in its inherence in a self that possesses consciousness, then it follows that objects such as jars would not be manifest;
this is what he means by the words "of jars, etc.
On the other hand, if that relation consists in being an object of consciousness, then it follows that both consciousness and the self would not be manifest.
Thus he says "of the self" (ātmanaḥ); that is, of consciousness (saṃvidaḥ). "Of him" (tasya) refers to the person (puṃsaḥ).
The underlying intention is that it is impossible for consciousness to be the object of its own manifestation— just as it is impossible for the tip of one's finger to touch itself—
and that it is likewise impossible for it to reside within the self due to the contradiction between being the object and the agent of an action.
Now, if this contradiction between object and agent is accepted, let it be that the conventional usage "the self manifests" occurs simply because the self is the locus of cognition.

Regarding the claim that for supersensible cognition (*jñāna*), "manifestness" (*prākaṭya*)—which is the cause of the linguistic usage "it shines forth"—is possible through an inference based on the mark of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), the author says: "dependent on cognition.
Furthermore, since the inference of cognition is rejected, the linguistic usage "it shines forth" must be explained as cognition shining forth by its very nature as cognition.
And thus, [if manifestness were required], it would have to exist in objects through manifestness, which is a property produced by cognition.

It is established that, according to this view, it is impossible for that [manifestation] to have a single uniform nature across all three— since it manifests as knowledge by way of being of the nature of knowledge, and as the self by way of being the locus of knowledge; thus, conventional usage [occurs] in these three cases.

Having thus, through the voice of the Guru, explained how the uniformity of the manifestation in linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is impossible regarding the object, the cognition, and the cognizer according to the Bhāṭṭa school, the investigator now raises the objection that even in the Guru’s (Prābhākara) view, the uniformity of suitability for linguistic usage among these three is impossible, stating: "In the self-luminous [cognition], in the object by way of being the content of cognition... and so forth.

The meaning is that even in the Guru’s system (Prabhākara), the discrepancy—which must be addressed as to how [the self] conforms to linguistic usage by being of the nature of knowledge in the case of cognition, and by being the locus of knowledge in the case of the self—is impossible to avoid.
He states another refutation as well: "In both systems, regarding the self... and so forth.
The doubt here concerns the sense faculty (*indriya*).

The meaning of the doubt is this: that cognition which is produced by a sense faculty, a logical mark (*liṅga*), or the like, in connection with an object, brings about either a state of manifestation (*prakaṭatā*) or a fitness for linguistic convention (*vyavahārānuguṇya*) regarding that object.
He indeed does not reject [the view] that it is not [required] once [the cause] has been obtained;
for an effect depends upon efficient causes only for its own production,
but not even for the production of its own effect once it has already arisen.
Otherwise, the fetching of water by means of a jar would occur only when a potter is present, and not elsewhere; such is the meaning.
The point is that if one maintains that cognition itself depends on its own cause for the accomplishment of its own effect, this very same inconsistency would follow.
"Having the same locus as the potter, etc. means having the same substratum as the potter, etc.
He states another point of disparity with the words "and not," etc.

The meaning is that since the destruction of the effect is not observed upon the destruction of the efficient cause (*nimitta*) in other cases, a disparity arises in both positions even by the admission that knowledge itself is destroyed by the destruction of its efficient cause.
What, then, is the justification for the manifestation (*prakāśa*) or the linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) [of the object]? To this it is said:

the intention is that one must accept, without resorting to an infinite regress, that cognition—which has issued forth through the door of the sense organs and the like, which is in contact with the object along with that [cognition], and which manifests the object—is the generator of the linguistic usage regarding the object.
This is the position of the proponents of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*).

"Likewise, it would not exist" means that if cognition were to possess activity and so forth simultaneously with the sense organ, then— given that the cognition is in contact with its object and illuminates it— the occurrence of positive and negative concomitance (anvaya-vyatireka) in accordance with the positive and negative concomitance of the contact between the sense organ and the object would be possible; otherwise, it would not.

The meaning is that if the contact between the object and the cognition mediated by the sense organs and so forth is not admitted, then since the destruction of the cause is not the cause for the destruction of the effect, there would be no cessation of cognition upon the cessation of the contact between the sense organ and the object.

Nor is it appropriate to counter-argue this by citing the example of number and so forth; for [in those cases], destruction is unestablished, whereas number [is destroyed] through the destruction of the cognition [of it].
Number other than the unitary number is also non-substantial, because it possesses the nature of number. //29//
For all numbers, which reside in a single substratum and apply to both permanent and impermanent objects, are accepted by all theorists as existing only as long as their substratum exists. (30)

Why is that number which exists in many things—beginning with duality and ending with the highest unit (parārdha)—not of such a nature [as being a universal], given that it possesses the common property of "number-ness" (saṅkhyātva)? //31//
But surely oneness is not a number,
because it does not exceed the thing's own nature; therefore, the example cited is devoid of the probans.
Not so; that is simply number, because it persists even when there is another substance.
If oneness were merely the intrinsic nature of a jar or the like, [it would not persist].
Consequently, there would be no commonality of oneness across all substances such as "one jar" and "one cloth";
for it is not possible for the essential nature of a jar to stand in grammatical coreferentiality with the essential nature of a cloth, as in "the jar is the cloth."
But that [oneness] does exist.
Now, one must admit that even the destruction of the cause is sometimes a cause for the destruction of the effect;
otherwise, the destruction of duality and so forth following the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) would be untenable.
He raises the objection that "the same will be the case here [in the present context]" with the words "na ca" (and not).
He refutes this with the words "asiddhatvena" (because of being unestablished).

The meaning is that since the destruction of duality and so forth by the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) is unestablished, it is impossible for the destruction of duality and so forth to serve as an illustration of the destruction of an effect through the destruction of its cause.

"Some" [hold that] because oneness, duality, and so forth are numbers, they persist as long as their substratum exists; thus, they do not perish through the destruction of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*).
By this, the [opponent's] lack of proof is established.

The formal argument (prayoga) here is as follows: duality and so forth, as long as they exist in their substratum, are numbers because they possess the nature of number, just like unity. // 29 // 30 // 31 //
He raises the objection that the reason is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the example with the words "But [there is] no unity";
he refutes this with "Not so," and explains with "If..."

If the specific nature of each individual object alone were the determinant of the cognition and linguistic usage of "one," then the occurrence of inclusive cognitions and usages such as "the pot is one" and "the cloth is one" would be untenable,
because the property of being that specific individual (tattadvyaktitva) is not inclusive.
The point is that if the number one were of such a nature, then because it would persist as oneness, the occurrence of a persistent cognition and so forth would be possible.
This is according to the method of the logicians (*tārkika*).
Furthermore: "Oneness as a number is like the number two or other numbers, because it is contradictory [to itself]."
For there is no cognition of grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the form "one" or "two."

As for the argument that "because it is a quality residing in multiple substances, number such as duality and so forth does not persist as long as the substance exists— just like conjunction"— that is inconclusive with respect to plurality;
for even when two things, such as a jar and a cloth, exist, their plurality does not perish.
Nor is that [duality] merely the number two,
for it would follow that it would be absent in the case of three;
nor is it merely the absence of oneness.
Since even that which is empty would fall into the error of manifoldness,
he raises the objection regarding the unestablished nature of the reason in the example with the words, "But is there not non-unity?
He refutes this with, "Not so."
Regarding the word "yadi":

if the specific nature (svarūpa) of each individual instance alone were the regulator of the uniform cognition and linguistic usage [of "one"], then such uniform cognitions and usages as "the jar is one" and "the cloth is one" would be untenable.
The meaning is that because each individuality (*tattadvyaktitva*) is non-continuous (*ananugata*),

whereas oneness (*ekatvasaṅkhyā*) is continuous in that way, the occurrence of a continuous cognition and so forth is possible through its continuity as oneness. This is according to the method of the logicians (*tārkika*).

Having stated the refutation against [unity] being the intrinsic nature (svarūpa), he also states the proof for its being a number (saṅkhyā) with the words "saṅkhyaikatve" (in the case of unity as a number).
Here the formal argument (prayoga) is: "Unity is a number, because it is opposed to other numbers, like duality and so forth. He applies the reason to the subject (pakṣa) with the word "ekam" (one).

In this regard, the following should be understood: since the paryāpti (inherence) delimited by the delimitor of the intended object (*uddeśyatāvacchedaka*) appears as a relation such as duality (*dvitva*), whereas the paryāpti delimited by singularity lacks the status of being a relation such as duality, the expression "one is two" (*ekaṃ dvau*) is not employed.
However, the expression "one possesses duality" (*ekaṃ dvitvavat*) might indeed be possible.

In this case, since it is the inherence of duality itself that appears by way of the relation of essential identity (*svarūpa-sambandha*), and since that [inherence] is not sublated even in a single [substance],
the state of being opposed to another number is characterized by the absence of a subsistence whose pervasion is delimited by a delimitor of the pervasion of another number.

By this much, the opponent's objection regarding the deficiency of the probans (*sādhanavaikalya*) in the example for the inference that duality and so forth exist as long as their substratum exists has been removed. // 32 //
Because duality and so forth are relative, because their counter-correlates are not apprehended,
and because the desire to know them has ceased, they are indeed real even though they are not apprehended.

Therefore, it is only for consciousness itself that its conformity to the presence of the object is logically established through contact with the object via the medium of the sense organs. Furthermore, according to you, cognition is the illuminator of the object;
and every illuminator is observed to be an illuminator only when in contact with the object to be illuminated, as in the case of the light of a lamp and so forth.
Therefore, it is logical to maintain that this [space] is also like that.
If it is argued that, being formless like space, it cannot possess action, then what indeed is this so-called "form" (mūrti)?
If it is argued that [consciousness] is a functional application for one who is separated from [the body],
and if it is defined as being occasional while possessing substantiality,
then that is indeed accepted in the case of sentience.
For that [atom] is not an all-pervading substance;
