if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the simultaneous accomplishment of all objects.
However, if it is localized, then when it is in contact with a single sense organ at one time, it is directed toward that specific object.
At that time, it does not preside over another sense organ;
for this very reason, there is no simultaneous arising of cognitions,
and it possesses unsurpassed velocity.
Because one perceives the simultaneous— or rather, extremely rapid— presiding over multiple sense organs,
the aforementioned lack of corporeality (*amūrtatva*) is unestablished;
for corporeality (*mūrti*) consists in possessing tangibility (*sparśavattā*).
If it is argued that [sound] is inactive because it is devoid of contact (*saṃyoga*);
[we reply that] this is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*) with respect to sound.

For sound, though devoid of touch, travels with its momentum from a very distant place such as the mouth of a conch shell, just like a clod of earth or similar objects, due to a particular impulse (*nodana*).

Even for the mental faculty (*manas*), which is devoid of contact (*sparśa*), its possession of activity is agreed upon by both parties—those who understand the meaning of words and those who understand the meaning of sentences.

If it is asked, "How can there be a conjunction with consciousness (*caitanya*) regarding the past and the future, which are non-existent? [the reply is: "Or how else could they possess the status of being objects (*viṣaya*)?"
Is it their state of being manifest,
or their connection with number and so forth? Whatever the resolution may be in that regard, [it applies equally].
Let that very [past and future object] be what is present here.
Moreover, since those two [the past and the future] exist even today by virtue of their being past and future, what inconsistency is there in their contact with consciousness in that form?
Furthermore, just as the eye comes into contact with the polar star, the sea-monster (śiṃśumāra), and so forth, which exist in a most distant place;
Likewise, by one such as the Self-Existent (Svayambhū) existing at a more remote time, spanning the beginning and end of a kalpa and so forth, there is no lack of evidence whatsoever. Furthermore,
he raises the objection of a counter-argument with the words "But [the case] where there are many," and he refutes it with the words "To that [we reply]."
Multiplicity (*nānātva*) means plurality (*bahutva*); and because it inheres distributively (*vyāsajyavṛttitva*), like duality and so forth, it is indeed a quality (*guṇa*),
but not of the nature of difference (*bheda*).
The meaning is that difference does not subsist distributively (avyāsajyavṛtti).

Now, if it is argued that since [duality and the like] exist as long as their substratum exists, it would follow that they must necessarily be perceived at the time the substratum is perceived—just as oneness is—[the author] says in response: "Because of relativity" (āpekṣikatvāt).

This is because duality and the like, whose cognition depends upon the apprehension of another related object, cannot be perceived so long as that other related object, which serves as their counter-correlate (pratiyogin), is not apprehended.

The point is that even if [duality] were grasped, it would not be perceived at all times due to the absence of the desire to know duality and so forth, as well as the absence of the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) which acts as its auxiliary cause in that perception.
Thus, it is stated that duality and the like are not suitable examples for [the principle of] being destroyed by the destruction of its cause.

In reality, however, since duality and the like—apart from a specific enumerative cognition—are themselves unestablished by means of valid cognition (*aprāmāṇika*), there is certainly no possibility of their destruction depending on the destruction of that [cognition]. This is how it should be understood. // 33 //
The past and the future cannot be distant from the intellect, because they are manifested by the intellect, just like the nature of the intellect itself and its knower. // 34 //

And thus, due to the unsurpassed velocity of consciousness, there arises the misconception of not perceiving the intervening space and time, just as there is the misconception of not perceiving the successive conjunctions and disjunctions with different points of space in the case of a whirling firebrand.
Furthermore, whatever specific form belongs to the sense organs, logical marks, mental impressions, and so forth, with respect to their respective objects—
Consciousness also emerges by adhering to that very [object], and it is brought into proximity precisely through its objective domain;

just as the word-power (*śakti*) of words such as "cow" relates only to the universal aspect within an entity that consists of both universal and particular aspects— though established by a single cognition— or just as an injunction (*vidhi*), setting aside the already-accomplished portion, touches only that portion of the productive urge (*bhāvanā*) which is not yet accomplished.
Therefore, it is logical that consciousness, through the gateway of the senses and so forth, goes out toward its respective objects.

As the Blessed One said: "It carries away his wisdom, as the wind [carries away] a boat upon the waters. And Manu says: "For if even one among all the senses leaks away," [it carries away his wisdom].
"By that, his wisdom flows away like water from the foot of a leather bag.
As for the objection, "How can consciousness, which is a quality, leave its possessor and go elsewhere?",
that is incorrect.
Because its abandonment is not admitted;
for even without abandoning the self, volition issues forth from here and there through the doors of the sense faculties and so on.
And it has been stated in the very scripture that the reconnection of such [volition] once severed is impossible.
Furthermore, qualities such as sound, odor, sunlight, and the luster of jewels are observed to possess motion and to transcend their substrates.
Indeed, sound is a material entity that is extremely subtle and characterized by traveling to a distance.
[Objection: Is it not the case that sound, like space, is all-pervasive, yet is perceived as if localized and as if moving due to the influence of the manifesting articulations (*dhvani*)?
For instance: sound is all-pervading because, while residing in a single substance, it is a quality of space, like its dimension (parimāṇa).
This is not so, because it is not a quality of that [space]. Sound is a quality of air.
Because it necessarily arises simultaneously with that [substance],
like its own touch;
and whatever quality necessarily arises simultaneously with a particular substance is indeed a quality of that [substance].
Just as visible forms and so forth are of such a nature,
sound also necessarily arises simultaneously with the wind;
for both are invariably produced by the conjunctions and disjunctions of the drum and the stick, or the bamboo and the blade, and so forth.
And sound is produced, because, while being perceptible by the sense organs, it possesses the nature of a quality (*guṇatva*), like odor and so forth;
and it is also produced, because it is perceived only after an action [of articulation], like conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and so forth.
Furthermore, one should not assume that effort and the like are merely manifesters [of sound], as that would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*).
Even when comparing the postulation of its being the cause of that cognition with the postulation of it being the cause [of the object], the latter alone is simpler.
Furthermore, manifestors manifest simultaneously multiple objects located in the same place that are perceivable by different sense organs;
for example, a lamp manifests color, number, dimension, and a water-jar and other such things existing in one location.
And since it is not the case that [the auditory organ] is produced by the air generated from the conjunctions and disjunctions of the palate and so forth, it is not a manifestor [of sound].
Having stated the refutation regarding the non-acceptance of sensory contact with the object for cognition, he states the proof for such contact with the words "and another.
He raises the objection that if cognition were to go outward, it would contradict its formlessness, using the phrase "like space."
He dispels this doubt by means of the alternative of corporeality with the words "What is this? and so forth, [concluding] with "For that is not... etc.
The meaning is that during the state of bondage, there is simply a lack of omnipresence (*avibhutva*) regarding knowledge.
Regarding the phrase "not that":

it means that at the time when [the soul] is presiding over one sense organ, it does not cause that [soul], which is in contact with another sense organ, to function for the sake of contact with its object.

The meaning is that, since "mūrtatva" (corporeality) is thus characterized by having a substance that is not all-pervading, its absence—namely "amūrtatva" (incorporeality)—is unestablished (*asiddha*) in the case of cognition (*jñāna*).
Regarding the position that "mūrtatva" consists in possessing touch (*sparśavattva*), he states the fault with the words "by sound" (*śabdena*).
The restrictive rule that "whatever lacks touch is devoid of action" (*akriyatva*) is unestablished.
The meaning is that since sound, though formless, possesses action,
there is likewise no logical inconsistency in the diffusion and so forth of cognition, even though it is intangible.
This demonstration of the inconclusiveness [of the reason] is made with respect to sound, according to the view that it is a substance.
Even if there is disagreement regarding its substantiality (*dravyatva*), he demonstrates it in another well-established instance with the words "in touch" (*sparśe*).
Alternatively, one might object: "Surely the movement of sound must be explained as occurring only through its substratum;
and since the substratum of sound is air, which possesses touch, there is no damage to the aforementioned rule. To this, he replies with the words "in touch."
The followers of Kaṇāda are experts in the meaning of words (*padārtha*), while the followers of Jaimini are experts in the meaning of sentences (*vākyārtha*).
The point is that both schools agree that the mind possesses action (*kriyāvat*), even though it is intangible (*niḥsparśa*).

One might object that if cognition reveals an object through contact with it, then since contact with a past or future object is impossible, the cognition and the conventional usage of revealing such objects would not be tenable;
thus he raises the doubt with the words, "How [could there be cognition] of the past?
He then offers a counter-objection with the words, "Or how [could there be cognition] of the future?"
The meaning is as follows: according to the Vaiśeṣika school, past and future things are objects of present cognition;
according to the Bhāṭṭa school, they possess the quality called "manifestation" (prakāśa), which is dependent upon present cognition.
In both systems, how can numbers such as duality and so forth—which are produced by a present enumerative cognition (apekṣābuddhi)—be logically established in relation to those two [past and future]?
He clarifies the parity with the subsequent [view] in the words "yastatra" ("that which therein").

Whether it be being an object of cognition or possessing a property dependent on cognition, the dependence of the object's existence upon cognition is not required; thus, even one who does not wish to accept it must admit this.
The sense is that we too establish the contact between cognition and its object in exactly that same way.

In fact, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), since those two [past and future objects] also exist at the time of cognition by virtue of their state characterized as the absence of destruction (*dhvaṃsa*) and prior absence (*prāgabhāva*), the contact (*saṃnikarṣa*) with cognition is indeed possible; thus he says, "Moreover" (*api ca*).
Regarding the phrase "what impossibility? (*kānupapattiḥ*), in some places the reading is "what indeed is the impossibility? (*kā nāmānupapattiḥ*).
Now, even so, there would be no apprehension of that specific time by the cognition, such as a present one.
Regarding the statement "because of its [the cognition's] absence now," he says "furthermore" (*kiñca*).
The meaning is that because cognition possesses extreme velocity, its apprehension of various objects through contact at their respective times is logically established.
An illustration of cognition contacting a temporally remote object is the visual light of the eye, which, despite being extremely swift, contacts a spatially remote object.
It was stated that even at a distance, contact with the intellect (buddhi) is possible;
now, however, he says "not in the past" to show that, from the perspective of the intellect, there is no such thing as distance at all.

The established conclusion (siddhānta), however, is that contact with the intellect consists precisely in the absence of distance from the intellect, which is common to the object to be known, the act of knowing, and the knower. // 34 //
For those who maintain that sounds are eternal, reside in partless space, and are audible, there is no reason for a restriction regarding their manifestation. (35)
For it has been shown that there is a single manifestor when there is identity of location and identity of the perceiver;
in the absence of that [identity], the air arising from effort is the cause of the sound. (36)

For this very reason, let it be accepted that there is multiplicity with each utterance, because what has already been produced cannot be produced again, owing to the difference in the completeness of its causes. (37)

Furthermore, how could properties such as acute accent, grave accent, length, and shortness—which reside in the phonemes *ga* and so forth and are perceived simultaneously—not differentiate their own substrates? (38)
Recognition also does not establish identity due to the similarity arising from the coincidence of location;
this has been made known by the reasons for difference, just like the recognition of a lamp-flame. (39)
But in that case, either a conjunction with consciousness or some kind of manifestation produced by conjunction would result;
yet neither of these two is possible in the case of consciousness.
Because a relation depends upon difference,
there is no conjunction of the self with consciousness either, since [consciousness] is the very attribute of that [self].
For the relation between a property and its substratum is not conjunction;
rather, it is inherence, because it is a relation between things that are inseparably established.
Conjunction (*saṃyoga*), however, is the reaching together (*prāpti*) of two substances established separately, caused by action;
or it is the state of being without interval (*nirantara-sthiti*) between those two, whether they be effect and cause, or between either of the two—
consciousness or conjunction— inherence (*samavāya*).

Alternatively, if mere relation were the manifestation, then non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) and over-pervasion (*ativyāpti*) would have to be demonstrated respectively with respect to the knower, the act of knowing, the object of knowledge, the body, and the senses.
Furthermore, the admission that there is a manifestation of a distinct reality (*tattvāntara*) is sublated by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*) and thus does not require further refutation.
Therefore, knowledge is that which is conducive to the arising of practical activity (*vyavahāra*).
Therefore, it is logical to accept that "it is that which shines forth.
However, the fact that consciousness possesses a nature conducive to the conventional usage of a triad is an incongruity of cause that cannot be questioned;
for natures do not admit of questioning.

If this is so, then it is reasonable to maintain that consciousness is the cause of linguistic usage even for an object that lacks both conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*), in accordance with the diversity of its causes.
To this it is replied: it has already been stated in this regard that an effect does not initiate its own activity by following the lead of its instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*).

Even if the meaning of the term *prakāśa* (manifestation) is a consciousness that conforms to empirical usage (*vyavahāra*), it is nonetheless difficult to avoid a difference in its *pravṛttinimitta* (the ground for its application).

For if one resorts to a *bahuvrīhi* compound, there would follow the undesirable consequence that manifestation does not exist in that [consciousness] itself, because of the absence of another consciousness [to manifest it].
If one resorts to a *karmadhāraya* compound, there would follow the undesirable consequence that the knower and the knowable are not manifestations, since they themselves are not consciousness.
And conformity with the emergence of linguistic usage must be understood from that very usage;
furthermore, before that, there occurs the cognition of being known and the act of verbal expression.
If this is so, what then is the object that is manifested?
For we do not perceive that which is faultless, uniform, and yet follows after the knower, the known, and the knowledge.
It is said in reply: Surely you have never heard the *Nyāyatattva* regarding the first topic (*prathamādhikaraṇa*).
For it has been stated therein by those establishing memory based on experience:
"Proximity to experience is the cause of memory.
What is meant by this is that proximity to consciousness is manifestation.
He asks: "What is this 'not distant' (*adūra*)? Is it something other than distant, its opposite, or its absence?
Likewise, is 'not distant' a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) or a mere incidental characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*)?"
If it were a qualifier, then in all three positions, there would have to be a cognition such as "it manifests preceded by a recollection of its distance from consciousness";
yet this is not the case.
If it were a secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*), another intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) must be stated.
And it has been stated that [the object] is not perceived by means of the sense-faculty.
To this it is replied: enough with this misplaced agitation.

Even so, since contact with distant space and time is invariably concomitant with contact with the intervening space and time, there would follow the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that even those things situated in the intervening spaces would be perceived; however, this consequence is accepted as being desired.
He refutes [the objection] with "If it were so... [and so forth].

Now, even if this is the case, since there is contact between the cognition extended by the eye and taste and so forth as well, how is the determination made that it is only form (rūpa) that is manifested by it, and not taste and so forth? To this he says: "Moreover... [and so forth].
That which is the form restricted to a specific object— that is, the capacity for producing cognition established only with respect to that specific object—
by means of that [form], namely the sense faculty and so forth restricted to that object;
and by means of its very domain, that is, only by means of the object suitable for that sense faculty and so forth.
And thus, the point is that there is no contact between visual cognition and taste and so forth.
Regarding the connection with only the "fitting" (yogya) aspect, there are both worldly and Vedic illustrations, namely "just as" (*yathā*) and "just as indeed" (*yathā vai*).

If the word-potency (*śakti*) of words such as "cow" were connected to a specific individual characterized by its particularity (*tadvyaktilakṣaṇaviśeṣa*), then from that particular word, there would be no cognition of other individuals.

However, regarding the connection with the general aspect (*sāmānyāṃśa*), it is held that the universal alone possesses the fitness for connection with words such as "cow" and so forth. Furthermore, since the connection of an injunction (*vidhi*) with an already established object is purposeless, its fitness for connection is held to be with that which is not yet established.
And by means of each [particular], the connection with each respective [object] is intended, as follows:

Thus, it should be understood that each respective sensory cognition and so forth is connected only with its corresponding object, such as the sense organ; otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of the non-existence of the blind, the deaf, and so on, as well as the consequence of a lack of systematic order— this is the intended meaning.

The Mīmāṃsakas maintain that although the efficient force (bhāvanā) is connected with the goal, the means, and the procedure, its purport lies specifically in the aspect of the means, since that is what has not yet been established.
It is directed toward that very object; it is solely intent on manifesting an object capable of being perceived by the senses.
Mere relation is not "contact" (sannikarṣa).
However, there is a specific relation;

and since that relation belongs only to a particular sense-cognition with respect to an object suitable for that particular sense-organ, the underlying point is that taste and so forth are not revealed by visual or other such cognitions.
However, there is one position that holds that visual and other types of cognition have no connection whatsoever with taste and so forth;
yet the previously mentioned position alone is logical.
He cites the venerable *Gītā* verse, "That of this [person]," as proof for the expansion of cognition toward the sense objects.
The first half [of the verse] is: “For when the mind follows after the wandering senses.

The meaning is that the mind leads the cognition—which is inclined toward grasping a self and directed toward the objects of the senses—facing toward the sense-objects by means of the doors of the senses; this is the statement regarding the mind in the expansion of cognition through the doors of the senses.
Regarding the phrase "of the sense-faculties" (*indriyāṇām*):
it flows out, meaning it moves toward external objects.
By means of that gateway of the sense-faculties, consciousness (*caitanya*) also issues forth, just as water [flows] through the openings of a leather water-skin bag; such is the meaning.
"Without abandoning" means that even without relinquishing its connection to the self—

that is, without abandoning the knowledge which possesses the qualities of contraction and expansion as an attribute of the self— the connection with external objects occurs through its state of expansion. He provides an illustration of a quality moving elsewhere from its substrate in the words "are seen."
The state of transcending the locus of the property-bearer (*dharmin*) consists in being related to a locus larger than that of the property-bearer.

Furthermore, "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) must here be defined as the state of being a mode (*prakāra*) that is not established separately (*ayutasiddha*), which is common to both substances and non-substances, because both non-substances— such as sound and odor— and substances— such as light and radiance— are included under the category of quality.
The possession of motion and other qualities by a quality occurs through its substratum;
nor should it be argued that this does not constitute overstepping the locus (*dharmyativartitva*),
for the intended meaning is the overstepping of well-known substrata such as the *śaṅkhapuṣpa* flower.
The scriptural statement, "the fragrance wafts from afar," declares that fragrance possesses motion.
As for sound, its possession of motion is established by the perception of "this is the sound of a conch" even when it is at a distance.
To the objection that, because sound is a quality of space (*ākāśa*), its motion—even via its substratum—is not tenable, he replies: "extremely subtle."
"Material" means produced from the primary elements (*bhūta*).

Sound arises in the air that has been set in motion by the striking of a drum with a stick and so forth. The point is that, due to the dispersal of portions of the supporting air, its connection with various directions is also possible.
Because of its extreme subtlety, the wind possesses the capacity to travel far;
it should be understood that the property of the substratum is metaphorically attributed to the thing supported by it.
Now, one might object that sound, as a quality of space, has no need for movement precisely because of the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of space itself.
One might object:

"Since sound is perceived only in a location connected with its manifestor (*vyañjaka*), there is no undesirable consequence of it being perceived everywhere even if it were all-pervading (*vibhu*). To this, he raises the objection, "But [the case of] space...
and establishes the all-pervasiveness of sound with the words, "Sound..."
The qualifying member in the reason is for the purpose of avoiding deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as the conjunction of the space within a jar (*ghaṭākāśa-saṃyoga*);
the qualified member is for the purpose of avoiding that [deviation] in cases such as the oneness of a jar (*ghaṭa-ekatva*).
He refutes this with "Not so."
He states the "unestablished nature of the essential character" (*svarūpāsiddhi*) with the words "because it does not possess those qualities.
This means because sound lacks the quality of being a property of space (*ākāśaguṇatva*).
If it is asked, "But since the fact that sound is a quality of space is established by the scriptures, how can it be rejected?", it is replied as follows:
According to scripture (*āgama*), even space itself does not possess omnipresence (*vibhutva*); how much less, then, can its quality [sound] possess it?
However, by reasoning (*yukti*) alone, it will be established that sound belongs solely to air (*vāyavīyatva*); this is the underlying intention (*hārda*).
He states that very reasoning with the words "belonging to air" (*vāyavīya*).
Having rejected the omnipresence [of sound], he also rejects its permanence as maintained by the Mīmāṃsakas, stating: "And it is produced.
By this, the non-establishment of the qualified part of the reason (*hetuviśeṣyāṃśāsiddhi*) in the inference of sound's being composed of air is also avoided.

Now, one might raise the objection that being perceived at a time subsequent to [its production] could also be accounted for by its being manifested (*vyaṅgyatva*), and thus the reason is inconclusive (*aprayojaka*).
He rejects [the opponent's view] with the words "and not" (*na ca*).

This is because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*): to postulate that [the cause] is the cause of its manifestation based on the assumption that it is the cause of that [cognition] itself involves complexity. The underlying point is that an argument (*tarka*) which results in complexity for the opposing position (*vipakṣa*) is what supports one's own position (*svapakṣa*).
He also states the impossibility [of the theory] under the position that [sounds] are manifested, saying: "And the manifestors...
The point is that if articulation were the manifestor of phonemes, there would be the undesirable consequence of all various phonemes being manifested simultaneously;
for it is the nature of a manifestor, when situated in one place and perceived by a single sense organ, to manifest everything [within its range].

Furthermore, it should be understood that there is excessive complexity (*atigaurava*) in postulating a distinct class (*vaijātya*) for the air that manifests phonemes (*varṇa*), consisting both in the postulation of its being the cause of manifestation and in the postulation of a distinct class among manifestors for the sake of establishing the fixed order of manifestation.
He demonstrates the very fault in [the air] being a manifestor with the following half-verse: "If [phonemes] were eternal... (*nityatve*).
The term "nityatvavādinaḥ" ends in the genitive case; the word "mate" (in the view) is to be understood as the ellipsis.
The two qualifiers—having a single substratum and being perceptible by a single sense organ—are thus indicated.

And thus, he concludes that on the view that [the phoneme] is manifested, there would be the undesirable consequence of all phonemes being manifested by a single utterance, stating: "In the case of identity of location" (*deśaikye*) and "due to the absence of that" (*tadabhāvāt*).

The meaning is this: because there is no manifestation of multiple [phonemes] by a single manifestor, the internal air (*kauṣṭhyamāruta*), arising from the effort of articulation and having reached the points of articulation such as the palate, is itself the producer of each respective phoneme.

Since it is impossible for [the phonemes] to be suggested (vyaṅgya), even the distinctness of the letter *ga* and others at each utterance—which follows from the position that they are produced (utpādya)—must indeed be admitted; thus he says, "For this very reason.
He establishes the difference of *ga* and so forth also through the perception of contradictory properties (*viruddhadharmopalambha*), saying, "Furthermore, in the case of the acute," etc.;
by the word "etc.," qualities such as high pitch and low pitch are to be understood.
It has been stated that because contradictory properties can coexist in a single entity through a difference in time, they appear simultaneously;
"appearing" (bhāntaḥ) means "manifesting" (bhāsamānāḥ).

The underlying intention is that it is also difficult to maintain the claim that the properties of the manifestor are superimposed upon the manifested solely because the latter cannot itself be a manifestor.
[Objection: But how can there be recognition (pratyabhijñā) such as "this is that very letter *ga*" if there is a difference with each pronunciation?
To this he says: "Because the place [of articulation] is the same" (*sthānaikye*).
The sense is that, because it is rooted in similarity, that recognition is of the nature of an error (*bhrānti*). // 35 // 36 // 37 // 38 // 39 //
Let it be far from experience, or let it be something else entirely, or even its opposite;
and let its nature be luminosity—what more need be said here? (40)
The manifestation "it shines forth" is also merely a discernment of the nature of an object conjoined with that cognition— a cognition which is the opposite of the remoteness of the intellect—
just like the external light.
For even in that case, the designations "manifest" and so forth regarding the light and the portion of ground pervaded by it are caused by the proximity of the light.
And just as in that case there is the cessation of total darkness caused by that [light], so too here there is the cessation of ignorance caused by the remoteness from knowledge.
For this very reason, there is a recollection at a later time that is similar to both the experienced object and the experience itself.

Thus, even the dilemma regarding the specific nature of the relationship with consciousness finds no footing; it is therefore merely a "cavil against what is not to be caviled at" (*niranuyojyānuyoga*). Furthermore, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is simply extreme proximity, a synonym for the term "immediacy" (*nairantarya*).

That same [proximity], when dependent on others, is the conventional ground for the Vaiśeṣikas' technical term "inherence" (*samavāya*); thus, since no distinct entity is accepted, such a dilemma is impossible.
And we shall demonstrate in the "Examination of Relations" how inherence is included within conjunction;
or rather, there is another kind of manifestation characterized by fitness for linguistic usage, which is brought about by proximity to cognition.

And although its own causes are complete, that [sound] does not arise with respect to other attributes of the self such as omnipresence and tangibility, nor with respect to the body and sense organs, due to obstruction or a lack of suitability— just as color, taste, and so forth do not appear in the waters of the Yamunā when they are in contact with the eye.
Thus, by refuting [the views of] eternality and omnipresence, it has been established through reasoning that sound possesses the quality of being aerial and that it is diffusive in nature.
Regarding the mere connection of the self’s quality, consciousness, with something else, the examples are sound and fragrance;
regarding its movement elsewhere without leaving its substrate, the examples are sunlight and the luster of a gem.
Thus, movement to another location is possible even for that which is not of a material substance.
The meaning of this section is that because the connection with the substratum is uninterrupted, its status as a property [of that substratum] is well-established.
Thus, the connection of consciousness with objects has been stated;
and it is intended that the linguistic usage "it shines forth" is occasioned by the connection with consciousness.
Here the Prābhākara raises an objection:

"But indeed, if it be so"—if the conjunction with consciousness (*caitanyasaṃyoga*) were the regulator of the manifestation and linguistic usage [of objects], then such manifestation and usage would be impossible for consciousness itself, for its substratum, and for the substratum of that [consciousness].
And if the inherence in consciousness (*caitanyasamavāya*) were the regulator, then such manifestation and usage would be impossible for both consciousness and its object.
If mere connection with consciousness were sufficient for such [cognition], then it would follow that the sense organs and so forth would also be manifest.

Therefore, one must accept that a particular cognition serves as the cause for the practical usage of its respective object only through a specific instrumental condition (*nimitta-viśeṣa*), while by its very nature (*svabhāvataḥ*) it serves as the cause for the practical usage of its own substrate. Thus, the postulation of a connection with consciousness is useless; this is the collective intention [of the argument].
Regarding the position that there is a conjunction of two all-pervading [substances], since action is absent therein, he defines conjunction in another way as "akārye" (in the non-produced).
The meaning is that conjunction is the state of two substances distinct from their parts and wholes existing in an unobstructed interval between them;
and that [conjunction] occurs through action in the case of what is not all-pervading.
The meaning is that pervasiveness belongs to [the object] by its very nature.
By the very rejection of the connection with an object, the position that there is the manifestation of another property produced by that [connection] is also rejected.
He states the sublation by non-perception regarding the manifestation of another property as well, saying "in another reality" (*tattvāntare*).
"It is not to be questioned" means that it is itself the cause of its own linguistic usage,
because it inheres in its own substratum.
The meaning is that the fact that the object conforms to its own cause constitutes a difference in the causal factor (*prayojaka-vaiṣamya*), which does not entail a fault.
The critical examiner states "it is said" (*ucyate*) to point out the defect even in the view of the Guru (*gurumata*). [He argues:

It is observed that the production of its own effect occurs only in a location possessing its own instrumental cause (*svanimitta-kāraṇavat*), and not elsewhere; thus, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is accomplished by cognition only with respect to an object where there is sensory contact (*indriya-sannikarṣavat*), and not otherwise.
The sense is "correctly.
He states another objection as well with the words "in practical usage" (*vyavahāre*).
Manifestation (*prakāśa*) is characterized by the knower and the knowable possessing a cognition that conforms to their own respective practical usages.

The meaning is that for cognition (*jñāna*), however, that [nature] characterized as being a cognition conformable to its own linguistic usage (*svavyavahārānuguṇajñānatva*) does not exist as a common factor (*anugata*) across the three [categories], such that it could serve as the regulator of a uniform linguistic usage (*anugatavyavahāraniyāmaka*) for the term "manifestation" (*prakāśa*). Now, one might object: let manifestation simply be the state of being conformable to linguistic usage dependent upon cognition, and let that be the common factor; to this he replies with the words "in the arising of linguistic usage" (*vyavahārodaye*).

The meaning is that since illumination, which consists in the fitness for linguistic usage (*vyavahāra-yogyatā*), is itself inferable only from such usage, it is logically untenable for the notions of "being known" and the corresponding linguistic usage to arise prior to that very usage. Thus, when the investigator has raised this objection regarding the referent of the term "illumination," the bystander objects: "If this is so," and [the opponent replies]:
"Indeed not."

The meaning is that the referent of the word "manifests" (*prakāśate*) is difficult to define, because the mere relation to cognition is common to objects that are not being manifested, and because [relations] such as inherence (*samavāya*) lack universal applicability (*ananugatatva*).

The term "referent of the word 'manifests'" refers to the meanings of the stem and the suffix that constitute the word *prakāśate*. The proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) provides the resolution with the words beginning "It is said" (*ucyate*).
The genitive case in "of the first topic" (*prathamādhikaraṇasya*) is a possessive genitive (*śaiṣika-ṣaṣṭhī*). "Recollection regarding experience" means a recollection whose object is experience.
[This refers to] "proximity to experience."

The meaning is that since the experience itself is indeed as proximate to the experience as the object is, recollection is thereby rendered possible. Now, let this be granted; what relevance does it have to the matter at hand?
Regarding this, he says: "This has been stated. It has already been effectively shown that even consciousness possesses a distance from itself;
thus, the meaning is that the referent of the term "manifestation" (prakāśa), which is of that very nature, is what persists through all three [states].
He raises a doubt with the words "What is this?

Since the negative particle (*nañ*) has multiple meanings, this is a doubt arising from the desire to know what its specific meaning is in the present context. Having accepted some particular meaning for the negative particle, he raises another doubt with the word "so" (*tathā*).
If distance, difference, and so forth were the referents of the term "manifestation" (*prakāśa*), then the cognition of them would necessarily be preceded by the cognition of distance;
yet it is not perceived as such.
If, however, they are merely qualifiers (*upalakṣaṇa*), then another form that is the qualified object (*upalakṣya*) must be stated.
That is not the case;
thus, the perception of the impossibility [of the object] in both positions is the seed of doubt.

Alternatively, the objection beginning with "What [could it be]? and so forth, is that because it cannot withstand conceptual analysis, consciousness would not be manifestation due to its distance from [the object].
He sets aside [the objection] with the words "It is said.
He addresses the first alternative with "Let it be so in the case of experience," and he addresses the second alternative with "And if that state [exists]."

Luminosity (*prakāśatva*), or being luminous (*prakāśamānatva*)— that is to say, the referent of the term "luminosity"— is either the state of being distinct from what is remote from experience, or the state of being opposed to what is remote from experience.
In this context, the word "experience" (*anubhava*) signifies cognition in general.

In this regard, the following is the intended meaning: just as in the expression "the branch is the moon," there is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the indicator (*upalakṣya*) and the indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), and [it is stated that] "that state is luminosity" (*tadbhāvaśca prakāśatvam*).
Thus, luminosity is the property characterized by its proximity to consciousness (*saṃvidadūratva*). // 40 //

Therefore, according to the principle stated above, the self is by its very nature the embodiment of consciousness; it is of the very essence of knowing, though it perceives other objects through the instruments [of the senses]. //41//
As for the argument that consciousness is adventitious because it possesses specific qualities such as pleasure and so forth,
that too results from a lack of understanding regarding the nature of qualities; for the investigation into the category of "light" was undertaken only as a digression.

With the verse beginning with "ataḥ," he concludes that which was previously established— namely, that the self has the nature of cognition (*jñānasvabhāvatva*) and that its manifestation depends on something else— in order to refute the claim that the manifestation of the self occurs only at the very moment of cognizing an object.
This is because it can be demonstrated that manifestation is common to the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), the act of knowing (*jñāna*), and the knower (*jñātṛ*).

Therefore, by the proof of the manifestation that follows upon the subject (pakṣa) and the similar instances (sapakṣa), according to the reasoning stated in the verse beginning with "sajātīya," the Self is established as self-dependent and self-luminous.
And that [Self] is indeed of the very nature of knowledge;
its knowledge is not adventitious.

The meaning of the verse is that the Self is the illuminator of even that which is other than the knowledge constituting the dharma (dharmabhūtajñāna) as it issues forth through the eyes and other sense organs.
The reading "hānasvabhāva" found in older printed editions is not correct. //41//
Attributes that are adjuncts of the essential nature (svarūpa) exist as long as their substratum exists;
pleasure and the like are not so, whereas cognition is an adjunct of the self's essential nature. (42)
And how the nature of the self has cognition as its limiting condition has already been established;
furthermore, pleasure and pain are not attributes of the self.
This is because the existence of those [qualities] is established only through the excellence or impairment of the sense faculties (*indriya*).
Furthermore, this will be explained on the occasion of supporting the final point; thus, the illustrative example (*nidarśana*) is also deficient in its probans (*sādhana*).
Moreover, passion, hatred, and so forth are particular states of the mind (*manas*), not directly qualities of the self (*ātman*).
For it is known: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intellect, and fear—all this is indeed the mind.
And it is sung: "Desire, aversion, pleasure, and pain," and "volition and steadfastness" as a single term, which is the definition of the field (*kṣetra*).
For the body is indeed an aggregate sustained by volition (*cetanā*);
it is what is called the "field" (*kṣetra*) because it functions solely through consciousness that conforms to its own specific mode of operation.
For this very reason, in the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa*, there are such designations as: "He whose body is the earth," "He whose body is the waters," and "He whose body is the self," and so forth.
And in the Purāṇa it says, "All those [are] within that.
What is this "intellect" (dhī)?
That is intended as a metaphorical conceit (utprekṣā).
It does not have cognition as its object, because its inherent nature is heard in that very scripture;
for it is heard: "There is no loss of the knower's knowledge."
And [the scripture says]: "For there is no loss of the vision of the seer, because of its imperishability.
This scriptural passage, establishing the imperishability of knowledge precisely because of the imperishability of the knower, shows that knowledge is inherent to the very nature of the knower.
Nor is it tenable to claim that the seer is mentioned merely as a qualifier of vision.
Because it would contradict the use of the masculine gender, and because it would result in the reason being equivalent to the probandum;
even if [the passage] were intended to specify the essential nature of the seer.
The view that the self is non-existent is untenable because it lacks a logical basis and results in the abandonment of one's own position;
however, the permanence of the self, established by numerous reasonings and scriptural authorities, is unshakeable and thus appropriately designated as the causal basis.
For when an entity exists, its essential attributes cannot fail to exist,
just as yellowness exists in gold and radiance in a lamp.

Therefore, this is the meaning: for consciousness (*cit*), which constitutes the very nature of the Self, there exists never any loss whatsoever—whether in the state of *saṃsāra* or *apavarga*—of its various designations such as seeing, smelling, tasting, speaking, hearing, thinking, touching, and knowing, which arise through its connection with specific external and internal objects while illuminating its own self.
"Just as a mass of salt has no interior and no exterior, but is entirely a single mass of flavor..."
Thus indeed, O King, this Self is without interior or exterior, an entire mass of consciousness;
likewise, "By its own radiance, by its own light," and "The Self is the light, O Emperor," so he said.
Similarly, at the stage of liberation, the Chandogas declare: "The seer sees neither death, nor disease, nor even suffering."

"He who sees sees everything, not remembering what is born," and "He, indeed, by means of this divine eye, the mind, beholding these desires, rejoices"; and other [texts] such as, "This person surely knows."

The Śrutis, such as "But he is not known by the intellect," which declare the awakening of the Self even during the state when all the instruments [of perception] have ceased, confirm its nature as consciousness.
Furthermore, the Purāṇas state, "This Self consists of liberation, consists of knowledge, and is stainless," and so forth;
and the Itihāsa states, "It is the light even of lights," and so forth.
The Blessed One and Śaunaka said: "Just as moonlight is not produced by the washing away of a gem's impurities,
so too knowledge of the self is not produced by the abandonment of defects."
Just as by the construction of a well, the space occupied by water is not created—since it already exists—it is merely brought into manifestation;
for how could there be the arising of that which is non-existent?

"Likewise, through the destruction of qualities to be abandoned, qualities such as consciousness and so forth are manifested; they are not produced, for they are indeed eternal attributes of the Self.
For this very reason, the author of the Sūtras states: "He is a knower, for that very reason."
(Thus, the eternity of knowledge as the nature of dharma is established by means of scripture and other authorities.

Therefore, in this way, the distinction in conventional usage— such as certainty, doubt, and so forth— belongs either to consciousness (*caitanya*) which constitutes the very nature of the Self when it enters into specific contacts with objects,
or to that consciousness as it partakes in those respective particularities.
For consciousness, a firm conjunction with an object is indeed certainty (niścaya); its simultaneous, non-firm conjunction with many objects is doubt (saṃśaya);
and its connection according to the latent impressions of knowledge is recollection (smaraṇa), and so forth.

And it has been said: "The conjunction of consciousness, which is the attribute of the self, with an object is called cognition. Nor does it follow from this that the object would also be a knower, since conjunction is dependent on both [relata] only insofar as there is no conjunction of the object with itself.
For its conjunction with consciousness is like that of external light;
indeed, just as even when there is a connection with light, it is the sun and such alone that possess the quality of illuminating, and not a jar or similar objects.

Now, if it is argued that because light is dependent on the sun and so forth, it is the sun itself— possessing that quality— which is said to be the illuminator of another object through its connection with it, then here too, since consciousness is a quality of the self, it is logically consistent that the self itself, by touching another object through that [consciousness], knows it. Thus it is established that this self, whose very nature is consciousness, exists as one who knows itself.
However, depending on the difference in the objective conditions (*nimitta*), it either knows or does not know [an object].
(Thus is established the internal differentiation of the knowledge that constitutes the nature of reality, such as doubt and so forth.
In this way, although this Self, whose nature is consciousness, is ever-shining, it is like a fish in a deep reservoir of water, or like milk mixed with water.

Because [the object] does not shine forth clearly when distinguished [from its substrate], the various prior types of inference and their supporting statements are respected as they follow the logic for establishing that [distinction].

Dissatisfied even with those, [the practitioners]— having had the impurities of the veil of non-purity destroyed by the performance of the limbs of yoga such as the restraints (yama) and observances (niyama)— seek immediate knowledge (*aparokṣajñāna*) which is distinct from all other objects, arising from the predominance of *sattva* when the stains of *rajas* and *tamas* have been blown away by the repeated smelting of the practice of cessation (*nirodha*).

They exert themselves [in this regard], and it is undisputed by all theorists that non-perceptual knowledge arises at the ultimate limit of the intensification of cultivation; therefore, no effort is made here to establish that point.
Now, as for that which was stated regarding adventitiousness as the counter-thesis to the inherent nature of consciousness:
Having restated that [position], he refutes it with the words "As for [the claim] that pleasure and so forth...
and "That too...";
"guṇavṛttam" means having the nature of a quality (guṇasvabhāva).
And what is that?
To this he says: "the adjuncts of the essential nature" (*svarūpopādhayaḥ*).
Being an adjunct of the essential nature means being that which defines the essential nature.
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of such phenomena is their persistence as long as the basis [of consciousness] exists;
however, for others, it is adventitious (*āgantuka*). This is the operation of qualities (*guṇavṛtta*). Let this be so; what follows from that?
To this, he replies: "It is not so.

While pleasure and the like, which are objects of experience, must indeed be adventitious, consciousness cannot be established as adventitious; for it is the defining characteristic of the self's own nature, and the permanence of the self will be established [later]. This is the intended meaning. //42//
Regarding the phrase "and as follows": *bodhopādhiḥ* is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.
The meaning is that the referent of the term "self" (*ātman*) possesses attributes that define its nature as non-different from cognition.
Thus, the self's status as having cognition as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) is established by the reasoning that it is perceived solely through its possession of cognition.
The sense is that although cognition colored by an object is perceived as occasional because its connection with an object is occasional, the nature of cognition itself is indeed eternal.
Although scripture will later be established as the authority for cognition being the very nature of the Self and being eternal,
nevertheless, since this treatise primarily relies on reasoning, it should be understood that reasoning alone is put forward here.

By this, it is stated that in the inference of the adventitious nature of cognition (*jñāna*), the limiting condition (*upādhi*) is "being distinct from the properties that define its own essential nature.
Then, he also states the unestablished nature of the reason (*hetvāsiddhi*) in that illustrative example (*nidarśana*) with the word "pleasure" (*sukha*).
For, in the established doctrine (*rāddhānta*), [pleasure] consists of nothing other than cognitions that are favorable or unfavorable.
They consist of the forms of pleasure and pain;
and because they are included within those [categories], they do not serve as examples.
Furthermore, pleasure and pain—characterized respectively by the proficiency and lack of proficiency of the instruments—are distinct from specific types of cognition.

The meaning is that since those two [pleasure and pain] do not possess the quality of being attributes of the self (*ātman*), the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).
"At the end" means at the occasion of establishing the portion [of the thesis] beginning with "naturally happy" (*svataḥsukhī*).

[Objection: Even so, passion (*rāga*) and the like would still serve as examples, because they are specific qualities of the self (*ātman*) and are adventitious (*āgantuka*). To this, he says "passion" (*rāga*): passion and the rest are particular modifications of the mind (*manovṛtti*), not properties of the self.
However, just as the properties of fire, such as heat, appear in a pot with which it is in contact, there is merely the perception of the properties of the mind within the self.
Thus it has been said: "This self consists entirely of nirvāṇa, consisting of knowledge and stainless;
the properties of suffering, ignorance, and impurity belong to primordial nature (prakṛti), and not to the self."
Such is the meaning.
He states that the fact that passion and the like are attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is also perceived in the Śruti by saying, "it is known.
Furthermore, he corroborates this point with the words of the Blessed One by saying, "and it is sung [in the Gītā]."
Because the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) is dependent upon the field (*kṣetra*), its qualities— such as passion and the rest— are described as being qualities of the field.
But is it not also recited here that "volition and fortitude" (*cetanā-dhṛti*) [are qualities of the self]?
Therefore, he says "the support of consciousness" (*cetanādhṛti*) to show that even consciousness does not have the nature of a self (*ātman*).
*Cetanā* and *dhṛti* are not two separate words;
rather, *cetanādhṛti* is a compound.

The meaning here is that the definition of the body is stated as "that which is supported by volition" (*cetanādhārya*), referring to that which is sustained by volition (*cetanena*) or by the act of willing (*cetanayā*); thus, the body is necessarily [the subject] here.
He says this in the phrase "its own function" (*svavṛtti*);
"function" (*vṛtti*) means existence (*sattā*).
Or it is activity (*pravṛtti*);
that which is active is "proceeding" (*pravartamāna*), meaning existing with excellence (*prakarṣeṇa vartamāna*) or having attained stability; or it is that which possesses activity (*pravṛttimat*).
The established meaning is that the body is that whose existence and activity are generally dependent upon its connection with the consciousness of the Self.

This alone is the correct definition of the body, because definitions such as "possessing hands and feet" and so forth suffer from defects such as being too narrow (avyāpti). Keeping this in mind, [the author] cites scriptural statements from the Śruti which declare that earth and the other elements are the body of the Supreme Self, beginning with the words "Therefore... (ata eva).
The sense is that because everything has its nature, existence, and activity obtained solely through the knowledge consisting of the Lord’s volition, its being His body is indeed primary.
Why is this so? [Objection: But surely even the intellect (*dhī*) is listed among the attributes of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*);
therefore, it is implied here as an objection that consciousness is not the very nature of the Self (*ātman*).
He refutes [the objection] by means of the term "imagination" (utprekṣā).
The meaning is that among the specific modifications of the mind, imagination is called "intellect" (dhī).
Even though it is held that desire and the other [afflictions] are also properties of the self (ātman), [they are not so in this context].
However, these [qualities] do not belong to the self by its very nature;
rather, they are dependent upon limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as karma.

Furthermore, the figurative identification of the mind with those various [states] in the Śruti is based on the fact that the mind possesses the activity which causes the respective modifications of the intellect (buddhi), such as desire and so forth—this is the established conclusion (siddhānta).

Furthermore, since passion and the like are themselves forms of cognition characterized by specific states, it is not possible for them to serve as examples in an inference regarding the occasional nature of cognition.
Nor should it be argued that, by means of such qualified illustrations, the adventitious nature of cognition in general is being established.
Since it is perceived only as qualified by its states, it is impossible to prove adventitiousness in cognition-in-itself, which is unqualified.

Furthermore, if that [cognition] is established by scripture, its eternity is likewise established by scripture; thus, there is sublation by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha*).
Moreover, because a non-existent thing cannot possess states, the eternity of cognition alone is logical—this is the intended meaning.
However, this is stated as an *abhyupagamavāda* (an admission for the sake of argument) according to what has been heard.
He cites scripture regarding the eternity of knowledge with the words "for it is heard.
What is intended here is the eternity of the essential nature of knowledge, which possesses states such as being cognized (*vijñātitva*) and being perceived (*dṛṣṭitva*).

"Viparilopa" means destruction. [Objection: But has it not been stated here that there is only indestructibility of knowledge, and not its beginninglessness and endlessness? To this, he says: "of the knower."
The sense is that, by virtue of being the determiner of its own nature, the fact that knowledge is produced by the nature of the eternal Self also results in its being ancient.
As for the phrase "na ca" (and not):
it is not logical for the word "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*) to function as a qualifier of the act of seeing (*dṛṣṭi*) through non-difference.

The sense is that, such being the case, there ought to have been an indication in the feminine gender as "draṣṭryā" (by the seeress). Having stated the contradiction with respect to the word, he states the contradiction with respect to the meaning: "of the reason" (*hetośca*).
"Equivalence to the probandum" (*sādhyasamatvam*) means its unestablished nature (*asiddhatvam*).
The meaning is that, just as the probandum—characterized by permanence consisting in existence at all times—is unestablished, so too is the reason—characterized by indestructibility—unestablished;
or rather, since indestructibility itself is the probandum, it is illogical for that very same thing to serve as the reason.
Having raised the objection that [the verse] intends a different meaning, he refutes it with the words "of the seer" (*draṣṭuḥ*).
In this formulation, the term *dṛṣṭi* (vision) has the abstract state (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning.
What is to be proven (*sādhya*) is the exclusion of non-conjunction with knowledge on the part of the seer.
Here, the point is that because the reason lacks probative force (*aprayojakatva*), its status as a non-reason—that is, its lack of capacity to prove the thesis—is unavoidable.
"Regarding *svapakṣe* (in one's own position):

the meaning is that for one who maintains the doctrine of adventitious knowledge (*āgantuka-jñāna-vādin*), the admission that the self (*ātman*) is of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna-rūpa*) constitutes a deviation from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*).
Furthermore, the intended refutation here concerns the meaning of the cited scripture as accepted by the Advaitins."

Just as when it is to be proven that the knower does not transcend the nature of cognition, the eternality of the self is not a valid reason because it is unestablished with respect to a different locus; and if one accepts that the "I" (the object of the notion of "I") is the self and is indestructible, there is a contradiction of one's own tenets (*apasiddhānta*). To state the intended meaning of the aforementioned scripture, he clarifies the subject matter in two sentences beginning with "But of the self... (*ātmanas tu...*).
"Nor indeed, because it exists" (*na hi satīti ca*).
By these two statements, the fact that knowledge possesses the nature of a quality (*dharma*) that defines the eternal self-essence (*ātmasvarūpa*) was indicated as the reason for its eternity.
Now, he states the meaning of the scriptural passage (*śrutivākya*) with the word "therefore" (*tena*).
The term "of the seer" (*draṣṭuḥ*) is a non-co-referential qualifier of vision (*dṛṣṭi*), which is knowledge as an attribute (*dharma*).
It has been stated that the self is eternal because it is indestructible.
Since "of the seer" is a designation of the substratum (*dharmin*), it is established that knowledge is an attribute that defines the very nature of the self.
And thus, he states the reason for the resulting [conclusion] with the words "of that which has become the very nature of the self.
The reason is the state of having the eternal self as its nature.
By this, the suspicion of a lack of proof due to a different locus (*vyadhikaraṇāsiddhi*) is refuted.

The manner of connection with a particular object is characterized by a specific relation between consciousness and its object, which depends on the various extensions [of consciousness] through the doors of the sense organs and so forth; the compound [dṛṣṭyādimat] means "that which has obtained the designations such as 'seeing' (*dṛṣṭi*) and so on" by means of that [connection]. Here, "seeing" (*dṛṣṭi*) refers to visual perception (*cākṣuṣa-pratyakṣa*).
Ghrāti is that which arises from the nose (olfactory cognition); rasayatiḥ is gustatory cognition (rāsana);
vaktiḥ is verbal cognition (śābda-jñāna).
Śruti is auditory perception;
mati is inference;
spṛṣṭi is tactile perception.
Cognition (*vijñapti*) is meditation (*upāsana*),
or it is direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) born of yoga;
[it belongs to] that which illuminates its own self— that is, that which is self-luminous (*svaprakāśā*).
Since knowledge has the nature of the self and is eternal, he cites other scriptural passages as well, beginning with "Just as...
The word "immediate" (*anantara*) refers to the external region,
while "not external" (*abāhya*) refers to the internal region in its entirety.
This is what is intended to be expressed.
Furthermore, the completeness of the self pertains both to its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and its attributes (*dharma*).
Thus, the self's being of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna-svarūpatva*) and its having knowledge as its intrinsic essence (*jñāna-svabhāvatva*) are always established.
Regarding the meaning of this statement, another scriptural passage says, "By its own radiance, by its own light.
Here, it is stated that [the Self] has the nature of illumination both in terms of its essential form (*svarūpa*) and its attributes (*dharma*).
The expression "self-light" (*ātmajyotis*) also has precisely the same meaning as already explained.
For the sun and other luminaries are both luminous and have light as their form;
likewise, the Self is also so.
It is like the illumination of the sun and other luminaries.
It is intended here that knowledge, which is of the nature of light, is innate to the self.
Regarding the persistence of knowledge in liberation, he cites scripture with the words "tathāpavarge.

The sense is that since liberation is characterized by the manifestation of one's innate form, the fact that knowledge is an inherent attribute of the self's nature is established through the persistence of knowledge [in that state].
Regarding the persistence of knowledge even during sleep, he cites another scriptural passage with the words "And others [say]...
The meaning of such passages as "He indeed knows" is that although knowledge exists, there is no manifestation of objects during sleep due to the absence of contact with those objects.
Furthermore, regarding the eternality and the nature-inherent quality (*ātmasvabhāvatva*) of knowledge, he provides examples from memory with the words "In liberation (*nirvāṇa*)," etc.
In the glorious Vaiṣṇava Purāṇa: "consisting of knowledge" (*jñānamaya*);
here the suffix *mayaṭ* denotes abundance.
The particle *eva* (only) is connected here as well;
the intended meaning is obtained through the restriction "only abundant in knowledge.
The phrase "even of the luminaries" refers to the *Mahābhārata*, specifically the *Śrī Bhagavad Gītā*.
The Blessed One introduces a clear statement from the *Śrīviṣṇudharma* regarding the eternity of knowledge and so forth, beginning with the words "The Blessed One... and so on;
the word "said" (*āha*) is to be supplied. He states "for this very reason" (*ata eva hi*) to show that the *sūtra* as well is an authority for the point already explained.
Therefore, the meaning of the Sūtra is that the Self is indeed a knower—that is, it is consciousness itself—based on scripture alone.
By the phrase "it is indeed a knower," the author of the Sūtra intends to show that knowledge is eternal and constitutes the very nature of the Self.
For this very reason, having raised the objection that if knowledge were eternal, there would be illumination even during deep sleep, he refutes it with the analogy of "manhood and so forth."

[Objection: If knowledge, which is an attribute of the self, is thus innate (*svābhāvika*), how can there be the distinction between doubt and certainty, as well as the distinction between memory and direct experience?
To this, he says: "In that case, thus...
[meaning] simultaneously and instantaneously.
"Without interruption" means up to that point.
The subtle aspect of cognition (*jñāna-sūkṣmāṃśa*) is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) dependent upon the experience of the impressions of cognition;
it is a specific form of the intimate union between consciousness and its object.
It has been stated that consciousness itself, as qualified by a specific connection with an object, receives the designations of "doubt," "certainty," and so forth.
Regarding this, an objection is raised against the first position with the words "And not thus.

The meaning is that since conjunction resides in both [relata], if the conjunction of consciousness with an object constitutes knowledge, it would follow that the object also possesses the status of a knower.
Since it might be possible to somehow accept the consequence that consciousness itself is the knower, the consequence that the object is the knower has been raised;
or else, "of the object" means "of that which has the object as its locus.
According to the literal reading, this would apply to the self as well.
In this position, there would be no status as the substratum of those respective cognitions.

Therefore, in this position, "knowership" must be defined as simply possessing cognition through the relation of being the substratum of its own substratum; thus, there is no unwanted consequence of knowership applying to the object.
He refutes [this objection] with the words "by the object."
The third case ending in "viṣayeṇa" is used in the sense of a cause (*hetu*).
The word "viṣaya" refers here to the operation of the object. The same applies later in the expression "cetanatvena."

The intended meaning is as follows: consciousness itself is indeed that which is active for the purpose of grasping an object. Thus, although the conjunction of the object and consciousness constitutes the cognition of each respective object, because that conjunction exists in the self alone—by virtue of its relation to the self as the substratum of the consciousness possessing the activity conducive to it—it is the self alone, and not the object or anything else, that possesses the status of the knower; this is established on the strength of experience.

This is just as, although the conjunction of light and an object constitutes illumination, the status of being the illuminator belongs to the sun and so forth alone, and not to the object, by virtue of the spreading of light which is their own attribute.
Alternatively, the meaning of the phrase "by means of the object" (*viṣayeṇa*) and so forth is "due to the absence of conjunction having the object as its correlate.
Its "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) refers to a conjunction having the object as its counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*).

Having thus established the first position, he establishes the second position—that consciousness itself, when connected with this or that object, is the cognition of that respective object—by way of raising an objection and providing its resolution.
The word "atha" [introduces the following]:
"prakāśaḥ-prakāśakaḥ" means the illuminator of light;

"sūryāditantratvam" refers to having one's essential nature, existence, and activity dependent upon the sun and other luminaries, as well as being an inseparably established attribute (*apṛthaksiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*) thereof.

The meaning is that, just as the sun and other luminaries possess the quality of illumination only by depending on light connected to their respective objects, so too the Self possesses the status of a knower only by possessing consciousness (caitanya) connected to its respective objects.
This alone is the primary position,
because the sense is that the status of being a knower is directly inherent in the Self.

The phrase "not having another means" (ananyasādhana) concludes that the self’s nature is consciousness and its realization is not dependent on anything else; this is established by the words "that is proven. "Having the nature of consciousness" means having the nature of being a knower.
By this, the view that knowledge is adventitious is refuted.
He remains knowing himself alone; he remains as one who is eternal, independent of anything else, and self-luminous.
By this, the adventitious nature of the Self's luminosity and its dependence upon knowledge are excluded.

"According to the distinction of the causal signs"—that is, by following the positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) with the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) such as the sense organs, the inferential marks (*liṅga*), and the contact between the object and the cognition.
The remainder is clear.
With the words "In this way," etc., [the author] establishes that the self, though self-luminous, is also the object of cognitions derived from verbal testimony and other means of valid knowledge.

The fish is the illustration for indistinct manifestation, and milk is the illustration for grasping through non-discrimination. Those [examples] follow the logic of that demonstration; they are to be employed by means of the five-membered syllogism which establishes the discrimination between the Self and the non-Self.
The varieties of inference (anumānabheda) refer to specific types of inference.
The statements (vacana) are authoritative sentences (pramāṇavākya) that conform to the treatises (śāstra). By "by those as well" [it is meant that they too are included].

Since inference and scripture, being causes for knowing only that which is beyond the senses, do not produce a clear manifestation [of reality], it is indeed appropriate for those who desire a clear manifestation of the Self to be dissatisfied with them alone.

It is indicated by the words "restraints" (*yama*) and "observances" (*niyama*) that the destruction of the defects obstructing the knowledge residing in the mind and other faculties is accomplished through the practice of the limbs of yoga.
"Practice of cessation" (*nirodhābhyāsa*) refers to the practice of yoga.

For the *Yogasūtra* states: "Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. Through the ripening of the practice of yoga, the turbidity of *rajas* and *tamas* ceases; thus, when the mind is characterized by an abundance of pure *sattva*, it becomes capable of the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the discrimination between the Self and [nature]. This is the meaning of the passage beginning with "through the practice of cessation" (*nirodhābhyāsāt*).
It is for the sake of the direct knowledge of the distinction residing in the Self.
They strive; that is, immediately after the completion of the [preparatory] accomplishments, they engage in the practice of contemplating the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*).

Regarding "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*): when yoga, characterized by the uninterrupted contemplation of the self, has been perfected at the culmination of the intensity of cultivation, [the goal is attained].
And there arises direct knowledge—the direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) of the true nature of the self produced by the purified mind, assisted by the merit born of yoga;
"arises" means "is born.
Thus, the self is established through itself, as well as through scripture and inference.
It is clearly revealed by the direct perception born of the practice of yoga. //43//
(Thus concludes the section on the determination of the means of self-cognition.

Now follows the examination of its delimitation by time. In this regard, those who follow the doctrine of the Sugata, proclaiming that momentariness is inherent in all that exists and considering the very view of a permanent self to be the root of all evil, maintain that this [self] is subject to momentary destruction.
"Whatever exists is momentary,
and this self exists. But how is it that momentariness is invariably concomitant with mere existence?
Because existence is impossible for that which is non-momentary;
for such a thing is incapable of producing any effect whatsoever, even ultimately the lineage of the omniscient consciousness.
Its existence cannot be conceived; therefore, for entities, being (*sattā*) consists precisely in the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritā*).

And since that [capacity] is not possible in a non-momentary thing—which lacks succession and simultaneity, which are its own pervaders—it follows by default that [existence] is necessarily bound to momentariness alone, as there is no other place for it to reside.
But how is it that succession and simultaneity are pervaders of causal efficiency?
Or how is there the exclusion of those two from that which is non-momentary? Listen: the meaning already stated is summarized as "thus the Self.

It is established by this much alone: that knowledge, which is an attribute (*dharma*) of the self-luminous Self, is employed by the Self in the apprehension of objects and the like, as well as in the apprehension of its own distinction from the body and so forth.
Thus, the examination of the means of valid cognition regarding the self is concluded. //43//

Now, he begins the investigation in order to establish permanence with the words "atha asya" (now, of this). "Of this" means of the self; "examination of the limitation by time" refers to the investigation concerning the relationship with time.
The word "proceeds" is to be supplied as the ellipsis.
Regarding the phrase "therein":
in the context of investigating the self's connection with time, some proponents (namely, the Buddhists) maintain that the self is perishable, existing for only a moment. This is the sense.
Their intention is that the connection with time is precisely characterized by momentariness;
it has been stated that the self possesses momentariness because of its existence.
This [argument] would be sound if existence were established as being pervaded by momentariness.
Why is that?
To this end, he prepares the definition of existence (*sattva*) as being worthy of being pervaded by momentariness, starting with "that which...
Existence is simply the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*).
And the intention is that this [continuity] is pervaded by momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*).
"Omniscient cognition" refers to the cognition of a Buddha.
He establishes the very pervasion by momentariness in the passage beginning with "na ca sā... (and not that...).
The meaning is as follows: the capacity to perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is pervaded by either succession or simultaneity.
Since this capacity is untenable in a non-momentary, stable entity, it necessarily establishes that capacity in a momentary one; thus, it follows that existence is indeed pervaded by momentariness.
[This refers to] the fact that either succession or simultaneity is the pervader of the capacity to perform causal efficiency, and of that...
In order to demonstrate the impossibility [of causal efficiency] in what is stable, the question is raised: "But how?
The answer begins with "Listen," and so forth.
Regarding the agency of entities in purposeful actions, there are two possible modes.
Whether successively or simultaneously, no other mode of occurrence is possible. //44//

Since, between existence and non-existence, the establishment of one occurs upon the cessation of the other, there is no possibility of a third mode for entities in the production of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*); thus, causal efficiency is necessarily bound to either succession or simultaneity.
Furthermore, neither succession nor simultaneity is possible in that which is non-momentary (*akṣaṇika*).
(Only this much of the *Ātmasiddhi* section of the work is extant.

Thus ends the *Ātmasiddhi*, within the *Siddhitraya* bestowed by the supreme teacher, the venerable Bhagavadyāmunamuni, who was the foremost bearer of the burden of propagating the illustrious Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrine.
"Artha" means: some performance of causal efficiency occurs sequentially, while some occurs non-sequentially—that is, simultaneously.
When simultaneity is impossible, there is sequence.

And in the absence of that [succession], simultaneity is necessarily established; thus, the meaning is that causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is necessarily pervaded by either succession or simultaneity.
Let this be so;
nevertheless, how is it that [causal efficiency] does not exist in a permanent entity?

Regarding this, he says "na ca" (and not). The subsequent portion of the text is not found anywhere from here on; therefore, a commentary has been provided based on the essence of what has been recovered.

Thus [composed] by the jewel among sons of the eminent teacher Śrī Kṛṣṇamācārya— the ornament of the lineage of Prativādibhayankarācārya and a preeminent scholar born in the divine land of Śrī Nāgapurī (Tirunāṅgūra)—

who has crossed to the further shore of the ocean of the four systems of philosophy, whose fame rests upon the horizon, who is an embodiment of compassion, who is a delighter in residing at Śrī Bhūtapurī as one descended from the divine lineage of the venerable Bhāṣyakāra, a sovereign among scholars of the Hārīta clan, and who has attained a mastery of the heart of the systems of *pada*, *vākya*, and *pramāṇa* through service at the lotus feet of the lordly teacher Śrīmad Āsūri Rāmānujācārya.

May the *Siddhāñjana*, a commentary on the *Ātmasiddhi* composed by the illustrious Vaiṣṇava servant Prabhāvaṇṇaṅgarācārya— a crest-jewel of Nyāya and Vyākaraṇa and a scholar of both Vedāntas— be victorious for a long time!
